News.title: Children among 10 dead after huge fire breaks out at popular tourist beach as people left trapped inside burning huts
News.content:
Next

AT LEAST 10 people – including young children – have been killed in a horror fire that ripped through a beach resort.

Emergency crews rushed to the scene in Bangladesh on Saturday, to find a destructive inferno engulfing a three-storey wooden structure.



Officials confirmed ten people died in the blaze – the youngest among them reportedly just five years old.

It is understood that guests became trapped inside the location, Tuptup Resto and Resort, when the fast-moving fire struck.



It broke out around 6.20am in Inani in the Cox’s Bazar district, a popular destination for domestic tourists.

Syed Mohammad Morshed Hossain, deputy assistant director of Fire Service and Civil Defense in the district, said the blaze spread quickly.

He later confirmed that children were sadly among the 10 fatalities, six of who have been formally identified.

Saiful Islam, a volunteer, said: “Some people had taken shelter in the washrooms to save their lives, but they died there.

“It was early in the morning, and the resort guests were asleep.”

Four additional people were injured and were transported to hospital.



Police have reportedly arrested the manager of the resort, according to the United News of Bangladesh.

The cause of the fire remains unknown as authorities launch an investigation.

It comes as 20 people were killed in a massive fire that devastated a restaurant in India.

Diners and staff were forced to jump from windows as the fire savaged the eatery in New Delhi in June.

A total of 37 people were rescued from the multistorey building and taken to hospital for treatment.



20 people died as a result.

Dramatic footage showed a woman leaping from the first floor to escape the flames and thick smoke.

Two water tenders, two water bowsers, a quick response vehicle and firefighting units battled to contain the blaze, officials said.

Later in June, a tourist died after a huge fire ripped through a luxury beach resort in the Dominican Republic.

Shocking footage shows thick plumes of smoke billowing above the Viva Dominicus Bayahibe resort where a total of 1,700 people were forced to evacuate.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The woman who died in the fire was an Italian tourist, Francesca Valentino, 46, who had been on the beach at the time the blaze broke out.

Preliminary investigations suggested that strong winds meant the fire spread quickly across flammable palm roofing.

News.title: Man in his 30s plunges to his death after falling from multi-storey London hotel sparking large police response
News.content:
HOTEL TRAGEDY Man in his 30s plunges to his death after falling from multi-storey London hotel sparking large police response







Next

A MAN in his 30s plunged to death from an eight-storey building in London, sparking a large police response.

Emergency services were called to Roomzzz Aparthotel at around 5pm on Friday after it was reported the man had fallen from a height.

He was found unconscious, and pronounced dead at the scene in Stratford, East London.

Officers blocked off the road, West Ham Lane, while they tended to the death for several hours.





Met Police have revealed the man’s death is not being treated as suspicious, and are working to inform his next of kin.

A spokesman said: “Around 17:12hrs on Friday, 16 October, officers attended West Ham Lane, Stratford, following reports of a fall from height in Roomzzz Aparthotel, Stratford.

“Police attended with the London Ambulance Service.

“A man, believed to be aged in his 30s, was found unconscious.

“He was sadly pronounced dead at the scene.

“Police are working to inform the man’s next-of-kin.

“The incident is not currently being treated as suspicious.”

News.title: Kemi Badenoch tells her shadow cabinet to get their manifesto ideas in as she gears up for early election
News.content:
Tory leader is getting battle ready in case the new PM calls an early general election

BATTLE READY Kemi Badenoch tells her shadow cabinet to get their manifesto ideas in as she gears up for early election







Next

KEMI Badenoch is getting “battle ready” for an early election – and has ordered her frontbench to submit their manifesto ideas.

The Tory leader has told her shadow cabinet ministers they must get their ideas in within the next month.

It comes amid mounting speculation that Andy Burnham will call an early general election.



A Tory frontbencher said: “We have been told to get our manifesto ideas in within the next month.



“Everyone is getting battle ready for a possible snap election. Everyone thinks that is what Andy Burnham is planning.”

The new PM denied he is secretly plotting an early election.

But he has fuelled speculation by delaying a string of big policy decisions.

Details of his big plan to fix the social care crisis are not expected for some time.

A government spending review to find savings to help fund defence has been kicked back until next year.

And the PM’s 10 year policy plan will be outlined later this year.



Some in Labour are urging Mr Burnham to call an early election so he can tear up Keir Starmer’s manifesto and hike taxes.

But other senior figures in No10 have warned against an early election gamble as they fear Labour will lose so many seats the PM will never be forgiven.

News.title: Boy, 14, stabbed in shopping centre car park & raced to hospital with ‘serious injuries’ as armed cops swarm high street
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

ARMED RESPONSE Boy, 14, stabbed in shopping centre car park & raced to hospital with ‘serious injuries’ as armed cops swarm high street







Next

A TEEN has been seriously injured in a stabbing at a shopping centre car park, with armed cops rushing to the scene.

Emergency services were called to Arndale Centre in Manchester at 3.20pm today, after receiving reports that a boy, 14, had been stabbed.



The attack reportedly took place moments after an alleged shoplifting incident, according to Manchester Evening News, with several other sources confirming the timeline.

More than one person is believed to have been injured in the stabbing.



Onlookers reported seeing multiple police vehicles parked outside the shopping centre.

At least two armed response units were also present at the site, alongside GMP’s Tactical Aid Unit.



Part of the ninth level car park remains cordoned off as forensic teams work at the site, with car owners unable to access any vehicles behind police tape.

A spokesperson for Greater Manchester Police said: “At 3.20pm we were called to reports of a stabbing in a car park at Manchester Arndale.

“Emergency services attended, and a 14-year-old boy has been taken to hospital with serious injuries.

“Enquiries are ongoing.”



They have not confirmed whether any arrests have yet been made.

News.title: Oregon shooter’s mom raised concerns years before deadly rampage as she insists son who killed 4 was ‘a good boy’
News.content:
Next

THE mom of the teen shooter who stormed a special education classroom raised concerns about her son years before his deadly rampage.

Griffin J. John II targeted the Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday, killing three children and one teacher, before being stopped by heroic bystanders.



The 16-year-old who was shot dead by an armed civilian was armed with over 60 rounds of ammunition and a pump-action shotgun bought by his mother around the time of his birthday in August.

Now, his sobbing mom Shauntai May Nickerson has broken her silence following the deadly rampage, and insisted her son “was a good boy,” the New York Times reported.



“He was a good boy, he really was,” she said, before adding, “I miss him.”

“I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss,” she said of the grieving families of those who were killed, per a CNN report.

read more on the shooting COLD BLOOD Teacher killed by Oregon shooter is pictured & family say it was her 'dream job'

“If I could have prevented this, I would have,” she said, the Times added.

She did not say how he ended up possessing the deadly weapon.



Her comments come as it emerges that she raised concerns about the wellbeing of John II six years before the shooting.

The then-10-year-old boy was struggling with remote learning and not getting the right help due to the pandemic, she said.

Nickerson told NewsChannel 21 in 2020 that returning to the classroom “will be great for Griffin, because I am not certified teaching a special need student.”

The program she was discussing with the news outlet was for children with “intensive behavioral and social skills challenges” to return to in-person lessons.

“I think it will be great for my son to get the help that he needs from the skilled teachers that he needs to get it from,” she added.



However, the nursing home health aide told CNN that she saw no warning signs before her son stormed the school armed to the teeth with weaponry.

Authorities revealed that John II was a former special education student at the elementary school.

This detail could point to a possible motive, which is still being investigated, and to how he was able to enter the secure building.



Police said that rather than use the front door, he entered from a vacant lot before jumping the fence in the playground and shooting through the locks on a door.

He headed for the special education classroom where he killed 5-year-old Rhoam Summer, an eight-year-old boy, an 11-year-old boy, and 25-year-old teacher Megan Lambert.

Saylor Graham, 7, who is bound to a wheelchair is fighting for her life after being shot in the face, and a 54-year-old teacher Becky Drury was also critically injured.



The teen shooter unloaded 15 shots across the room and still had 44 rounds left before he was gunned down by hero dad Kaylub Giamanco, 36.

He was driving home for his lunch break when he heard gunshots and saw the boy running towards the school and opening fire at a bystander.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

An investigation into the shooting is ongoing as Bend police chief Mike Krantz told reporters on Friday, “Everyone wants to know why, including us.”

In Oregon there is no criminal law prosecuting parents of children who use their weapons for deadly attacks.

News.title: Mystery of Amelia Earhart could finally be solved as new snaps offer clues over pioneer pilot’s disappearance
News.content:
HUNT FOR CLUES Mystery of Amelia Earhart could finally be solved as new snaps offer clues over pioneer pilot’s disappearance







Next

A TROVE of never-before-seen photographs could finally crack the 89-year mystery surrounding the disappearance of legendary aviator Amelia Earhart.

The extraordinary images show a remote Pacific island where the pioneering pilot may have crash-landed before meeting a horrifying fate.



The American trailblazer, 39, vanished in July 1937 while attempting to become the first woman to fly around the world.

A total of 47 high-resolution aerial photographs have been released for the first time, offering fresh hope of uncovering what happened to Earhart and her missing plane.



Now, almost nine decades later, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand has published the remarkable collection taken just 17 months after she disappeared.

The black-and-white snaps show Nikumaroro, a tiny island in the South Pacific where investigators believe Earhart may have spent her final days stranded.

Captured on December 1, 1938, the images were taken during a military survey searching for potential airbase locations.

Matthew O’Sullivan, the museum’s Keeper of Photographs, discovered the negatives more than a decade ago.

While a handful of grainy copies previously surfaced online, the complete collection has never been publicly released in high resolution.

Veteran Earhart investigator Ric Gillespie hailed the discovery as a “goldmine”.



The release coincides with a fresh expedition to the isolated atoll, where a 17-strong team is hunting for the wreckage of Earhart’s Lockheed Electra.

Researchers believe a mysterious shape lurking beneath the island’s lagoon could be the remains of the doomed aircraft.

Dubbed the “Taraia Object”, the strange formation was spotted in satellite imagery from 2020.



Led by archaeologist Dr Richard Pettigrew, the team travelled 830 miles to Nikumaroro aboard the Marin Mainiku before beginning their painstaking search on Tuesday.

Scientists from Purdue University and the Archaeological Legacy Institute are using powerful magnetometers and sonar equipment to detect submerged wreckage.

Any promising discovery could eventually be excavated and transported to the US for examination.

But severe weather has already disrupted the high-stakes mission, with investigators expected to provide an update on the mysterious object.

Pettigrew said: “We understand the tremendous interest in what we’re doing at Nikumaroro, and we appreciate everyone’s patience.



“This is a complex scientific process. You don’t simply arrive at a site and immediately identify what’s there.



“We have to carefully collect the data, analyse it and reach sound conclusions.”

The search could also expose a far darker truth about Earhart’s final days.

Pettigrew previously suggested the aviation pioneer may have survived an emergency landing before slowly starving to death on the deserted island.

Under the gruesome theory, her remains were then devoured by giant coconut crabs.

He told the Daily Mail in 2025: “The very idea that she wasted away on the island and eventually died and got eaten by coconut crabs – that’s a horrible, horrible vision.



“I don’t like thinking about it, but it’s inevitable.”

Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan vanished on July 2, 1937, while flying from Papua New Guinea towards Howland Island.

The record-breaking pilot, who became the first woman to fly solo nonstop across the Atlantic, had radioed that she was running dangerously low on fuel.

Her disappearance sparked a frantic 16-day US Navy search, but no trace of the pair or their aircraft was found.

The longstanding official theory is that the plane ran out of fuel and plunged into the Pacific near Howland Island.



But investigators have long suspected Earhart instead managed to land on a coral reef at Nikumaroro, formerly known as Gardner Island.

Researchers from TIGHAR have pointed to her final radio transmission and mysterious distress calls apparently made after her disappearance as possible evidence she survived the landing.

Previous searches also uncovered signs of a possible castaway campsite and artefacts, including glass thought to have come from a cosmetic cream jar.



However, none has conclusively linked Earhart to the island.

And the latest suspected wreckage has already divided experts, with Gillespie warning the Taraia Object could simply be a fallen tree.

There is also no obvious sign of the mysterious shape in the newly released 1938 photographs.

Previous attempts to solve the riddle have repeatedly ended in disappointment.

A multimillion-pound search led by renowned ocean explorer Robert Ballard in 2019 failed to locate the aircraft near Nikumaroro.



In 2024, explorers from Deep Sea Vision believed they had discovered an aircraft-shaped object on the Pacific seabed, only for a second expedition to reveal it was a cluster of rocks.

Other theories suggest Earhart and Noonan were captured by Japanese forces after landing on Mili Atoll and later died in captivity.

But despite decades of investigations, no verified wreckage or human remains definitively linked to the missing aviators have ever been recovered.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Now, with fresh photographs under scrutiny and scientists combing the remote lagoon, investigators hope the latest mission could finally end one of aviation’s greatest mysteries.

Pettigrew previously declared: “Finding Amelia Earhart’s Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime.”

News.title: Our tiny village survived 1066 & William the Conquerer – now our homes are CRUMBLING because of thundering new invasion
News.content:
Next

AN ANCIENT village that survived the 1066 Norman Conquest is being wrecked by an invasion of lorries, locals have said.

Hundreds of HGVs plough through the picturesque village causing daily quakes that furious residents liken to “living in a washing machine”.



Pevensey Castle is over 1,700-years-old and was originally built by the Romans in AD 290.

It’s even included in The Bayeux Tapestry along with reams of embroidered linen illustrating William the Conqueror’s invasion – and is just 10 miles from the site of the Battle of Hastings.



But the historical gem is being ruined by “thundering” lorries grating and vibrating the castle wall, according to locals.

Huge lorries clatter through the Tudor streets of Pevensey Village at 30mph every day, each of them causing quakes in the stonework as they pass.



Locals are sick of the shaking and fear the traffic could even be risking pedestrians’ lives.

It’s got so bad that 500-year-old Tudor wall paintings in a local visitor centre are crumbling.

The abandoned Roman fort that once stood on the site of the castle became a stronghold for thousands of Norman troops during the invasion of 1066.



After sinking an arrow into King Harold’s eye and slaughtering thousands of English fighters the blood soaked invaders set up camp in the castle ruins.

Then in the 1070s William the Conqueror ordered a huge stone fortress to be built which still stands today.

During The Sun’s visit we watched dozens of lorries pelting round the corner of Castle Road, missing the fortress wall by centimeters.

It’s been battered so many times that a huge two metre chunk of wall has been destroyed.

Now a petition has kicked off to stop the traffic chaos.



Locals want a HGV weight restriction and the speed limit cut to 20mph.

The campaign is spearheaded by Peter Lowton, chairman of Pevensey Parish Council, who is appalled by the situation.

He told The Sun: “I think it’s shocking.



“We’re very lucky in this country to have such wonderful heritage and we should be protecting it not allowing it to disappear.

“The reality is the damage that’s been caused to the castle is obvious and there will be further damage.

“When you look at the Tudor wall paintings of The Mint House, it’s just shocking.

“They’re trying to restore the building whilst at the same time lorries are destroying it.

“Their case to get funding will rely on whether things are put in place to stop the lorries from damaging it.”



The Mint House is a Tudor inn steeped in English myths and legends of sword fights, royals, ghosts and murders.

The quakes have damaged the building so much that crumbling plastering has uncovered hidden 400-year-old wall paintings.

The half a millennium old art was crafted by travelling merchants who offered innkeepers the chance to decorate their businesses.



Restoration has already cost £600,000 and future funding relies on stopping the shakes.

During our visit we felt the wooden floor boards vibrating under foot whilst lorries almost as tall as the building trundled past.

Project manager Joe Seaman has been looking after the building since 2021 and says the condition is getting worse.

He told The Sun: “You can literally feel the building shaking as they go past, because it’s 500-years-old the surfaces vibrate and it’s not good for it at all.

“This hasn’t sprung out of nowhere, the damage has been going on for a number of years and the corner of the castle has been hit a number of times.



“Because we’re restoring the building we’re finding more and more wall paintings.”

He added: “But there’s no point us putting in £1million if it’s still going to be damaged by the road.”

The traffic isn’t just damaging the village’s Tudor relics, Joe says it’s risking pedestrian safety.

With almost 70,000 visitors to the castle each year, the road is bustling with tourists.

He continued: “It’s a constant worry that someone will come round the corner too fast, it’s an accident waiting to happen.



“We’re not saying turn the whole village into a museum, but we want people to be able to cross the road without getting run over.

“I don’t like nimbyism, but I do think when there are institutions like National Highways then maybe they should help rather than be the block.

“We’d love to work with them to find a solution, it’s not about blaming it’s about working with people.”

The street is a B road which means online sat navs send unsuspecting truckers through the village instead of on the nearby Pevensey Bypass.

Katherine, a local resident, supports the proposed speed limit cut.



She told The Sun: “It’s a complete blind spot when you try and cross next to the castle.

“It’s just lethal because you can’t see anything round the corner.”

Mark Penderton has lived in the village for 33 years and had to pay for a structural engineer after a lorry cracked his wall.

He said: “We’ve had our property damaged three times by lorries and a number of near misses.

“We hear a lot of noise and vibrations, our neighbour’s possessions vibrate on the window ledge and their car mirrors were knocked off by lorries.”



East Sussex County Council is responsible for the road and said: “We have yet to receive the petition, but the concerns raised will be considered in full once we do.”

English Heritage manage and conserve Pevensey Castle.

A spokesman told The Sun: “We are aware of concerns about large vehicles passing close to Pevensey Castle’s historic walls and the potential impact this may have.

“We take these concerns very seriously and include the external wall faces in our regular site checks.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The road is outside English Heritage’s control, but we welcome the local authority’s invitation to discuss measures to address the issue, including road speeds and restrictions on large vehicles.



“We hope these discussions will help identify practical ways to reduce any potential risk and protect this important historic monument.”

News.title: Putin builds new air defence towers near his forest palace as Ukraine steps up attacks on Russia
News.content:
Next

VLADIMIR Putin has thrown up four new missile defence towers around his secret forest palace amid mounting Ukrainian attacks.

The paranoid tyrant now has 30 air defence towers guarding his heavily fortified Valdai hideaway.



One towering missile launcher stands just 1,312 feet from the palace where Putin is believed to live with his secret lover Alina Kabaeva, 43, and their two young sons.

The latest military build-up was exposed by Radio Svoboda using satellite imagery of the sprawling estate in Russia’s Novgorod region.



Four newly constructed towers are among the closest permanent missile defence positions to the dictator’s bolthole, some 230 miles northwest of Moscow.

And locals have revealed how troops have descended on the surrounding woodland as the Kremlin continues to tighten its iron grip on the estate.

One resident said: “See that tower? They’ve brought in a lot of soldiers – they’re building things there, constantly building.”

A teacher in the nearby village of Roshchino described how the ominous air defence machinery has become a familiar presence.

They said: “That’s the air defence system – you wouldn’t recognise the sounds.

“If it’s spinning, it means there’s no immediate danger overhead.



“If it stops, it means something is flying over us.”

The latest additions come amid mounting fears of Ukrainian drone strikes penetrating deep into Russian territory.

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky previously claimed Putin had deployed nearly 90 air defence launchers to the wider Valdai area, stripping other Russian regions of vital protection.



He said: “They have moved nearly 90 air defence launchers to Valdai from other Russian regions, and a special air defence division is being formed there to ensure the peace of the Russian leadership.”

Zelensky also warned in June that the Kremlin was scrambling to protect its most prized locations.

“The Russian leadership is moving more air defence systems to Moscow, to Valdai, and to Putin’s bridge across the Kerch Strait,” he said.

The military shield has grown dramatically since 2024, when just seven air defence positions guarded the secluded fortress.

Earlier research by Radio Liberty identified 27 emplacements around the estate, including at least eight towers installed within four months.



Most were believed to house formidable Pantsir missile systems, each costing up to £16million.

At least one was understood to be an S-400 system, with a staggering price tag of up to £800million.

Combined with sophisticated radar equipment, the arsenal protecting Putin’s private sanctuary is estimated to be worth well over £1billion.



The lavish military protection dwarfs the defences guarding many Russian cities.

Moscow and its surrounding region, home to some 20 million people, reportedly have just 100 air defence emplacements between them.

Other Russian cities are understood to have even fewer, while Putin pours military resources into protecting his secluded family retreat.

The latest security frenzy follows a bitter row over the dictator’s claims that Ukraine had tried to attack his palace.

In December, Ukrainian forces launched a long-range drone strike against the Akron chemical plant in Veliky Novgorod, around 85 miles from Valdai.



The industrial site plays a key role in Russia’s explosives production.

But Putin claimed more than 90 Ukrainian drones had instead been directed towards his private residence.

He even complained to US President Donald Trump that Kyiv had attempted to target him and his family.

Western and Ukrainian intelligence dismissed the explosive accusations as false, with Trump also rejecting the Kremlin’s account.



Despite the claims being disputed, Putin pressed ahead with bolstering his palace defences.

Reports also suggested Kabaeva had refused to remain at the heavily guarded estate amid fears for her safety.

The former Olympic gymnast is believed to share the sprawling complex with Putin and their sons Ivan, 11, and Vladimir, seven.

The boys, whose existence the Kremlin has never publicly acknowledged, are reportedly being raised under the surname Spiridonov.



They are educated by private tutors rather than attending ordinary schools and are said to be keen young gymnasts.

Their secret surname is believed to honour Putin’s paternal grandfather, Spiridon Putin, who worked as a chef for some of the Soviet Union’s most notorious figures.

Putin’s hidden family life has become the subject of repeated investigations into the luxury surrounding his lakeside fortress.

The vast woodland estate is believed to contain a nuclear bunker, private hospital and separate residence for Kabaeva and the children.

Investigative outlet Proekt previously exposed an enormous private spa complex tucked away inside the grounds.



It reported: “Located about the same distance from Putin and Kabaeva’s houses is a huge spa complex with a solarium, a cryo chamber, a 25-metre swimming pool, a hammam, a sauna, a mud room, massage baths, cosmetology and dentistry areas.”

Investigators also uncovered evidence of a secret playground and karting track built for the dictator’s young sons.

Proekt reported a “constant presence of children in the residence”.

The fortress is so heavily guarded that Putin reportedly travels there aboard his own armoured train rather than relying on ordinary transport.

Proekt revealed: “For this reason, a secret, guarded station was built near his residence.”



The Kremlin’s frantic fortification comes as Ukraine ramps up retaliation attacks on Russian soil.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

In June, Moscow had been blitzed by Ukraine’s biggest attack of the war so far – with dramatic clips showing 400 drones raining hell on Vladimir Putin’s doorstep.

Extraordinary footage showed huge plumes of smoke rising over the Russian capital amid the onslaught – part of Volodymyr Zelensky’s endgame blitz.

News.title: More NHS staff sacked over attacks victims' records
News.content:
Further members of staff have been sacked by an NHS trust for inappropriately accessing medical records of the Nottingham attacks victims.

Nottingham students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, who was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.

In May, Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust confirmed it had dismissed 11 members of staff and, in an update on Friday, said a total of 15 people had now been sacked as part of its investigation.

Dr Sanjoy Kumar, Grace's father, said: "I am appalled, it's time to get a handle on these failures."

He added: "Clearly, the way that the highest confidential data, which is medical data, is being looked at by voyeuristic people in the NHS is disgraceful."

Dr Manjeet Shehmar, medical director at NUH, said: "There is simply no excuse for accessing the records of a patient without a legitimate reason and I hope this sends a really clear message â we will investigate and we will take action.

"To lose a loved one in the way that the families of Ian, Grace and Barnaby have is heartbreaking enough.

"I am so sorry that they have had this further compounded by the actions of these staff members."

News.title: UK must protect against Russian 'hybrid attacks', ex-national security adviser says
News.content:
The government must do more to protect key infrastructure against "hybrid attacks" from Russia, a former national security adviser has told the BBC.

Lord Ricketts said more money should be spent on the defence budget, as well as improving the resilience of energy, transport and air traffic control.

He warned hybrid attacks were becoming "more reckless, more dangerous" and that people could end up being killed.

It comes after MI5 chief Sir Kevin McCallum said in his annual speech earlier this week that threats from foreign states, including Russia and Iran, had quadrupled in the last decade.

Lord Ricketts told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that ministers had to warn British people about what might be coming.

"Not only is [Russian President Vladimir] Putin trying to break morale in Ukraine, he's also trying to undermine morale in European countries," he said.

He said there had been a stark warning from the head of MI5 that there could be worse to come in terms of hybrid attacks in the UK or on other Nato territory.

Responding to a question about the impact of disruption by Russia, Lord Ricketts said: "I'm not saying there's going to be industrial war with tanks rolling across the north German plain.

"But yes these hybrid attacks are getting more reckless, more dangerous...people are going to end up getting killed somewhere."

Hybrid attacks tend to use non-military methods, such as hacking, in an attempt to destabilise a country.

Moscow is suspected to be behind many such attacks in Europe since the start of the war in Ukraine, but it has always denied involvement.

As well as cyber-attacks, hybrid attacks can include attempts at sabotage and efforts to spread misinformation.

Lord Ricketts's warning comes after US President Donald Trump blocked sanctions on Russia. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said the decision "only encourages him [Putin] to keep attacking" Ukraine.

The former national security adviser, who also previously ran the Foreign Office, said the UK's focus should be on putting more effort into the coalition of the willing, rather than attempting to act as a bridge between Zelensky and Trump.

"I don't think in Trump's current mood there is any influence Britain can have in the short term," he said.

A growing number of European leaders have warned that Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.

Last month, Germany said Russia was responsible for a drone attack on an airport in Leipzig, in which an explosive failed to detonate close to Ukrainian cargo planes.

French President Emmanuel Macron warned in September that the threat of hybrid attacks by Russia against Europe and France had intensified.

News.title: Scotland 'not like Manchester', Swinney says in dig at PM Burnham
News.content:
John Swinney has taken aim at those who think Scotland "should be just like Manchester" as he vowed Scotland would soon be an independent nation.

In a closing speech at the SNP conference that did not mention Prime Minister Andy Burnham by name, Swinney issued a veiled retort to the former Greater Manchester mayor after he visited Scotland.

The first minister, speaking in Aberdeen, also announced that the country's bus network would be brought under public control by the end of the parliamentary term in 2031.

Swinney made further pledges to extend a Â£2 bus fare cap to the north east of Scotland, launch an independence campaign, fund anti-racism initiatives and tackle misogyny in schools.

News.title: Why people who have never smoked are getting hooked on vapes
News.content:
When vaping first took off at Gracey Mungulu's school, she was vocal about the fact she found it as repulsive as smoking.

"I literally used to tell people like, 'Er, why are you doing that?'" she says.

But Gracey says the habit became so common among her classmates that by the age of 16 she too had taken it up, even though the first time left her coughing rather than inhaling.

"The more you see it, the more you start trying it a bit more," Gracey says, "and then eventually I just got used to it and I was just doing it all the time."

Now 21, she buys a refillable vape every day, using it whenever her hands aren't busy with her work as a hairdresser and in a school.

Gracey is among the more than one million people in the UK who say they have never smoked but now vape, according to recent Office for National Statistics (ONS) survey data â and that number has risen year-on-year.

When vaping first came to the market it was seen as a way to help smokers quit cigarettes.

Vaping nicotine, a highly addictive substance, is less harmful than cigarettes, but the long-term effects are not yet clear, according to the NHS.

News.title: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
News.content:
Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder

Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.

Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.

Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.

"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.

"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."

Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.

News.title: Two-week half terms: The school holiday no one can agree on
News.content:
Samantha Buckland is bracing herself for a tough fortnight. The single mum lives in Reigate, Surrey, and her seven-year-old son goes to a state school that has just introduced a two-week half term.

Buckland has two jobs: teaching medical students at a hospital in Brighton and working at a vintage shop in her home town. The 45-year-old receives universal credit and is worried about the cost of looking after her son while school is closed.

"What I'm trying to do is find out who I can get childcare from and work around that," she says. "I'd like to work, I need money. It's not cheap to live these days."

But money isn't Buckland's only concern. She's also trying to piece together the patchwork of childcare needed to cover the break.

There's a local holiday club, but it's only running for one of the two weeks, which Buckland says "parents are up in arms about". She'll also have to work at the hospital some days.

As a result, she's considering asking family to help, or even going to stay with a fellow mum so they can take turns with the kids.

News.title: Boy, 16, and 80-year-old man die in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond
News.content:
A 16-year-old boy and an 80-year-old man have died following a light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond in Scotland.

Emergency services were called to the scene of the crash near the village of Drymen, in the Stirling Council area, at about 16:45 BST on Friday.

The boy and man were pronounced dead and their next of kin have been informed, police said.

Temporary airspace restrictions are currently in place over the area while the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) conducts its inquiries.

An AAIB spokesperson said: "A team has travelled to the accident site near Drymen, north of Glasgow, to make inquiries and gather evidence as part of the process of conducting a safety investigation."

News.title: Man jailed for Starmer-linked arson attacks is deported
News.content:
A man who plotted to carry out arson attacks on property connected to Sir Keir Starmer has been deported, the Home Office says.

Stanislav Carpiuc, 28, was one of two men convicted over the attacks, which took place in May last year and targeted a car and two houses.

The Ukrainian-born Romanian national was sentenced to two years in prison in June. The Home Office said he had been removed from the UK, without specifying where he had been sent.

The BBC revealed the attacks were ordered on behalf of Russia, with an anonymous handler known as EL promising payment to Carpiuc's accomplice, Roman Lavrynovych.

Lavrynovych, a 22-year-old Ukrainian national, was sentenced to seven years imprisonment in June.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "This was an abhorrent attack and the conviction and imprisonment of these men should send a clear message to anyone blinded by the promise of money from strangers. You will be caught and face severe consequences.

"This individual has now been deported from the UK," it added, referring to Carpiuc.

News.title: Nurse stole £750k from 99-year-old woman for cosmetic surgery and home improvements
News.content:
A nurse who stole Â£750,000 from a vulnerable 99-year-old and spent the money on cosmetic surgery and home improvements has been struck off.

Rebecca Louise Burwood exploited the resident who was living at Bryn Yr Haul Care Home in Mold, Flintshire, where she was deputy manager, for her own personal and financial gain.

She coerced the pensioner from 2017 to 2023 and also bought a car and campervan with the stolen money, as well as obtaining ownership of the woman's home.

A Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) hearing found Burwood's fitness to practise was impaired by reason of misconduct and imposed a striking-off order, meaning she will be removed from the nursing register.

The NMC hearing was told Burwood had a longstanding relationship with the woman before she moved into the home in 2018.

The panel heard the resident had no family members and was vulnerable after a fall. She was dependent on Burwood for friendship and social contact.

It found that, between 2017 and 2023, Burwood abused a position of trust and power, becoming the resident's lasting power of attorney, while also overseeing her care.

Burwood withdrew money from the woman's bank account, accepted ownership of her house and received thousand of pounds, which was used for her own benefit, including for building work and the purchase of vehicles.

Evidence presented showed more than Â£370,000 had left the resident's account over five years, with Â£160,000 of that from making large cash withdrawals at ATMs.

She also took the resident to the solicitors and got her to transfer the ownership of her Â£400,000 house.

The hearing was told there was "evidence to show Mrs Burwood used the funds for house improvements, utility bills and council tax", and there were "allegations that Mrs Burwood used some of the funds for personal cosmetic surgery".

She convinced the resident to pay Â£20,000 for a car and Â£9,000 for a campervan, which she said was purchased so the pair could go on days out.

Burwood claimed the work on her home had been so the elderly woman could live with her in the event of another outbreak of Covid - however it had been paid for before any Covid lockdown in the UK.

News.title: Why hasn't the UK had any named storms yet?
News.content:
With November already on the horizon the UK is yet to see its first named storm of the season.

Deep Atlantic lows responsible for more turbulent conditions have been steered away by dominant areas of high pressure.

This year the headlines have been about worsening drought rather than the impact of gales.

However, could this be the calm before the storms as the Met Office predict a growing chance that late autumn and early winter will turn wetter and windier as El NiÃ±o strengthens in the Pacific.

News.title: Husband calls for PM to intervene after wife detained in Egypt
News.content:
The husband of a woman who was detained by the Egyptian authorities has called for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to get involved and help with her release.

Eman el-Shazly, from Handsworth Wood, in Birmingham, was taken from her mother's house in Cairo two months ago, allegedly in relation to her sister's online activism.

Her husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, said that their family felt "very helpless" and that their "only possible solution" was for Burnham to "make a phone call to Egypt" to end the detainment.

The BBC has approached the Egyptian consulate in London for a response. The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said it was in contact with authorities in Egypt.

Moustapha said he had had "no contact whatsoever" with his wife, but had heard from her mother that her health had deteriorated due to a lack of food and medical assistance.

"It's not a five-star hotel, there's 30 individuals sleeping in a cell with one toilet and one shower," he said.

He told the BBC that his wife had travelled to Egypt to look after her elderly, sick mother, who had been undertaking 18-hour round trips to take food to el-Shazly's two brothers in detention.

News.title: DIY SOS to be 'rested' next year to save money, BBC says
News.content:
The long-running home renovation TV series DIY SOS will be "rested" next year in the light of "savings challenges", the BBC has said.

It will be replaced by a spin-off show featuring highlights from past episodes. Sources denied reports in the Sun newspaper the programme would be axed as part of a plan to make savings.

Presented by Nick Knowles, DIY SOS sees a team transform the homes of families who are facing severe illness, disability, bereavement or building disasters.

It was first broadcast in 1999 and is currently airing its 35th series on BBC One and iPlayer.

The decision comes during the corporation's drive to save Â£500m over three years. It has already cancelled several well-known TV shows including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind and Live At The Apollo.

A BBC spokesperson said: "In light of the BBC's savings challenges we have taken the decision to rest DIY SOS in 2027 and commission a new spin-off show instead from producers South Shore.

"DIY SOS Rebuilt My Life will revisit successes from the show's past and expand the brand on the BBC in a more cost-effective way next year."

News.title: Miranda's tears, joy and dance moves steal show as deadly boredom sets in on The Celebrity Traitors
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode six of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

For a show that likes to keep participants and viewers on the edges of their seats, gripped by suspense and skullduggery, it was ironic that Friday's episode of The Celebrity Traitors came down to which one of its stars would die of boredom.

The climactic final scene switched between a series of faces as we waited to see which of the famous faithful would... yawn.

Some dramatic editing and music attempted to build fevered anticipation, but this was a slow-motion, low-energy premise for a murder in plain sight.

The trio of traitors had been tasked with being as boring as possible, and yawned theatrically in one of the castle's communal rooms in the hope that their apparent fatigue would be contagious.

News.title: Third runway at Heathrow Airport would drive growth, Healey says
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey has said building a third runway at Heathrow Airport has "always been a case for growth" after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say if he backed the expansion.

Healey said airport expansion, including at Heathrow, had been "a big part of jobs and growth" in recent decades, speaking at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok.

His comments came after Prime Minister Andy Burnham was more sceptical, telling the BBC last month it was "a matter for London and Londoners".

Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves had put the airport's expansion at the centrepiece of an argument that Britain was open for business.

Earlier this week Heathrow's chief executive Thomas Woldbye warned that not building a third runway at the UK's busiest airport would be a "huge missed opportunity".

Healey told reporters: "The case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth."

He added: "The formal position now is that the consultation is closed, led by the Transport Department.

"We're reviewing those, and then further decisions and announcements will follow."

The third runway been debated for decades, with the project facing opposition from residents, politicians and climate campaigners.

Last year, Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying "a third runway is badly needed", and the government could not "duck the decision any longer".

Asked about the project in September, Burnham suggested it was an argument for London to decide.

"I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he added.

The Department for Transport has said it is "considering the appropriate next steps" following the public consultation on its National Policy Statement, which provides the basis for deciding whether to grant a new runway at Heathrow.

The airport's consortium of owners has said they need explicit backing from Burnham before the end of the year in order to proceed with the project.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme earlier this week, Woldbye said it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project.

He said he hoped the prime minister would "come along" with the project, adding that a third runway was "not just for Londoners".

"Benefits will be felt all over the country because our supply chain reaches all the way from the north all the way to the south of the UK," Woldbye said.

Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built.

The project, which has an estimated price tag of Â£33bn, would see hundreds of homes demolished, rivers diverted and the M25 motorway rerouted through a tunnel between junctions 14 and 15.

The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues.

News.title: These are the signs you have bedbugs in your hotel room
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

As the threat of a serious bedbug invasion takes hold of transport from the UK to Italy, the thought of the tiny pests is more than enough to make skin crawl.

For those travelling this autumn, there’s a chance hitchhiking bedbugs may have made themselves at home on clothing and luggage ready for a rent-free life in mattresses and skirting boards.

A Qantas flight from Italy to Australia was cancelled after the aircraft had to be grounded for a “deep clean” following a bedbug outbreak.

Southeastern trains operating from the affected West Marina train depot near Hastings in East Sussex have also reportedly been taken out of service as a result of bedbugs in October.

Here’s how to check if you’re rooming with an uninvited plus one and what to do if you spot the bloodsucking bugs in your hotel room.



What are bedbugs and what do they look like?

Bedbugs are wingless, small, dark yellow, red or brown insects with oval, flat bodies that feed on animal and human blood.

They typically bite the head, arms and legs – areas on show while you are sleeping – in a zig-zag pattern of raised red bites that are known to be itchy but are unlikely to cause other health problems.

Are bedbugs common?

Cases of bedbugs are rising by about 20 per cent a year in London and other major European cities, a bedbug monitoring company has said.

The blood-sucking pests were seen in one in every 42 hotel rooms observed by Valpas, which produces bedbug traps and monitors, The Times reported.

While there has been a huge rise in global bedbug numbers in the last decade, frequent travel and insecticide resistance are predicted to be escalating the problem now.

Dr Cassie Krejci, vice president of transformation at pest management company Forshaw, said: “Bedbugs are a problem for all travellers, regardless of destination. They are not a symptom of uncleanliness or bad habits otherwise, but rather the consequence of an insect’s success.”

“Visitors should worry about bringing bed bugs home from any trip, particularly those in cities where we are seeing a notable increase in the number of infestations reported.”

How can I check for bedbugs in my hotel room?

As the presence of bedbugs isn’t determined by cleanliness, even five-star suites put you at risk of taking home the unwelcome house guests.

Although the bugs are particularly hard to get rid of or even spot with your own eyes, there are tips to detect the tiny insects once you’ve checked in.

“My biggest tip is to always roll your suitcase into the bathroom or another tiled area prior to starting an inspection of your hotel room”, Krejci recommends.

Turn off the lights – Before you unpack, turn off the lights and use your phone’s torch to inspect your hotel room for the best chance of spotting the nocturnal bugs. Check the mattress, furniture and appliances – Bedbugs are most commonly found in the crevices and seams of mattresses and sleeping areas. Rust-coloured brown and red dots, exoskeletons, tiny blackish specks (dried excrement) and small yellow eggs can all be indicators of a bedbug infestation. Follow your nose – A musty odour from the bugs' alarm pheromones, sometimes likened to the scent of expired raspberries or coriander, is a tell-tale sign of a large group of bedbugs. Lift wall hangings – Bedbugs are expert hiders; dark stains on the walls or in picture frames would clue you into their presence even if you don’t come across the bugs themselves.

Krejci adds that cushions and throw pillows should also receive the same “flip and inspect” treatment upon arrival.

What should I do if I spot bedbugs in my hotel?

“Most hotels will have protocols in place that involve relocating you and guests in adjoining rooms to mitigate the spread of bedbugs, along with contacting a professional pest control company for inspection and treatment of the infested areas,” said Krejci.

Notify hotel staff or your rental host immediately with photos of the bedbug evidence you have found. Keep your luggage away from the bed and walls by storing it in the bathroom – preferably on a clean countertop. Do not store clothing in chests of drawers. Instead, use the wardrobe, as bedbugs can’t fly. Once home, seal your luggage in a dark plastic bag and unpack your clothes on a hardwood floor away from the bedroom so you can spot any suitcase stowaways. Dry every item of clothing from your case straight away in the tumble dryer to kill any bugs that crept past customs.

News.title: Business as usual for victorious Man City despite lingering state of limbo
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Business as usual for Manchester City. Or should that be business as unusual? City may be in a strange kind of limbo but their new normal looked distinctly similar to the old variant. They won. Whatever punishments may await in the wake of the 114 guilty verdicts, which City are appealing, for now they are constructing a title challenge which, perhaps, the Premier League could do without. They are leaders with a six-point advantage at the summit and, some would say, an asterisk or two.

But Enzo Maresca’s stellar start has given him outright possession of a record. The Italian has seven victories out of seven in the top flight, the longest winning start to a reign in the Premier League. Beating Ipswich took him past Carlo Ancelotti, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer and his predecessor Pep Guardiola, all tied on six. “For sure I didn’t expect to win seven games out of seven,” said Maresca. “It’s a matter of winning games in this business.” It has been at City, anyway.

So life in the wake of the independent commission’s damning conclusions rather resembled the time before it. There was the statutory Erling Haaland goal, as he scored a second successive brace. The Norwegian has 12 goals in his last eight outings for City. A weakened City team had a talisman in attack ensuring that Ipswich’s competitiveness did not earn them a point. Even when Maresca’s policy of picking Haaland seemed to backfire, after he hobbled off at the end, the Norwegian could reassure his manager. “He said he was okay so hopefully it is nothing serious,” said the Italian.

open image in gallery Erling Haaland was once again Man City’s talisman at the top of the pitch ( Getty )

If so, Haaland was not the only City forward with reasons to enjoy the day. Outside the Etihad Stadium, they did a roaring trade in inflatable bananas. Some are manufactured by their old striker Imre Varadi, the man nicknamed “Imre Banana” in his playing days. If commercial deals involving City have come under the microscope of late, this one will benefit a man who scored goals for them in the second tier in the 1980s.

Maresca’s children were among those trying to buy bananas – “I will ask them now,” he said, waiting to hear if they succeeded – and, in their somewhat surreal way, the bananas form part of the City fans’ response to a ruling that could bring all this to an end. Call it gallows humour or defiance but fans chanted “Stockport away”, envisaging a rather different fixture list. When Jeremy Doku was fouled, they chorused “same old City, always cheating”.

Otherwise, however, it had the air of another of City’s Saturday 3pm kick-offs, just as the Paris Saint-Germain game felt like a big Champions League game. In the interim, anyway, the guilty verdicts may not have changed much.

There was one significant difference, however: Phil Foden ended a 35-game goal drought for City with a belated first strike of 2026. The local marked his first appearance since his Manchester derby red card by slotting home after Doku’s cutback. Maresca, who had predicted Foden would score, looked prophetic. “He’s one of the best Premier League players and it’s my duty to help him be one of the best players,” said the manager.

Foden owed his presence to a wholesale policy of rotation after City’s considerable efforts against PSG. Maresca made six changes, giving Ayyoub Bouaddi a first Premier League start. With Enzo Fernandez and Elliot Anderson held in reserve, City’s bench cost more than the starters, around £500m. The Argentinian was summoned earlier than expected when Mateo Kovacic, who had been excellent, hobbled off. While five City players sustained problems, Maresca was most concerned about the substitute Antoine Semenyo. “The only one we need to wait on is Antoine,” his manager said.

Kovacic had made City’s second goal as Haaland struck for an eighth game in a row, heading in after a lovely bit of skill and a deft chipped cross from Kovacic. Iliman Ndiaye was the provider of the Norwegian’s first goal against Paris Saint-Germain with a cross for a towering header. This was a different kind of assist, with a perceptive pass, followed by two terrific Haaland touches, the second dispatched beyond Christian Walton. Briefly it seemed that Haaland had his ninth Premier League hat-trick, hooking in a volley after Ndiaye had hit the bar, but Fernandez was offside.

open image in gallery Phil Foden ended his goalless streak but scoring City’s opener at the Etihad ( PA )

Instead, it brought Ipswich back into the game. They had levelled when Daizen Maeda scored his first goal for Ipswich after darting in behind Marc Guehi. It was not Guehi’s finest day: he fouled the Ipswich substitute Azor Matusiwa for a late penalty that Zian Flemming converted. City have now conceded nine goals in their last three home matches in all competitions and the last few minutes were fraught.

“I am disappointed we haven’t taken points,” said Ipswich manager Gary O’Neil. His team had begun well organised in a 5-4-1 formation he has used against City before and ended on the front foot. They looked a side who will be in the Premier League next year. Will City?

News.title: This uncrowded Spanish city rivals San Sebastian for food
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

I watched, fascinated, as waiter Manuel expertly separated the flesh from the bones of my salt-baked sea bass. Behind him, diners spilt out of the restaurant onto the cobbled streets of Ciutadella’s port, drinks in hand, chatting in Spanish. The scent of paella hung in the warm early-autumn air.

Spain has always been my favourite destination for good food. I was last here on my birthday, intent on consuming my body weight in Basque cheesecake. But instead of heading to San Sebastian (where the dessert has found fame), I found myself in Ciutadella… and liked it enough to return just months later for another friend’s birthday.

It’s easy to understand why San Sebastian might be the obvious choice for travellers with food on their minds. The Basque city has one of the highest concentrations of Michelin stars per square kilometre in the world (nine restaurants with 16 Michelin stars within a 25 km radius), along with its famed pintxos bars. The food is hyper local, and menus follow the seasons.

Yet Ciutadella rivals much of what makes San Sebastian an appealing food destination. Three of its restaurants – Smoix, Godai and Aquiara – feature in the Michelin Guide, alongside Ca Na Pilar, Torralbenc, Santa Mariana and Es Cranc in the surrounding area, and, much like San Sebastian, Ciutadella has a strong tradition of kilometre zero gastronomy, where restaurants draw heavily on ingredients produced close to where they are consumed.

open image in gallery Ciutadella in Menorca has a food scene to rival San Sebastian ( Getty Images )

The city participates in Menorca’s Custòdia Agrària, or land stewardship scheme, which works with local farms to reduce the environmental impact of agriculture and livestock farming and helps connect participating producers with markets, shops and businesses across the island.



Aquarium, where I ate the salt-baked fish, is a good example of how that approach extends beyond simply sourcing ingredients locally. Much of the restaurant's seafood comes from fishermen in Ciutadella, and the kitchen uses almost everything that arrives, adopting a nose-to-tail approach. A single lobster can be used across several dishes, including caldereta, Menorca’s traditional seafood stew.

Back at the table, the waiter squeezed lemon over my fish before bringing out Aquarium’s red tuna japo taco. It won first prize for Spain’s best bluefin tuna tapa at the national GourmeTapa competition in 2023. One bite made the win easy to understand: the crisp taco shell cracked to reveal unctuous tuna and creamy guacamole lifted by zingy Japanese spices.

open image in gallery The award-winning red tuna japo taco dish at Aquarium restaurant in Ciutadella, Menorca ( Queenie Shaikh )

The sun was setting over Ciutadella, and there was little room for dessert, but Manuel insisted I try their Basque cheesecake.

“I can guarantee that it is the best Basque cheesecake you will eat in all of Menorca,” he said, with such conviction that I gave in.

I gently tapped my spoon against the cake’s crust. Breaking through the dark, caramelised top revealed a soft, almost molten centre, and there was a Menorcan twist: the cheesecake was made with the island’s protected Queso Mahón Menorca, for which the milk must come from local cows, rather than the commercially available cream cheese more commonly used in San Sebastian cheesecakes. Manuel’s confidence turned out to be entirely justified.

The next day, I continued my foodie exploration, making my way through the town centre towards its waterfront promenade. It was noon, and groups of friends lingered over coffees and tortillas at pavement tables, discussing plans to visit the 17th-century Castell de Sant Nicolau watchtower. Tourists filed out of the Cathedral Basilica of Santa María de Ciutadella, a 14th-century Gothic cathedral built on the site of a former mosque, its neo-Classical facade glistening in the autumn sun. There were certainly visitors, but none of the sense of being swallowed by the crowds that have become increasingly difficult to escape in San Sebastian.

When I arrived at Fang i Aram, a popular vegetarian and vegan restaurant near the sea, for lunch the interior was packed, with diners seated on mismatched recycled chairs.

open image in gallery Writer Queenie Shaikh on a coastal walk in Ciutadella ( Queenie Shaikh )

Like the Basque Country, Menorca’s Mediterranean diet features plenty of vegetables, and at Fang i Aram, I found an inventive menu that put them to creative use: aubergine cannelloni with sweet potato sauce, courgette ravioli stuffed with cauliflower sauce, and stuffed piquillo peppers with a pea and spinach sauce. On the walk back to the port, I detoured to Sa Farola Lighthouse, which sits on a hill overlooking the Balearic Sea toward Mallorca.



Dinner that evening was at the Mexican-Mediterranean fusion restaurant Katú de Smoix, set up by Smoix's chef. It reminded me of San Sebastian’s Topa Sukaldería, which takes a similar approach by combining Basque ingredients with Latin American cooking.

Despite the changing seasons, the evening was pleasantly warm, with diners spilling out onto the outdoor patio. It was my friend’s birthday, and we ordered the set menu: six tapas-style dishes per person, chef’s choice. Highlights included corn fritters, Katú’s signature fish ceviche, and green bean pasta served with a seasonal fruit salad. Instead of a traditional birthday cake, staff brought out plates of tarta tres leches – the classic Mexican milk cake.



In typical Spanish fashion, most diners in the city were just heading to dinner as we left Katú around 9pm. Pampa, another famed tapas restaurant close by, was filling up, with tables sharing cheeseboards and cocktails. Neighbourhood cats gazed up hopefully at diners’ feet, waiting for someone to share a bite.

open image in gallery Salt-baked seabass at Aquarium restaurant in Ciutadella ( Queenie Shaikh )

As night fell and another evening of wining and dining commenced, it was clear that other visitors were also in love with Ciutadella’s restaurant scene, much of it shaped by a commitment to sustainable practices. The Basque Country may have its pintxos bars, but here, on the other side of Spain, the Balearic island of Menorca was making a compelling case in its own right. Two visits to Ciutadella in a matter of months had proven that for me too. I strongly suspect there will be a third.

How to do it

Fly direct to Mahón, the capital of Menorca, from London with easyJet, Jet2, Ryanair, British Airways and TUI Airways from £41 per person, return without baggage. You can also reach Mahón from Manchester, Birmingham, Bristol, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Liverpool, Newcastle, Leeds Bradford, East Midlands, Bournemouth and Belfast, although many routes are seasonal.

From Mahón Airport, take the number 10 bus to Mahón bus station (€2.80; £2.37), then the L01 bus to Ciutadella (€5.75; £4.87). The journey takes approximately 90 minutes, depending on connections. Alternatively, a prebooked private transfer to Ciutadella costs around €57 (£48) one way, and takes about 50 minutes.

Where to stay

S’Enclova Petit Hotel

Rooms start from £61 per night for a deluxe double room based on two adults sharing. The hotel is a five-minute walk from the Cathedral Basilica of Santa María de Ciutadella and a 15-minute walk from Platja Gran (Gran Beach).

Hotel Los 5 Sentidos

This five-bedroom bed and breakfast has rooms starting from £110 per night (standard room for two adults), including breakfast. It is set a five-minute walk from the town centre.

News.title: France’s highest hotel is over 2,600m – and it just reopened
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The highest hotel in France, 2,620m above sea level, has just opened in the Pyrenees.

Hôtellerie des Laquets reopened its doors to guests in late September, having been closed for over 30 years.

The former stop-off for tourists and scientists, built between 1930 and 1933 on the route to the Pic du Midi, has been reopened after closing in 1996.

Following an extensive renovation, 16 rooms, a bar, restaurant, sauna and a steam room will be on offer to guests of Hôtellerie des Laquets.

The hotel restaurant offers a menu created by chef Stéphane Tournié, who was awarded a Michelin star at Les Jardins de l'Opéra in Toulouse.

The spa area with a sauna and steam rooms is due to open in December 2026.

open image in gallery Hôtellerie des Laquets features 16 rooms ( AFP/Getty )

To check in, travellers will have to take the cable car to the summit of the Pic du Midi at 2,877m, before connecting to the hotel via a private cable car.

Half-board double rooms, some in a historic wing of the original 1930s building, feature private bathrooms and panoramic views of the Pyrenees from €599 (£506) per night.

Hôtellerie des Laquets reached heights above Refuge de Solaise, a luxury hotel in Val d'Isère, 2,551m above sea level in the Alps, for the accolade of the highest French hotel.

The hotel sits just 257m below the Pic du Midi observatory, the world’s oldest high-altitude astronomical observatory at 2,877m.

open image in gallery The hotel restaurant offers a menu created by Michelin-starred chef Stéphane Tournié ( AFP/Getty )

Pic du Midi was designated France’s first International Dark Sky Reserve in 2013, and room rates include a daily planetarium show introducing the constellations.

This is not the only landmark hotel to be opening in Europe this year.

Tourists in London will soon be able to check in to one of the city’s landmarks with the opening of a new luxury hotel in Admiralty Arch.

Waldorf Astoria London, Admiralty Arch is set to welcome overnight guests for the first time in its history in autumn 2026, following an extensive restoration of the grade-I listed monument.

The monument is located on the opposite end of the Mall to Buckingham Palace, close to Trafalgar Square.

The hotel will feature 114 rooms and suites, with some named in reference to the building’s history and naval heritage, including the Nelson Suite, St James’s Residence and Victory Residence, named after HMS Victory.
