World.title: Counterfeit goods worth more than R160m seized from Joburg CBD
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The National Counterfeit and Illicit Goods Unit seized counterfeit goods worth more than R160 million during a multi-disciplinary operation in the Johannesburg CBD this week.

Police spokesperson Colonel Amanda van Wyk said the team, with support from the Public Order Policing (POP) Unit in Pretoria, the South African Revenue Services (SARS) Customs Division, and brand protectors, executed search-and-seizure warrants at several identified shops located in a retail building.

"This resulted in the seizure of more than 62 000 counterfeit items including high-end branded clothing, footwear, cosmetics, watches, jewellery, and sunglasses.

"The operation forms part of ongoing nationwide efforts to dismantle illegal trade, manufacturing, and distribution of counterfeit and illicit goods in the country," she said.

World.title: 'No favours for connected friends' - Zille tells DA rally
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - DA Johannesburg mayoral candidate Helen Zille has declared war on corruption.

She has promised an independent investigation into alleged corruption, with public hearings and published findings, and calls for stronger protections for whistleblowers.

Speaking during her campaign for the city, Zille also called for stronger protections for whistleblowers.

"Joburg needs its own Madlanga moment We will initiate an independent investigation into the corruption that has crippled this city, with public hearings and published findings. We will act on the evidence from the Auditor General, from whistleblowers, the Zondo Commission, and others.

"We will rebuild this city's anti-corruption capacity, shield it from political interference, and do whatever is possible to protect whistleblowers.

And we will scrutinize city contracts, starting with the biggest and the most suspicious. We will open up procurement to public scrutiny. Who got the contract? Why? What were they paid? And what did they deliver? No more secret deals. No favours for connected friends. No work, no pay," she said.

World.title: 'Cockroach' party founder released from Indian police custody
World.content:
NEW DELHI - India's Cockroach Janata Party founder Abhijeet Dipke was released from detention on Saturday, a day after his arrest during a police crackdown on protests against the election authority.

Dipke, 31, was detained on Friday in New Delhi as he headed to join a rally that the CJP protest movement had called in the capital's central Connaught Place district.

He walked out of a police station on Saturday afternoon, waving to the media and giving a thumbs up as he was driven away, an AFP photographer saw.

"Abhijeet Dipke released," CJP legal affairs chief Ratna Singh said on social media.

Opposition parties and CJP activists have defied a security crackdown, rallying to demand the resignation of India's chief election commissioner after accusing the poll body of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling party.

The commission, which oversees voting in the world's most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing.

Two other senior CJP leaders, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, were arrested on October 14 after entering Jantar Mantar, a decades-old protest site that police have declared off-limits for demonstrations. They remain in custody.

Members of Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India's electoral rolls.

Rights groups and critics however say Modi's government has eroded democratic freedoms during more than a decade in power, citing pressure on journalists, civil society groups and political opponents -- allegations the government rejects.

World.title: Joburg Crisis Alliance sounds the alarm on city's problems
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Joburg Crisis Alliance warns that Johannesburg cannot afford another five years of poor service delivery and crumbling infrastructure.

The alliance calls for stronger civic structures and greater community participation to hold the incoming city council accountable.

JCA co-convener Neeshan Balton said urgent action is needed to keep the city from sliding deeper into crisis.

The alliance met in Parkview earlier.

"It needs to now move beyond being a crisis alliance to something more formal to do the work that has been outlined here. Because the JCA itself must become a democratic organisation that must bring together people, that must build these civic structures.

"And when we build them, we need to make sure that all the education and advocacy work that we've spoken about here takes place across the length and breadth of the city.

"Because on the 4th, a new government comes into place in Johannesburg. They will be there for five years until 2031. Now, keep that in mind. 2031, we are going to be having these summits, and we will gather here in 2031. And very little would have changed besides having to pay more for very little. I don't think we can afford that. I don't think we can afford for this city to collapse."

World.title: Nepal floods 'defining moment' for climate action: UN
World.content:
KATHMANDU - Nepal's devastating floods should be a turning point for global climate action, with the international community helping the Himalayan nation recover, a top UN official told AFP on Saturday.

The country suffered one of the worst disasters in its history on August 26, when a mountain collapse near the China border triggered catastrophic floods that killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing.

Scientists said climate change played a significant role in that disaster.

Jorge Moreira da Silva, executive director of the UN Office for Project Services (UNOPS), which implements humanitarian and development projects, said he had witnessed "massive devastation" during a visit to affected communities.

Nepal, a largely rural country of 30 million people that contributes little to global greenhouse gas emissions, estimates reconstruction will cost $4.78 billion.

"This is a defining moment not only for Nepal, this is a defining moment for the international community," Moreira da Silva told AFP in Kathmandu.

"It's not fair to ask a country that emits almost nothing of CO2 to suddenly pay alone the consequence of something that was not generated by the country," he added.

"That's why it's fundamental that global solidarity is brought to this equation."

- 'Climate justice' -

Moreira da Silva said reconstruction and resettlement must account for future climate risks, while the international community must "renew its commitment to climate".

"It's also about climate justice and climate responsibility," he said, warning that low-emitting countries would continue to bear the brunt of climate change.

"This is going to happen unless those countries that emit the most... change their pathway," he said.

Moreira da Silva said Nepal was rebuilding as global disruptions threatened food security. He also leads the UN task force for the Strait of Hormuz.

"The simultaneous disruption of the three maritime shock points... the Strait of Hormuz, in the Black Sea and in the Red Sea, poses a significant challenge, particularly on food security," he said.

The UN and its humanitarian partners launched a $49.6 million appeal last month to provide emergency assistance to flood victims.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah told the United Nations last month that the flooding "was a warning to the world" about the growing dangers of climate change.

By Paavan Mathema

World.title: Albanian capital sees fifth straight day of violent clashes
World.content:
TIRANA - Albania's capital Tirana saw clashes for a fifth straight day Saturday as protesters demanded the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who pledged to listen to their criticism.

Several hundred people, some masked, gathered around noon in front of the ministry of education, with protests later spreading across the city.

Protesters threw rocks at the police and set litter bins on fire, using them as barricades to prevent the police from advancing.

After police officers had used megaphones to call on those gathered to desist from violence, they used water cannons and tear gas to temporarily disperse the crowd.

Violent demonstrations have rocked Tirana since Tuesday, with thousands of protesters calling for Rama to step down over university conditions and high tuition fees.

At the beginning of the protest demonstrators set a suitcase on fire and threw it in the education ministry courtyard, symbolically showing they do not want to leave Albania.

Journalism student Sinan Billa said the protest was "a reaction to express discontent at the silence of our government."

"Young people have awoken for our parents, too," Billa told AFP.

"We are not asking for privileges. We are demanding our rights, our future and a better country," he said.

While visiting local business damaged in the demonstrations, Rama said he respected the students and added that "their right to protest must and will be protected.

"Their voices, the voices of young people and of every citizen who has taken part in protests today, must and will be heard with respect," Rama said.

However, he added that he "will not allow anyone to jeopardise the future of this country".

Local media reported further protests in the coastal town of Durres, where demonstrators smashed the windows of the post office and blocked roads with burning barricades.

On Friday night police deployed tear gas and water cannons as protesters hurled stones at security forces, burning dustbins to block roads across the city. The clashes continued into the night in several parts of the city.

Police said 10 people were arrested after Friday's demonstrations, with criminal proceedings lodged against a further 22.

The health ministry said 25 people, including nine police officers, sustained minor injuries during clashes in Tirana, Vlora and Lezha on Friday.

This week's escalation of unrest comes after months of anti-government protests in the Balkan nation, initially sparked by a controversial resort development linked to US President Donald Trump's family.

World.title: Jayawardene quits as coach of five-time IPL winners Mumbai
World.content:
MUMBAI - Mahela Jayawardene stepped down as head coach of Mumbai Indians on Saturday to end a nearly decade-long association with one of the Indian Premier League's most successful teams.

The 49-year-old former Sri Lanka captain led Mumbai to three titles in his first stint between 2017 and 2022.

He rejoined the team in 2024 but was unable to replicate his success as five-time IPL winners Mumbai finished fourth in 2025 and ninth out of 10 teams in 2026.

"Together we have shared some unforgettable moments, overcome challenges and built something we can all be proud of," Jayawardene said in a statement.

"I leave with immense pride in what we have achieved together and will always carry a special place in my heart for MI.

"I wish the team every success in the years ahead."

Jayawardene represented Sri Lanka in 149 Tests, 448 one-day internationals and 55 T20 matches between 1997 and 2015.

World.title: Leaders weigh 'huge benefit', risks of AI for global economy
World.content:
BANGKOK - The artificial intelligence boom has been a key driver of global growth, but also poses economic risks should investment in the technology falter, experts and policymakers said this week at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.

Propelled by spending on data centres and microchips, AI has helped cushion the economic shock of rising global energy prices caused by war in the Middle East, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said in a report on Tuesday.

The fund's chief economist Silvana Tenreyro noted this week that global trade rose 8.3 percent between 2023 and 2025, a figure she said would be closer to 4.6 percent without AI-related products.

"It is everywhere in the global economy," Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said of AI on Friday.

"You see it in GDP. You see it in the stock market. You see it in the bond market... So it is here, and it's just the beginning."

But some top officials gathered in Bangkok this week cautioned against relying too heavily on AI investment.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh called AI the "most consequential change" to the global economy in his lifetime, and said it had "a huge benefit". Still, he warned the road ahead would be "bumpy".

"The path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one, bumpy in our understanding of the technology, bumpy because we really don't know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies," he said.

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva similarly noted the AI boom's boost to global growth, but she told AFP that any slowdown in the industry "would be felt across the world".

"If there is loss of confidence and money runs away from AI, that can lead to financial stability risks," Georgieva said.

An IMF report released this week projected that a decline in AI investment could reduce global GDP by 0.4 percent by 2028.

"Weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction," the report said.

- War and regulation -

While AI investment and trade have softened the global economic impact of the Middle East war, economists at Moody's Analytics have warned that if the conflict drags on it could "puncture" the boom.

They said higher energy prices and tighter financial conditions could push up operating costs and interest rates, adding to doubts over "the long-term profitability and viability of AI business models".

"A drawn-out conflict would put serious strain on the economics behind AI investment," the group said.

The uncertainty around regulation has also clouded the technology's outlook.

Leaders like US President Donald Trump have urged more limited government regulation, even as some in the industry have called for legislation to mitigate risks.

Georgieva, the IMF chief, appeared on Friday to link such regulation to future investment.

"If there are no safeguards, then the risks may exceed the opportunities," she said in Bangkok.

By Asad Hashim

World.title: GSU officers forcefully occupy Moi land
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

GSU officers have occupied private property near the Eldoret State Lodge owned by the family of former President Daniel arap Moi.

General Service Unit (GSU) officers have occupied a prime property owned by the family of Kenya’s second President, the late Daniel arap Moi, near the Eldoret State Lodge.

The property, registered as Eldoret Municipality/Block 8/62, was invaded Friday afternoon after what those in the know claim was an order from State house to evict current occupants.

Lawyer Moses Mutisya of Gordon Ogola and Associates, who represents the Moi family and Willowdale Investments Limited, said GSU officers ordered caretakers at the property to vacate.

Mutisya said that upon making inquiries, he was informed by the officers that they were acting on firm instructions to enforce the directive.

By Saturday afternoon, occupants had moved out of the property, according to the lawyer.

The parcel is strategically located near the main entrance to the State Lodge.

The area around the State Lodge was under tight security yesterday, with only government officials reportedly allowed to use roads leading to the protected area.

Photographs obtained by The Standard showed deserted premises within the property.

Mutisya, who spent much of the midmorning and afternoon at the property, said his pleas to stop the occupation were brushed aside.

He described the alleged occupation as unlawful and demanded immediate redress, warning that the owners would take legal action if the matter were not resolved.

Efforts to get a comment from the Government Spokesman Charles Owino were futile as he neither picked calls nor replied to text messages.

The advocate said caretakers were shocked when GSU officers later informed them that they were occupying government property.

“The said officers entered the property unlawfully and informed the caretakers of our client that a senior government official had directed that all adjoining properties to the State Lodge be vacated immediately,” Mutisya said during a media briefing in Eldoret.

He added: “My client has been in occupation of the property since 1996 and had a title to that effect.”

Some cows, which Mutisya said did not belong to his client, were seen grazing on the disputed property.

“We are hereby demanding that this injustice be remedied, failure to which we will take appropriate legal action,” he said.

It was not immediately clear whether the alleged eviction was linked to a land dispute or a security measure. However, the owners, through their lawyer, maintained that they had documents proving ownership of the property.

Mutisya said the land had not been the subject of any dispute for nearly three decades and that no eviction notice had been issued before the officers moved in.

World.title: Kenya confirms third Ebola case
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kenya has confirmed a third case of Ebola involving a 65-year-old woman who is a close relative of the first two patients.

The Ministry of Health, in a statement, said the woman developed a fever, sore throat and malaise while in quarantine, prompting her isolation and testing.

Her samples tested positive for Ebola at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI).

According to the Health Director-General Patrick Amoth, the patient has been transferred to an infectious disease unit, where she is receiving supportive care and being monitored.

“Having been in quarantine, she was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care, improving her chances of recovery while limiting the risk of further spread of the disease,” the statement read.

The second patient, on the other hand, is in stable condition and responding well to supportive care.

The latest case brings the number of confirmed Ebola infections in Kenya to three.

According to the Ministry, of the 130 contacts identified so far, 127 had been traced and placed in quarantine, with efforts ongoing to trace the remaining three.

World.title: From 'Chogo' to senator? Winnie Odinga steps into her own political spotlight
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

From Raila Odinga’s shadow to her own political path, Winnie sets her sights on the Nairobi Senate seat in 2027. [Courtesy]

The hat was more than a hat. Literally.

As Raila Odinga’s body made its final journey home from India, his youngest daughter, Winnie, held tightly to his familiar cream-coloured fedora. It was one of the few things she could still protect, a small piece of a man whose presence had filled her life and Kenya’s political imagination for decades.

The image of Winnie carrying her father’s hat was deeply personal. The country was mourning a political giant, but she was mourning her father.

A year later, on the first anniversary of Raila’s death, Winnie has announced her intention to contest the Nairobi Senate seat in the 2027 General Election.

The timing is poignant. On a day devoted to remembering her father, she has declared her own political ambitions, signalling a shift from being one of the most recognisable faces of the Odinga family to a politician seeking a mandate in her own right.

“As Edwin Sifuna seeks a higher office, I see an opportunity in Nairobi, which is why I have decided I will vie for Senator of Nairobi County,” she said.

And just like that, the conversation shifted from the daughter who carried Baba’s hat to the politician who wants a seat of her own.

The last-born girl

To many Kenyans, Winnie is Chogo, the last-born child of Raila and Ida Odinga. The nickname carries the familiarity of family life, a reminder that behind the powerful surname is a daughter who grew up in a household where politics was never far from the conversation.

Her father was no ordinary political figure. His name could summon crowds, ignite debate and divide opinion. His decades-long career placed the Odinga family at the centre of Kenya’s political story.

Growing up as Raila’s youngest daughter meant sharing him with a country that claimed a piece of his time, energy and, eventually, his final goodbye.

Yet Winnie was not simply a spectator in her father’s political world. She worked around his campaigns and communications before stepping into politics herself, eventually winning a seat in the East African Legislative Assembly.

In November 2022, Parliament elected her to represent Kenya in the regional legislature, where she took office in December that year. Based in Arusha, Tanzania, she became part of the East African Community’s legislative institution, serving a five-year term running to 2027.

The EALA offered Winnie a political platform beyond her father’s immediate circle and an opportunity to participate in regional affairs. Her current tenure has also given her experience in legislative politics before her proposed move into elective politics at home.

The Nairobi Senate bid would take her into a different contest, one in which voters will have to decide whether her experience, ideas and political programme merit their support.

The hat she could not let go

For years, Raila’s trademark headgear had been part of his public identity, appearing at political rallies, meetings and public ceremonies. But in Winnie’s hands, it became something else: a personal possession tied to the final journey of a daughter and her father

She explained how protective she had been of it throughout the journey, describing it as one of the few things she could still hold on to.

The image captured a kind of helplessness that public figures’ families rarely get to show. Crowds could mourn Raila, politicians could speak of his legacy, and supporters could debate who would inherit his political movement. Winnie, however, had been left with the painful task of bringing her father home.

The symbolism of the hat has since acquired another layer. At a ceremony in Bondo earlier this month, elders placed a traditional hat on Winnie’s head in a symbolic gesture associated with the possibility of her carrying forward her father’s political mantle.

Winnie’s political journey has not started with this Senate announcement.

Her election to the East African Legislative Assembly placed her among Kenya’s representatives in a regional institution whose work concerns cooperation among East African Community partner states.

The role gave her a platform in regional legislation while her father remained a central figure in national politics.

The Senate is responsible for representing counties, participating in lawmaking on matters concerning counties and exercising oversight over revenue allocated to county governments. A Nairobi senator must therefore make a case on issues that touch residents directly, from public spending and service delivery to the accountability of county leadership.

The capital is also a demanding political terrain. Its electorate is diverse, its concerns immediate and its contests fiercely competitive.

A famous surname may open doors, but it cannot replace a convincing programme on jobs, housing, transport, healthcare and the management of public resources.

Winnie will have to demonstrate that she understands Nairobi beyond its place in her father’s national political story.

Can she translate the loyalty associated with Raila into support for her own agenda? Can she persuade voters that she is more than the daughter of a political icon?

Those questions will follow her into the campaign.

The Odingaism

Political inheritance can be both an advantage and a burden.

Raila’s name carries a formidable history of opposition politics, democratic reform and a loyal support base. It also invites comparisons that few politicians have to contend with.

Winnie’s challenge will be to honour that history without allowing it to become the entirety of her political identity.

Raila’s death left a space in the Orange Democratic Movement and among supporters who had looked to him for direction through decades of political contests. The question of who will carry his legacy has inevitably turned towards his family and the wider political movement he helped build.

Winnie’s Senate bid will require her to turn recognition into a political proposition that voters can interrogate. Her experience at EALA gives her a legislative starting point; the Nairobi contest will demand that she demonstrate how that experience can serve residents of the capital.

She must also navigate the expectations attached to her father’s name while making room for her own ideas, priorities and leadership style.

There is a temptation to see Winnie’s future entirely through the lens of inheritance. She is Raila’s daughter, the last-born known as Chogo, the woman who carried his hat and the politician whom some supporters hope will continue his legacy.

But she is also a woman making a decision about her own future.

The Senate bid offers her an opportunity to define what that future means, beyond the grief surrounding her father’s death and the weight of a name that has shaped Kenyan politics for decades.

The hat remains an unforgettable image from Raila’s final journey home. A daughter attempted to protect the last tangible thing she could hold on to.

The Senate will demand something different: a political vision, a campaign and the votes of Nairobi residents.

Chogo has announced her next move. Will Winnie Odinga turn the memory of Baba into a mandate of her own?

World.title: Motorists, households face fresh fuel price hikes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

EPRA attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East. [FIle, Standard]

The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) has increased fuel prices, raising the cost of super petrol by Sh12.93 per litre, diesel by Sh9.90, and kerosene by Sh28.49.

The new prices, effective from October 15 to November 14, 2026, will see motorists in Nairobi pay up to Sh226.96 per litre for super petrol, Sh227.76 for diesel, and Sh219.85 for kerosene.

EPRA Director-General Edward Mwirigi Kinyua attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East, which has disrupted petroleum supply chains and driven up the cost of importing fuel.

The rise in kerosene prices is likely to hit low-income households that rely on the fuel for cooking and lighting.

Meanwhile, higher diesel prices could raise the cost of transporting goods and operating public service vehicles, potentially driving up fares and commodity prices.

Diesel is a key fuel for the country's freight transport sector and a significant portion of public service vehicle operations, meaning the increase could have a ripple effect across the economy.

The latest review comes after EPRA maintained pump prices during the September 15 to October 14 pricing period, despite a decline in the cost of importing petrol.

World.title: Oburu Oginga to leave hospital soon - ODM
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

ODM SG Catherine Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician.

ODM Secretary General Catherine Omanyo has dismissed social media reports about the health of party leader Oburu Oginga, saying he is recovering well and is expected to be discharged from hospital either today or tomorrow.

Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician, accusing them of exploiting his health condition to attract online attention and increase engagement.

“It's unfortunate what I've been reading on social media. Those people who are seeking to have more likes or viewers, they will be disappointed because he's up, he's well, he's fine. In fact, he's headed home either today or tomorrow,” she said.

Omanyo insisted that the reports had exaggerated his situation, dismissing claims of his death and assuring the public that he was doing well.

She noted that health conditions could fluctuate, saying Oburu's position as ODM party leader had made his well-being a subject of heightened public interest.

“Everybody, everybody, including you and me, our health is not static. You can be under the weather any time. It's just that he's a party leader, and it makes breaking news,” Omanyo said.

She urged social media users to exercise restraint when discussing the health of public figures, warning against spreading unverified reports, particularly claims of death, before confirmation from credible sources.

Her remarks come amid growing speculation on social media about Oburu's health, with some users circulating unverified claims about his condition.

World.title: Kenya declares Ebola a formidable epidemic disease, sets new rules
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, who declared Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus a formidable epidemic disease under the Public Health Act. [File,Standard]

Kenya has declared Ebola virus a formidable epidemic disease, introducing new rules governing screening, isolation, quarantine, contact tracing and the handling of bodies.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale issued the declaration through a legal notice published in the Kenya Gazette on Monday, October 12, under Section 35 of the Public Health Act.

The declaration follows Kenya’s confirmation of its first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease on October 6, after a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo travelled through Uganda to Nairobi. The patient died despite receiving supportive treatment.

The case prompted health authorities to trace people who may have come into contact with the patient and strengthen screening at points of entry.

In an update on October 12, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Kenya had listed 127 contacts, with 94 in quarantine, and screened more than 665,000 travellers at points of entry.

WHO also supplied protective equipment and testing materials worth about US$70,000 to support the response.

The government published two legal notices on October 12. Legal Notice No. 203 declares the disease a formidable epidemic, while Legal Notice No. 204 establishes the Public Health (Ebola Disease) Rules, 2026.

The regulations provide for screening at points of entry, medical assessment, isolation, referral, quarantine and monitoring.

They also assign responsibilities to transport operators, health facilities, medical practitioners and laboratories.

Health authorities will conduct investigations and contact tracing, while designated health facilities will manage suspected and confirmed cases. The rules also provide for the inspection and decontamination of premises.

The regulations cover the safe and dignified disposal of bodies, burial procedures, record-keeping, transportation and repatriation. They also address public communication, media houses’ responsibilities in public sensitisation and assistance from enforcement agencies.

The rules provide for offences and penalties, although the Gazette extract does not specify the penalties for individual violations.

What the declaration means

Bundibugyo virus disease is a form of Ebola that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or contaminated materials.

Contact with the body of someone who has died from the disease can also expose people to infection during unsafe burial practices.

Symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat, followed by vomiting and diarrhoea. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days.

WHO says no approved vaccine or specific treatment currently exists for the Bundibugyo strain, making early detection, isolation, supportive care and contact tracing central to controlling its spread.

The health agency has advised against travel or trade restrictions on Kenya, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo based on the information available.

The new rules establish a legal framework for managing the disease, from identifying suspected infections and monitoring contacts to caring for patients and preventing exposure during burials.

World.title: How Hegseth’s Pentagon tenure is shaping his possible political future
World.content:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has rarely shied away from controversy, but his latest spectacle — announcing that the convicted Fort Hood mass shooter’s execution would be livestreamed — proved a bridge too far even for President Donald Trump.

While Trump pulled the plug on the broadcast Thursday, the episode underscores the risks behind Hegseth’s increasingly provocative public persona — one that some of his closest advisers believe could carry him all the way to the White House, but which others caution could jeopardize his possible political future.

Hegseth’s push to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad initially surprised Trump, as CNN has previously reported. Two Trump advisers described the move as an attempt by Hegseth to play into the impulses of Trump and the MAGA base. But Trump’s eventual decision to backtrack on the idea amid bipartisan backlash was also viewed by some inside the administration as a blow to Hegseth — and a warning about the combative, made-for-TV image he has cultivated at the Pentagon.

Still, Hegseth’s push to livestream a public execution overlaps with his future political ambitions, two sources familiar with the matter told CNN. The livestream was “pure id,” one of the sources said, noting how it comports with Hegseth’s eye for theatrics as a former TV personality who believes he knows what resonates with the American public.

Conversations with more than a dozen current and former administration officials, Trump allies, Republican operatives and people familiar with Hegseth’s political orbit reveal a defense secretary who, while never holding elected office, is taking steps that could set up a political future. He has cultivated a macho public image, empowered a small group of media-savvy advisers and tested messages that appeal to the MAGA base — even as his record at the Pentagon and his appetite for controversy threaten to narrow his path.

As he’s sought to craft his “warrior” image, Hegseth has surrounded himself with former Fox News producers and social media personalities — chief among them his wife, Jennifer Hegseth. Sources said that group wields outsized influence within the shrinking circle of advisers he still trusts.

Many of those advisers have encouraged Hegseth to consider political office — including a possible presidential run in 2028, sources said. Their argument: The two main alternatives, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, may not run and face an uncertain path to the nomination. Hegseth, they believe, should keep his options open.

“A lot of them are all in,” said one administration official who supports Hegseth’s political ambitions. Many of those closest to Hegseth are focused on his political future in part because they see elected office as one of his few viable options after the Pentagon, the source added.

His closest advisers also argue that Hegseth has the “look” of a candidate and presents a stronger image than some of the other likely contenders to replace Trump. However, some also acknowledge the criticism his overhaul of the Pentagon has sparked, and that his consistently combative attitude toward those who question his views or policies present headwinds toward winning over the electorate.

Unlike Vance, who has served as the Republican Party fundraising chair this past year, and Rubio, a 2016 presidential contender, Hegseth also lacks deep connections to the donors needed to mount a White House bid. Meanwhile, a super PAC close to Texas Sen. Ted Cruz remains active as he publicly flirts with another presidential campaign.

Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth attend a bilateral meeting with President Donald Trump and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, in the Oval Office of the White House on March 3. Win McNamee/Getty Images

Some Trump allies told CNN they believe Hegseth would entertain a 2028 presidential bid only if Vance decided not to run.

Vance has the inside track to get Trump’s support — choosing a potential successor was part of the calculus in selecting the Ohio senator as a running mate in 2024 — and Hegseth would face a steep climb without the president’s backing, sources added.

NBC News first reported on Hegseth’s private discussions about a possible 2028 run in August. At the time, Hegseth called the report “100% false.”

In response to CNN’s questions for this article, Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson said in a statement that “Secretary Hegseth is not running for president, and his only priority is leading the War Department.”

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell in a statement said that Hegseth had “not once” discussed any of what CNN was reporting. “As one of Secretary Hegseth’s senior advisors, I can attest that he spends every single day working to protect the nation and give our service members everything they need to be successful,” Parnell said.

While Hegseth’s image and blunt style have obvious appeal with a MAGA base that will be looking for a future home after Trump’s presidency, his oversight of the Iran war is a significant challenge. America’s latest military campaign in the Middle East is deeply unpopular with voters, and polls show it driving down support for both Trump and Republicans in the midterms.

Hegseth’s political activity — including traveling to Iowa earlier this year to rally for a GOP House candidate — has helped fuel speculation that he could someday run for office.

His political movements are watched with increasing interest in Tennessee, where his family moved several years ago, though GOP sources there say he has not taken steps in the state yet that might suggest he harbors political ambitions there.

“We’re very proud that he is serving us,” said Scott Golden, chairman of the Tennessee Republican Party. “And I would just say I hope he considers running for office at some point, at some level, whatever level he wants to do.”

The making of a ‘warrior’

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth lifts weights as he meets with troops at the US naval base at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, on June 10. Phil Stewart/Reuters

Hegseth has focused much of his efforts at the Pentagon on crafting a particular public image for himself, based around the idea he is leading a charge to root out so-called “woke-ism” from the military.

At times referred to inside the Pentagon as the Secretary of Culture War, Hegseth’s priorities have included slashing the number of generals in the military, changing the Department of Defense to the “Department of War,” and even creating a screening program for “testosterone deficiency.”

“We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that? No fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors,” Hegseth said at a September “State of the Force” speech. “The ideological clowns are out. The patriotic cowboys are in — with testosterone testing on top.”

In what is seen as an effort to manufacture the specific public image he wants, Hegseth has largely insulated himself from the press and often declines to answer questions on his decision-making. Press conferences held near the beginning of the war with Iran began on many occasions with Hegseth’s ranting against the press and reporters’ coverage of the conflict, which he found to be “incredibly unpatriotic.”

The Pentagon has also taken on a more political tone in some of its public messaging, particularly on X, where an official Defense Department Rapid Response account dedicates itself to sharing images of Hegseth and snippets of his speeches.

Several far-right social media personalities and accounts — including at least two active-duty Army officers— routinely and vigorously defend Hegseth’s decisions and attack his critics on X. (This despite strict regulations for how service members can conduct themselves online.) Several of the individuals are employed at the Pentagon and many in the building see the small group as an online army tasked with influencing public perception of Hegseth and his policies.

Hegseth has repeatedly insisted his overarching goal is to make the military more “lethal” by removing guardrails intended to prevent things like civilian casualties and by endorsing legally dubious combat operations — including some that have prompted allegations of war crimes.

Those moves have garnered criticism from officials both inside the Pentagon and elsewhere within the Trump administration. But they appear to have also helped Hegseth maintain the one relationship that matters most if he envisions some sort of political future for himself: the president.

Secretary of DefensePete Hegseth walks near President Donald Trump before departing for Baltimore County, Maryland, on October 6. Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

While Trump has remained a steadfast defender of Hegseth, others close to the president — including some in the West Wing — are less enthusiastic, sources familiar with the matter told CNN.

Hegseth has been at the center of controversies even before the execution livestream, many of which the White House has brushed off, but some have left a lingering unease among White House officials and even some other Cabinet members.

One such issue is the Signal chat scandal, in which Hegseth shared specific operational details with senior administration officials in a Signal messaging app just hours before the US military carried out strikes on Houthi rebels in Yemen. His messages laid out exact timelines and target surveillance prior to the March 15, 2025, operation. Unbeknownst to Hegseth and the group, the editor-in-chief of The Atlantic was part of the chat.

The president’s then-national security adviser Mike Waltz took the brunt of Trump’s ire following the controversy, but many advisers thought at the time Hegseth should have faced stronger repercussions.

“These people have long memories,” one Trump adviser told CNN.

Hegseth’s eagerness to go to war with Iran and his removal of high-ranking military officials have also put him at odds with some senior advisers to the president.

In the immediate lead-up to the first bombs being dropped on Iran, Hegseth was one of the biggest cheerleaders for military intervention.

While the debate played out internally, Hegseth not only validated Trump’s idea to move forward, he downplayed the inherent risks of the conflict spiraling, CNN reported at the time — a reality that’s now come to fruition.

White House principal deputy press secretary Anna Kelly said in a statement that the White House and Pentagon “are fully aligned on ensuring justice is brought to evil traitor Nidal Malik Hasan who killed 13 innocent people.”

“Secretary Hegseth is doing a great job leading the Pentagon — and the results of Operations Epic Fury, Absolute Resolve and Midnight Hammer speak for themselves,” she said, referencing US military operations in Iran and Venezuela.

The episode over the Fort Hood shooter has resurfaced some of these frustrations over Hegseth’s movements. And, notably, it was Vance, whose own 2028 ambitions cast a shadow over all possible contenders, who was among the first to publicly express doubt about Hegseth’s plans to livestream an execution.

“I mean, look, if it’s all through live stream, I’m not going to be watching it,” Vance said.

In search of a political home

Pete Hegseth, then a Republican Senate candidate, in March 2012. Bruce Bisping/Star Tribune/Getty Images/File

A turn to politics would not be new for Hegseth. Before joining Fox News, he ran for Senate in Minnesota in 2012, when he was leading a conservative veterans’ advocacy group.

An adviser for Hegeth’s Senate campaign told CNN that while Hegseth was a young candidate at 32 years old, he had natural talent on the campaign trail.

“Pete was great on the stump,” said the adviser, who requested anonymity to candidly discuss Hegseth’s Senate campaign. “He’s one of those people that when he’s talking to you, he’s talking to you. He has an amazing ability to do that. His eyes are focused on you.”

But Hegseth ultimately dropped out of the race after the Minnesota GOP convention that year, when he lost the party’s nomination to Kurt Bills, as a candidate who eschewed 2012 GOP presidential candidate Ron Paul’s libertarian-leaning ideology.

Hegseth now owns a home in Tennessee, a state much more amenable to Trump’s brand of politics.

Trump held a rally last weekend in Clarksville, Tennessee, where questions about Hegseth’s political future have at times become fodder for speculation for his post-Pentagon career. That speculation has intensified at times, like when Hegseth’s nomination was jeopardized by revelations about a past accusation of sexual assault — which Hegseth has repeatedly denied — and during early scrutiny of his uneven start as defense secretary.

But GOP officials there say Hegseth hasn’t made any moves that would suggest he’s eyeing a run for office there.

“I, for one, would love him to run for office at some point in the future. But honestly, there’s not been a lot of talk,” said state Rep. Aron Maberry of Clarksville, Tennessee. “But we love him. And we are excited that he’s in DC in the Department of War and a Tennessean.”

A senior GOP official in the state said that other than some rumors and intrigue, there was never any serious discussion about Hegseth potentially running for governor or senator back when his confirmation vote in the Senate was in jeopardy.

The official never got the sense that Hegseth or anyone close to him was lining up support from county chairs or that there was pressure coming from Washington to help him find a safe landing spot.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth speaks at the 2026 International Christian Media Convention in Nashville, Tennessee, on February 19. Seth Herald/Reuters

He could have the same challenge turning to Tennessee politics now, should he leave the Pentagon.

“His biggest challenge is, he’s a Minnesota guy, he’s a DC guy, he doesn’t have real Tennessee ties,” said Steve Gill, a conservative political commentator and editor and publisher of TriStar Daily, a digital media publication in Tennessee. “He has work to do if he wants to create that base of connections and support. I’m not seeing any indications yet that he’s doing that.”

At Trump’s Tennessee rally, Hegseth received mostly rave reviews from the MAGA faithful. Many attendees CNN spoke with had close ties to nearby Fort Campbell and approved of Hegseth’s military overhaul.

Kris Grempler is the owner of a school that teaches members of the 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment how to drive armored vehicles. Speaking to CNN at Trump’s rally, he said that morale among service members is noticeably improved since Hegseth took over the Pentagon.

“I love him to death. You know, getting to see him like do PT and stuff with these guys still, like he’s just — he’s a guy’s guy. And these troops love that,” Grempler said.

Emily Vierra, 47, a teacher at a Department of Defense school at Fort Campbell, said she thinks Hegseth could have a future in politics. “I can see it 100%. I can see him doing it in a heartbeat,” she said. “He’s a great communicator, able to deliver and relay the message in a way that resonates with people.”

“I don’t think he needs to change a thing,” Vierra said as she waited for Trump to arrive in Clarksville. “I think he needs to be authentic and true to who he is.”

But there was also some skepticism at Trump’s Tennessee rally. Hunter Meade, a 22-year-old server from Nashville, said that Hegseth struck him as overly performative, pointing to the defense secretary’s appearance in Memphis during a National Guard deployment earlier this year. He also found the animated comedy series South Park’s recent portrayal of Hegseth as a social-media obsessed brute amusingly accurate.

So while Meade said he’d keep an open mind if Hegseth ran for office, he has his doubts. “Do I care for Pete Hegseth as a person or as a leader? Not particularly,” Meade said. “I think he’s more like for show.”

World.title: What happens if AI agents start speaking their own language?
World.content:
Part of Chris Painter’s job is to help figure out what happened when AI goes rogue, then publish the results in public reports.

He and METR, the nonprofit AI research group he helps lead, have been busy lately: They helped OpenAI untangle the Hugging Face hack this year, and Painter recently testified in front of a Senate subcommittee following a string of other rogue AI incidents.

Researchers at METR pore over AI agents’ scratch pads – the “chain of thought” data that can help humans see the steps bots took before responding to a request. That information was key in METR’s investigation of the Hugging Face incident.

But Painter is worried that job could soon get a lot harder.

Humans’ ability to check up on AI agents depends on being able to communicate the way the bots communicate, in a shared language.

What happens if we stop speaking the same language?

Or what if AI agents stop showing their work entirely?

“If they’re becoming less monitorable, then they have more opportunity to kind of do things that we don’t intend,” Painter told CNN last month.

Understanding how AI models think

Many AI models — and the AI agents they power — use a method known as “chain-of-thought reasoning” that outlines their process for completing a task. Chain of thought reasoning breaks down processes into a logical sequence of steps, which can help AI models arrive at more accurate answers.

For researchers, chain-of-thought data can provide clues to what went wrong.

If an AI agent goes rogue and breaks into other systems, researchers can see whether the chain-of-thought data included mentions of deceitful actions, like hacking. METR examined roughly 1,300 raw chain-of-thought transcripts during its investigation into the OpenAI Hugging Face incident.

Painter expressed concern that paper trail may one day become unintelligible if AI models begin using their own language to track their steps.

“If that were to happen, then like when an investigator goes in, they’ll look around and it’ll all just be numbers everywhere,” he said.

AI models could use shorthand references, similar to how a human would when transcribing notes, that are intended for the model to understand so that it can work faster, according to Mark Riedl, an artificial intelligence professor and director of the machine learning lab at the Georgia Institute of Technology.

But much like most humans when looking at shorthand, it would probably look like gibberish.

Chris Painter, who helps lead the nonprofit AI research group METR, speaks during a Senate subcommittee hearing on September 30. Finn Gomez/Getty Images

There are a few theories for how the chain-of-thought process works, but researchers aren’t sure which ones are correct, says Jacob Andreas, an associate professor at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. An AI model may also decide the best way to meet the criteria it was trained for, like using less power or taking fewer steps, involves producing a chain-of-thought that doesn’t look like legible English.

That’s just one concern — another is that models are getting better at executing tasks without even logging their chain of thought. Riedl said newer models can reach the same conclusions without producing a traceable chain-of-thought.

While companies can train their models to produce a chain of thought, doing so is more expensive and slower than having the model process tasks internally.

OpenAI found that its monitoring systems would be less likely to detect when its new Astra model behaves in undesirable ways through chain-of-thought compared to older models, according to documentation from early September. It also found that Astra could accomplish more tasks without using chain-of-thought reasoning and that it was more capable of controlling its chain of thought.

The company wrote that it would lose confidence in its current systems’ ability to detect misaligned behavior – that is, when models take unsanctioned steps that don’t align with human values – if that trend continues.

Jakub Pachocki, chief scientist at OpenAI, wrote in a September blog post that AI was getting better “manipulating its own reasoning process” and that models are becoming “smarter even without using verbalized reasoning at all.”

OpenAI said in a statement last week that it’s investing “significant resources” in the ability to monitor AI models. This came after the company fired three safety and alignment researchers, though OpenAI said the dismissals were not tied to employees voicing safety concerns.

In its Astra-related documentation, OpenAI said it’s investigating why the model is more capable of controlling its chain-of-thought, along with methods for protecting against potential misalignment that could be caused by a lack of chain-of-thought.

OpenAI pointed CNN to its Astra documentation and Pachocki’s post when asked why Astra is less monitorable and whether the company plans to make future models more monitorable.

Branding for Claude Code at a conference in London on May 19. Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Trying to understanding AI under the hood

The other challenge is that chain of thought doesn’t provide the full picture of why AI models make certain decisions.

Complex tasks can require multiple agents generating thousands of words worth of logs outlining their steps, which could feel like trying to monitor a thousand people talking out loud, Riedl said. While AI could help summarize those texts, there’s been some evidence that suggests AI omits important details, he added.

Chain-of-thought data shows what an AI model did before arriving at an answer or taking an action but doesn’t reveal why. Humans can control the data and parameters that AI models are trained on, but they don’t understand how these factors may influence the way models behave.

It’s possible to look for patterns in an AI model’s neural network – a computational model often used in AI that’s meant to resemble the human brain – but it’s difficult to prescribe precise meaning to those patterns, said Andreas.

Anthropic published a research paper in July indicating that it had found small collections of neural patterns within Claude associated with certain words.

Still, that doesn’t mean Claude is saying that word.

“I think we’re still very far from being able to claim that we have any sort of fine-grained understanding of how the model is actually arriving at a solution,” MIT’s Andreas said.

AI’s rapid advancement makes this issue all the more pressing to Painter. With AI increasingly being used in AI research, he worries that information may come out faster than people are able to process it.

But he also thinks the Hugging Face saga has cast a spotlight on concerns about rogue AI that have been prominent among AI researchers for years.

“I think it has been heartening,” he said. “It really feels like people, when they were talking about this a long time ago, were underestimating how much help there would be from the whole world when the whole world is paying attention.”

World.title: Trump waives Russia-related sanctions before they even kick in as Ukraine ties worsen
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has waived a further slate of sanctions related to Russian fossil fuel sales, days before they were to take effect under a bill he signed into law last month.

The waiver announced in an executive order Friday comes as Trump increasingly feuds with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, and cracks appear in Washington’s support for Kyiv in its four-year-old war against its invading neighbor, deepening alarm among European allies.

The White House has heaped pressure on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil facilities, as it seeks to ease oil prices ahead of midterm elections at home. Ukraine briefly acceded to the request, but has since resumed attacks – and Russia has continued to pound Ukraine’s energy infrastructure throughout the week.

Zelensky condemned the move, which came as Russia carried out what he said was one of their biggest attacks on Ukrainian energy.

“At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end,” he said.

“This Act could have helped enormously – and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters.”

Despite the current tensions between Zelensky and Trump, the Ukrainian president said negotiators from the two countries talked on Friday and could meet next week. In a WhatsApp media chat with reporters on Saturday, he said details of a potential meeting were being worked out.

The latest reprieve by Trump for Moscow’s depleted coffers quickly triggered criticism from both sides of the aisle in Washington on Friday evening.

The forestalled legislation would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% on – among other things – goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, the sale of which is crucial to funding the Kremlin’s war machine.

“I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States,” Trump said in the order released by the White House on Friday.

The order did not specify why the decision served the national interest, and said the waiver will remain in effect until the Trump administration determines that “further action is appropriate.”

The measures were included in the Graham Act, legislation named after former Senator Lindsey Graham, a noted Russia hawk who died in July.

Kirill Dmitriev, head of Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, hailed the waiver in a post on X as “an important and truly historic moment,” adding that “economic cooperation between Russia and the United States serves the interest of both nations.”

US legislators, however, condemned the waiver. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren called it an “abject and predictable failure in leadership,” citing “strong bipartisan support” for Ukraine.

Republican Rep. Don Bacon said Trump “is prolonging the war, not ending it.”

In a post on X, Don Beyer, who represents Virginia in the House, said: “Trump’s latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression.”

And Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who helped draft the bill, said on X: “These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin.”

A bitter feud

The turnaround caps a turbulent week for US-Ukraine relations that has fueled concerns in Washington and Europe that Trump is taking a series of steps to actively help Putin.

Relentless attacks continue, with overnight Russian strikes targeting energy facilities across the country. The whole city of Vinnitsya was left without power, Ukraine’s energy ministry said.

Russia’s defense ministry, meanwhile, said that it intercepted 610 Ukrainian drones.

Trump blindsided European leaders last week when he struck a deal allowing Russian diesel exports – a move Zelensky said had left him feeling betrayed. The deal also drew bipartisan blowback at home.

The US president has blamed the rise in fuel prices on the Ukraine-Russia war, eager to deflect attention from his war in Iran which remains deeply unpopular with voters.

Ties between Ukraine and its most important backer the United States have also been strained by the apparent withdrawal of US intelligence sharing, and restrictions to the Starlink satellite internet service.

Earlier this week, Zelensky said his government had received “no early warning from our partners” before a deadly ballistic missile attack hit a major power plant in Kyiv and damaged a residential building. Trump, however, said the US had not stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.

And Ukrainian authorities have said they were caught off-guard by restrictions on the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink, disrupting operations of Ukraine’s drone missions and early-warning systems, and reducing the military’s capabilities for frontline logistics, communications and reconnaissance.

Zelensky said on Friday that the Starlink operations had improved but had not yet been fully restored.

Trump also lashed out at the Ukrainian leader in an interview with Newsmax on Thursday, saying: “I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.”

Rising tensions come as CNN reported that Kyiv has run out of missiles for the US-made Patriot air defense system, even as Russia continues to launch devastating air and drone strikes against Ukrainian energy plants.

The interceptors are among the few defensive weapons capable of knocking down a ballistic missile, and Zelensky has been vocal about his constant struggle to obtain more stocks.

Meanwhile, European leaders are rallying around Zelensky. In a veiled swipe at Trump on Friday, the Ukrainian president praised “real leaders” in the continent at a summit in Belgium.

European Union leaders said they were preparing a new package of sanctions against Russia – the 22nd package since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In contrast with the Trump administration, they were keen to stress that sanctions against Moscow would be strengthened unless Putin stops the war.

World.title: Russia deal, execution plans and deportations tell a defining tale about Trump and power
World.content:
Donald Trump is trying to make America more like him.

But voters will soon get to deliver a verdict on the president’s efforts to redefine how the government he leads wields power at home and abroad.

Three flashpoints illustrate how his coercive and transactional instincts are changing the character of the country and how the rest of the world sees us.

Ever since World War II, America has nurtured democracy. But by allowing Russia to supply markets with diesel, Trump will reward a ruthless authoritarian, President Vladimir Putin, who is killing scores of Ukrainian civilians as he aims to crush their independence.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream the death by firing squad of the Fort Hood mass shooter meanwhile risks putting the United States in the category of Iran, the Taliban and Hamas in carrying out public executions.

And the shooting by federal agents in New York last week of a citizen of the Dominican Republic while a 5-year-old was in the car was the government’s latest flex of violent force in public in an intensifying deportation crackdown.

Each event sparked a political backlash, and each raises questions about the unconstrained use of presidential authority and how eroded legal and behavioral standards will ultimately sit with the national conscience.

But each also directly flows from the personality of a president who made no secret of his intentions when he was twice chosen by voters in democratic elections and who represents the views of tens of millions of citizens.

The midterm elections are being dominated by high prices for food and housing, a backlash against AI data centers, and public fury over the Iran war.

But the election also marks 10 years since Trump first won power, and it will serve indirectly as an accounting of his attempts to define 21st century national greatness through a prism of his truculent and idiosyncratic values.

Growing concerns about the Russia diesel deal, a potentially livestreamed execution and Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity may hint at Trump’s eroded political clout nearly halfway through his second term.

And the shift of the electoral calendar to a presidential cycle in a few weeks will begin a debate on whether Trump’s redefinition of American exceptionalism is an aberration or whether it will linger in his image when he’s left office.

Smoke rises from an oil refinery following a Ukrainian drone attack in Moscow on June 18 in this picture obtained from social media. Social Media via Reuters

A startling deal with Russia

Trump’s deal with Putin to send diesel onto international markets is a blunt demonstration of “America First” in action and the US president’s tendency to use foreign policy to promote his political goals.

The move shatters the international sanctions regime that battered Russia’s economy after the invasion of Ukraine; delivers a huge propaganda victory to Putin; and reflects the US president’s pattern of accommodating the Kremlin strongman.

It deals a new blow to the morale of Ukrainian civilians, who are under escalating Russian attacks, including at least 33 who died when two public buses were targeted.

It opens a huge rift with NATO allies at a moment when Moscow is accused of a campaign of sabotage, harassment and airspace violations in Europe. The Dutch defense minister last week branded Russia “our enemy.”

And Trump’s demand Saturday for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky — a key Moscow condition — will renew fears that he’s siding with Kremlin war aims. Those fears were also recently exacerbated by Trump’s failure to license Kyiv to produce Patriot missiles.

But there is a logical explanation for Trump’s decision.

He’s in a political and economic bind because the cost of diesel has hit record levels, hammering US agriculture and raising food prices. Most of this is because of his war in Iran, and it is unclear whether the deal will lower prices quickly. But he had a burning domestic political imperative to do more, whatever the expense.

“It’s another example of our president thinking out of the box,” House Majority Whip Tom Emmer told ABC News’ “This Week” on Sunday. Emmer added: “Our president is trying to find every answer possible to help the American people.”

But former Vice President Mike Pence balked at easing the economic vise on Russia. “America should not be throwing a lifeline to Putin’s war machine. Now is the time to stand strong against Russian aggression as we did during the first Trump administration,” Pence wrote in a post on X.

Trump rejects the kind of hawkish, traditional Republicanism that Pence represents. The president has a narrower definition of national and personal interest: On the same day he delivered a huge win for Putin, an accused war criminal, and again warned he may destroy Iran, Trump slammed his latest Nobel Peace Prize snub as “an embarrassment” and “disgraceful.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks during an event at Sparrows Point Shipyard in Baltimore County, Maryland, on October 6. Eric Lee/Reuters

What Hegseth thinks people ‘need to understand’

Nidal Hasan is a US Army major convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder for targeting soldiers headed to Afghanistan. The question is not whether his victims deserve justice following a judicial process. It’s whether staging a public execution would infringe constitutional protections; whether it is consistent with America’s modern values; and if it would hand Hasan the martyrdom he sought.

Hegseth explained last week that the execution would be public because “people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.” The defense secretary favors the performative use of force and is contemptuous toward those who fear it violates American principles. He has, for example, defended US strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats in the Caribbean and the Pacific that have killed at least 221 people and that critics call unconstitutional extrajudicial assassinations.

A backlash could still scupper the livestream execution plan. Trump said over the weekend that he will decide whether it will happen.

But opponents worry that going ahead will stain America’s moral reputation and reward extremist groups with a propaganda triumph.

“What is he mimicking, ISIS executions?” Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy told CNN’s Erin Burnett on Thursday. “I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public executions is medieval.”

Some Republicans are also concerned. “I absolutely support the sentence of death, but livestreaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that,” said Georgia Rep. Austin Scott. And Utah Sen. John Curtis warned on X, “A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment.”

President Donald Trump is reflected in the sunglasses of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles as he speaks to the press on the South Lawn of the White House on October 5. Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

‘He was a thug’

The public use of military-style force in law enforcement and a narrative of governmental toughness also underpins the deportation crackdown. It has come with grave consequences, including the deaths of protesters Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota.

In the latest controversy, Oscar Belgal, 28, from the Dominican Republic, suffered a superficial wound to the neck when he was shot by immigration agents in the Bronx last week. His child was not physically injured. Federal authorities said officers believed that their lives were in danger. The injured man had previously pleaded guilty to fourth-degree grand larceny and received five years of probation, according to court records.

Critics see such confrontations as unacceptable examples of untamed federal government power. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the officers involved were not wearing uniforms and that ICE agents are “making the city terrified.”

But Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told CNN’s Jake Tapper on “State of the Union” on Sunday that Belgal was to blame. “The truth is this guy was an awful human being. He was a thug. He was a gangbanger,” Mullin said. He placed the blame on Belgal for putting his child at risk: “The last thing I would have done is put my son or one of my kids in danger.”

Mullin’s comments are consistent with the views of many Americans who favor stronger immigration enforcement and who responded to Trump’s searing promises to launch law and order crackdowns in his campaigns.

Yet while a majority wanted more action on the border after the Biden administration’s neglect, there are signs the aggressive tactics are a political liability. In a Pew Research poll in May, 52% said the administration was doing “too much” on deportations. Still, only 19% of Republicans thought so, underscoring that confrontations might please GOP midterm base voters.

Law enforcement gather near a damaged vehicle at the scene after a shooting reportedly involving US Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers in the Bronx borough of New York on October 8. Eduardo Munoz/Reuters

An existential question voters must answer

American history is scarred by violence and stifled justice: lynchings; the crushing of civil rights protests; internments in wartime; and foreign wars that killed thousands of innocent civilians. So Trump’s muscularity is far from the first time that government power has challenged traditional perceptions of US values.

Yet few modern presidents have been as willing to test American ideas about limited government power, the restrained use of force, international alliances and American global leadership.

Ultimately, citizens must decide at the ballot box if this is what they want.

World.title: Here’s why Moody’s has upgraded Egypt’s credit rating
World.content:
The credit rating agency Moody’s has upgraded Egypt’s long-term credit rating from Caa1 to B3, while maintaining a positive outlook.

This upgrade is supported by several factors, including the stabilization of the exchange rate against the US dollar, a sustained period of fiscal consolidation, and structural economic reforms that have successfully reduced public debt indicators.

The agency highlighted a track record of robust primary budget surpluses—which reached 4.9 percent of GDP in the 2026 fiscal year—as a key driver behind this decision.

Furthermore, efforts to mobilize revenue —combined with expenditure controls and adjustments to energy prices —have contributed to reducing total government debt to 81.8 percent of GDP as of June 2026, down from 95.2 percent three years earlier.

Economic strengthening

According to Moody’s, reforms initiated since the beginning of 2024 have also significantly strengthened the economy’s capacity to absorb exchange rate volatility.

The shift toward a flexible exchange rate regime and a tighter monetary policy has eliminated chronic foreign currency shortages, allowing official reserves to rise to US$57 billion by September 2026.

Egypt’s updated policy frameworks have shown their resilience in the face of regional geopolitical developments and rising global oil prices, preventing a sharp depletion of reserves.

Official foreign currency inflows—driven by tourism and remittances—have rebounded sharply, helping to offset the decline in Suez Canal revenues and the broader trade deficit in the hydrocarbons sector.

This continued positive outlook reflects expectations that sustained fiscal discipline could help reduce government debt and borrowing costs more rapidly than currently anticipated in the baseline scenario.

Further gains remain contingent upon potential divestments under the State Ownership Policy, as well as a prospective recovery in domestic energy production and maritime traffic.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Egypt named among 7 destinations recommended by Forbes for 2027
World.content:
Forbes magazine has included Egypt in a list of seven tourist destinations recommended for a visit in 2027, based on selections by OvationNetwork, a company specializing in luxury travel.

This recognition highlights the appeal of Egypt as a diverse tourist destination— with offerings ranging from ancient monuments to luxurious Nile cruises.

According to the report, Egypt has once again caught the attention of travelers seeking profound tourism experiences.

This is bolstered by the country’s rich array of archaeological and historical sites, as well as an expanding selection of luxury Nile cruises that connect Luxor and Aswan, offering visitors the chance to explore temples and ancient landmarks along the banks of the Nile.

The report cites a travel advisor at OvationNetwork as noting that improved political stability has brought Egypt back into the tourism spotlight—a trend bolstered by an expanding range of luxury Nile cruise offerings.

The report also recommends visiting the Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza, highlighting it as a premier cultural attraction alongside the Pyramids of Giza, which stand as an extraordinary symbol of ancient Egyptian civilization.

The list further includes the Dolomites in Italy, Lima (the capital of Peru), the coast of Montenegro, Bangkok and northern Thailand, Ireland, and Brazil’s Pantanal region—an area renowned for its ecological diversity and wildlife.

World.title: Egypt ranks 3rd in Africa for tourism in 2026 Travel & Tourism Development Index
World.content:
Egypt has secured the third position in Africa—and 63rd globally—in the 2026 Travel & Tourism Development Index, published by the World Economic Forum in collaboration with the Zurich Insurance Group, as reported by the African economic news agency “Ecofin.”

Mauritius ranked first in Africa (59th globally), followed by South Africa in second place (61st globally), with Egypt placing third.

The index does not directly measure the number of tourists, the volume of spending, or tourism-related revenue.

It instead assesses the environment that enables countries to attract tourism and develop it sustainably, as well as their capacity to provide the conditions necessary for the sector’s growth.

The index covers 110 countries and is based on 102 sub-indicators—categorized into five key dimensions—that encompass security and stability, infrastructure and air transport, policies and visa regulations, price competitiveness, digital services, tourism resources, and sustainability.

While Egypt’s achievement of the third-place ranking in Africa is significant, the results also highlight areas for improvement—specifically regarding the quality of services, the streamlining of procedures, the expansion of hotel capacity, the enhancement of the tourist experience, and the strengthening of sustainability and air connectivity.

Egypt’s true challenge lies in transforming substantial assets into greater outcomes—namely, higher tourist numbers, increased average spending, and longer stays—thereby propelling the country toward a more prominent global standing.

World.title: Air Cairo extends suspension of flights to Riyadh until Tuesday
World.content:
Air Cairo announced the continued suspension of all flights to King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh—departing from Cairo, Assiut, and Sohag—until Tuesday, October 20, pending the resumption of normal airport operations.

The airline explained in a statement that this decision was made in coordination with the civil aviation authorities of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, in light of temporary operational measures affecting air traffic to and from the airport.

Air Cairo said that it is closely monitoring developments and advises customers with bookings for Riyadh-bound flights to contact the airline or their travel agent for the latest information regarding their reservations, and to stay updated through the company’s official announcements.
