World.title: CCPC urged to intensify sensitisation campaigns
World.content:
Mwine Lubemba Chitimukulu of the Bemba people has called on the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) to intensify sensitization campaigns on consumer rights.

Speaking when officials from the Commission paid a courtesy call on him at his palace in Mungwi District, the Mwine Lubemba, Chitimukulu says many consumers continue to suffer violations of their rights due to limited awareness.

The traditional leader has expressed concern that a number of people are unaware of the mechanisms available for seeking redress when they are unfairly treated by traders.

“A lot of people have suffered because they do not know their rights, some have been denied justice simply because they do not know where to report their complaints,” he said.

The Mwine Lubemba noted that many consumers fail to receive compensation when they purchase defective products or encounter unfair business practices because they lack information on procedures to follow.

He urged the Commission to strengthen its outreach programmes and make greater use of radio stations to reach communities with consumer protection messages.

“Make use of radio stations to sensitize the community. We are not benefiting in any way when people continue to be suppressed of their rights because they do not know where to seek help,” Mwine Lubemba Chitimukulu said.

And Northern Province Competition and Consumer Protection Commission Investigator, Milner Kazembe, has pledged the Commission’s continued commitment to enhancing public awareness on consumer rights and responsibilities.

Mr Kazembe said the Commission has rolled out various community engagement programmes aimed at ensuring that consumers are equipped with knowledge that enables them to make informed purchasing decisions.

“We are doing everything possible to scale up sensitization across the country so that members of the public understand their rights whenever they purchase goods and services,” he said.

He added that traditional leaders are critical partners in the commission’s awareness programmes because of their influence within communities.

“Traditional leaders look after large sections of the population, making them important stakeholders in disseminating information on consumer rights and protection, the Commission will continue to engage and work together to ensure communities are made aware of their rights and responsibilities, ” Mr Kazembe said.

And Competition and Consumer Protection Commission Kasama Office Investigator, Samson Musonda, has advised consumers to exercise caution when purchasing products by carefully checking all details before making payments.

Mr Musonda has urged consumers to carefully check details on products before they make payments and has stressed the need for consumers to obtain and keep receipts for all purchases.

“Consumers should always ensure they collect receipts after buying products because receipts serve as important evidence when lodging complaints or seeking compensation,” he said.

He further encouraged members of the public to promptly report cases of unfair trading practices to the Commission.

World.title: K1.5 million Solwezi Water Treatment Plant Weir progresses
World.content:
Construction of the K1.5 million Weir at the Solwezi Main Water Treatment Plant has reached 80 percent completion.

The project is being implemented by the Northwestern Water Supply and Sanitation Company Limited with funding from the Ministry of Water Development and Sanitation.

Company Manager for Corporate Planning, James Phiri, told the media in Solwezi today that the project is expected to be complete by the end of October 2026.

Mr Phiri says the project which started in October last year is aimed at improving raw water availability for the water supply system especially during the dry season.

” Construction works resumed in July 2026 following delays caused by unfavorable weather conditions. With concrete casting works completed and overall progress standing at 80 percent, the company is undertaking the remaining activities to meet the targeted completion date,” Mr Phiri said.

He said the project involves the construction of a weir on the Solwezi river to raise and maintain water levels at the abstraction point, supporting reliable supply of raw water to the company’s main water treatment plant.

Mr Phiri says the weir is a critical investment in strengthening the reliability of water supply in Solwezi as the main treatment plant depends on the Solwezi river as a key source of raw water.

“By improving water levels at the abstraction point, the infrastructure is expected to enhance raw water abstraction, support the efficient operation of pumping equipment and strengthen the Company’s capacity to meet customer demand,” he said.

Mr Phiri said upon completion, the project is expected to benefit an estimated population of over 40,000 people by improving raw water security and supporting more reliable water supply services.

He said the Solwezi Weir project demonstrates the water utility’s commitment to strengthening critical water supply infrastructure, improving operational efficiency and enhancing service reliability to meet the growing water needs of Solwezi.

World.title: Nigeria: Nigeria's Hunger Crisis Takes an Emotional Toll on Caregivers #WorldFoodDay
World.content:
Fatima Ibrahimâs 23-month-old daughter, Aisha, was admitted to the Nilefa Kiji nutrition facility in Maiduguri after battling meningitis and repeated convulsions. The three weeks spent in hospital were filled with conflicting emotions. While grateful to see her daughter improve, Fatima could not stop thinking about the eight children she had left at home.

As millions of people across northern Nigeria face severe food insecurity, children continue to bear the consequences of a deepening malnutrition crisis. But the impact is far beyond the children in treatment. This can be a source of significant anxiety, exhaustion, and emotional distress for parents and caregivers, particularly those who spend weeks in the hospital when a child is severely malnourished and are concerned about starving children at home.

The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) estimates that 34.7 million people in Nigeria are in crisis levels of food insecurity during the lean season, while more than 5.4 million children are acutely malnourished. In northern Nigeria in 2025, MSF teams provided treatment to 425,634 children who were suffering from acute malnutrition.

The food crisis has particularly affected Nigeria's northeastern states of Borno, Adamawa and Yobe. It is estimated that by 2026 nearly 5.8 million people will be severely food insecure. In Borno State, conflicts, climate shocks and displacement are interfering with people's means of livelihood and damaging local food production, putting about 15,000 people at risk of suffering from catastrophic hunger.

The World Food Programme (WFP) has warned that ongoing insecurity is worsening hunger by forcing communities to flee their homes, preventing farmers from accessing their land and restricting the delivery of humanitarian assistance.

Monica Genya, Association Director at Doctors Without Borders (MSF) Southern Africa, described the "situation as critical," with medical teams treating children suffering from severe acute malnutrition and related illnesses.

In MSF nutrition facilities such as Nilefa Kiji in Maiduguri, she said, teams see intensive care units full of children fighting severe acute malnutrition. Many arrive severely wasted, and because malnutrition weakens their immunity, many also have illnesses such as measles, diphtheria and malaria, she said.

"It is severe, and it is life-threatening for many children," said Genya.

In 2025, MSF treated 353,989 children for severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and 90,723 for moderate acute malnutrition (MAM). She said that SAM is the most dangerous form that continues to claim young lives in the region. Children are severely wasted, and their immune systems are weakened. Some arrive at treatment facilities already suffering from diseases such as measles, diphtheria and malaria. Treatment can last anywhere from a week to more than a month, leaving caregivers facing prolonged separation from the rest of their families.

Genya said MSF treated 41.8 per cent more children for acute malnutrition in 2025 than in the previous year, reflecting a worsening crisis. Admissions have risen steadily since 2022, driven by insecurity, displacement, food shortages, disease outbreaks, economic hardship and cuts to humanitarian funding.

"These pressures compound one another, so more families are pushed to the edge each year," she said.

The rising number of children requiring treatment also raises questions about whether humanitarian resources are keeping pace with the need. MSF supports the state Ministries of Health in Zamfara, Katsina, Kebbi, Borno, Bauchi, Sokoto and Kano.

Abba Adamu Musa/MSF Inside a ward of MSFâs facility, Nilefa Kiji, in Maiduguri, Borno State, northeast Nigeria. Here, MSF provides care for children suffering from malnutrition.

Supporting caregivers as part of treatment

Genya said that the emotional burden carried by caregivers is often overlooked in discussions about child malnutrition, where attention tends to focus on medical treatment, admissions and recovery rates.

"Medical statistics capture admissions and recovery rates, but they cannot measure the emotional burden carried by the person at the bedside, who is most often the mother," she said. Caregivers endure fear, anxiety, guilt, uncertainty and emotional exhaustion, and some develop symptoms of depression."

The consequences extend beyond their own wellbeing. This matters for the child's recovery too. A caregiver's emotional wellbeing influences how engaged they stay in treatment, whether they follow medical advice and how well they can care for the child after discharge.

"Caring for the caregiver is part of caring for the child," she said.

The competing demands on caregivers are evident in the experiences MSF counsellors encounter at its nutrition facilities in northern Nigeria. "Caregivers are pulled in two directions," said Genya. "Many arrive with a critically ill child while having left other children at home, sometimes with no one to look after them and little to eat."

Their worry does not stop when treatment begins. Genya recalled the experience of a mother in Maiduguri.

"One mother in Maiduguri told us she had left eight children at home, and when she heard one had a fever and there was no money for treatment, she cried and could not eat. Another was asked by her eldest son when she was coming home, because the children were hungry without her," she said. In another case, counsellors met a mother of six who had to leave the hospital because her husband had left the children with neighbours and she could not bear to stay.

"These stories show how guilt, worry and separation can put a child's treatment at risk, which is why we listen and respond," she said.

Recognising the emotional toll of malnutrition, MSF incorporates mental health and psychosocial support into its nutrition programmes.

At Nilefa Kiji, caregivers receive psychological first aid on arrival, followed by individual counselling and group sessions where they can share experiences, express their fears and learn coping strategies. Caregiver education helps families understand and manage the emotional and behavioural challenges that can arise during and after treatment. Children take part in structured play activities that help restore a sense of normalcy during recovery.

"The support is also practical," she said.

Counsellors help distressed caregivers reach relatives by phone, and in some cases supervised home visits let a caregiver briefly check on their family before returning to finish their child's treatment. She said that this helps caregivers cope, builds their confidence, supports treatment adherence and contributes to better recovery. "Many regain hope as they watch their children get better, and some come back after discharge just to show how healthy their children have become," said Genya.

Beyond treating malnutrition

For MSF, addressing the crisis requires more than treating children after they have become severely malnourished. Families must also be reached earlier, before food insecurity and other pressures push children into life-threatening conditions.

Abba Adamu Musa/MSF MSF counsellor-educator Keturah John engages Adamaâs daughter, Fatima, in a play therapy session at MSFâs facility, Nilefa Kiji, in Maiduguri, Borno State, northeast Nigeria. Fatima is an inpatient and has been receiving treatment for malnutrition.

"Treating children once they are already severely malnourished saves lives, but we also need to reach families before they get to that point," she said.

Insecurity and displacement, disease outbreaks and economic hardship continue to undermine families' ability to provide adequate food and care. Genya said prevention and treatment must go hand in hand, alongside support for caregivers who bear much of the responsibility for children's recovery.

She added that the pressures pushing children into malnutrition, including insecurity and displacement, food insecurity, disease outbreaks and the economic crisis, are not easing. Sustained funding is needed not only for nutrition services but also for mental health and psychosocial support, she said. Governments and humanitarian organisations must work to ensure families can access essential assistance before children reach the point of severe malnutrition.

"This is why MSF's work focuses on both prevention and treatment, and why we care for the whole family, including the caregivers at the bedside, through counselling and psychosocial support. This work depends on public support," she said. "Donating to MSF's humanitarian efforts helps our teams keep reaching children across northern Nigeria, treating them early and supporting the families who care for them."

With over 5.4 million children acutely malnourished this year, every contribution makes a difference, she said.

As the world marks World Food Day, the experiences of families in northern Nigeria underline the need to recognise the human cost of food insecurity beyond the physical effects of hunger.

Genya said that addressing the crisis requires supporting caregivers alongside treating children. She said that there is a need to support caregivers through mental health and psychosocial services. She said that behind every child in our facilities is a caregiver, most often a mother, living with fear, anxiety, guilt and exhaustion. Many are worried sick about children left at home without enough food. Their emotional wellbeing shapes whether they can stay engaged in treatment, follow medical advice and keep caring for their child after discharge.

"Recognising and supporting caregivers is therefore key to ending this crisis, not a side issue," she said.

She urged donors to reconsider humanitarian funding cuts and sustain investment in nutrition care, including mental health and psychosocial support, to ensure children and their caregivers receive the help they need. "Behind every statistic is a caregiver's mental health impacted by malnutrition," said Genya.

The fear of losing a sick child, combined with guilt over being separated from other family members, can take a significant toll on their mental well-being. "A mother sits at a hospital bedside, grateful that her child is improving, while worrying that her other children at home have nothing to eat. She is afraid of losing the child in front of her, and guilty about those she can't be with," she said. "These are people showing extraordinary resilience under immense strain, and their stories rarely get told."

"Healing is not only about restoring a child's weight," said Genya. "It is also about restoring hope and resilience to the person who sits at the bedside every day."

World.title: Nigeria: Aircraft Loses Door Mid-Air, Makes Emergency Landing in Abuja
World.content:
The aircraft, a CL60 with registration number T7-SEI and flight identification DWC052, was departing Abuja for the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos, when the incident occurred.

An aircraft operated by Triton Aviation made an emergency landing at the Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport, Abuja, on Thursday after its crew reported that a door had opened mid-air shortly after take-off.

The aircraft, a CL60 with registration number T7-SEI and flight identification DWC052, was departing Abuja for the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos, when the incident occurred.

According to a serious incident report, the aircraft took off from Runway 22 at 4:17 p.m. Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) and, about three nautical miles from the airport, was climbing at 3,000 feet when the crew issued a distress call at 4:20 p.m.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The crew reported an open door in flight, prompting air traffic controllers to direct the aircraft back to Abuja for an emergency landing.

Airport fire and rescue personnel and the medical team were subsequently alerted and placed on standby in preparation for the aircraft's return.

The incident report stated that at about 4:29 p.m. UTC, the crew asked the Abuja control tower to confirm whether the door was open.

The duty air traffic controller attempted to observe the aircraft with binoculars but could not establish the door's condition because of the aircraft's position.

The crew was informed that the controller could not visually confirm the situation.

The aircraft landed safely on Runway 22 at approximately 4:34 p.m. UTC, about 14 minutes after the Mayday call.

After landing, the controller observed that the aircraft's door was missing from the fuselage.

The aircraft was subsequently taxied to the international apron extension, where it was parked with the assistance of a marshaller.

Meanwhile, a video circulating on social media appears to show the aircraft's missing door. In the footage, an unidentified man said some farmers found the door while returning from their farm in the Abuja area.

He suggested that it had fallen from an aircraft but did not provide further details about the discovery. The circumstances surrounding the reported discovery have not been independently verified as of the time of filing this report.

The cause of the incident and the circumstances surrounding the door's detachment have not been established.

The number of people on board is also not immediately available.

The Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau (NSIB) confirmed that the incident occurred and said investigators have been deployed.

"Yes, it happened. The investigators are there. We will be releasing an official statement shortly," the bureau's media team said.

Close 

The Director of Public Affairs and Consumer Protection at the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA), Michael Achimugu, also confirmed the incident but said the NSIB has jurisdiction.

However, Triton Aviation could not be reached for comment when this report was filed.

World.title: South Africa: Lions Player Dies From Suspected Cardiac Arrest in French Hotel
World.content:
A Lions player has apparently died in a hotel room in France, where the South African team has been preparing for the Champions Cup debut against La Rochelle.

French media are reporting that a Lions player has died in a hotel room on the Île de Ré, where the South African team has been preparing for the Champions Cup debut against La Rochelle.

Île de Ré is an island off the western coast of France, and connected via a bridge to the mainland city of La Rochelle.

According to media reports in France, the player was found unresponsive in a shower cubicle.

Paramedics attempted to resuscitate him but were unsuccessful. He was pronounced dead. The player, in his thirties, was in cardiac arrest when emergency services arrived shortly before 10.30am.

Sources have independently confirmed the news to Daily Maverick, but the player's family have yet to be informed, so his name cannot be released.

It is unclear at this stage whether the Champions Cup match against two-time champions La Rochelle will go ahead, originally scheduled for Saturday, 17 October 2026. DM

World.title: America's softest generation isn't the kids — it's their parents
World.content:
The biggest babies at a girls' flag football tournament in Revere, Massachusetts, weren't the girls. They were the grown men running the game.

A coach and referee got into a fight in front of children who had come to play football, not watch two adults lose their tempers. Both men later apologized, but what kind of example were they setting?

We hear plenty about how soft kids have become. They can't handle losing, expect trophies for showing up and need constant praise. But as a psychotherapist, I wonder whether we've been blaming the wrong people. Maybe the problem isn't that children can't handle disappointment. Maybe it's that their parents can't stand watching them experience it.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Spend a Saturday at a youth sporting event and you'll see parents screaming at referees and treating a missed call like a personal insult. A father tells his son to stop making excuses after striking out, then berates the umpire.

A mother tells her daughter to be a good sport, then complains that the coach didn't give her enough playing time. These are often the same people complaining that America is raising a generation of wimps. Yet the moment a referee makes a call they don't like, they behave like toddlers.

A parent who would punish his child for screaming at a teacher may have no problem screaming at a referee. He sees nothing wrong with it because he believes he's standing up for his kid. But defending your child doesn't give you a free pass to behave like a bully.

YOUTH FOOTBALL COACHES FIGHTING & ACTING LIKE FOOLS IN PENNSYLVANIA ISN'T THE LEAST BIT SHOCKING

For some parents, their child's athletic success has become tied to their own self-esteem.

When the child wins, they feel successful. When the child loses, they feel embarrassed. A father who never made varsity may see his son's benching as another personal rejection. The child is playing a game, but the parent is still trying to settle something from 25 years ago.

Your child's athletic career isn't a second chance at your own. If you didn't make varsity in high school, screaming at your son's Little League coach isn't going to change that.

Youth sports have become an expensive business.

Families spend thousands on travel teams, private lessons and tournaments. Some start talking about college scholarships before their children are even teenagers. After all that investment, parents can begin to feel they're owed something. If their child isn't starting, the coach must be playing favorites. If the team loses, someone must be incompetent. Sometimes your kid just isn't that good. Sometimes he has a lousy game. Sometimes the other team is better. That's sports, and arguing with the coach won't change it.

We've gotten so used to treating children's disappointment as something that needs fixing that ordinary setbacks have become emergencies. Losing isn't a crisis. Sitting on the bench isn't trauma. A coach telling your kid he needs to improve isn't abuse. Yet some parents respond as though their children have suffered a serious injustice.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

A child who gets benched may be upset for an hour or two. He complains on the ride home, and moves on. His father, meanwhile, is still angry three days later, replaying the coach's decisions. The kid who struck out has forgotten about it. Dad is still furious on Tuesday.

These parents are depriving their children of some of the most useful experiences sports can provide. Kids need to learn that trying hard doesn't guarantee winning, that someone else may be better and that unfair things sometimes happen. They need to figure out what to do when they're disappointed rather than expect an adult to intervene.

I've seen adults struggle with this same habit. They get passed over for a promotion and assume the boss has something against them. They receive criticism and spend days complaining about how unfairly they've been treated. They devote more energy to proving somebody else was wrong than considering what they might do differently.

Of course, parents should intervene when a coach is abusive or a child is genuinely being mistreated. But not making the starting lineup isn't mistreatment. Neither is losing a game or being told to practice more. There's a difference between protecting children from harm and protecting them from disappointment.

Which brings us back to Massachusetts. Whatever prompted the disagreement, two adults at a children's football tournament ended up fighting in front of the players. Had one of the girls behaved that way, she probably would have been removed from the game. Instead, the adults were the ones who needed to be separated.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Those girls showed up to play football. Instead, they watched two grown men make fools of themselves. Maybe the next time we complain that kids today can't handle disappointment, we should look at the adults standing on the sidelines. If your child's Little League game can ruin your entire weekend, your child isn't the one who needs to grow up.

World.title: Three men get 158 years each for murdering American and Australian surfers, dumping bodies in Mexican well
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Three men in Mexico received 158-year prison sentences Friday for the murders of Australian surfers Callum and Jake Robinson and their American friend Carter Redd Rhoad.

A federal judge in the town of Ensenada, Baja California sentenced Jesús Gerardo García, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús each to 158 years and nine months in prison for murder, robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.

An accomplice of García's — Ary Gisell Silva Raya — was also convicted of aggravated robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence and sentenced to 20 years in November after agreeing to an abbreviated trial.

AMERICANS WARNED POPULAR TRAVEL ROUTES THIS SUMMER COULD CARRY CRIME AND KIDNAPPING RISKS

García, Francisco and Jesús were convicted last week of killing the Robinson brothers and Rhoad, which authorities said was carried out in order to steal the tires from the deceased men's truck.

"The attackers pull out a gun they were carrying and kill the person who initially resisted the robbery, then on the other two," Baja California prosecutor María Elena Andrade said, according to a report from The Associated Press.

THREE WOMEN FOUND DEAD IN POPULAR AMERICAN TOURIST HOT SPOT AS LOCAL POLICE SEARCH FOR CLUES

Mexican authorities found the trio's bodies in a well in the state of Baja California in May 2024.

The three men traveled to Punta San José, about 50 miles from where their bodies were found in Ensenada, for a surfing trip in April 2024.

MEXICAN SPORTS JOURNALIST ROBBED AT GUNPOINT DURING LIVE REPORT

The parents of the Robinsons attended the sentencing, telling reporters the moment marked a significant conclusion to the tragic two years since their sons' deaths.

"Today’s guilty verdict is a significant moment in our long and painful journey to seek justice for our beautiful sons, Callum and Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad, whose lives were so cruelly taken from them in 2024," Matin Robinson said.

POPULAR CRUISE LINE'S GIANT BEACH PARK BLOCKED BY MEXICO AFTER LOCAL BACKLASH ERUPTS

The deaths captured international attention and rocked the local economy, which authorities said was heavily reliant on tourism.

Antonio Otañez, president of the Baja California surfers association, said he was happy to see justice served but admitted the incident led to a "major drop" in tourism.

"I always recognize he's the president of the United States, he does what he thinks is good for the United States. And that's exactly what he does. I do the same for Israel," Netanyahu said. "And I'm glad that it often, very often, this meshes."

TRUMP WELCOMES NETANYAHU TO WHITE HOUSE AS RAGING IRAN WAR THREATENS TO SOUR US-ISRAEL RELATIONSHIP

"Aside from the fact it's fun being with him, I mean, I don't know. Most people don't know that he has a wicked sense of humor. I mean, he can be very funny and very warm. And so, I treasure this relationship," he added.

'BIBI'S HAIR ON FIRE': TRUMP-NETANYAHU PUBLIC 'RIFT' MASKED UNIFIED FRONT AGAINST IRAN, ANALYST SAYS

World.title: Former US ambassador says South Korea prosecuted him over speech made on American soil
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A former U.S. diplomat appeared in court in South Korea Friday facing charges of defamation against President Lee Jae Myung for comments made on American soil in a case that has left him stranded in the Asian country.

Morse Tan's troubles began after he delivered a talk in June 2025 at the National Press Club in Washington, D.C., and responded to a question where he brought up the South Korean leader's alleged involvement in a crime as an adolescent.

Since visiting the country in May, Tan has not been allowed to leave due to the case against him, having been charged under the Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc., and the Criminal Act.

Tan issued his remarks about Lee’s alleged juvenile crimes at a National Press Club event titled: "Report on Election Fraud in the June 3 South Korean Presidential election." In response to a question about President Lee and other issues, Tan responded by citing allegations from a few years back that Lee was involved in a gang rape and murder when he was a teenager. He added that Lee, now 62, was sent to a juvenile detention center and did not complete junior high and high school.

SOUTH KOREAN PRESIDENT JUMPS TO INVEST IN MILITARY AFTER TRUMP CUTS JOINT EXERCISES

South Korean prosecutors say the criminal allegations against Lee are unsubstantiated, according to the Korea JoongAng Daily. The outlet wrote that they said Lee had not "been prevented from attending middle or high school due to such a criminal record."

Another South Korean news outlet, KBS World reported that "the prosecution previously verified that there was no record of Lee’s being incarcerated at a juvenile detention center and concluded that the rumors about his incarceration were false."

Asia Business Daily reported that Tan's attorney said that "Even if jurisdiction is recognized, the statements did not present false information, and Tan was not aware that they were false," adding, "He had no intention to defame."

Tan told Fox News Digital on Friday that he "pleaded not guilty because I believe that Lee Jae Myung is guilty" during his hearing at the Seoul Central District Court.

OVER 50 HOUSE MEMBERS ACCUSE SOUTH KOREA'S NEW LEFT-WING GOVERNMENT OF ATTACKING US COMPANIES, FAVORING CHINA

Tan, who has taught constitutional law and served as the dean of Liberty University’s law school, told Fox News Digital his "protected speech is about as protected as it gets." He said South Korea’s prosecutor invoked "criminal defamation, a dubious category which does not exist in the U.S.," to prosecute him.

A spokesperson for the South Korean Embassy in Washington, D.C. told Fox News Digital, "This case is being handled in accordance with the relevant laws and regulations, established principles and due process in the Republic of Korea and the restriction on departure is also imposed and reviewed accordingly."

Tan says he is disappointed that the U.S. Ambassador to South Korea, Michelle Steel, a former Republican congresswoman from California, has not publicly commented on Tan’s legal case — both Steel and Tan are Korean-Americans.

A U.S. State Department spokesperson declined to comment on the specifics of the case.

"The Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "Due to privacy and other considerations, we have nothing further to share at this time."

Tan said the case against him violated his due process rights, and the South Korean judicial system lacks jurisdiction to bring the case. He added that the second charge against him involves his July 2025 talk in South Korea, where he "raised some issues as questions" involving the president. "This is political lawfare. This is a persecution, not a prosecution," he said.

TRUMP SHOULD PRESS XI ON CHINA’S PERSECUTION OF BELIEVERS AT HOME AND ABROAD

Tan believes the motivation for seeking to criminalize his free speech stems from the South Korean government’s view of him as a "threat" and an outspoken critic of Lee’s alleged appeasement policy toward the North Korean communist regime.

"People consider me to be leading a movement against the communizing of South Korea," Tan said.

Tan accused the present government of being aligned with North Korean and Chinese communist regimes "against the U.S. and the Korean people."

Tan points to bias against him by South Korean authorities, who he says prohibited him from attending the funeral of his grandmother, while it allows South Korean prisoners to attend funerals for family members.

KBS World reported that the "Police, who had initially decided not to hand over Tan’s case to the prosecution, launched a reinvestigation at the prosecution’s request."

World.title: Here's some tips on how to organize photos with keywords on your phone
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Your phone probably holds thousands of pictures. Some are important family memories, while others are screenshots you saved because you thought you might need them later. Then comes the frustrating part. You remember taking a particular photo, but finding it feels like searching for a needle in a digital haystack.

Apple's iOS 27 offers a way to make that search easier by letting you add keywords to individual photos. Instead of scrolling through months of pictures, you can search for a word you've assigned to a photo and pull it up again.

Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel users have similar ways to organize their pictures, although the tools work differently. Here's how to take advantage of them and spend less time hunting for photos.

Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com.

YOUR PHONE CAN FIX BADLY FRAMED PHOTOS AFTER YOU TAKE THEM

How to add keywords to photos on iPhone

Apple's Photos app can already recognize people, pets, places and objects. However, automatic searches don't always understand why a particular photo is important to you. That's where manually assigned keywords can help.

For example, you might photograph a parking spot at an airport or save a picture of a particular appliance model number. Adding a keyword you will remember later can make the photo much easier to find.

Add keywords to photos in iOS 27

These instructions are based on an iPhone 15 Pro running iOS 27.

Open the Photos app on your iPhone.

Find and open the photo you want to organize.

Tap the Info (ⓘ) icon or swipe up on the photo.

Tap Add Keywords.

Enter the keyword or keywords you want to associate with the picture.

Tap the checkmark icon to save your changes.

If you want to edit or add more keywords later, you can tap Edit .

Choose words that make sense to you. For example, a picture of your car's license plate might get a keyword such as "license plate." You could also tag pictures from a family vacation with a memorable trip name.

How to find photos using keywords on iPhone

Once you've added keywords, searching for those pictures takes only a few seconds.

Open the Photos app.

Tap the Search icon, which looks like a magnifying glass.

Type one of the keywords you previously added.

Look for a suggested search result with the Aa symbol.

Tap that result to see photos and videos associated with the keyword.

You can also manage your keywords by opening Photos > Collections > your profile icon > Manage Keywords. From there, you can rename keywords, delete them or add frequently used keywords to your favorites.

Pro tip: Start with photos you actually struggle to find. Important documents, appliance labels and travel information are useful candidates. There's no need to spend an entire weekend tagging your photo library.

How to organize photos on Samsung Galaxy

Samsung Galaxy phones also let you add tags to pictures using the built-in Gallery app. That means you can assign your own keywords and search for them later, much like you can on an iPhone. Depending on your Galaxy model and Gallery version, the exact location of the tagging controls may vary. However, Samsung supports manual photo tagging on compatible devices.

Add tags to photos on Samsung Galaxy

Here's how to tag a picture using Samsung Gallery.

Open the Gallery app.

Select the photo you want to organize.

Swipe up on the photo to open its details, or tap the Details icon (ⓘ) if it appears at the bottom of the screen.

Select Add tag.

Enter a keyword or phrase that describes the picture.

Tap Save.

On some Galaxy versions, you may need to tap Edit in the photo's details to add a tag. If you don't see the option, make sure your Gallery app is updated.

How to find tagged photos on Samsung Galaxy

Once you've tagged a photo, you can use the Gallery's search feature to find it again.

Open the Gallery app.

Tap the Search icon.

Enter the tag you assigned to the photo.

Select the matching picture from the search results.

For example, you could tag pictures of your home appliances with their model names. Later, when you need a serial number or replacement part, you can search for the tag instead of scrolling through your entire camera roll.

Create an album on Samsung Galaxy

Albums offer another way to keep related pictures together, especially when you want to organize several photos from the same event or project.

Open Gallery.

Tap Albums.

Tap the plus (+) icon or the option to create a new album.

Choose Create album or Album if prompted.

Give your album a descriptive name.

Tap Create.

Select the photos you want to add.

Tap Done.

If prompted with "Copy or move items?", choose Move to move the photos into the new album or Copy to create duplicates in the new album.

For example, you could create an album for home repairs and keep pictures of paint colors, appliance labels and receipts in one place.

Pro tip: If you regularly photograph product labels or serial numbers, keep them together in an album called "Home information." You'll appreciate having those pictures handy when something breaks.

HOW TO SAVE A VIDEO FRAME AS A PHOTO ON YOUR PHONE

How to organize photos on Google Pixel

Google Pixel phones take a different approach. Instead of relying on manually assigned keywords, Google Photos uses automatic recognition to help you find pictures based on what's in them. For example, you can search for "dog," "beach" or "receipt" and Google Photos may find relevant pictures without requiring you to tag them first. You can also create albums to organize pictures you want to keep together.

How to find photos using Google Photos

Google Photos can recognize many objects, places and other details in your pictures. Here's how to use its built-in search feature.

Open the Google Photos app.

Tap Search at the bottom of the screen.

Enter a word describing what you're looking for , such as receipt , dog or beach .

Browse the matching pictures.

Google Photos can often identify objects and locations without requiring you to manually label every picture. However, results depend on what the app can recognize, so you may need to try a different search term if your first attempt doesn't find the right photo.

How to create albums on Google Pixel

If you prefer organizing pictures yourself, albums offer a straightforward way to group related photos.

Open Google Photos.

Touch and hold a photo, then select any additional pictures you want to organize.

Tap Add to album.

Create a new album.

Enter a descriptive album name.

Tap Done.

To find your albums later, open Google Photos > Collections > Albums.

You can create albums for vacations, family events or important household information. That way, pictures you frequently need are grouped together instead of scattered throughout your photo library.

Find receipts and documents in Google Photos

Google Photos also offers a useful feature for organizing certain documents automatically. On supported versions, backed-up pictures of receipts and other paperwork may appear in a dedicated Documents collection.

To check, open Google Photos > Collections > Documents. If Google Photos recognizes documents in your backed-up pictures, you may find them organized into categories.

This can be particularly helpful when you're trying to locate a receipt or another document you photographed months ago.

Pro tip: Try searching Google Photos before creating dozens of albums. You may discover that it already recognizes much of what you're looking for.

Smart ways to organize photos without wasting hours

You don't need a complicated system to keep your pictures under control. In fact, a few consistent habits can make a bigger difference than spending hours organizing every image you've ever taken.

Start with photos you know you'll need again. Travel confirmations and warranty information are good candidates. Then choose simple names that you'll remember when searching.

Avoid overly specific labels that might be difficult to recall months later. For example, "kitchen repair" will probably be easier to remember than the exact date you photographed a broken dishwasher.

Also, remember that photo organization doesn't replace a backup. Important pictures should be protected through a trusted cloud backup service or another reliable backup method. And if you're photographing sensitive information, think carefully about whether you want those pictures stored in a cloud account.

STOP LOSING PHOTO QUALITY WHEN YOU SHARE PICTURES

Kurt's key takeaways

I've lost count of how many times I've taken a photo specifically so I wouldn't forget something, only to spend several minutes trying to find it later. A simple keyword or well-named album can solve a surprisingly annoying problem. What I like about Apple's approach is the ability to assign a word that means something to you. Your phone might recognize a picture of a car, but it doesn't necessarily know that you took it because you needed to remember where you parked. Samsung Galaxy users can take advantage of manual tags, too, while Google Pixel owners have powerful automatic search tools built into Google Photos. My advice is to start small. Organize the pictures you'll actually need again, and let your phone's built-in search handle the rest.

Would you rather have your phone automatically analyze every picture to make it searchable, or would you prefer more control over how your personal photos are labeled and organized? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

There are a couple of anti-aircraft guns and part of the USS Indiana, including the mast, sitting outside Memorial Stadium on the campus of Indiana University in Bloomington.

It’s all a tribute to the men and women from Indiana who have served in the armed forces of the United States.

As No. 5 Indiana, the defending national champion, hosts No. 4 Ohio State in a Big Ten college football mega-tilt on Saturday at Memorial Stadium, OutKick's Game of the Week, the connection between sporting events on campus and the military is undeniable.

THE CIGNETTI EFFECT IS REAL: INDIANA FOOTBALL SPARKS AN UNBELIEVABLE 'REVIVAL' IN BLOOMINGTON

The importance of the military every single day at Indiana University is also undeniable.

"IU definitely has an upper echelon of military history, and they do really treat their military personnel with a lot of respect," said Vasiliios Koultourides, a senior at Indiana and a member of the Indiana National Guard. "They do really care about us. "

EXCLUSIVE: NEW AMERICA 250 MONUMENT LETS FAMILIES FIND MILITARY RELATIVES IN SECONDS: 'I HAD TEARS IN MY EYES'

And Indiana University cares about its military history, not just by displaying relics outside the football stadium, but by chronicling the military service of every single person with ties to the university with a cherished, one-of-a-kind piece of history carefully and respectfully housed inside the school’s Memorial Student Union on campus.

The Golden Book at Indiana has its own hallowed room there. Dating back to 1898, the book is now a fragile specimen, protected in a clear plastic box that still allows for viewing.

A GENERATION CANNOT REMEMBER 9/11. WE HAVE A DUTY TO MAKE SURE THEY LEARN

The Indiana Daily Student began the initiative to document military service by IU students and staff by publishing a list of those who served in the Spanish-American War. Next was an effort to compile a list of those who had served in the Civil War.

According to Indiana University’s website, each of the 152 pages of the book "lists the names of veterans as well as donors to IU’s Memorial Fund, which sponsored the construction of three buildings on campus in honor of those men and women: Memorial Hall, Indiana Memorial Union, and Memorial Stadium.

UNIVERSITIES ACROSS AMERICA HONOR THE VICTIMS OF THE 9/11 TERRORIST ATTACKS WITH MEMORIAL STAIR CLIMBS

"Inside the book, carefully written by hand, are the names of IU alumni who served in the War of 1812, the Black Hawk War, the Mexican War, the Civil War, the Spanish-American War, the Philippine Insurrection, the Mexican Border Expedition, World War I, and World War II."

In 2016, Indiana University began a digital version of the Golden Book and now more than 25,000 names are listed.

‘THEIR SOULS ARE IN THAT STEEL’: 9/11 BEAM MAKES EMOTIONAL STOP IN INDIANAPOLIS BEFORE RETURN TO NYC

"I just think it's the coolest thing ever, and I think it's so unique," said Indiana student Zainab Diouf, who is a member of the Indiana National Guard. "No other school has that, so I think it's such a cool thing, and I really encourage if you're here at IU to go see it."

Koultourides certainly remembers the first time he saw the book. He was touring the Indiana campus while still in high school. The Golden Book mesmerized him.

VAN HIPP: WHY THE ARMY SHOULD RESTORE ITS GRASSROOTS LINK TO AMERICA'S COMMUNITIES

"I was like, whoa, I’ve never seen anything like this before. It's like a little chapel kind of, but I remember walking up to the book and just looking at it, and that's when it kind of hit me like, oh, this is a memorial for everyone that's ever been (in the military). It’s amazing to see how they've kept such in-depth records about these people's lives and service. It means a lot to know that you're not forgotten, and you'll forever be there and remembered. It's really cool to see."

"The Center for Veterans and Military Students is awesome," Koultourides said." It's a nice area where you can sit, study, and then also meet individuals that are just like you who have shared experiences. Which is really important for a lot of people who have gone and actually deployed, and they come back to school."

Elsewhere on campus, Indiana’s military members are treated with equal importance.

World.title: College Football Playoff expansion is just the latest example of why 'growing the game' isn't always healthy
World.content:
"Grow the game."

It's a phrase you hear quite often on social media these days, particularly with more "niche" sports like hockey or golf.

Just this past week, a different sport has made yet another attempt to "grow the game," as college football announced it will be expanding its playoff from 12 to 24 teams sometime in the near future.

Plenty has been written on why this is a bad idea, mostly with regard to destroying what was once the greatest and most consequential regular season in sports, and while I share those sentiments, I'm looking to attack this from a different angle.

This isn't even the first time college football has attempted to "grow the game" and appeal to a wider audience.

HERE'S WHY THE COACHES ASSOCIATION'S 24-TEAM COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF COULD RUIN THE SPORT

The College Football Playoff, since its very inception, was created in part to appease those who cried that the BCS was an unfair and antiquated system.

So we went to a four-game model, then a 12-game model, and now that 12 isn't enough, we have moved to 24.

CFP, NCAA TOURNAMENT EXPANSION BOTH DRAW BACKLASH, BUT ONE IS DEFINITIVELY WORSE THAN THE OTHER

Surely, that's the end of it, right?

If 24 is good, is 32 better? Where is the limiting principle?

And it's not just the Playoff, either.

Conference expansion and realignment, as well as an unfettered transfer portal, has college football looking more and more like the NFL by the day, and that's by design.

SEC, BIG TEN ARE DOMINATING COLLEGE FOOTBALL THANKS TO MASSIVE ADVANTAGES OVER OTHER CONFERENCES

One of the biggest arguments I've seen in favor of the expanded CFP is that the NFL has a certain percentage of its teams make the postseason, and that a 24-team model will have those numbers look closer to the NFL.

With all due respect, if I wanted to watch the NFL, I'd just watch the NFL.

HERE'S WHY, EVEN WITH ALL ITS PROBLEMS, COLLEGE FOOTBALL IS STILL BETTER THAN THE NFL

Can we stop trying to turn college football into something that "everyone" wants to watch?

Because you're not just appealing to a wider audience, you're appealing to a lowest common denominator as a result.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

College football was never the most popular sport in America, but it was certainly the most beloved.

Fans were insanely passionate and regionally focused, and the game reflected that.

The folks who "didn't get it" were more than welcome to tune out.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

I understand from a money perspective why college football is trying to "grow the game," and my colleague Trey Wallace wrote a great piece about that, but sacrificing the will of loyal fans for the almighty dollar is unhealthy for the sport long term.

I mentioned the NHL trying to "grow the game," and while that has gotten them slightly more exposure, it's also attracted fans who read "Heated Rivalry" with pronouns and "Free Palestine" in their social media bio.

College football isn't for everyone. It never was.



So stop trying to include the ones who weren't on board from the start.

If you like the NFL, that's great. But let us enjoy our Saturday religion while you enjoy your Sunday corporate clash.

World.title: John Goodman admits he felt 'frightened' after the  sudden fame he experienced from 'Roseanne'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

John Goodman is getting real about the downside of starring in one of the biggest sitcoms of all time.

During a conversation with the SAG-AFTRA Foundation, the 74-year-old actor admitted he was "frightened" by the level of fame he achieved following his starring role in "Roseanne" and other projects.

When asked what his biggest pitfalls were that he wished he would have foreseen, he replied he wished he would have understood fame better.

"I wish I would have taken to it better," he said. "I didn't. I was frightened … I'm my own worst enemy, by far."

ROSEANNE BARR HASN’T SPOKEN TO TV SISTER LAURIE METCALF SINCE SHOW’S CANCELLATION

Earlier in the conversation with interviewer Joe Neumaier, Goodman was asked about the way his career picked up in the late ‘80s and early '90s, and how he shifted from being a more independent actor to being a celebrity.

"It changed ,'" he said. "That's when I was told, ‘You better get a publicist and get a hold of this stuff.’ And I just … I had a bad time dealing with how famous I got all of a sudden, and just [said], ‘Well, that ain’t me.'"

He added, "It took a long time to deal with it, so I got that out of the way. But just the negotiations you have to go through, the things you have to do to sell a film, they're not ideal, but they need to be done. People put a lot of money into these things, and let's help each other out and get this done. They have a job to do, and you have to support it."

At another point in the interview, Goodman shared he agreed to do "Roseanne" "to quit living out of a suitcase," adding that he "hit it off with [Roseanne Barr] immediately, to the point where, and not in an arrogant way, I just knew when I left that I had the job."

"Roseanne" aired on ABC for nine seasons from 1988 to 1997, releasing 222 episodes in its first run and winning four Emmy Awards.

"At the time, the hot shows in television were all wealth porn, like 'Dynasty,' 'Dallas,' stuff like that. And we were sober reality," he said. "Rose said something early on that 'just because we're poor doesn't make us stupid.' And the reason that family stayed together was because of laughter and obvious love. And I think that showed on the screen in a real way."

Following his time on "Roseanne," Goodman starred in many successful movies, including "The Flintstones," "The Big Lebowski," "Monsters Inc." and others, before returning to the role of Dan Conner in the "Roseanne" reboot in 2018.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

While successful, the reboot only lasted one season, as it was quickly canceled after Barr made a racist statement on social media in reference to President Barak Obama's senior advisor, Valerie Jarrett.

Just a few weeks later, ABC announced that the show's cast would be returning for a new spin-off, "The Conners," without Barr. The show aired for 112 episodes from 2018 to 2025, with Goodman filming that and "The Righteous Gemstones" at the same time.

"I didn’t think [the 'Roseanne' reboot] was going to go beyond the initial five or six episodes. I thought it’d be a one-off thing, and then we got picked up, and Roseanne got fired," he told The Hollywood Reporter in July 2025. "I thought that was it, and as soon as they dismissed the cast, I picked up 'Righteous Gemstones.' Then we got to do the show again as 'The Conners.' I didn’t know how long it would last, but I sure enjoyed it while I was there."

When speaking to the outlet, he also shared that he and Barr had not spoken "for about seven or eight years" at the time, adding "I’d rather doubt if she wants to talk to me."

Barr told listeners of her podcast, "The Roseanne Barr Podcast," in March that she felt "betrayed" by Goodman due to his decision to scale back his appearances on the show in the later seasons.

"I don't think I heard it from his agent, I think I heard it from the producers of the show actually [that] he doesn't want to be on the show anymore," she explained. "I think they said he'll do six of the 24 or something like that."

World.title: Oregon school shooting victims include 5-year-old whose family is ‘broken and lost’
World.content:
The victims killed in a special needs classroom at an Oregon elementary school Thursday included a 5-year-old boy whose family said they are “broken and lost” after the shooting and a young teacher working her “dream job.”

The shooting occurred at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend. Officials said an armed bystander fatally shot the teen gunman, putting an end to the shooting spree.

“A school should be a safe place where children can learn and feel secure. What happened today should never happen,” Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler said Thursday.

Rhoam Summer, a 5-year-old with long, curly hair, was identified as one of the victims by a family member.

Rhoam Summer. Swan Amity

Rhoam’s mother, Kelik Summer, posted to a Facebook group last night, saying Thursday was “the worst day of my life. My son Rhoam was killed in a school shooting.”

“We are broken and lost, but are surrounded by friends and family who are keeping us safe,” Summer wrote.

Officials did not identify the other slain children, ages 8 and 11, at the request of their families.

Rhoam’s family said they are “broken and lost” after the shooting. Swan Amity

Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said that when officers arrived, two boys and a teacher were dead at the scene. Officers and medics attempted lifesaving care on another boy, he said.

A 7-year-old injured in the shooting was stabilized in serious condition at a hospital, Krantz said. Another teacher, Becky Drury, 54, had “serious but non-life-threatening injuries,” police said.

Megan Lambert, 25, a central Oregon native and Boise State University graduate. Bend Police Dept.

The family of the teacher killed in the attack identified her on Friday as Megan Lambert, 25, a central Oregon native and Boise State University graduate who dedicated her life to both teaching and coaching girls in the Central Oregon Volleyball Club.

She was a substitute teacher before getting her position as a full-time teacher, the family said in a statement read during an afternoon news conference.

“She loved Silver Rail,” the family said. “This was her dream job.”

She also loved volleyball and rejected a salary during her first year as a coach so girls whose families couldn’t afford the costs of participating could play, the family said.

“She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs,” it said.

Rebecca Drury was injured in the shooting. Bend Police Dept.

In a statement, Drury’s husband thanked people for their support.

“The kindness and concern shown to our family and everyone affected mean more than we can express,” her husband wrote.

“Right now, our focus is on my wife, Becky, and her recovery, and on supporting our family through an unimaginably difficult time,” he wrote. “We respectfully ask for privacy and space as we navigate the days ahead.”

The attack began just before 1 p.m. Thursday, police said, as the shooter scaled a perimeter fence at the school, shot at and breached a set of double doors, and entered Lambert’s special needs classroom, where he opened fire.

Krantz said another teacher, who was not named, threw a cellphone at the shooter during the attack and tackled him. “She almost certainly help prevent more bloodshed,” he said. That teacher was uninjured.

The bystander who shot the attacker entered a classroom in which a teacher and the gunman were in the middle of a physical altercation, Krantz said.

The shooter had been a special needs student at the school, Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said at the news conference. A possible motive remained under investigation.

Kaylub Giamanco. via Facebook

Kyle Giamanco identified the person who took down the gunman as his brother, Kaylub Giamanco, 36, a father of two children who attend the elementary school.

Kaylub Giamanco is a hero, his brother told NBC News, but doesn’t feel like one. He can’t get the children out of his head and feels guilty he didn’t save more people, Kyle Giamanco said.

Kyle Giamanco also said he is friends with the family of the 7-year-old child who is in the hospital. The child, who is in a wheelchair and was shot in the face, is recovering from surgery.

World.title: Pope Leo discharged from hospital after lung cancer surgery
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV was discharged from the hospital on Saturday after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, with his surgeon saying he could be fully recovered in about 10 days.

Dr. Stefano Margaritora told Vatican News there were “no clinical reasons” preventing the pontiff from making his planned trip to Latin America next month.

The pontiff, who had been recovering at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital since Tuesday, walked out unaided before spending a couple of minutes speaking with well-wishers. He appeared to accept a gift of a homemade smiling Pope figure before getting in a car and being driven back to the Vatican.

“Following the conclusions reached by the medical team this morning, Pope Leo XIV will be discharged today from Gemelli Polyclinic Hospital, where he was admitted for surgery on his right lung,” the Holy See Press said Saturday in a statement, before the Leo left the building mid-afternoon.

He is expected to recite the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment at St. Peter’s Basilica on Sunday, according to the statement.

The pontiff’s personal doctor, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and Margaritora, said that in light of blood tests and a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning, and after an assessment of his clinical condition, “the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge from the hospital.”

So far, Leo’s doctors have given no indication that the pontiff might need any further treatment. And the Vatican has not indicated whether the cancer might have spread.

Leo, who is a Chicago native, resumed working from the hospital on Thursday, his doctors and the Vatican reported.

Pope Leo XIV leaves the Gemelli University Hospital on Saturday. Tiziana Fabi / AFP via Getty

The Vatican on Friday released the first images of Leo since his surgery, showing him celebrating Mass inside the hospital, as doctors said that tests confirmed the “continued improvement” in his recovery.

The photos show Leo standing up at the altar in green vestments celebrating Mass in a makeshift chapel that has been set up for him. Spokesman Matteo Bruni said he presided alone over the liturgy, distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present and delivered a homily.

His discharge from the hospital comes less than a month before Leo is scheduled to jet off for a two-week trip to South America, which is set to start Nov. 11.

Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, in an interview on Peruvian television, said the pace of the pope’s recovery could determine whether Leo makes his weeklong apostolic visit to Peru.

“I want the pope to know that here in Peru, millions of us are praying for his speedy recovery,” Fujimori said Wednesday.

A drawing of Pope Leo XIV at the statue of John Paul II outside the Gemelli University Hospital, where Pope Leo XIV is recovering after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung. Alberto Pizzoli / AFP via Getty

Leo was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer, after doctors examined the nodule they had removed from his right lung.

Non-small cell lung cancer accounts for 80% of all cases of the disease, according to the American Lung Association.

This type of cancer affects both smokers and nonsmokers, although Leo is not known to ever have been a smoker.

The initial lump was detected during a routine check, the Vatican has said. The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics took the rare step of revealing the health issue — the first of his papacy — during his Sunday noon prayer last week.

Leo waved to crowds outside Rome’s Gemelli Hospital as he entered Tuesday.

As Margaritora led the procedure, Gemelli’s medical staff recited the rosary prayer in the hospital chapel.

World.title: 71-year-old man dies after alligator attack while fishing in Florida, police say
World.content:
A 71-year-old man died after an alligator attacked him while he was fishing, authorities said on Friday.

Steven Hamilton was fishing at Dr. Bradford Memorial Park in Winter Garden, Florida — a city about 15 miles west of Orlando — when he was bitten by an alligator, according to a statement from the Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation Commission.

Responding emergency personnel relayed reports that witnesses had seen someone possibly grabbed by an alligator and pulled into the water, according to a recording radio traffic. He was pronounced dead at the scene, the FWC said.

The Winter Garden Police Department confirmed the incident in a statement, adding that FWC authorities trapped and killed the roughly 12-foot-long alligator.

The FWC said that “serious injuries caused by alligators are rare in Florida.”

In June, a 31-year-old woman died after an alligator bit off one of her arms and mauled the other at nearby Little Big Econ State Forest.

“Always be aware of your surroundings. Always be safe,” Winter Garden police Capt. Michael Mason told reporters, according to NBC affiliate WESH 2 News. “Local wildlife, respect it, keep your distance. It looks like it’s docile, it looks like your Florida emblem, but it can be dangerous.”

Mason encouraged witnesses of the incident to reach out to authorities.

World.title: ‘The house was toast’: Surf swallows California homes
World.content:
LONG BEACH, Calif. — It was 3:30 a.m. on Oct. 9 and the unthinkable was happening all around Shawn Curtis: The boardwalk in front of his two-story beachfront apartment building was gone. The 25-foot-wide sand beach was gone. Salt water poured in from all sides. And now the building was slanting down into the ocean.

Curtis couldn’t make sense of what he saw. “The doorframe was crooked. The window was crooked, and then I saw a big wave crash,” he told NBC News on Thursday.

The surf crashed all the way up to the second floor. Neighbors across the street said they could see water cascading down onto the roof of Curtis’ home of nine years. Booming waves were loud enough to wake him and shake his apartment as though an earthquake rippled through, he said.
