World.title: Egypt's Ssisi says he'll defend Saudi Arabia, if asked
World.content:
The Egyptian president said his country was ready to defend Saudi Arabia "if requested." The comments come amid escalating Houthi attacks.

Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sissi on Saturday said that his country stood ready to defend Saudi Arabia, if asked to so.

Sissi said that while Egypt was "not looking for a role to play" in regional conflicts, it was "inconceivable that we would allow Saudi Arabia, ⁠its security ⁠or stability to be harmed."

The comments came as Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have ramped up attacks on Saudi targets, including strikes on energy facilities and Riyadh's main airport.

'We are speaking only about defense,' says Sisi

"Egypt, of course, with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, will carry out any measure to protect you or defend you," Sissi said at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian military academy.

"I'm not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone," Sissi said. "We are speaking only about defense."

"I know this ​requires the approval of the Egyptian parliament, and I ask that an emergency session be held so that it can give us that ⁠authorization ​if we are asked," the Egyptian leader said.

An emergency session in Egypt's parliament is expected to be held on Sunday to consider whether to authorise potentially assisting in Saudi Arabia's defence.

Saudi Arabia on the backfoot in the war against the Houthis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Houthi-Saudi conflict

The Houthis have clashed with Saudi Arabia since the kingdom stepped into Yemen's civil war to lead a military coalition against the Iran-backed fighters in 2015.

The Houthis have launched repeated attacks against Saudi Arabia, also attacking the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

A week ago, one of those attacks killed 13 people in what was the deadliest in the country in over a decade.

Egypt and Saudi Arabia share strong strategic and economic ties. Egypt was part of the Saudi-led coalition that stepped in 2015 to support the Yemeni government against the Houthis.

Disruption in the Red Sea as a result of Houthi attacks has impacted the revenue coming from shipping traffic in the Suez Canal.

World.title: West Bank: Israeli settlers attack EU diplomats, French mayor
World.content:
A group of Israeli settlers attacked vehicles carrying European diplomats in the West Bank. Belgium has condemned the attack.

Belgium's Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said on Saturday that masked settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank had attacked Palestinians, Catholic representatives, and Western diplomats and officials.

Prevot said that the Belgian consul general and French and Polish diplomats, as well as a French mayor, were among those attacked.

In a post on X, he condemned "in the strongest terms" the attack in which a Belgian vehicle was also damaged.

Israeli police said they have opened an investigation into the alleged assault of diplomats in the occupied West Bank.

In a separate statement, the Israeli military said the visit was not coordinated with them and there were no soldiers present.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office reacted to the incident by criticizing an alleged a "smear" campaign against settlers.

"These reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge," his office said in a statement, using the biblical name for the West Bank.

What do we know about the incident

According to witnesses, cars from the French, Belgian, and Polish embassies had brought diplomats to visit Taybeh, a predominantly Christian village in the occupied West Bank.

Settlers then descended on the area to prevent Palestinians from gathering olives.

Masked men reportedly surrounded a diplomatic vehicle with their off-road vehicles, then demanded identification and smashed a window.

A witness and two diplomats also told the AFP new agency that the settlers beat up Bernard Baudoux, the 78-year-old leftist mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, a town in northern France.



West Bank olive harvest under attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

French mayor says attackers were 'completely enraged'

Badoux told AFP that he was fine, having suffered minor injuries, but he expressed concern about the residents in the area.

"The whole world needs to know what's happening there," Badoux said.

Badoux said he was visiting Taybeh with the French consul general in Jerusalem, along with a priest from his home parish, to sign a goodwill cooperation agreement with his city, which has an olive emblem.

The mayor, who was wearing a sash in the French tricolour, said that the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground.

"It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged."

"It's absolutely incredible that settlers can behave like this," he said. "I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government," he added.

Israel FM condemns 'rioters'

In a rare statement critical of settlers, which was released before Netanyahu's statement, Israel's foreign minister condemned the attack by Israeli "rioters" on the European diplomatic delegation in the West Bank.

"I strongly condemn the severe acts of violence by Israeli rioters in the area of Taybeh," said Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, who also faulted the diplomats for not coordinating with the Israeli military.

The West Bank has experienced an especially violent olive harvest season this year. Israeli settlers have tried to stop Palestinians from harvesting their crops by using physical force.

Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine was injured on Friday when she was attacked by a group of Israeli settlers while reporting in the occupied West Bank.

This violence is occurring during the final days of the election campaign. In hopes of gaining their support in the upcoming election, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has championed the cause of the settlers.

World.title: How big is Russia's threat against Germany?
World.content:
Experts believe that, so far, Germany has been ill-prepared — both militarily and mentally — for Russian provocations. They also warn against the idea that ending support for Ukraine would make Germany safer.

Warnings keep mounting about Russia's threat to Germany. On October 12, Sinan Selen, president of Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, said that Russia's covert attacks and destabilization efforts against Germany and other European countries are "not a temporary development but a long-term hybrid attack."

Even if the war in Ukraine were to end, said Selen, the Russian threat would not disappear. "For Russia, this is about completely redrawing the map of Europe and redefining its own role within Europe and in global politics."

He added that Russia's aggression would continue to be felt not only in Ukraine, but also in the Baltic states, in Poland and in Germany.

Russia is tied down in Ukraine — for now

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has described the threat situation as one in which "our country is not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare." Russia's goal, he said, is not to defeat Germany militarily "but to subdue us politically and socially."

Security experts, however, are not so sure that Russia is only interested in exercising political and social influence. Last year, political scientist Carlo Masala told the political talk show Maischberger that "Russia is preparing for a major war." And he didn't mean just a cyberwar. Inspector General Carsten Breuer, the Bundeswehr's highest-ranking officer, agreed.

For now, though, Russia remains tied up in its war against Ukraine. According to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, there is no immediate military threat to NATO territory. But according to military experts, European intelligence agencies, and the German Defense Ministry, Russia will have the personnel and equipment to wage a conventional war against NATO by 2029. The Russian defense industry is running at full speed, and Moscow plans to expand its armed forces to 1.5 million soldiers.

At the moment, Russia has other objectives, believes Stefan Meister, an expert on Eastern Europe at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP): "I don't think Russia has any interest in a direct military conflict with NATO right now. It wants to test NATO and also display its capabilities," he tells DW.

If Russia attacked NATO, would Germany be prepared? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An accidental military confrontation?

An example of Russia's hybrid war might be the failed attack with an explosive-laden drone against a Ukrainian transport aircraft at Leipzig-Halle Airport in August. Soon after, the German government stated that it was certain Russia was behind the attack.

Security expert Nico Lange told DW at the time that Germany was very lucky the explosives did not detonate: "Honestly, it was pure coincidence and not the result of German defensive measures."

As for why Germany was targeted specifically, Lange said: "I believe that Germany has always been a primary target of Russian influence and hybrid warfare. Russia believes that Germany is the key to European decision-making. Germany is now leading the way in supporting Ukraine."

Moscow swiftly responded to the German government's accusation with an angry denial. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said it was "the beginning of a real war," though there was no immediate further escalation.

Nevertheless, there is always the risk that things could spiral out of control following a Russian provocation and subsequent response, according to Stefan Meister: "Accidentally shooting down an aircraft that they were trying to intimidate would trigger a counter-reaction. But I don't believe that Russia is currently aiming for a direct war but rather for provocations, polarization, and sowing uncertainty among the population."

AfD says less money for Ukraine means more for Germany

Not everyone shares the assessment that Russia poses a threat to Germany — some believe that the threat can be averted.

Despite the war in Ukraine, politicians from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the populist left-wing Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) want to improve relations with Russia, resume Russian energy supplies and end support for Ukraine.

AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said in early September, "People are fed up with this escalation against Russia, with the billions being squandered there on a system that is actually funded by German taxpayers' money."

The message appears to have resonated among the population, especially in eastern Germany. The AfD saw strong gains in all three state elections in September. In Saxony-Anhalt, it became the strongest party by far and may even run the government there soon, which would be the first time that a far-right party has held power in Germany since the end of WWII.

The CDU's security policy expert Roderich Kiesewetter disputed the claim made by the AfD and BSW that ending aid to Ukraine would mean greater security and more money for German schools and infrastructure: "Spending on education, social policy, and infrastructure is only possible if we live in freedom and democracy — and, above all, in peace and security. Anyone who believes that we'll have more money for social programs if we stop supporting Ukraine and let Russia have its way is either gravely mistaken or is making themselves a tool of Russian propaganda."

German high school students have gone on strike to protest plans to reintroduce military conscription Image: Snowfield Photography/picture alliance

A decades-long pacifist mindset

The perceived security threat has led the German military, the Bundeswehr, to fast-track significant modernization through substantial investment. But it is struggling to find enough recruits for its planned expansion. Many young Germans have taken to the streets to protest against plans to reintroduce conscription. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius faced criticism from inside his own party, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), for saying that Germany must become "capable of waging war." Many found the statement to be too militaristic.

Is Germany prepared for a military threat? "Not at all. Germany is not well prepared militarily or in the civilian sector, and the population isn't mentally prepared for it either," said Meister. "Just look at the demonstrations against conscription and the military that continue to take place, even though Germany needs a draft. For decades, we've grown up in this culture of pacifism, in a comfort zone. I believe there is very limited societal resilience, but above all, we are not at all mentally prepared for war."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) are under increasing political pressure — especially from the far right — to scale back support for Ukraine. But Merz never tires of emphasizing that Ukraine will continue to receive support under his chancellorship, calling it a matter of Germany's security. He recently visited Kyiv once again and, together with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, surveyed the destruction caused by Russia.

But this also means that the threat from Russia will continue and even intensify, says Stefan Meister: "I believe we will see a massive increase in attacks such as the one in Leipzig, of provocations involving drones. We will see attacks on infrastructures and possibly also on specific individuals within the military-industrial complex. I believe this is the real, concrete danger facing Germany in the coming months."

This article was translated from German.

World.title: China's influence in the gaming industry is growing
World.content:
Home to more than 700 million gamers, China is the world's largest gaming market — but it's also one of the most tightly regulated. The effects reach far beyond China, impacting players around the world.

In a dark underground hideout, dim light spills from a handful of oil lamps. A comrade fiddles with a rifle. A red flag hangs on one of the roughly hewn stone walls, bearing a hammer and sickle on a white star — the symbol of the ChineseWorkers' and Peasants' Red Army. Weapons are scattered on the ground. One is picked up, and soon the action moves into the snowy forest, where gunfire erupts among the trees.

Such a scene could fit in a new installment of "Call of Duty," the popular first-person shooter game that transports players to battlefields past, present, and future. But it is actually from "The Defiant." The game is currently being developed by the Chinese studio Hoothanes Technology in Hangzhou. It tells the story of Chinese forces fending off the Japanese army in the 1930s and 1940s.

Developer Connor Xu tells DW the weapons featured in the game are unique. They were used only in Asia and are therefore unfamiliar to many Western players, he says. The same goes for the story, which Xu says has never before been told in a video game.

Game developer Connor Xu wants to tell stories from Chinese history Image: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

"The Defiant" is also designed to appeal to an international audience. In just a few years, China has emerged as a major player in the global gaming industry despite strict regulations, censorship and a former ban on video game consoles.

Gaming is part of everyday life in China

More than 700 million people in China regularly play video games. According to market research company Newzoo, most consider gaming an important part of their lives. Many use games to stay in touch with friends.

"Games make life more interesting," developer Xu says. "I can try different roles, different stories, different characters, because we only have one life to live, but we can play a role in another story. That's really attractive, I think, to Chinese users."

'Honor of Kings' is largely unknown outside China, but it's one of the country's most popular games Image: Tencent/Level Infinite/TiMi Studio Group

People in China primarily play games on PCs and smartphones, while consoles are much less common. There are historical reasons for that: While gamers in Europe and North America debated whether PlayStation or Xbox was the better console in the early 2000s, the devices were not officially sold in China between 2000 and 2014. Chinese authorities said the restrictions were intended to protect children and teenagers from becoming addicted to gaming.

Limits on gaming time and extensive controls

Minors in China are currently allowed to play online games for no more than three hours a week. There are no such limits for adults, but gaming is subject to strict controls. Anyone who wants to play must register using their real name and a personal identification number. That effectively allows the state to track who plays what and when, as well as whom they communicate with.

There is also a gray area that the Chinese government appears to tolerate. Some players log in using VPNs, giving them access to games that are not officially available in China. Some younger players use their parents' accounts to get around the limits on gaming time.

The Chinese role-playing game "Genshin Impact" bears visual and gameplay similarities to "The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild" Image: Cognosphere/miHoYo/HoYoverse

Despite its strict controls on underage gamers, China has become increasingly receptive to video games in general, having recognized the industry's enormous economic potential. Early on, games released for Chinese players often appeared to be copies of Western titles. At the same time, Chinese tech companies such as Tencent and NetEase invested in numerous Western gaming companies.

No license? No sales in China

One distinctive feature of the Chinese market is its licensing system. "Unlike a lot of the other big video games markets in the world, China has a tightly regulated and licensed official video games market," George E. Osborn tells DW. The journalist advises NGOs and governments on video games and spoke at the Gamescom congress. In his book "Power Play," he describes how authoritarian states use video games to pursue political objectives.

The strategy game 'Heroes of Might and Magic III Remake' is currently being developed by Ubisoft's studios in Chengdu and Shanghai Image: Ubisoft

The rule for all games in China is simple: No license, no sales. "That system essentially forces developers who want to release their video games to go through multiple layers of approval from China's Ministry of Propaganda, Ministry of Culture," Osborn says.

Strict criteria for video games

Games are prohibited from containing material that threatens China's unity, sovereignty or territorial integrity, among other restrictions. Pornographic content and gambling are also banned. Games may not incite crimes that threaten national security or spread information authorities believe could disrupt public order.

"The whole point around this criteria is that it's deliberately designed to be pretty vague," Osborn says. Whether a game violates the rules is a matter of interpretation. Sometimes games are altered even after release. In the 2025 action role-playing game "Wuchang: Fallen Feathers," for example, enemies based on famous Chinese figures from the Ming Dynasty suddenly could no longer be killed. Instead, they would collapse from exhaustion.

Chinese culture is an international hit

The Chinese action role-playing game "Black Myth: Wukong" became an unexpected international hit in 2024. By then, it was clear Chinese developers could do more than cater to the domestic market — they could create successful games for a global audience as well. The game was inspired by the 16th-century Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West."

The video game 'Black Myth: Wukong' became an international hit Image: Game Science Interactive Technology Co

Osborn sees nothing wrong with bringing Chinese culture to audiences around the world. The question, he says, is how much the state actually intervenes in the games themselves. "I think in general, video game players are actually quite deeply skeptical of these kinds of things. They are generally very good at spotting when someone might be selling to them or someone might be propagandizing. And so I think if it's too obvious, it won't work," he says.

The problem of self-censorship

Because of the licensing system, Western developers also have to comply with government requirements if they want to sell their games in China. And they do want to, Osborn says, because the market is too big to ignore. "But I think when you start thinking about the potential impact this has on creative standards around the world, I think it's really important that developers ask themselves the question of what will we or won't we compromise on here?"

He fears the real danger lies in self-censorship. That could lead developers, for example, to leave queer characters out of their games. That would represent a major step backward, he says, because games help many people explore their identities.

China is not the only country where games are modified to comply with national regulations. In Germany, for example, symbols that violate the country's constitution, such as the swastika, may not be shown in games unless the game in question explicitly contributes to the country's culture of remembrance. Depictions of extreme violence also have to be removed from German versions.

History from a Chinese perspective

Glorifying violence is prohibited in China, too, yet Xu's team is still allowed to develop a war game. How does this add up? Xu explains it this way: "I think in this game, the most important thing is not violence. The most important thing is to tell history."

Xu says the team is committed to delivering a historically accurate product. Whether it succeeds will be for historians to judge.

This article was translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal.

World.title: Pope Leo leaves hospital after cancer surgery
World.content:
Four days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo left the hospital in Rome. His doctors said he was well enough to return home.

Pope Leo XIV left the Gemelli hospital in Rome on Saturday afternoon. He returned to the Vatican four days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.

The 71-year-old pope walked unaided to his car and stopped to speak with well-wishers outside the hospital.

"I am better, thank you," Leo XIV said as he was driven away in a black SUV. Leo XIV entered the Vatican ten minutes after leaving the hospital.

After conducting blood tests and imaging scans of his chest, the pope's doctors said he was well enough to return home.

Currently, Leo is undergoing physiotherapy to help him breathe more easily.

What to know about Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What do we know about the Pope's health?

On Tuesday, Leo XIV had the lower lobe of his right lung removed after doctors identified a nodule suspected to be cancerous. The surgery confirmed that he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

The doctors said his surgery was successful and complication-free. However, they have not yet disclosed the size of the tumor or if the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes. These factors are key in determining the prognosis.

The diagnosis of the relatively young and energetic pontiff, elected in May 2025, came as a shock. It raised questions about the future of his papacy as he deals with the illness.

On Sunday, Leo is expected to lead weekly prayers with pilgrims in St. Peter's Square at noon (10:00 a.m. GMT), which will be his first public engagement since his surgery.

Skip next section Supreme Court says access to internet fundamental right for children, calls blanket bans 'disproportionate'

10/17/2026 October 17, 2026 Supreme Court says access to internet fundamental right for children, calls blanket bans 'disproportionate'

India's top court declared that access to and use of the internet is a fundamental right of every individual, including children, legal news outlet LiveLaw reported Saturday.

It said that a blanket ban on children's internet activity could make them vulnerable to greater risks rather than protect them from online abuse and exploitation.

The Supreme Court also issued directions to bolster the processes for detecting and removing child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) from social media and other online platforms, the report said.

The court stressed that the right to freedom of speech and expression also incorporates the right to know, receive and impart information and ideas, LiveLaw reported.

The two-judge bench described the internet as a "marketplace of ideas, creative expression and information" and said that its value went beyond the material it contains, as it provides opportunities for children in remote areas and those with disabilities.

"For many children, particularly in remote areas, it is often the only source of learning and information," the court said, according to LiveLaw.

For children with special needs, the internet is often the only platform where they can find company with others like them, the court said.

The court acknowledged that the internet, in its current form, poses safety risks to children. But it said that keeping children away from the internet because of failures by platforms and the relevant authorities to detect and remove harmful content would amount to mistaking the victim for the problem, LiveLaw reported.

What did the court say on blanket restrictions on internet use for children?

The Supreme Court said that a legal ban would not stop children from using the internet, and that they could move to other unregulated platforms.

"Any blanket restriction on the access of internet by children is nothing more than unproven measures of proven disproportionality," LiveLaw cited the court as saying.

The Supreme Court called for safeguards to ensure online child safety and the regulation of content accessible to children.

It suggested measures such as a "child mode" for social media accounts, LiveLaw said.

Saturday's Supreme Court judgement comes amid a global debate on the ban of social media for children over risks from harmful content. Australia declared the world's first social media ban for under-16s last year.

France followed suit this summer, before its Constitutional Court blocked the move.

World.title: Russia wants blackout in Ukraine as winter comes — Zelenskyy
World.content:
Ukrainian President Zelenskyy says Russia is trying to cut electricity and heating to civilians ahead of winter. He also called the US president's waiver of new sanctions on Moscow a boost for Vladimir Putin.

Russia is stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in a bid to cut electricity and heating in the country as winter approaches, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday.

His remarks come as Moscow intensifies its attacks on civilian targets in the capital, Kyiv, and elsewhere, with key observers saying its objective is to render the country virtually unlivable.

Overnight strikes on Zaporizhzhia killed a 64-year-old man Image: Daria Nazarova/AFP

What did Zelenskyy say?

In a post on social media platform X, Zelenskyy said Russia had just carried out one of its biggest attacks on Ukraine's energy sector since it began its full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.

"More than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities were targeted across different regions of Ukraine," he wrote.

"Restoration work is ongoing, with all necessary services and all available resources of Ukrainian energy companies involved," he added.

Zelenskyy said that Russia was planning to leave Ukrainian citizens in the cold this winter.

"Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine — right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating," he wrote, calling on allies to put pressure on Moscow to stop this happening.

He said Russia had "expanded ‌its campaign ​against the energy system" and was trying "to stretch ⁠Ukraine's ​reserves ​and repair ​capacity as ‌thinly as possible." ​

Russia claims multiple infrastructure attacks

The Russian Defense Ministry, for its part, said on Saturday that its forces had attacked several infrastructure targets in Ukraine overnight.

Among those named was an electricity substation in the northwestern city of Zhytomyr.

However, it also said Ukraine's largest steelworks, in the city of Kryvyi Rih, had been hit, saying the facility supplied steel products to the Ukrainian military-industrial complex.

It said another steel plant in ​Zaporizhzhia, a city near the front ​line, had also been struck.

Ukrainian authorities have also said that one person — an ambulance driver — was killed ​and ‌19 others injured, including a child, in a Russian airstrike on Kherson in southern Ukraine.

Russian state news ​agency TASS has also reported the death of one woman as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes in Russia's Belgorod region that also injured a man.

Russia's overnight attacks hit numerous civilian sites Image: REUTERS

Trump's sanctions waiver a boost for Putin: Zelenskyy

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy also reacted to US President Donald Trump's decision to waive a package of new sanctions on Moscow, saying the move would only encourage Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

"A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking," Zelenskyy said.

On Friday, Trump signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia's energy revenues, two days before they were due to take effect.

The waiver has been hailed by a Russian presidential envoy as a "historic moment."

"The Trump administration's suspension of the [Lindsey] Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev said on social media.

Dmitriev said the act, named for the late US senator who sponsored the bill, "would have caused "serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets."

Trump's move came as he increasingly criticizes Zelenskyy, fueling speculation that the US leader is siding with Moscow in the conflict.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: El regreso de los ‘chalecos amarillos’ y la rabia estudiantil incendian Francia
World.content:
Las manifestaciones desembocan en escenas de caos y enfrentamientos entre la policía y los jóvenes, que protestan desde hace semanas por el deterioro educativo

La rabia ha vuelto este sábado a las calles de Francia. Estudiantes, funcionarios, transportistas y el espectro de los chalecos amarillos acudieron masivamente a la cita en unos 500 puntos del país. La movilización social, convocada originalmente contra el encarecimiento del coste de la vida y la pérdida de poder adquisitivo, a la que después se sumaron los estudiantes, ha terminado incendiando las calles de las grandes ciudades de Francia. El presidente de la República, Emmanuel Macron, llamó a la calma el viernes por la noche. No sirvió de nada, como la mayoría de su acción de gobierno en el último año. La policía cargó violentamente contra los manifestantes con pelotas de goma, gases lacrimógenos y cañones de agua en las principales ciudades del país, cuyas calles empezaron a arder pasadas las dos de la tarde. Y, a partir de ahí, se desató el caos.

Los líderes de las protestas habían convocado alrededor de 500 acciones y más de 90 manifestaciones. Unas 800.000 personas, según los organizadores, acudieron a la llamada. Urbes como Lyon (la tercera más poblada del país) amanecieron con algunas calles cortadas por barricadas formadas por bicicletas de alquiler, contenedores y neumáticos. En París, la policía ya había detenido a media mañana a más de un centenar de personas y en ciudades como Marsella (la segunda en población) comenzaron temprano las cargas policiales contra los primeros manifestantes, que incendiaron contenedores y papeleras. Un olor a plástico quemado, pólvora y gas lacrimógeno invadió de repente el aire de París. Y ya no desapareció.

Las llamas prendieron en todo el país y quemaron comercios, mobiliario urbano y vehículos aparcados. Pero también ardieron los últimos restos del macronismo, un decenio político que ha terminado desatando la cólera de los ciudadanos, que presienten hoy la sensación una vida peor que hace diez años. A seis largos meses de las elecciones presidenciales, con un gobierno hecho jirones que deberá aprobar un presupuesto con recortes de 54.000 millones, una deuda disparada (119% del PIB) y la ultraderecha a las puertas del Palacio del Elíseo por primera vez desde la Segunda Guerra Mundial, crece la sensación en la calle de que no hay interlocutor en el poder. Hay gritos, pero nadie escucha. “La sensación es la del final de un reinado”, opina el sociólogo Jérôme Fourquet.

Lo mismo, exactamente, perciben los manifestantes y su indisimulada violencia. Al mediodía, un grupo de agitadores entró y vandalizó una comisaría y ocupó luego la entrada del Ayuntamiento de Marsella, forzando la puerta. El alcalde se vio obligado a pedir refuerzos personalmente a Macron. “La comisaría de policía municipal de La Canebière ha sido vandalizada, las puertas del Ayuntamiento han sido forzadas, numerosos comercios han sido dañados”, lamentó el regidor. Lo mismo ocurrió en otras ciudades como Lille o Rennes. En Lyon ardió la oficina de turismo. “Es un drama”, lamentó su alcalde, Grégory Doucet. Un grupo de personas saqueó la resiencia del delegado del Gobierno en Burdeos. A media tarde comenzaron también los pillajes e incendios intencionados en centenares de comercios de París. La sensación a esa hora era ya de un pérdida total de control por parte de las fuerzas de orden.

La protesta, y esa también es la novedad respecto a los últimos días de conflicto, confirma un cierto regreso de los chalecos amarillos a Francia, cuya indumentaria apareció discretamente a las primeras aglomeraciones en la plaza de la República de París, donde empezó a las 14.30 la gran manifestación en la capital. La marcha, pacífica y ordenada, fue lo más tranquilo. Mientras decenas de miles de personas marchaban, en las calles adyacentes los antidisturbios y agitadores vestidos de negro con gafas de esquí y mascarillas se enzarzaban en una batalla campal con proyectiles de todo tipo. Ardieron coches, motos, bicicletas y contenedores. Y las barricadas que formaron los manifestantes en la calle solo se abrieron cuando pasaban los bomberos y las ambulancias, siempre aplaudidos por los estudiantes. “Ellos no son como la policía. Están con nosotros. Su lucha también es nuestra”, explicaba August, estudiante de 17 años.

Algunas fases de la protesta, que dejó más de 400 detenidos pasadas las ocho de la tarde, estaban perfectamente organizadas. Muchos manifestantes prepararon desde hace semanas la denominada operación escargot [caracol]. Llenaron huevos y botes con pintura y excrementos para cegar los cascos de la policía, a la que distrajeron en muchos momentos. Tantos, que lograron el objetivo original y vetado por el ministerio del Interior de llegar a la plaza de la Concordia, lugar donde hace 230 años se colocó la guillotina que decapitó a Luis XVI en enero de 1793 y, nueve meses después, a María Antonieta.

Jornada de protestas en París, este sábado. Thibault Camus (AP Photo)

“Hemos vuelto. Han pasado ocho años, pero todo sigue siendo una mierda. La gasolina es más cara, somos más pobres. Se ríen de nosotros, Macron se ha reído de nosotros”, protesta Philippe Doué, 54 años, parado. El hombre, que ya participó en las primeras protestas de los chalecos amarillos, ha venido a París desde Nanterre con un grupo de amigos. “Los sábados salimos en bici o nos juntamos en el bar. Hoy toca luchar por nuestros derechos y por los de los jóvenes”, insiste al pie de la estatua de la Marianne, símbolo de la Revolución Francesa, que terminó con un enorme chaleco amarillo donde podía leerse: “2026, la policía mutila estudiantes”.

Una hora más tarde, comenzaron también las cargas policiales en la propia plaza, cuyos manifestantes fueron dispersados con gases lacrimógenos y con un camión con cañones de agua. La plaza de la República terminó envuelta en una columna de humo, como tantas confluencias de la ciudad, y con algunos heridos en el suelo. El fuego ya no volvió apagarse.

A pocos metros, algunos diputados de La Francia Insumisa (LFI), el único partido que ha podido participar en las protestas y aprovecharlas políticamente, se paseaban entre los manifestantes. Encabezaba la comitiva su líder, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, sonríente, con aire indismulado de satisfacción. Le acompañaba Mathilde Panot, jefa del grupo en la Asamblea Nacional, advertía a EL PAÍS que “todo terminará como quiera el Gobierno”. “De momento no han respondido más que con la fuerza policial, con gases lacrimógenos, bombas que arrancan las manos a estudiantes o les dejan tuertos... ¿Lo ve? Ahí lo tiene“, dice mientras vapea un cigarrillo electrónico tranquilamente y la policía empieza a cargar hacia donde se encuentra ella (y el periodista).

El ministro del Interior, Laurent Nuñez, autorizó que la policía pudiese recurrir a granadas aturdidoras y otros medios antidisturbios en caso de enfrentamientos graves. El anuncio llegó después de que, el miércoles de la semana pasada, el ministro ordenara suspender temporalmente el uso de un tipo dearmas tras un incidente ocurrido en Lens (norte), donde un manifestante de 15 años sufrió la amputación de una mano durante las protestas relacionadas con el bloqueo de institutos. Nuñez, que acusó el sábado a La Francia Insumisa de alentar la violencia, precisó entonces que la suspensión se limitaba al movimiento estudiantil y que se mantendría mientras se investigaban las circunstancias de lo ocurrido. Pero los artefactos volvieron. Y, de nuevo, causaron la amputación de una extremidad a un manifestante en Saint Étienne.

La protesta de este sábado empezó con un clip en TikTok, un malestar generalizado por el encarecimiento de los combustibles y una fecha: 17 de octubre. La convocatoria nació en redes sociales hace un mes y se convirtió en el nuevo objeto político-mediático de septiembre. La petición ―que incluía una especie de póster diseñado con inteligencia artificial― reclamaba una movilización nacional de chalecos amarillos con ocupación de rotondas y plazas en todo el país mientras sonaba de fondo una canción con el estribillo: “Macron, dimisión”. La misma letra que corearon este sábado todos los manifestantes. “Macron, estás jodido, la calle no está contigo”, cantaban algunos.

Agentes antidisturbios detienen a una manifestante en París, este sábado. Carl Court (Getty Images)

Nadie tomó demasiado en serio, al principio, la convocatoria de los chalecos amarillos en redes. Pero las protestas de los estudiantes han incendiado el país en los últimos días y el malestar generalizado ha encontrado una vía de canalización este sábado a través de la protesta. La violencia, sin embargo, ha desbordado todas las previsiones. También la policial.

El movimiento de los chalecos amarillos surgió en Francia en 2018 como una convocatoria en redes contra el alza de los precios de los combustibles impulsada por el Gobierno de Macron, y se definió a sí mismo como ciudadano, transversal, sin portavoces ni líderes oficiales y sin adscripción a ningún partido. El 17 de noviembre de 2018, su jornada fundacional, reunió a 282.000 personas que se manifestaron en todo el país. Ahora, ocho años después, como si fuera una profecía, su regreso se produce también un día 17, un mes antes en el calendario, justo al final del mandato del presidente a quien recibieron entonces a pedradas.

La convocatoria también ha reunido ahora a organizaciones juveniles, colectivos ecologistas, agricultores y sindicatos. La confluencia de luchas y de organizaciones implicadas refleja la amplitud de las reivindicaciones sociales, que van más allá de una única cuestión y reúnen distintas expresiones de descontento frente a la situación económica y las dificultades cotidianas de numerosos ciudadanos. Todo ocurre cuando el Parlamento debe debatir unas nuevas cuentas públicas que incluyen recortes de hasta 54.000 millones de euros para controlar una deuda disparada cuyo coste supone ya una carga mayor que la partida de Educación Nacional.

“No nos dejaremos intimidar”, advirtió Sébastien Lecornu. El primer ministro acusó a “grupos de extrema izquierda” de haber “organizado la violencia en varias ciudades de Francia”. “Delincuentes se mezclaron entre ellos para saquear y destruir”, lamentó X. Más allá de algunos mensajes más en redes sociales, el paisaje de fondo no favorece que pueda haber una respuesta efectiva del Ejecutivo para calmar las aguas.

El Banco de Francia rebajó hace apenas unos días su previsión de crecimiento para 2026 hasta una horquilla de entre el 0,4% y el 0,5%, muy por debajo del 1% que manejaba a finales de 2025, y elevó su pronóstico de inflación hasta el 2,5% para este año, casi un punto porcentual más de lo calculado meses atrás. La propia entidad admite que esa atonía económica, combinada con el encarecimiento de la deuda, empujará el déficit público al 5,2% del PIB en 2026, una décima más que en 2025. La inflación interanual ya se situó en agosto en el 2,4%, acelerando desde el 2,1% de julio, con una energía que se ha encarecido casi un 17% en el último año.

Más información La crisis energética aboca a los gobiernos a tomar más medidas a las puertas de un superaño electoral en Europa

La secretaria general de la CGT, Sophie Binet, considera que la jornada de movilización pone de manifiesto la gravedad de la situación económica que atraviesan numerosos trabajadores. Binet afirmó en la cadena de radio France Inter que productos cotidianos como los tomates y los calabacines, así como el combustible, se han convertido en gastos cada vez más difíciles de asumir para una parte de la población.

Agentes de la policía antidisturbios francesa (CRS) patrullan junto a comercios protegidos con paneles de madera en los Campos Elíseos de París, este sábado. Abdul Saboor (REUTERS)

El sábado 17 de octubre de 2026 pasará a engrosar el álbum de fotos de las grandes revueltas francesas. Desde el inicio del movimiento, unos 210 estudiantes de secundaria han resultado heridos, junto con 150 miembros del personal educativo y 900 integrantes de las fuerzas del orden. Este balance humano va acompañado de 8.000 detenciones policiales, de las cuales el 85% corresponden a menores de edad, y de una treintena de investigaciones encomendadas a la Inspección General de la Policía Nacional (IGPN), el organismo encargado de investigar posibles irregularidades policiales. En cuanto a los daños materiales, estos ascienden a “un mínimo de 30 millones de euros”, según indicó el Gobierno el viernes de la semana pasada.

World.title: Fea, malquerida y polémica: el fiasco inmobiliario de la torre más alta de París
World.content:
El ambicioso proyecto de renovación del edificio de Montparnasse debía arrancar este otoño, pero la mayoría de los propietarios ha rechazado el plan por su elevado coste

La llaman la torre malquerida. Tiene las mejores vistas de París porque con sus 209 metros es la torre más alta, pero también, dicen los parisinos, porque desde lo alto del rascacielos no se ve su propia fealdad en el horizonte. La Torre Montparnasse, que a pesar de su impopularidad es uno de los edificios más característicos de París, se encuentra desde hace meses en un limbo inmobiliario, pues el ambicioso proyecto para renovarla, que empezó a perfilarse hace una década y cuyas obras iniciales tendrían que haber comenzado este otoño, ha sido rechazado por la mayoría de sus propietarios por su elevado coste: 800 millones de euros.

La Torre Montparnasse se empezó a construir en 1969 y se inauguró en 1973. Formaba parte de una operación urbanística más amplia, que incluía un centro comercial y otros dos edificios de oficinas. Hasta entonces no había rascacielos en la capital y se convertía así en el segundo punto más alto del horizonte parisino tras la torre Eiffel (276 metros, considerada monumento). El rechazo popular al moderno edificio fue tal que el Consejo de París votó años más tarde una ley para prohibir construcciones dentro de la capital de más de 37 metros de altura.

Ubicado junto a la estación de Montparnasse, la cuarta con más tráfico en París (61 millones de viajeros al año), en este medio siglo el rascacielos no se había renovado. En 2005 se detectó la presencia de amianto y empezó a cobrar fuerza la idea de aprovechar las obras de retirada del mismo para darle una nueva imagen a la torre.

El proyecto de renovación se empezó a perfilar en 2017, a cargo de los arquitectos del colectivo Nouvelle AOM. La idea era darle un nuevo horizonte a París y transformar esta torre de hormigón y vidrio oscuro en un edificio con fachadas de cristal, más luminoso, y con un menor consumo energético. El proyecto incluía, además de oficinas, un hotel con centenares de habitaciones, repartidas en varios de los pisos, comercios y una zona ajardinada en la cima, para que el público siguiera disfrutando en la cubierta de sus vistas excepcionales. La Torre Montparnasse iba a ganar una decena de metros de altura.

Sus 59 pisos, 120.000 metros cuadrados, se vaciaron de inquilinos el pasado mes de marzo para que los primeros trabajos de la retirada de amianto y desmontaje parcial de la fachada comenzaran este otoño. Estaba previsto que las obras finalizasen en 2030. Este verano algunos de los copropietarios mostraron su rechazo al proyecto por el elevado coste y lo condicionaron a buscar financiación. A finales de septiembre el 76% de los copropietarios rechazó el proyecto durante una asamblea general, que era la última baza para desatascar la situación e iniciar las obras, tras meses de desacuerdos. El futuro de la torre ha quedado en el limbo, pues el permiso de construcción expira a finales de noviembre.

300 dueños

La gestión de la propiedad ha sido siempre compleja. Un monopoly de altura donde empresarios e inversores compran lotes por pisos. Llegó a tener 300 propietarios, pero los de mayor peso comenzaron a adquirir su parte a los más pequeños. El mayoritario, con un 30%, es LFPI (financiera patrimonial de inversión), que ya mostró en julio su rechazo al proyecto. Otros de los más importantes son los empresarios Xavier Niel y Frédéric Lemos, y las aseguradoras Axa y Mgen, con un 10%.

El alcalde de París, Emmanuel Grégoire, ha tenido que llamar al orden a las partes, pues, aunque el proyecto de renovación del rascacielos es privado, hay un interés público en la revitalización del espacio urbano en la zona. El ambicioso proyecto de renovación, que ha movilizado en estos 10 años a cuatro prestigiosos despachos de arquitectos, queda ahora olvidado: ni fachada luminosa, ni hotel ni jardín en la cubierta. La torre sigue vacía de inquilinos y ahora se habla de su “rehabilitación”. Se impone una solución más modesta y menos costosa que se limite a retirar el amianto y devolverle algún sentido a un edificio que, a pesar de su impopularidad, ha encontrado su lugar en el paisaje urbano parisino.

World.title: Información genética para una medicación más segura y eficiente
World.content:
Con una simple muestra de saliva, la farmacogenética permite el análisis de decenas de genes y cientos de fármacos de uso habitual y revela por qué un simple analgésico quita el dolor a una persona y a otra le produce una reacción adversa

Según estima la Agencia Española de Medicamentos y Productos Sanitarios, entre el 3% y el 6,5% de la población tiene una variante genética que provoca que su hígado transforme la codeína (un compuesto presente en medicamentos o soluciones tan frecuentes como las pastillas para la tos) en morfina. Este proceso, que se produce a gran velocidad incluso si la dosis administrada es normal, puede desembocar en una sobredosis accidental, que en algunos casos termina en el fallecimiento del paciente.

El ejemplo lo pone Javier Suela, director técnico del laboratorio de genética de Sanitas (Madrid). Él mismo pertenece a este pequeño grupo poblacional de riesgo: “Hay mucha evidencia acumulada de la toxicidad de ciertos medicamentos en ciertos pacientes. Estas reacciones adversas van desde un brote cutáneo hasta la muerte en casos extremos, como este mismo de la codeína”, explica.

Suela trabaja para reducir esa peligrosidad al mínimo. En el laboratorio que dirige, desde el pasado mayo, se extrae el perfil genético de quien lo solicite para “determinar si tiene un componente genético, una proteína, que produce que determinados fármacos se procesen de una forma que no es habitual”, sintetiza.

El perfil genético, en tres pasos 1 Recepción de las muestras e identificación de cada paciente El paciente lleva una muestra genética (basta la saliva, por ejemplo) en un tubo. Este tubo va a una primera máquina que realiza una preanalítica y transforma las muestras en placas que identifican a cada persona: en la posición A1 está la muestra de un paciente concreto y en la B1, otro, y así sucesivamente. 2 Procesado del material genético El material genético de la placa, que contiene muestras de hasta 96 pacientes, se prepara y depura (se corta, se colorea...) en otra máquina para el análisis final. Lo que se obtiene, tras cuatro horas de refinado, es la placa definitiva (en la imagen) que se usará para extraer el perfil genético. 3 Obtención del perfil genético La placa, con el material genético ya refinado, se introduce en un escáner que analiza cada celda, que contiene más de un millón de variables (cada una asociada a un genotipo) que procesar. Cuando este escáner finaliza se obtiene el perfil genético del paciente, el resultado final del proceso.

Esta disciplina se conoce como farmacogenética y en Sanitas está disponible para todos sus asegurados bajo el nombre de Mi Farmagen. “Un ser humano puede metabolizar todos los fármacos, pero en función de ciertas variables genéticas los metaboliza a distintas velocidades; entonces el medicamento puede funcionar demasiado bien o demasiado mal. Esto es lo que da lugar a reacciones adversas o reacciones inexistentes, es decir, cuando el fármaco no funciona”, detalla.

29 genes y 125 fármacos analizados

Mi Farmagen analiza hasta 29 genes y más de 125 fármacos de uso habitual, y ofrece un informe con las reacciones a cada uno de estos medicamentos. Y siempre es útil, tanto si se obtiene antes o después de la prescripción, ya que “permite ajustar la medicación sin perder efectividad, pero evitando posibles efectos adversos y aumentando la seguridad”, incide Suela.

Hay casos en los que un cambio anticipado de medicación puede salvar la vida del paciente, pero también situaciones más cotidianas en las que esta información es de mucha utilidad. Así lo explica Andrea Azcárate, jefe de servicio de Endocrinología del hospital Sanitas de La Moraleja (Madrid): “Es el ejemplo de un paciente con colesterol alto al que le sienta mal un tipo de estatina, que es el tratamiento habitual para esta patología. Para corroborarlo, se le hace la prueba farmacogenética. A partir de ahí, probablemente escojamos otro tipo de estatina que vaya a tolerar mejor”. Sin embargo, cada caso, en opinión de Azcárate, no es blanco o negro: “Lo que el análisis nos da es una predisposición de respuesta, una información probabilística que nos permite individualizar el tratamiento”, puntualiza.

0:00 ANDREA AZCÁRATE, jefe de servicio de Endocrinología del hospital Sanitas de La Moraleja (Madrid)

Azcárate y Suela inciden, precisamente, en la importancia de la interpretación facultativa de esta información, que por sí sola vale poco. “Es fundamental la interpretación y el ajuste, algo que siempre se ha hecho: la medicación, en función de las características clínicas del paciente, las casuísticas y las edades, se individualiza”. Y eso mismo se hará a partir de ahora, subraya: “Ajustaremos caso a caso, pero con más información. Es una herramienta más, muy buena y útil, pero hay que tener prudencia a la hora de incorporarla”.

En esa misma línea se expresa Suela: “El informe son páginas de metabolización, nada más. No vale de nada sin facultativo detrás que las interprete. Y, sobre todo, hay que combinar toda la información: igual tienes un paciente del que el análisis dice que el fármaco le va a sentar muy bien, pero esa misma persona tiene unas condiciones físicas complicadas o es un paciente polimedicado, en el que es fundamental medir las interacciones entre fármacos”. Es una cuestión de personalización, como dicta la tendencia actual en la medicina, pero con un conocimiento más preciso.

Así funciona Mi Farmagen Mi Farmagen analiza cómo las variantes genéticas influyen en la respuesta a determinados medicamentos.
