Hacia un pasaporte genético

En el futuro, coinciden los especialistas, se abre paso la idea de que todo ciudadano cuente con un carnet genético. Esta posibilidad existe gracias a la tecnología, explica Suela, que ha multiplicado el poder de las técnicas de genotipado: “Antes hacíamos un solo caso, un solo paciente, con cientos de marcadores. Ahora procesamos hasta 96 casos y en cada uno analizamos millones de marcadores. El salto es impresionante”.

0:00 JAVIER SUELA, director técnico del laboratorio de genética de Sanitas (Madrid)

El objetivo es que la farmacogenética sea útil, no un mero postulado teórico. Y ya lo es, pero todavía a pequeña escala. Mi Farmagen acumula ya mil análisis farmacogenéticos a pacientes con aplicación real. “Necesitamos que poco a poco todos tengamos un carnet farmacogenómico. En la actualidad esa información que tenemos ya nos salta a la historia clínica de forma automática como alerta a la hora de prescribir medicamentos con un programa propio, Farmacheck, y esta información también está a disposición del paciente en su app para poder ajustar e individualizar el tratamiento. En pocos años será un estándar”, señala Azcárate. Suela añade: “Nuestro sueño sería que en más del 90% de las prescripciones se tuviese en cuenta esa información genética de manera previa”.

Todo con un fin: obtener la mayor seguridad para el paciente, ya que, hasta hoy, “a la hora de prescribir algunos fármacos, operábamos con un método prueba-error: si no funcionaba uno, o si funcionaba mal, se probaba otro. Pero con la farmacogenética se abre otro camino, de máxima seguridad, basado en evidencias clínicas rigurosas”, afirma Suela.

World.title: Els contes de Jordi Cussà: l’art de seduir el lector
World.content:
Ens agrada que Actuació de gala, una selecció de contes que Jordi Cussà (Berga, 1961-2021) no va reunir mai en cap llibre i que abasten gairebé quaranta anys d’escriptura, finalitzi amb una faula titulada ‘Un present per a l’eternitat’, que sembla un aeròlit desprès d’El primer emperador i la reina Lluna (2021), aquella majestuosa i immensa novel·la on reconstruïa de manera aproximada les circumstàncies històriques de la Xina del segle III aC i sublimava, sobretot, la convicció que l’autor tenia sobre la naturalesa de l’ofici de narrar com l’art de seduir-nos a través de qualsevol argúcia, ja fos gràcies a la creació d’un suspens, a les revelacions truculentes, al fet extraordinari, al detall efectista, a l’habilitat de convertir en versemblant i indispensable el que en un principi no ho semblaria gens. De manera indirecta, les quatre proves que han de superar els candidats nobles a esposar-se amb la filla d’un rei, en el conte esmentat —una cacera amb llança i arc, el simulacre d’una batalla, un exercici de dialèctica social, la construcció d’un castell de focs—, i que guanya un simple llenyataire arribat d’unes muntanyes remotes on hi havia només “gorgs i cingles” —com Berga, potser—, glossen a la perfecció el que localitzem en les vint peces que configuren l’antològic regal sorpresa que és Actuació de gala: la justa precisió amb què Jordi Cussà atrapa cada frase, les emboscades imaginatives amb què ens arravata, l’escenificació d’uns diàlegs en cap moment afectats o falsos —aquí respira el dramaturg: llegirem algun dia les seves obres teatrals?—, l’esplendor d’unes trames que esclaten, s’encenen i perduren a la memòria com si el seu destí fos no apagar-se mai.

Más información Les 30 recomanacions de ‘Quadern’ per a La Setmana del Llibre en Català

A Actuació de gala, Jordi Cussà ens delecta de variades maneres. Causarà estupor en els lectors que només coneguin de l’autor Cavalls salvatges o Formentera Lady llegir ‘Totes les ànimes del tronc’ —davant l’amenaça d’un concurs boletaire, els bolets opten per amagar-se—, o ‘Nadala’, on una vaca i un bou, l’endemà de Reis, s’estimen més no presenciar la matança del porc i se’n van, “amb la calma del seu mil·lenari pas”, cap a “la pau que omple les muntanyes”, dues filigranes en miniatura que semblen sorgides d’un almanac molt antic; ens deixa atònits la força narrativa de ‘Noblesa obliga’, un thriller polític que usa a consciència tot el repertori de convencions del gènere per acabar fent-nos creure que no n’hi ha ni una, de convenció, com si l’únic manament vàlid fos no morir; i ens embadaleix amb els simulacres de crònica social —ardits, subterfugis i pretextos— sobre la misteriosa tensió de la soledat de les relacions sentimentals que traça en dues de les peces més audaces i majúscules del conjunt, ‘En minúscula’ i ‘La guionista i el personatge’. D’Actuació de gala tampoc en sortiran decebuts ni insatisfets els que hi busquin el que esperen trobar en un llibre de Jordi Cussà: ens esglaia el monòton i desesperat galop cap a l’autodestrucció, sense glorificar mai el sofriment, que trobem a ‘Urbana subterrània’ o a ‘De matinada, una telefonada’; ens commou —o ens acontenta, ens anima o ens fascina, tant li fa— la militància estoica del supervivent a pesar seu, com la dels protagonistes de dos altres contes magistrals, ‘Un duet nu’ i ‘Persones i llibres’, esforçats a recuperar la vida passada perquè fer-ho amb el futur els està vedat, com si es concentressin en si mateixos abans de dissoldre’s del tot; i quedem bocabadats davant de l’exhibició de l’extraordinària habilitat artesanal i l’enginy tècnic dels jocs metaliteraris de ‘Narració sense títol’ o ‘Contraplans’, que homenatgen la mateixa ficció, l’avidesa creativa, l’ambició literària.

A ‘Hah!’, el narrador conclou que la màxima addicció és escriure “perquè al capdavall, de manera conceptualment semblant a totes les altres drogues, també et crema les hores i et xucla, arranca, esbudella i tanca dins la teva pròpia ostra, menys i menys divertida a mesura que sumes lletres i frases i. Solitud”. Segurament deu ser cert, però la casualitat ha fet que la lectura d’Actuació de gala hagi coincidit amb la d’uns aforismes d’Elias Canetti, on n’hem trobat un que pot servir de colofó sobre Jordi Cussà i la seva literatura: “Inventa una història nova, una història completament nova, com mai n’hi havia hagut cap abans. Qui ho aconsegueixi haurà viscut, i no haurà de reprotxar-se haver mort”.

World.title: A los ricos no les basta con la piscina: las zonas comunes se adaptan al gusto del comprador extranjero en los edificios de ultralujo
World.content:
Si para muchos españoles tener una piscina en casa ya es un lujo, a los ricos parece que les sabe a poco. Dentro de las comodidades que ofrecen los nuevos edificios de ultralujo en Madrid, las piletas han pasado a un segundo plano, son un elemento que se da por hecho o, incluso, se prescinde de ellas para dejar espacio a otros amenities, término que se usa en el sector inmobiliario para referirse a los servicios comunes de un edificio. En unos años en los que ya no es descabellado hablar de 20.000 euros por metro cuadrado, e incluso 30.000 euros en ciertos proyectos singulares, en las zonas más prémium de la ciudad, los productos a la venta se han ido refinando y adecuándose a los gustos de los compradores extranjeros que han puesto sus ojos en la capital.

En esa evolución de la oferta se enmarca la tendencia por tener cada vez más amenities a disposición del dueño de un piso. Sin embargo, también hay quien considera que no es más que otra estrategia de venta que ayuda a elevar, aún más, unos precios que no paran de subir, aunque empiezan a mostrar síntomas de moderación.

Natalia Pérez, consultora sénior de ­Knight Frank, explica que es una tendencia que ha llegado en los últimos años de la mano principalmente de compradores latinoamericanos y, en menor medida, estadounidenses, “que demandan las mismas comodidades que tienen en sus países”.

Una visión que comparte Álvaro González, consejero delegado de Spain Sotheby’s International Realty, cuando señala que el 90% de los compradores de este tipo de producto inmobiliario son extranjeros. “Y, a veces, algunos empresarios nacionales con mucho éxito, o de provincias”, pero aún no “el madrileño de toda la vida”. Sin embargo, Pérez cifra en “un 50% internacional, 50% nacional” al referirse al perfil del comprador. “El español se ha sofisticado muchísimo en los últimos años y lo demanda también. En un proyecto high end (gama alta) cuyo metro cuadrado tenga un precio elevado, pregunta por las amenities. Si no hay, no paga esas cantidades”. Poder incrementar el precio y mejorar sus expectativas de ventas son dos de las razones que, según González, han llevado a que los promotores “metan estas amenities a la hora de rehabilitar edificios clásicos de Madrid”.

Por su parte, Beltrán Soto, director de Messer Living, comenta que los primeros promotores que “se atrevieron” a enfocarse en este producto fueron los internacionales. “Los españoles tenían un poco de miedo, porque no estaban acostumbrados a tanto peso de estos espacios comunes. No es solo lo que tenían que invertir para construirlos, también los metros cuadrados que debían sacrificar de los destinados a vivienda”. Dicho sacrificio conllevaba “menos pisos, pero de mayor calidad y con un incremento del precio por metro cuadrado”.

Evolución

El sector ha ido evolucionando, sostiene Soto, y hoy en día no hay ningún proyecto de obra nueva de cierto nivel que no venga con amenities. “Y no estamos hablando de los de ultralujo, también hay edificios que rondan los 14.000 euros por metro cuadrado en zonas del centro que tienen espacios comunes”. Los primeros, describe el director de Messer Living, fueron la piscina interior y una sala de gimnasio con varias máquinas. “Conforme ha ido evolucionando el modelo, ahora eso se ha convertido en un estándar. Comercialmente tienen cada vez más peso, por lo que los promotores se han tenido que poner más creativos con estos espacios”.

Recreación de la vinoteca proyectada en el edificio Santa Catalina 5, en Madrid. Cedida por Knight Frank

Ahora, en los catálogos de venta de los edificios se ven recreaciones de bodegas, coctelerías, salones para comidas privadas, salas para hacer yoga o pilates, soláriums en azoteas con barras de bar, bibliotecas y salones de peluquería. Y no suele faltar una zona de spa que, dependiendo del espacio, puede albergar baño turco, jacuzzi, piscinas de inmersión y salas de masajes. “Me he dado cuenta de que el lujo antes era llevar un bolso de una marca cara y hoy en día es el bienestar. Ahora la piscina, que no utilizaba nadie, se ha convertido en una zona wellness con todo tipo de servicios para el descanso y la relajación. Hay proyectos en los que veo plantas enteras dedicadas solo a esto. Es lo que más se demanda”, relata Natalia Pérez, responsable de la comercialización de un edificio con amenities en la calle Santa Catalina, 5, de Madrid.

Una demanda que concuerda con las conclusiones de un reciente informe de Sotheby’s International Realty, en el que se destacaba la creciente influencia de la longevidad y el bienestar en las decisiones de compra de los grandes patrimonios. Sin embargo, el consejero delegado de la consultora inmobiliaria en España muestra cierto escepticismo sobre los amenities, a los que califica como “elementos comerciales, para vestir el inmueble”, pero de los que se hace un uso limitado. “En América están acostumbrados a hacer vida dentro de un condominio o de un edificio por temas de seguridad. Cuando los latinos llegan aquí, se compran una casa en Lagasca, ven que tienen el parque del Retiro al lado y que pueden salir y hacer ejercicio allí, en lugar de en un gimnasio sin ventanas, porque el edificio no da más posibilidades”.

Servicios a la carta

En estos proyectos inmobiliarios con tanto peso de zonas comunes, el reto principal, según Beltrán Soto, es una “gestión residencial” que vaya más allá de la que hace un “administrador de fincas habitual”. “Se requiere más sofisticación para dar el servi­cio y que se puedan aprovechar esos espacios”. Una “necesidad” que está detrás del nacimiento de la rama living de Messer, firma que llevaba años trabajando en la conceptualización, posicionamiento y desarrollo de marcas para activos residenciales. Soto compara al residencial manager con la figura de un director de un hotel boutique, que esté pendiente de todos los detalles, desde el uniforme del portero hasta avisar si se estropea la sauna. La empresa ofrece, además, un catálogo de servicios a la carta que el dueño de la vivienda puede contratar, desde un corte de pelo o un masaje sin salir del edificio hasta que le tengan la nevera llena cuando llegue a casa.

Para los ricos internacionales que compran casa en Madrid, este tipo de facilidades y de amenities suelen ser algo común en su día a día en otros países, por lo que también están acostumbrados al desembolso mensual de unos gastos de comunidad que pueden llegar a ser de varios miles de euros. No obstante, aseguran fuentes del sector, al español aún le cuesta hacerse a la idea. “Es lo primero que preguntan cuando se interesan por un edificio de este tipo”, expone Soto. Mientras que Pérez afirma que “hasta el español es consciente de que no va a pagar menos de 1.000 euros al mes”. Y que mientras que a aquellos que adquieren un inmueble por un precio que ronda el millón de euros “les cuesta muchísimo”, los que desembolsan “de tres millones de euros para arriba lo dan por hecho”.

González, por su parte, argumenta que, “cuando se pasa un tique, como puede ser una casa de cinco millones de euros, preocuparse por los gastos de comunidad es como comprarse un Ferrari y preguntar cuánto gasta”.

World.title: Viaje a la remota isla escocesa de Islay y a la aún más inaccesible Jura, donde Orwell terminó ‘1984′
World.content:
Una escapada entre destilerías, turba y ciervos donde el paisaje se mete en el cuerpo, las canciones guardan la memoria de quienes se fueron y aún parece posible perderse entre acantilados e historias

Cuando George Orwell llegó a la isla escocesa de Jura para aislarse del mundo en 1946, escribió en su diario: “Este es un lugar extremadamente inaccesible”. Basta con intentar llegar hasta su casa en Barnhill para comprender que no exageraba: Jura está al otro lado de Islay y, una vez en esa isla, todavía hay que seguir avanzando hacia el norte por carreteras y caminos que parecen empeñados en devolver al viajero al punto de partida. Tengamos en cuenta este dato: en Jura viven 250 personas y 5.000 ciervos. Jura es la hermana pequeña de Islay, una de las islas más narcóticas de las West Highlands escocesas (las tierras altas del oeste) y donde viven 3.000 personas que gozan del lujo medioambiental yendo a donde el viento quiera, un viento con propiedades altamente saludables, que despeja y ventila como una verdad incómoda y con el que uno acaba empatizando porque, al fin y al cabo, él también parece tener prisa por detenerse a contemplar.

Para llegar hasta estas dos islas de las Hébridas Interiores, lo primero es aterrizar en Glasgow (bendito problema), la ciudad más divertida del Reino Unido, y si hay que pasar la noche, mucho mejor, porque los bares Nice ‘N’ Sleazy y Stereo no cierran nunca.

Más información En la isla de Rügen, un patrimonio entre lo mitológico y lo real

Observando la silueta de Islay por la ventanilla de la avioneta antes del aterrizaje, uno ya intuye que lo mejor será ser presa de la isla, un grano de arena entregado al aislamiento. Islay tiene algo de territorio que se ha quedado al margen por vocación. El mar, el viento y la turba han definido el carácter de las cosas, y hasta el silencio tiene una textura particular. Es una isla de horizontes bajos, carreteras estrechas en las que más de una vez hay que echarse atrás para dejar pasar al que viene, playas que cambian de humor con la marea y pequeños pueblos donde la vida transcurre como debería transcurrir la vida en todas partes. El whisky parece estar flotando en el aire, en las bodegas y en una forma de entender el paisaje. Islay no se visita, se entra en ella para dejarse llevar.

Vista de Portnahaven, un pequeño pueblo situado en el extremo sur de la isla de Islay. Paul Carroll Y Mhairi Carroll (GETTY IMAGES)

Veamos cinco puntos fuertes para hacernos una composición de lugar y extraerle el mayor partido más allá del tópico de las destilerías y apostar por el paisaje, la fauna, el bienestar, la gastronomía y la hospitalidad local.

1. La costa de Islay desde el mar

Una manera de acercarnos a esa hospitalidad de sus gentes y de su territorio es dejar las cosas en el hotel y acudir a la localidad de Port Ellen para sumarse al recorrido en bote de tres horas con comida (inolvidable) incluida de Islay Sea Adventures. El capitán Harold nos recibe empuñando una gaita cuyos fogonazos conmovedores consiguen caldear el viento.

La destilería de whisky Lagavulin, y los restos del castillo Dunyvaig, en la isla de Islay. Patsy Davies (Alamy / CORDON PRESS)

Desde el mar se contemplan las tres grandes destilerías del sur —Laphroaig, Lagavulin y Ardbeg— y, delante de cada una, la tripulación sirve un trago de whisky para que cada marca se fije en la memoria con el pegamento de haberla probado allí donde nace. Así continuamos hacia el Área Especial de Conservación de Islay, un espacio protegido al que solo se puede acceder para contemplarlo desde el agua. Mientras los simpáticos patrones van contando historias de la isla, su pasado y su patrimonio, recorremos la costa sudeste, entendiendo uno de sus paisajes más hermosos y también uno de los más ricos en fauna. Aquí vive una importante colonia de focas, además de delicados ciervos rojos que te miran con una pureza con la que mira un niño a su rey mago. Con un poco de suerte, durante la travesía pueden aparecer incluso águilas de cola blanca y delfines.

Parte de la actividad organizada por Islay Sea Adventures consiste en un pícnic de marisco tras un paseo en barco. Ben Shakespeare (Islay Sea Adventures)

El momento más extraordinario llega al alcanzar las aguas tranquilas de los islotes del sudeste de Islay (South-East Islay Skerries), porque es entonces cuando empieza el festival del marisco fresco capturado prácticamente a la puerta de la mesa: del mar al plato apenas hay unos pocos kilómetros. Langosta, bocas de buey de mar, salmón ahumado y, aparte, las vieiras, que son las protagonistas. Porque es un placer ver cómo Harold las cocina a bordo, sobre una barbacoa, con mantequilla, ajo y chile. Se agradecen el pan fresco, la ensalada y las salsas caseras, pero como decoración. Comer así es la experiencia que mejor explica la isla. Ningún folleto, ningún libro, ninguna foto puede superarlo. El único problema de esta actividad puede ser el precio: 115 libras (unos 135 euros, al cambio actual)

2. Vida de isla: tartán, ‘fish and chips’, folclore, Hollywood y Port Charlotte

Con un clima tan contradictorio, en el que un amanecer soleado puede transformarse en cinco minutos en un chubasco pasajero, conviene vestirse correctamente. Se explica así que la lana y el tartán sean tan importantes y se hayan convertido en una de las señas de identidad de las Highlands. Para hacerse una idea de hasta qué punto forman parte de su cultura, merece la pena visitar Islay Woollen Mill, una fábrica con una historia estupenda: allí se diseñó y produjo el tartán utilizado en la película Braveheart. La propia fábrica conserva y comercializa la colección Braveheart y ha trabajado también para otras producciones cinematográficas. El tartán es ese tejido de líneas de distintos colores que se cruzan en ángulo recto formando una trama de cuadros y que acabó convirtiéndose en uno de los signos visuales de Escocia. El que aquí se fabrica lo hemos visto también en Rob Roy, Highlander, Harry Potter (forma parte del uniforme de Hogwarts) e incluso en Forrest Gump, aunque en esta película el tartán juega ya como estampado universal y no tanto como emblema escocés.

El taller de Islay Woollen Mill, que trabaja con los tejidos de forma artesanal. Kenny Lam (VISIT SCOTLAND)

Al hilo de la tradición y para ver esas vestimentas, nada como una noche en el pub del Port Charlotte Hotel, en el pueblo de Port Charlotte, uno de esos rincones dulcemente extendidos frente al mar, reconocibles por sus casas blancas de dos alturas, tan bien conservadas. El local es un punto de reunión donde convergen la nostalgia y la identidad. Su fish and chips es tan interminable como irresistible. La sala tiene el encanto de los negocios eternos que abren fuera de temporada. La cerveza acompaña la llegada de los músicos, que se van sumando como si bajaran a la calle para encontrarse con sus amigos. El fiddle (violín tradicional), el acordeón, las guitarras, las mandolinas y la gaita van llenando el pub de canciones y viejas melodías de las islas, como si cada una trajera consigo un pedazo de memoria o una lágrima que se disuelve en el vaso. Cuando suena Westering Home, no hay nada ni nadie que pueda deshacer el nudo del estómago.

Esas canciones, esa música tradicional gaélica o folk, parecen creadas por la naturaleza, el viento, la lluvia, en ese mar que se lleva a la gente de aquí a probar suerte en otros mundos que difícilmente serán mejores. Y es que cuando uno se va, lo único que de verdad se lleva encima, incrustado, es la música: la canción de cuna que le cantaba su madre, las canciones que moldearon su infancia. Es la prenda mayor.

3. Excursión a Jura

Si Jura no es una isla inventada para perderse, no lo es ninguna. Lo que decíamos antes —250 vecinos rodeados por unos 5.000 ciervos— se comprueba nada más cruzar en ferri el kilómetro —apenas cinco minutos— que separa ambas islas. Bienvenidos a las montañas, las turberas, las costas solitarias y los Paps de Jura, esas tres cumbres que dominan el horizonte como una presencia casi mitológica.

Tres ciervos junto a la costa de la isla escocesa de Jura. Chris Morson (Alamy / CORDON PRESS)

Hacia el norte está Barnhill, la remota casa donde George Orwell se refugió para terminar 1984. Pero la historia del escritor británico y Jura había empezado antes. Él y su mujer, Eileen, llevaban tiempo pensando en abandonar Londres y marcharse a las Hébridas. Tanto era así que Orwell ya había iniciado las gestiones para encontrar allí una casa cuando, en marzo de 1945, Eileen murió inesperadamente durante una operación. Tenía 39 años. Orwell se quedó viudo y con Richard, el hijo que ambos habían adoptado pocos meses antes.

Un año después, David Astor, su amigo y editor del periódico The Observer, le sugirió que se marchara a Jura. La familia de Astor tenía propiedades en la isla y conocía Barnhill, una granja aislada en su extremo norte. Orwell llegó en mayo de 1946 y acabó alquilando la casa. Lo que había sido un proyecto compartido con Eileen se convirtió así en su refugio: un lugar donde alejarse de Londres, del periodismo y del ruido del mundo. En Barnhill, sin electricidad, teléfono ni vecinos a mano, encontró el aislamiento que buscaba y terminó escribiendo 1984.

Más amable es la parada en Lussa Gin, donde la ginebra se elabora con botánicos recolectados en la isla. Georgina y Claire nos enseñan su huerto, donde crecen algunos de sus ingredientes: enebro, rosas y tomillo limonero. Allí nos presentan su licor, extraordinariamente botánico, antes de mostrar su nueva creación, una ginebra homenaje a George Orwell llamada Nineteen Eighty Four, con notas de té Assam, cardamomo y rosas. El licor sirve también para hablar del escritor, que nació en la India en junio de 1903, hijo de un funcionario del Imperio británico. Con apenas un año, su madre se lo llevó a Inglaterra. Luego participó en dos guerras, experiencias que acabarían alimentando buena parte de su obra.

Parte del equipo de la destilería Lussa Gin. Lussa Gin

Cuando nos vamos, le digo a Georgina que pensamos comer en The Antlers. Su respuesta llega inmediata:

-Oohh, The Antlers... Desde que abrió, la gente de Jura está más gorda y es más pobre.

Le sobra razón. Esta bakehouse (panadería) roba el corazón hasta a la persona más evitativa con su pastrami y sus sausage rolls (rollos de salchichas). En The Antlers, la gastronomía vuelve a poner los pies en la tierra después de tantas millas de paisaje. En Jura todo parece estar desproporcionado: hay más ciervos que personas, más naturaleza que habitantes y una sensación de espacio que hace que incluso el silencio parezca perdido.

4. El imprescindible paseo al American Monument

Hay que dejar el coche en el aparcamiento de la reserva natural de The Oa, al final de la carretera que atraviesa esta península del sur de Islay. Desde allí comienza el camino hacia el American Monument, un paseo de unos treinta minutos, aunque lo razonable es hacer la ruta circular completa, de unos tres kilómetros y medio, sin ninguna prisa. Y, sobre todo, reservar otra hora para quedarse allí.

El camino es un abrazo constante de la naturaleza: la hierba, el viento del Atlántico, el salitre y esa sensación de ir dejando atrás el mundo... Hasta que aparecen los acantilados, el mar y el monumento, levantado en memoria de los soldados estadounidenses que murieron en los naufragios del Tuscania y el Otranto en 1918, que desde lejos parece suspendido sobre el océano.

El faro de Carraig Fhada, situado en la isla de Islay, es un faro emblemático en forma de torre cuadrada. Catherine Gilbrook (Alamy / CORDON PRESS)

Hay algo de templo en este lugar: un santuario sin techo ante el que uno acaba pidiendo deseos al mar, como quien deja una ofrenda y confía en que alguien, o algo, se encargará de ella. Y luego está el viento, que aquí parece tener permiso para hacer lo que quiera. Empuja, despeina, zarandea, te da la vuelta y te hace gritar al vacío. Un grito que mezcla la alegría y el dolor, la satisfacción de estar allí y la emoción que uno carga.

Después de este paseo solo quedan dos opciones: volver al whisky o entregarse al hotel. La primera pasa por Bowmore, una de las destilerías históricas de Islay, fundada en 1779 y una de las más antiguas de Escocia. Está a orillas del Loch Indaal y conserva uno de los elementos que mejor explican su carácter: sus almacenes de maduración, algunos de ellos situados prácticamente al nivel del mar. Aquí el whisky sigue teniendo algo de paisaje: turba, agua, sal y años de espera convertidos en una bebida.

La segunda opción es bastante más peligrosa para el presupuesto: irse al hotel, pero, en fin, tampoco todos los días se despierta uno en Islay.

5. The Machrie, un hotel convertido en galería

El hotel The Machrie está frente al Atlántico, entre dunas y junto a una playa de siete millas, pero quizás lo más sorprendente está dentro. La colección de arte, reunida y comisariada por su fundadora, Sue Nye, convierte el alojamiento en una especie de galería habitada: las obras aparecen en los pasillos, las habitaciones, el restaurante, la recepción o el gimnasio. Hay artistas escoceses como John Bellany, Pat Douthwaite, Peter Howson o Elizabeth Blackadder, junto a nombres como Tracey Emin, Antony Gormley, Peter Blake, Picasso, Miró, Dalí o Banksy. El arte forma parte de la vida cotidiana.

El hotel y campo de golf The Machrie. KEVIN MURRAY (THE MACHRIE)

Y luego está el paisaje, la ubicación. The Machrie recibe también a muchos jugadores de golf, que encuentran aquí un tapete verde frente al Atlántico. Para quien disfrute dándole a una pelota con un palo y persiguiéndola después por la hierba, probablemente no se pueda pedir más. Para los demás siempre queda sentarse frente al mar. Porque las vistas de la hierba y el océano son de esas que consiguen que uno se quede un rato sin hacer absolutamente nada. Uno mira cómo el viento mueve la hierba y cómo la isla continúa con su vida. Quizá ese sea el lujo verdadero de The Machrie. Y, puestos a confesarlo todo, quizá también el único que importa, junto a la poesía, porque ante este paisaje por fuerza vuelven a la cabeza aquellos versos de Wislawa Szymborska: “Comprendo que mi tristeza no frenará la hierba. Si los tallos vacilan será sólo por el viento”.

World.title: US ambassador to the NL gave $1m to Trump ballroom
World.content:
The US ambassador to the Netherlands, Joe Popolo, donated $1 million towards president Donald Trump’s new White House ballroom, according to a leaked list of project donors.

The Washington Post, which obtained the list, said the gift was made late last year, around two months after the businessman was appointed ambassador. Popolo declined to comment further to the paper.

The list runs to the end of September and records 67 donations of $10,000 or more, with a total of $333 million pledged. Tech, AI and arms manufacturers made up a large share of the donors. Some, who asked to stay anonymous, accounted for $77 million.

According to the paper, about half of the money came from companies or individuals with business before the federal government. Democratic politicians had previously asked for the donor list without success.

The fund managing the money agreed with the government not to reveal the identities of its backers, which US non-profits are generally not required to do.

Trump said last year the ballroom would be paid for entirely by himself and a few friends, but the list shows no contribution from the president. The Washington Post reported earlier this year that half the construction costs, now estimated at $600 million, are being met from public funds.

The White House snubbed the criticism, saying the same critics would complain if taxpayers were paying for the renovations.

The ballroom, which the president says will hold nearly 1,000 guests, is being built on the site of the White House east wing, which Trump had demolished last year. The plans include a military bunker underneath.

World.title: Limburg named the world’s “most intelligent region”
World.content:
Limburg has been named the world’s smartest region by the US-based think tank Intelligent Community Forum (ICF). The southern province, known for its hills and regional dialects, beat finalists from countries like Taiwan and Canada.

The award was presented to Brightlands, a network of four business and research campuses in the province that focus on health, AI, sustainable chemistry and food research. The ICF, a federation of 200 cities and regions, ranks areas around the globe each year on factors like economic and social development.

The jury praised the cooperation between government, business and research institutions at the campuses, as well as the way Limburg rebuilt itself after its coal mines closed half a century ago. After natural gas was discovered in 1959, “the region lost not only jobs but also security and hope,” ICF founder Robert Bell said.

Brightlands was set up in 2014 by the provincial government, education institutions and local businesses, according to L1 Nieuws.

The Maastricht campus focuses on health and is linked to the university hospital, while Heerlen, home to pension fund ABP and the national statistics office CBS, specialises in data and AI.

The materials campus is on the Chemelot chemical site in Sittard-Geleen, and Venlo’s food campus uses infrastructure left over from the 2012 Floriade horticultural expo.

Limburg beat six other finalists, from Brazil, Turkey, the US, Canada, Spain and Taiwan. Last year’s winner was Durham Region in Canada. The Brainport region around Eindhoven won in 2011.

World.title: Self-employment declines as freelancers quickly find new jobs
World.content:
After two decades of mostly uninterrupted growth, self-employment in the Netherlands has declined this year for the first time, with former freelancers quickly finding new jobs, according to the Dutch central bank (DNB).

There are 10% fewer self-employed workers this year than in 2024. Their numbers have fallen by some 131,000 since the end of 2024, when they peaked at almost 1.3 million.

In mid-2026, around 12% of the workforce was primarily self-employed, still a substantial share by international standards.

Little impact on unemployment

But according to the DNB, the decline has had little impact on unemployment, with half of former freelancers finding paid work within three months. About a third move to permanent positions or to jobs with prospects of a permanent contract. Others move into flex work. Only 7% become unemployed, which is comparable to previous years.

“Leaving self-employment therefore mainly results in movement within the labour market rather than a greater flow into unemployment,” the DNB said.

About half of former self-employed workers move to different sectors entirely, especially healthcare and social care, education and government, retail, transport and hospitality.

The DNB says this confirms that the Dutch labour market is dynamic. However, its research does not show how people’s income, productivity or employment conditions change after they leave self-employment for new work.

The DNB says it cannot say definitively why the decrease is happening. It does note that stricter enforcement against so-called false self-employment since 2025 may play a role.

“We observe relatively high levels of movement between self-employment and employment in sectors where false self-employment is frequently debated, including healthcare, construction, facility services and business services,” it said.

World.title: Former parliamentarian targeted for banned Israeli wine purchase
World.content:
A complaint has been filed against former orthodox Protestant SGP MP Roelof Bisschop, who said publicly that he had bought wine in protest against the Dutch ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements, public broadcaster NOS reported.

Pro-Palestinian group BDS Netherlands (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions) filed the criminal complaint with the public prosecution service (OM). Activists had earlier reported Bisschop to the fiscal investigation service FIOD.

Bisschop bought two bottles on September 23, the day after the ban took effect, and posted a photo of them on social media. Two days later he told Christian television channel Family7 that the purchase was a “statement” against the ban.

Since September 22, the Netherlands has banned imports of goods from illegal settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories and the Golan Heights. The rules also ban buying and selling such goods, intermediary trade and any form of circumvention.

In its complaint, BDS Netherlands said Bisschop had deliberately acted against the sanctions policy and promoted this on several platforms.

“Anyone who, as a former MP, publicly announces they are deliberately testing the law can expect the OM to look at whether that is a criminal offence,” the group said in the complaint.

It is not yet clear whether the wine is covered by the ban. The producer, Teperberg Winery, has vineyards in the occupied West Bank and is on a UN list of companies active in settlements. However, it says these wines are made just inside Israel. Bisschop told NOS he did not know exactly where the bottles came from.

The OM said it is aware of the complaint and will assess whether there are grounds to open an investigation.

World.title: Dutch wartime biography pulled from shelves over falsehoods
World.content:
The biography of 99-year-old Dutchman Willem Wilbrink, Getekend voor het leven in Dachau en Indië (Marked for Life in Dachau and the Dutch East Indies), has been taken off bookshelves and online platforms at the publisher’s request after researchers found his claims of being a resistance hero and Dachau survivor were likely untrue.

The 2023 biography by author Laurens van Aggelen recounts Wilbrink’s claims that he was imprisoned in the Dachau concentration camp at the age of 16, where he allegedly saved 40 people’s lives. He claimed he took people who had been sent to the incineration ovens but were still alive to the infirmary.

But an investigation published in the history magazine Historisch Nieuwsblad earlier this month by Hans Vogelzang, whose wife’s father was imprisoned in Dachau, found no supporting evidence for Wilbrink’s claims in either camp memoirs or archives. He wasn’t even listed in the camp’s complete prisoner list, which is said to be extremely accurate.

Wilbrink is a well-known figure, a regular at Second World War commemorations where he wears medals that have also come under suspicion, including a Polish “hero title”. Several Dachau survivors have no memory of the stories he told.

Lingering doubts

According to GLD news, the Dachau Committee has doubted Wilbrink’s war story since 2024. “We have been closely involved in the article for several weeks,” said Wimar Jaeger, mayor of Zutphen and chairman of the Dutch Dachau Committee. “It’s not a surprise. The biography of Wilbrink that came out… raised a lot of questions for us. We couldn’t believe what was in there. It was almost impossible.”

At the time, the committee tried to get the publisher to withdraw the book. “We’re not out for a publicity wave that harms a 99-year-old man,” Jaeger told GLD. “He is a vulnerable elderly gentleman whose war trauma may have left him with images in his head that are not in line with reality. As a committee, we know what war trauma can do to memories and we are empathetic and understanding about it.”

But as the falsehoods continued to be presented as facts, the committee took more public action. “Then we have no choice but to make clear in this way that it’s not right. Facts and reality must be safeguarded, because if they turn out not to be correct, you no longer have a cautionary tale. That is especially important at a time like this, which in various respects resembles the run-up to the Second World War.”

Author Van Aggelen has rejected the criticism and says he stands by his biography, while Wilbrink himself has called the Historisch Nieuwsblad article “slander and libel” and maintains Dachau’s records were incomplete. The publisher, White Elephant Media in Arnhem, has yet to comment.

World.title: Police quietly seize left-wing activist server for US government
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Amsterdam police have seized a server belonging to Autistici/Inventati (A/I), a dissolved hacker network that provided online services and support to left-wing political groups. The US says this included Antifa, which the Trump administration has designated a terror organisation.

The server, located at the Science Park in the east of the city, was taken without any public announcement by local police. A spokesperson told NRC that an image of the server would go “straight to America”.

Trade association Dutch Cloud Community has demanded clarity over why the police agreed to the US’ demand. The public prosecution department has also made no official statement about the incident.

Politicians have also expressed dismay over the seizure. MP Barbara Kathmann, of opposition party PRO, told the Volkskrant it “sets a dangerous precedent”.

In September, after A/I shut down its services, Kathmann and D66 MP Sarah El Boujdaini warned in a letter to parliament that the US could paralyse European internet providers for political purposes.

Similar fears have arisen over the potential acquisition of Solvinity, the cloud provider that hosts Dutch government services like DigiD, by an American company.

World.title: ABN Amro caught in crossfire amid ICC sanctions
World.content:
Dutch bank ABN Amro, which handles the finances of the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, could face heavy US penalties if it keeps doing so once American sanctions take effect next April, RTL has reported.

The US government announced sanctions against the ICC last week, a significant escalation after it had already sanctioned 13 of the court’s judges and officials. The US says the court threatens American service personnel, and has attacked its decision to issue arrest warrants for Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant.

The sanctions will freeze any ICC assets in the US and bar Americans from providing funds, goods or services to the court. The measures have been delayed for 180 days to allow time for diplomatic talks, and are due to take full effect on April 7, 2027.

ABN Amro is exposed through ABN Amro Clearing, the division that settles share trades for clients and has a large US business. RTL reported that this gives Washington the leverage to fine the bank, bring criminal charges or, in the worst case, put ABN Amro itself on the sanctions list.

The Financieele Dagblad reported that the clearing division made a net profit of €298 million in 2025. The Dutch state is ABN Amro’s largest shareholder.

It is not clear how real the risk is. “The legislation is not at all clearly worded,” Cedric Ryngaert, professor of international public law at Utrecht University, told RTL. He said the uncertainty creates a “chilling effect”, because companies cannot tell whether they are covered.

The cabinet has condemned the sanctions. Prime minister Rob Jetten called them “deeply regrettable” but said dialogue with Washington was still important.

Legal experts and campaign groups want the European Commission to activate the EU’s blocking statute, which would bar European companies from complying with the US measures.

The cabinet previously told MPs it would push for activation if new sanctions were expected to seriously hamper the court’s work.

If that happened, ABN Amro could be forced to choose between breaking EU rules and breaking US ones, RTL said.

Many more municipalities in Poland will be allowed to charge a daily fee for tourists and other overnight visitors after a change to the law dropping environmental requirements for levying such charges. Kraków, which received 8.7 million overnight tourists last year, had in particular been pushing for the change. However, Poland as a whole has seen a recent boom in visitor numbers, recording the EU’s second-fastest growth in the number of nights in tourist accommodation last year. #Krakow #opłataturystyczna #ustawa 🚨🔥Z OSTATNIEJ CHWILI! 🔥🚨 📢 Prezydent RP podpisał nowelizację przepisów dotyczących podatków i opłat lokalnych, PIT oraz PCC. 🏨 Najważniejsze zmiany dla branży turystycznej dotyczą opłaty miejscowej i uzdrowiskowej. 🗓️ Od 2027 r. za jej… pic.twitter.com/9ATvENvNol — Kraków (@krakow_pl) October 15, 2026 Until now, a “visitor’s fee” could be levied by municipalities with beneficial climatic features, “scenic qualities” and the capacity to accommodate people visiting to benefit from these attributes, as well as localities in areas with the status of a “spa protection area”. In practice, this largely applied to seaside and mountain resorts. Kraków did charge a visitor’s fee between 2004 and 2015, but was subsequently unable to do so due to a toughening of environmental requirements. The city has long suffered from bad air pollution, though it has taken significant steps to tackle the issue. Now, under new legislation proposed by the government earlier this year and signed into law by President Karol Nawrocki this week, the requirement for beneficial climatic features has been scrapped, meaning many more places will be able to charge the visitor’s fee. From 1 January, municipalities with scenic qualities will be able to charge visitors up to 5 zloty (€1.14) for each night they stay in hotels, guesthouses and short-term rental accommodation for up to one month, a rise on the current maximum of 3.46 zloty. Additionally, whereas previously only people visiting for the purposes of tourism had to pay, the fee now applies to all visits, including for work or health purposes, reports broadcaster TVN. People with significant disabilities, children with certified disabilities and their carers will be exempt from the fee. In another change, fees will be collected directly by accommodation providers, who will be required to maintain detailed records, reports the Infor news service. Passing fees on in a timely manner will entitle providers to receive at least 10% of the money they collect. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 In 2024, Kraków appealed to the government to be allowed to charge tourists a fee, noting that “overtourism leads to tensions and social discontent”, as the “local community suffers” and “residents increasingly feel like tourists in their own city”. With its UNESCO-listed Old Town, Wawel royal castle, and former Jewish district of Kazimierz, Kraków is regularly named as one of Europe’s best tourist destinations. Last year, a record 16.25 million people visited the city, of whom 8.7 million stayed overnight. While that is a boon to the local economy, it also often causes tensions with residents, who complain about noise and disruption. In 2024, the city created the new position of “night mayor”, whose role is to reconcile the needs of tourists, businesses and residents. Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb. Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026 Following this week’s change to the law, Kraków city hall confirmed that it would now again be able to collect a visitor’s fee “if the statutory conditions are satisfied and the municipal council adopts an appropriate resolution”. The city’s recently elected new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, who will be sworn in next week, said before Sunday’s election that he was in favour of a tourist tax of at least 20 zloty per night, four times the new maximum. “In western European cities there are rates of that size and higher,” Gibała said, quoted by financial news service Money.pl. “Maintaining the city in the face of the influx of tourists is costly. In Kraków, private business owners profit from tourism, whilst the city and its residents foot the bill.” Poland as a whole has also experienced a boom in tourism. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-largest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Its increase of 7% was behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta (9.9%). Poland’s interior ministry has withdrawn a proposal to make it a criminal offence, punishable by up to three years in prison, to provide support to migrants who are in the country illegally. The idea had prompted criticism from human rights groups and even opposition from within the government. The interior ministry said the amendment had been intended to clamp down on migrant smuggling. But activists feared it would criminalise humanitarian aid, such as that provided to migrants who have irregularly crossed the border from Belarus. Za udzielenie bezinteresownej pomocy migrantom nie będzie groziła kara do trzech lat więzienia. Po burzy, którą wywołała publikacja „Rzeczpospolitej” i po sprzeciwie resortu rodziny, MSWiA wycofuje się z pomysłu „karania za podanie posiłku”.https://t.co/Q0N52IMRVn — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 15, 2026 Under current Polish law, anyone who facilitates the illegal stay of a person in Poland in exchange for financial or personal benefit can be jailed for up to five years. However, this week, the interior ministry proposed an amendment that would also have penalised anyone who knowingly “enabled or facilitated” the illegal stay of someone in Poland, even if not for financial or personal benefit. The offence would have been punishable by up to three years in prison. “Currently, this behaviour is not criminalised, creating a loophole for those who exploit such situations and, under the pretext of helping migrants, aid them in their illegal stay, thus serving as a springboard for further illegal migration,” wrote deputy interior minister Czesław Mroczek, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily. That immediately prompted concern that the law could be used against volunteers and residents of border areas who provide aid – such as food, water, medical treatment, clothing or shelter – to migrants who have crossed illegally from Belarus. Since 2021, tens of thousands of people, mainly from Asia and Africa, have tried to cross that border with the encouragement and support of the Belarusian authorities. They have sometimes used violence against Polish border officers. Poland and the EU accuse Belarus of “weaponising” migration as part of the “hybrid warfare” being waged by Russia and its allies against European countries. They have implemented tough border protection measures to prevent crossings and facilitate “pushbacks” of those who cross. However, many human rights and aid organisations argue that the migrants – over 100 of whom have died around the border since 2021 – are often victims of this process and need humanitarian support. Two dead bodies found in the river on Poland's border with Belarus likely belong to migrants from a group seen being pushed into the water by Belarusian officers as part of efforts to encourage irregular crossings into the EU, says a Polish minister https://t.co/xsnPd6FeO3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2025 In response to the interior ministry’s proposal, 61 organisations, including Amnesty International, the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights and the Auschwitz-Birkenau Foundation, signed a joint statement condemning the plans, which they said “violate international standards binding Poland”. The organisations warned that the proposed wording could expose medical staff treating migrants, lawyers providing legal assistance, facilities working with children, and organisations supporting victims of human trafficking to criminal liability. “This measure is not aimed at smugglers, but rather at activists or residents of border areas who provide humanitarian aid to foreign nationals who have crossed the border illegally and are present in Poland,” attorney Radosław Baszuk told the Rzeczpospolita daily. Baszuk previously represented five Polish activists who were prosecuted for providing food, clothing and shelter to a group of Middle Eastern migrants who had entered Poland from Belarus in 2022. A group of five activists have been found not guilty of enabling the illegal presence in Poland of Middle Eastern migrants whom they provided aid to after they had irregularly crossed the border from Belarus. Prosecutors had been seeking prison sentences https://t.co/RpfhVWL4hY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 8, 2025 They were acquitted last year, with the ruling made final in March this year after an appeal. But Baszuk told Rzeczpospolita that, under the interior ministry’s proposed amendment to the relevant law, his clients could been convicted. On Wednesday, Poland’s commissioner for human rights, Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram, also wrote to the justice ministry to “express concern” that the proposed changes “could lead to criminal liability for charitable or humanitarian activities undertaken towards individuals whose residence status has not yet been regulated”. Even a member of the government, the minister for family, labour and social policy, Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk, expressed her “firm opposition” to the plans on social media. She is from The Left (Lewica), one of the junior partners in Poland’s ruling coalition. ‼️ Ciepły posiłek, nocleg, potrzebne leki – za to wolontariusz ma trafić do więzienia nawet na 3 lata? 😡 Nie ma zgody Lewicy na kryminalizowanie pomocy humanitarnej! Ministra Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk zwróciła się do ministra Waldemara Żurka ze stanowczym sprzeciwem wobec… pic.twitter.com/QskUfJmgsu — Lewica (@__Lewica) October 14, 2026 In response to the growing criticism, the interior ministry announced on Friday that it was withdrawing the proposal, saying it decided to do so “to eliminate any doubts and prevent the misinterpretation of regulations”. “From the beginning, the ministry’s sole objective has been to tighten the system and target the organisers of this practice [of migrant smuggling],” said the ministry, quoted by Rzeczpospolita. “Legal provisions must effectively protect the state’s borders against organised crime, while simultaneously fully safeguarding humanitarian values ​and life-saving activities.” The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Both the former Polish government and the current one, which took power in December 2023, have regularly faced criticism from human rights groups over their response to the migration crisis on the Belarus border. Earlier this year, the previous human rights commissioner, Marcin Wiącek, expressed concern over a ban on asylum claims introduced by the government in March 2025. He noted that the measures had been described as a temporary solution, but have remained in place ever since. The government, however, argues that its measures have been effective in preventing the illegal trafficking of migrants. Its data show that attempted border crossings from Belarus fell from around 15,500 in the first half of last year to less than 250 in the same period this year – a drop of over 98%. It also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally. Było to pierwsze bezpośrednie, robocze spotkanie szefów tych instytucji od 2018 r. ➡️ Stronie polskiej przewodniczył kierujący… pic.twitter.com/qHpZwLeCEa — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) October 14, 2026 News of the meeting was announced on social media by Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which noted that it was “the first direct, working meeting between the heads of these institutions since 2018”. The IPN is currently headed by its deputy president, Karol Polejowski, because Poland’s parliament has been unable to agree on a permanent new president. The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINR) is led by Oleksandr Alfyorov. “The first topic of discussion,” according to the IPN, was the planned reburial of 115 Polish soldiers recently exhumed in Lviv, where they died in 1939 defending the city (then part of Poland and known as Lwów) during the Nazi-German and Soviet invasions. Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of 115 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending Lviv – now in Ukraine but then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of WWII https://t.co/yQNeq2D54E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026 Their exhumation resulted from a diplomatic breakthrough last year between Warsaw and Kyiv that saw Ukraine lift a moratorium on exhumations that had been in place since 2017 in protest at the dismantling in Poland of a monument to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). Ukraine has also allowed the exhumation on its territory of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres, which were led by the UPA. Poland likewise recently granted permission for Ukraine to search for Ukrainian victims of a massacre led by the Polish Home Army in the village of Łasków (Laskiv in Ukrainian). At this week’s meeting, the UINR gave an update on its work in Łasków, where it has uncovered the remains of 30 people. The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance has found 30 human remains in a village in Poland where Polish partisans killed Ukrainian civilians in WW2 It thanked Poland for permission to search the site, calling it a step towards "true reconciliation" https://t.co/BeeEtl6gCa — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026 The IPN and UINR also discussed planned exhumation work in the now-depopulated village of Huta Pieniacka (Huta Peniatska in Ukrainian), where the local Polish population was massacred in 1944 by a Nazi SS regiment mainly made up of Ukrainians. There was also “willingness on both sides to restore cooperation in the field of historical scientific research”, said the IPN. “The possibility of undertaking joint educational initiatives was also discussed.” The two sides also agreed to hold another meeting in Warsaw, though no date has been set. This week’s meeting comes after a period of tension over historical issues between not only Poland and Ukraine more broadly, but also the two countries’ remembrance institutes. In February this year, the IPN criticised Alfyorov over an interview in which he initially called the Volhynia massacres “one of Poland’s state myths”, before later appearing to correct himself and saying it was “not a myth, but one of the key elements of the Polish grand narrative”. By contrast, “for most Ukrainians, this is just a local episode of history”, added Alfyorov. Referring to Poland’s recognition of the massacres as a genocide – a term Ukraine rejects – he asked if Polish massacres of around 28,000 Ukrainians during the war should also be called a genocide. In response, the IPN called Alfyorov’s remarks “outrageous” and declared that the Volhynia massacres were “not an ‘episode’, but rather one of the largest genocides against civilians in 20th-century Europe”. It also condemned Ukraine for honouring figures associated with the massacres. The UINR, for its part, criticised a law proposed by Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki (a former head of the IPN), that would criminalise the promotion of ideologies associated with World War Two Ukrainian nationalist groups. Ukraine has criticised a law proposed by Poland's president that would criminalise promotion of historical Ukrainian nationalist ideologies, equating them with Nazism and communism It warns of "retaliatory measures" if the bill is passed https://t.co/TaX2Vj5z8v — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2025 In another sign of reconciliation, in May the UINR and Poland’s Mieroszewski Centre held a historical congress in Warsaw, bringing together more than 100 historians “to discuss complex issues of the shared past and explore common approaches to their interpretation”, in the words of the Ukrainian foreign ministry. However, that same month, President Volodymyr Zelensky prompted a diplomatic crisis by approving the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. Since then, both sides have made efforts to reach a diplomatic solution, including a pledge by Zelensky to “grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. World.title: Ukraine finds remains of 30 people in search for victims of massacre by Polish WWII partisans
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINR) has reported the discovery of 30 human remains at a site in Poland where Polish partisans killed Ukrainian civilians during World War Two. The head of the UINR, Oleksandr Alfyorov, thanked Poland for granting permission to conduct research at the location, which he said would help advance “true reconciliation” between the two countries over their difficult shared history. Ukraine has likewise recently allowed Poland to search for and exhume the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists during the war. At the end of August, the Polish authorities approved a request from Ukraine to conduct a search in the village of Łasków in southeastern Poland, around 10km from the border with Ukraine. On 10 March 1944, units of the Home Army (Armia Krajowa) and Peasant Battalions (Bataliony Chłopskie), two major Polish underground resistance movements that emerged during the Nazi-German occupation, attacked Łasków, which had a predominantly ethnic Ukrainian population. Estimates suggest that around 300 civilians were killed. Among them was a local Orthodox priest, Lev Korobchuk. On the same day, members of the Home Army also attacked the nearby village of Sahryń, where they are estimated to have killed hundreds more Ukrainians. Ukraine has also submitted an application to carry out exploratory work there. Poland has granted permission for Ukraine to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during WWII https://t.co/4JeAAhYJcY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 2, 2026 Work began in Łasków on 6 October and, on Wednesday this week, the UINR announced that it had “discovered the remains of 30 victims…[who] died as a result of the attack of the units of the Home Army and the Peasant Battalion in March 1944″. Svyatoslav Sheremeta, the head of the Lviv-based Dolya memorial and search centre, which carried out the work on behalf of the UINR, said that they now hope to “conduct exhumation, rebury the dead, and honour their memory with dignity”. “Thank you to the Polish side for the opportunity to conduct research,” added Alfyorov. “Our common task is to ensure a worthy commemoration of all victims, regardless of their origin and nationality.” “True reconciliation begins with respect for everyone’s memory, recognition of the pain of the other side, and the common desire for understanding,” said the head of UNIP, which shared images from the search site in Łasków’s Orthodox cemetery. At the time of writing, Polish officials had not yet commented on the development. However, when search work began last week, Rafał Kościański, a spokesman for Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), told Radio Lublin that IPN staff were participating as observers. Wiesław Koman, from the Provincial Office for the Protection of Monuments, added that cooperation between Polish and Ukrainian archaeologists at the site had been “impeccable”. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, told the broadcaster that the work in Łasków was “a step towards reconciliation between our nations”. “This is happening on both sides of the border and demonstrates the openness of both sides to commemorating the victims of the past conflict,” said Bodnar. “There are differing voices from different sides of the political arena, but this is the right path, one we should have been on for a long time.” Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of 115 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending Lviv – now in Ukraine but then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of WWII https://t.co/yQNeq2D54E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026 The legacy of wartime massacres has long overshadowed relations between Poland and Ukraine, who have otherwise become close allies since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches on its territory for Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists massacred around 100,000 ethnic Poles, mostly women and children. Poland has recognised those massacres as a genocide. Ukraine rejects the use of that term, and also points to anti-Ukrainian repression in the interwar Polish state and the massacres of Ukrainian civilians carried out by Polish partisans during the war. In a diplomatic breakthrough last year, Kyiv agreed to lift its moratorium on exhumations. Since then, it has granted permission for Poland to conduct searches and exhumations at a number of locations. The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 However, tensions over historical issues reemerged this year, when President Volodymyr Zelensky approved the naming of a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”, the group that led the Volhynia massacres. That prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. However, the two sides subsequently made efforts to reach a diplomatic solution, including a pledge by Zelensky to “grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. Poland’s energy ministry has signed an agreement with two state-owned companies, Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe (PEJ) and Polska Grupa Energetyczna (PGE), setting out responsibilities for preparing for the construction of Poland’s planned second nuclear power plant. “This is an investment in our security, sovereignty and economic development,” declared energy minister Miłosz Motyka. “Having our own stable energy sources strengthens Poland’s resilience to crises and reduces dependence on external suppliers.” ❗️ @ME_GOV_PL, @PEJ_PL i @Grupa_PGE podpisały dziś porozumienie określające zasady współpracy przy przygotowaniu budowy drugiej polskiej elektrowni jądrowej 🇵🇱 Polska jest 20. gospodarką świata, ale nasze ambicje sięgają wyżej. Nie będzie silnej, niezależnej gospodarki bez… pic.twitter.com/eQ7zWFEolh — Miłosz Motyka (@motykamilosz) October 13, 2026 Under the agreement, PEJ, which is also responsible for developing a first nuclear project that is already underway on Poland’s northern Baltic Sea coast, will act as the investor and coordinate the project. PGE, the country’s largest power producer, will prepare preliminary feasibility studies and analyse potential locations for the plant. However, a decision on selecting an international partner for the project is not expected to be made until next year. The potential candidates include US company Westinghouse, which is involved in the first nuclear power plant, France’s EDF, and Canada’s AtkinsRéalis. The second plant was initially envisaged as a joint project with Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP), a South Korean company, under a letter of intent signed in 2022 under Poland’s former government. However, the partnership was never formalised and fell through last year. Once the new partner has been selected, it will work with PGE to analyse potential sites. The current preferred locations are Bełchatów – home to the largest coal-fired power station in Europe, owned by PGE – and Konin, both in central Poland, because of their existing energy infrastructure and experience in electricity generation. According to the Polish government’s nuclear strategy – which was last month updated for the first time since 2020 – construction of the second plant is scheduled to begin in 2032, with its first reactor potentially entering service in 2040. That would be one year behind the previously planned schedule. The government has updated Poland's nuclear strategy for the first time in six years, with the new plan confirming that the first nuclear plant will launch three years later than previously planned, in 2036, and the second in 2040, one year behind schedule https://t.co/vgtuSXLDjZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 3, 2026 Meanwhile, Poland plans to begin construction of its first nuclear power station in 2028, with the plant beginning operation in 2036, three years later than previously planned. Together, the two plants are expected to have a combined capacity of up to 9 gigawatts. The move is part of Poland’s transition away from coal – which still generates around half of electricity, by far the highest proportion in the European Union – and towards cleaner sources of energy, particularly nuclear and renewables. Under a national energy and climate plan approved in June, Poland aims by 2040 for coal to account for only 0-5% of the energy mix. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%).
