World.title: Everything you need to know one year ahead of Poland’s parliamentary elections
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles Poland will hold parliamentary elections a year from now. The outcome will decide who governs the country for the next four years – although, given how close the polls are, and with questions over coalition formation, it could also result in uncertainty, chaos, and even new elections being called. Below, we explain how the elections work, which parties will be standing, what kind of outcomes are possible, and which issues may animate the campaign. When will the election take place? Assuming early elections are not called, the vote must take place on a non-working day in the last 30 days before the end of the current four-year parliamentary term, which began on 13 November 2023. Because elections in Poland are held on Sundays, that gives four possible dates: 17, 24 or 31 October, or 7 November (though 1 November and 11 November, which are public holidays, are also theoretically possible). It is the president, Karol Nawrocki, who will choose the date. He must do so no later than 90 days before the end of the current parliamentary term. How does voting work? The 460 members of the more powerful lower house, the Sejm, are elected through proportional representation, meaning that seats are distributed more or less on the basis of the share of the vote parties receive (using the so-called D’Hondt method for allocating seats from electoral lists put forward by each party). However, parties must receive at least 5% of the vote nationally to enter parliament (a figure that rises to 8% for coalitions of parties who stand on a single electoral list). The 100 members of the upper-house Senate are chosen through a first-past-the-post system similar to how members of the US Congress or British House of Commons are elected, with the candidate in each district that receives the most votes winning the seat. How is a government formed? A government can only be formed if it can win a vote of confidence in the Sejm. After the elections, the president designates a prime minister, who is tasked with forming a government – which would almost certainly be made up of a coalition of parties – that must then win a vote of confidence. If they fail to do so (as happened in 2023), the Sejm votes to choose an alternative prime minister, who likewise must try to form a government that has the confidence of the Sejm. Parliament has chosen @donaldtusk as Poland's new prime minister. That paves the way for him to form a new government in the coming days, ending the eight-year rule of the national-conservative PiS party https://t.co/iZUKh2rxnP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2023 If that fails, the president has a second chance to pick a prime minister, who must again win a confidence vote. However, whereas the previous two votes require an absolute majority (większość bezwzględna) to be carried, this time only a simple majority is needed, making it easier to form a minority government. If this third and final attempt does not work, then parliament is dissolved and new elections are called. Who is likely to form the next government? At the moment, it is incredibly difficult to say. Polls suggest an even split in support between parties generally aligned with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – and the right-wing opposition. However, the 5% electoral threshold complicates the picture. According to current polling averages compiled by Polish website eWybory and Politico Europe, Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) leads with 32%. One of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), is on 7%, while two others, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), are on around 3% and 1%, respectively. Another left-wing party, Together (Razem), which previously caucused with the ruling coalition but split in 2024, is on around 4%. Meanwhile, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, is on 20%. Two far-right opposition groups, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have 14% and 9%, respectively. The right-wing Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which broke away from PiS this year, is at around 5%. If we treat those as two potential blocs, parties more or less aligned with the current government are on around 47% while the right-wing opposition is on 48%. However, PSL and Poland 2050 currently look likely to fall below the 5% threshold if they stand alone, meaning votes for them would not count. That would significantly harm Tusk’s chances of forming a new government. If Rozwój Plus stood alone and fell below the threshold, that would harm the opposition. It is therefore likely that, as the elections draw nearer, parties that seem likely to fall below 5% will seek to join forces with other groups. In 2023, PSL and Poland 2050 stood together in the so-called Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance. But they have made clear they do not intend to do that again. That leaves them with limited options. They could join forces with KO on a single electoral list, but that does not guarantee that their voters will follow them. Indeed, some may baulk at voting for Tusk’s party. The Polish People's Party's parliamentary survival is on a knife edge, and could determine whether @donaldtusk's coalition remains in power after next year's elections.@AleksSzczerbiak looks at the challenges facing PSL and how it may respond to them https://t.co/MmswSLNWJE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026 Meanwhile, there are some wildcards in the pack. KKP, led by radical-right extremist Grzegorz Braun, is shunned by the mainstream right for its antisemitism, anti-Americanism and sympathy towards Russia. PiS’s leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, has declared that he would not allow Braun to join government. Development Plus has taken a similar position. Both parties value relations with the US and the Trump administration, whose ambassador to Poland has reportedly pushed them to rule out working with Braun. However, if KKP maintains its current level of support, it looks almost impossible for the opposition to form a parliamentary majority without it, meaning there would be a strong temptation to somehow work with Braun. Kaczyński’s determination to remove Tusk from power may outweigh his dislike of Braun and desire to keep the Americans onside. The Together party – if it manages to pass the 5% threshold – could likewise represent a challenge for Tusk when forming a coalition, given that it has criticised the government for failing to keep promises on healthcare spending, public sector pay, and liberalising the abortion law. There also remains the possibility of some elements from each camp joining the other side – either entire parties or individual MPs defecting – in order to help form a government. PiS has long sought to tempt PSL to its side (and recent reports suggest that even President Donald Trump tried to persuade PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, to do so). It is conceivable that Rozwój Plus could work with parts of the current ruling camp, though its hatred of Tusk would make that very difficult. All of the difficulties outlined above mean there is a significant chance that it will not be possible for anyone to form a government, necessitating fresh elections – something that has never happened before in Poland. If that happens, it would mean uncertainty and a lack of clear leadership at a time when Poland is facing major security challenges and a worsening fiscal situation. What about the Senate? The Senate, like the Sejm, is currently controlled by the ruling coalition. Indeed, Tusk has an even larger majority there than in the lower house, making it harder for the opposition to flip. Although the Senate is much weaker than the Sejm – and control of it does not determine who forms the government – it does have some powers that make it a useful asset. It can slow down the passage of legislation, though not block it. The Senate also must approve the appointment of certain officials, such as the heads of the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights (RPO). In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) https://t.co/QUsqfDNh4s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026 The upper house is also required to approve proposals by the president to hold national referendums. This year, the Senate has twice blocked moves by Nawrocki to hold a referendum on EU climate policies. In a situation where Tusk’s coalition controlled the Sejm, and was therefore still in government, but the right-wing opposition held the Senate, that would give the president a powerful tool to call referendums on policies important to him and the opposition. To that end, there have been calls for the right-wing and far-right opposition to form a so-called Senate pact, of the type that Tusk and his allies used to win control of the upper house in 2019 and 2023. What that means in practice is that the parties forming the pact agree to stand only one candidate between them in each of the 100 Senate districts, making it more likely that they will scoop up votes from supporters of all the parties in the pact and win the winner-takes-all contest. What role will Nawrocki play in all of this? Presidents are in theory expected to be non-partisan. In practice, however, they will seek to boost parties or coalitions aligned with them, and with whom it will be easier to work. Since Nawrocki was elected last year, relations and cooperation between the president and government have reached unprecedently low levels. Within just 10 months, Nawrocki had vetoed more bills than any previous president in history over their entire terms. He has made it abundantly clear that he would prefer to work with a government formed from the right-wing opposition. During his first year, President Nawrocki has transformed his office into a centre of resistance to the government and become a unifying figure for the fragmented right. But he faces new challenges moving towards the next election, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/uNYrFOppSp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 However, the extent to which he will be involved in the election campaign is unclear. Some figures on the right hope that Nawrocki will act as a figurehead, using his positive relations with parties across the right-wing opposition to bring them together. In practical terms, this could involve him acting as the patron of a Senate pact (something the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet recently said the president was willing to do), as well as helping right-wing parties form a coalition government after the elections. Nawrocki also continues to enjoy strong approval ratings among the conservative electorate, meaning that his presence during the election campaign could act as a boost for the opposition. What issues are likely to feature in the campaign? A major issue will be the question of sovereignty. The right-wing opposition accuses Tusk of being Brussels’ and Berlin’s lapdog, handing over ever more power to the EU and prioritising Germany’s interests over Poland’s. The ruling coalition, meanwhile, argues that PiS is too beholden to the Trump administration and warns that the opposition is pushing Poland towards “Polexit” from the EU, which would leave the country isolated and vulnerable, as well as much poorer. Those battle lines extend to security policy too, with the Tusk government shifting emphasis towards Europe as a defence partner but PiS insisting that only the US can truly guarantee Poland’s security. Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base has already become highly politicised. If progress stalls, the opposition will blame the government. If Washington confirms that the base will go ahead, Nawrocki will seek to take the credit, based on his good relationship with Trump. On this point, though, it is worth noting the split within the opposition. While PiS and Rozwój Plus are strongly pro-American, Confederation and, to an even greater extent, KKP, are opposed to a greater US presence in Poland. President @NawrockiKn says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”. He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump” https://t.co/uGGJSBe5nr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 23, 2026 Where the right-wing opposition has been united, however, is on pushing for a tougher position towards Ukraine and Ukrainian refugees in Poland. While tensions have calmed significantly since the crisis sparked in May by President Volodymyr Zelensky naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, it is likely that relations with Ukraine and the large-scale presence of Ukrainians in Poland will remain important issues during the election campaign. The ruling coalition, meanwhile, will be keen to emphasise its tough overall approach to immigration, which it says was out of control under the former PiS government. It can point to the falling number of new residence permits being issued, the growing number of deportations, and tougher measures on the Belarus border, including a ban on asylum claims. Poland has forcibly removed 2,100 foreigners from the country this year, around twice as many as in 2024. The figures come after the government introduced a tougher new migration policy last year, which has included more deportations of foreign criminals https://t.co/zOBxPLipy8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 31, 2025 The economy, public finances and cost of living are also likely to be major issues. As long as the current global energy crisis sparked by the conflict around Iran continues, the opposition will seek to place the blame for record fuel prices on the government. They will also cite large deficits and the ballooning public debt as evidence that Tusk is mismanaging the economy. The ruling coalition will point to continued strong economic growth and blame Nawrocki, who has vetoed revenue-generating tax bills, for the fiscal situation. In one of his first policy announcements since being elected on Sunday, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of its annual LGBT+ equality march. Łukasz Gibała, who has been supportive of LGBT+ rights in the past and has previously attended the march, argues that the event has become too “partisan”. He stood for election as an independent and has pledged to depoliticise city hall. His decision does not prevent the march from taking place. But it means that it no longer has the official support of the city. Łukasz Gibała: Nie obejmę patronatem Marszu Równości. Polityka progresywna nie zawsze się sprawdza https://t.co/vIw8ZsSPQK — Radio Kraków (@RadioKrakow) October 12, 2026 Kraków’s equality march, which was first held in 2004, draws thousands of participants when it takes place each year in May. The event is used to demand greater LGBT+ rights in Poland, which is ranked as one of the worst countries in Europe for LGBT+ people. In 2021, the city’s former mayor, Jacek Majchrowski, became an honorary patron of the march. In 2024, his successor, Aleksander Miszalski, became the first mayor to attend the event, declaring that Kraków should be “a home for everyone”. However, Miszalski was removed from office earlier this year in a recall referendum, necessitating a new election, which was won by Gibała. He beat Monika Piątkowska, who, like Miszaski, is a member of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Kraków's new mayor has announced that he will attend the city’s LGBT parade next week, something his long-serving predecessor never did. "I want to build a tolerant Kraków, a home for everyone," says @OlekMiszalski, who took office this week https://t.co/ZQ9SzZiHp4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 9, 2024 The day after his victory, Gibała was asked by local broadcaster Radio Kraków if he would continue city hall’s patronage of the equality march. The new mayor, who takes office next week, declared that he would not, saying he “will avoid sponsoring events that have a partisan character”. “I have the impression that, over the past three years or so, the community that organises equality marches has simply become partisan,” said Gibała. “These are people who ran for parliament and local government on the lists of specific political parties.” Gibała did not indicate who he was referring to. However, one of the organisers of the equality march in Kraków is Magdalena Dropek, who has three times stood as a candidate for The Left (Lewica), one of the groups in Tusk’s ruling coalition, in elections to the Polish and European parliaments. Gibała emphasised that he has himself attended equality marches in the past “and does not regret it”. He was previously an MP for both KO (when it was known as Civic Platform, PO) as well as for the liberal Palikot’s Movement (Ruch Palikota), later known as Your Movement (Twój Ruch). During the recent mayoral election campaign, Gibała told broadcaster TVN that, as an MP, he had supported the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships in Poland, and said that his views had not changed. When asked if that meant that, as mayor, he would continue the city’s practice of transcribing foreign same-sex marriages into the civil registry – as Poland was ordered to do last year by the Court of Justice of the European Union – Gibała said that he would. However, he added that he was doing this as a “legalist” who respects the current legal situation. “If a different political party wins [parliamentary elections] next year and changes the law in Poland, it [recognition of foreign same-sex marriages] won’t happen,” he told Radio Kraków. In fact, although the current government supports recognition of foreign-same sex marraiges, it has not changed the law in that regard. Polish law still does not recognise any form of same-sex union. The government, aware that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki would veto any change to the law, instead issued a regulation (which does not require presidential approval) empowering local authorities to transcribe foreign same-sex marriages into their registries. Many municipalities, especially more liberal larger cities, have begun to do so (some even did before the regulation was issued). But others, especially in more conservative places, have refused to, often arguing that there are legal doubts around the issue. Data provided to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) by the digital affairs ministry last week showed that 516 foreign same-sex marriages have so far been registered in Poland. The largest numbers were in Warsaw (209), Wrocław (73) and Kraków (46). The Polish government has granted same-sex couples who married abroad the same tax rights as other married couples It follows an EU court ruling ordering Poland to recognise such marriages even though domestic law does not allow any form of same-sex union https://t.co/3gE1PQU9AQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 25, 2026 In the same interview this week with Radio Kraków, Gibała was asked if he would “return to your political roots” and be a “progressive mayor”. He responded by saying that, while “there are some issues where progressive policies actually work, there are others where they don’t”. Asked for an example of the latter, Gibała said that, “if we look, for example, at what’s happening in western European cities, there are entire neighbourhoods in which there is a fear of entering for people of our skin colour”. The firm will invest over 200 million zloty (€46 million) in the facility, creating more than 100 long-term jobs. “The new facility will support Polish industry and defence capabilities and strengthen Kongsberg’s presence in Poland,” declared CEO Eirik Lie alongside Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz at the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year serving as the official partner nation. In January, Kongsberg signed an agreement to supply a new anti-drone system to Poland in partnership with Polish state defence group PGZ. World.title: Meet Paulo Dias, the Expat Behind Prague’s Pintz Beer App
World.content:
Finding a good beer in Prague is rarely a difficult task. Finding the right pub, knowing what a pint costs and deciding where to go next is a different question.

For Paulo Dias, that challenge became the idea behind Pintz, a web app built to help people navigate Prague’s rich beer scene.

Originally from Portugal, Paulo has spent almost 15 years living abroad, moving between Slovakia and the UK before eventually taking a job in the Czech Republic.



He first arrived in the Czech Republic in 2021, spending several months in Opava before moving to Prague in February 2022. Even after the move, he was cautious about settling in. “When I moved to Prague, I wasn’t buying many things for my apartment, because if I moved again, I’d have to pack everything,” Paulo recalls.

That changed once his new job became more stable. By the end of the year, he was already thinking about staying.

I think the quality of life in Prague is quite amazing. It’s one of the best, if not the best, of the cities I know. I feel good here, I feel at home. That’s why I decided to stay.”

Prague’s pub culture

Prague’s pub culture became one of the ways Paulo built a social life after moving to the city. He started with local pubs in Žižkov.

“I started to make friends there, and then I thought it was a good opportunity for me to become more social.”

What struck him was how different the culture was from Portugal. He describes drinking there as more centered around wine, home gatherings, watching football with friends or celebrating birthdays, rather than regularly meeting at pubs during the week.

“I know people who meet every Monday. It’s impossible in Portugal, this mindset. People just stay at home or go for a coffee after dinner. There’s no culture like going to a pub.”

In Prague, meeting for a beer could instead become part of an ordinary weekday. That was something Paulo gradually came to appreciate about his new home.

“I don’t need to wait for the weekend to have my social life active.”

From sneaker prices to Pintz

The idea for Pintz grew out of a sneaker-price platform “The Real Sneaker Index” Paulo had been working on in his spare time. The two projects are quite different, but the first gave him a way of thinking about how prices could be collected and compared.

The connection to beer came almost as an afterthought. Paulo was already spending time in Prague’s pubs, and the idea eventually brought his side project closer to something he was experiencing himself.

“I was thinking, maybe I could apply the same idea to something more connected to everyday life. And then I thought, why not use it to track beer prices?”

What started as a price tracker gradually expanded into a way of exploring pubs. Users can now add information about individual places, from terraces and beer gardens to the beers they serve, while ratings give people a way to share their own experiences. “It’s not only about finding the cheapest beer. It started that way, but it’s really about quality.”

Pintz is now present in the US, Mexico, Atlantic Islands and across many countries in Europe.

Building it alone with AI

Paulo has been building Pintz alongside his Lead AI Platforms job, developing the platform himself with the help of AI. He works on it in the evenings, at weekends and whenever he can find the time.

“I’m not a coder, I’m not a developer, but I know what I want to do.”

AI has allowed him to take those ideas further without having to build every part of the platform from scratch himself. He sets up processes, monitors how they work and keeps adding and improving features as the project develops.

The speed at which he can turn an idea into something functional has been one of the biggest surprises for him.

“What impressed me the most is the capability of building anything with AI, especially digital products.”

What’s next for Pintz?

For now, his focus is on getting more people to use Pintz and bringing more pubs, breweries and beer brands onto the platform. He is also looking at sponsorships and other ways of turning the project into a sustainable business.

At the same time, he is conscious of how easily monetisation could get in the way of the experience he is trying to create. He does not want users to feel like they are constantly being sold something while using the app.

“I don’t want this to become an advertising app that people are annoyed to use.”

World.title: Prague Light Park at Žluté Lázně Takes Visitors Back to the 14th Century
World.content:
Prague’s Žluté lázně has opened a new edition of the Story of Lights, a seasonal light park inspired by the city’s medieval history.

Running from October 16, 2026, to January 31, 2027, the event features illuminated sculptures, interactive installations and, from November, evening boat trips on the Vltava River.



The park takes visitors back to 14th-century Prague during the reign of Charles IV, the Bohemian king and Holy Roman Emperor whose rule helped shape the city’s development.

Thousands of LED lights illuminate the grounds after dark, forming a route through displays inspired by the architecture, symbols and history of medieval Prague.

Among the installations are illuminated representations of Charles Bridge, Gothic towers, church arches, royal crowns and coronation regalia. The displays reinterpret historical motifs using modern lighting technology.

Some installations are interactive, with the organizers targeting families with children as well as adults looking for an evening activity outdoors.

The historical theme focuses on a period when Prague underwent major urban development.

Charles IV initiated the construction of Charles Bridge, founded the New Town in 1348 and helped establish Prague as an important political, cultural and religious centre in medieval Europe.

From November 6, visitors will also be able to combine their visit with an illuminated boat trip along the Vltava. The evening cruises are scheduled for Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays.

World.title: Prague Expands Tram Network With Five Projects Underway
World.content:
Prague is expanding its tram network, with five projects now under construction across the capital.

Two new projects began in October 2026, extending the network from Malovanka to Strahov and from Libuš to Nové Dvory.

Work is also progressing on the tram line across Wenceslas Square, where the tracks have been connected between Vinohradská Street and the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.



The projects aim to improve public transport connections to developing residential areas and strengthen links with other transport services, including the future Metro Line D.

New tram line to connect Malovanka with Strahov

Construction of the new tram line from Malovanka to Strahov began on October 5, following preparatory work. The tracks will run along Vaníčkova Street, starting at Bělohorská Street and continuing toward Strahov Stadium.

The Malovanka stop will also be modified and moved to a position before the intersection, allowing it to serve trams heading toward Strahov.

The existing Stadion Strahov stop, currently used for passengers to disembark, will be renamed Strahov.

Tram extension to Nové Dvory will complement Metro Line D

Construction of the second new line, extending the tram network from Modřany through Libuš to Nové Dvory, began on October 7, 2026.

The extension will introduce two stops, Přírodní and Nové Dvory. At Nové Dvory, the line will end in a loop using Durychova, Libušská and Chýnovská streets.

The new connection is being developed alongside plans for Metro Line D and the wider expansion of the surrounding residential area. It will provide a direct tram connection to central Prague, including the Palackého náměstí area, with a future connection toward Smíchov also planned.

The extension will change operations on tram line 17. Once the project is completed, the temporary dead-end terminus in Libuš will be removed, allowing single-ended trams to return to longer routes. A second tram line is also planned for the new tracks after Metro Line D opens.

Hodkovičky gains a new tram stop

The new Hodkovičky stop, located between Belárie and Černý kůň, is another addition to Prague’s tram infrastructure in the south of the city.

The stop is intended to improve access to public transport for residents of the growing residential developments nearby. Further housing construction is also expected in Nové Dvory, where the planned tram extension will provide additional transport capacity.

Tram tracks connected across Wenceslas Square

Work on restoring tram services across Wenceslas Square is also progressing. In early autumn, construction crews connected the tracks running from Vinohradská Street, past the National Museum, across the square and toward the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.

The track infrastructure in this section is complete. Remaining work includes finishing the surrounding surfaces and installing overhead power lines.

Once these works are finished, the new line will restore tram services across Wenceslas Square, strengthening public transport connections in central Prague.

World.title: Prague Christmas Markets 2026 Start in November – Dates and Locations
World.content:
Prague’s Christmas markets will return in November 2026, with the first stalls opening at Náměstí Míru on November 20.

The main markets in Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square will follow on November 28, bringing traditional Czech food, handmade decorations and a program of seasonal performances to the city center.

Náměstí Republiky follows on November 25, and Tylovo náměstí opens on November 26.



The main markets at Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square begin on November 28 and continue until January 6, 2027. The other markets close on Christmas Eve, December 24.

Here are the opening dates and hours for the main locations.

– náměstí Míru — November 20 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– náměstí Republiky — November 25 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

– Tylovo náměsti — November 26 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– Old Town Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

– Wenceslas Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

Smaller Christmas Markets Across Prague

Several markets open before the main city-center venues and offer alternatives for visitors who want to explore different neighborhoods.

Further options include the market at Anděl and Lesser Town Christmas on Kampa Island.

náměstí Jiřího z Poděbrad will host farmers’ markets during Advent, with a design market joining them every Sunday during the season. These events offer opportunities to browse locally made products and find gifts beyond the usual Christmas-market stalls.

World.title: Modeselektor to Open Spectaculare Festival at Prague’s ROXY
World.content:
Berlin electronic duo Modeselektor will open the 14th edition of Spectaculare on 3 March 2027, bringing their live show to ROXY alongside new music from their latest album, MDSLKTR

Gernot Bronsert and Sebastian Szary will perform a set combining techno, electro, hip-hop and bass music, accompanied by visual projections and lighting.

The concert comes shortly after the release of MDSLKTR, an album that revisits the sound and influences that have shaped the duo’s nearly three-decade career.



The record follows Classics Vol. 01, a project that revisited material from their early albums Hello Mom! and Happy Birthday! and drew on years of studio recordings and unfinished ideas.

With MDSLKTR, Modeselektor return to the sounds that first defined their music, drawing on Berlin rave culture, techno, electro, IDM and hip-hop while continuing to move between genres.

Since emerging from Berlin’s underground electronic scene, the duo have built an international following through their studio albums, live performances and collaborations with artists including Radiohead frontman Thom Yorke, Tommy Cash, Flohio and Blixa Bargeld.

They also formed Moderat with producer Apparat and run the independent record label Monkeytown Records.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Festival Spectaculare (@spectaculare_music)

Berlin-based multi-instrumentalist Philipp Johann Thimm will open the evening. A longtime collaborator of Apparat, Thimm has worked across electronic and acoustic music as well as audiovisual projects. His work on Apparat’s album *LP5* contributed to a Grammy-nominated project, while his solo work explores the meeting point between electronic composition and live instrumentation.

World.title: Prague’s Día de Muertos Festival Returns to Holešovice on November 5th
World.content:
Prague’s Holešovice Market will host the fifth annual Día de Muertos festival on November 5, bringing Mexican food, live music, traditional decorations and family activities.

The event, organized in cooperation with Jarritos and Nuevo Progreso, will run from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Halls 13 and 11 will host a Mexican market and a carnival for children.

Visitors can arrive throughout the day, with the food stalls opening at lunchtime.



The selection will include Mexican and South American specialties, tortillas, grilled dishes and Jarritos soft drinks. A special beer brewed by Falcon brewery for the occasion will also be available.

The food zone will remain open until 10 p.m., giving visitors time to sample different dishes and explore the festival’s other attractions.

One of the main attractions will be a traditional ofrenda, or Day of the Dead altar, prepared by the Mexican Embassy. Decorated with photographs, flowers, candles and personal objects, the altar will introduce visitors to the traditions behind the holiday.

Día de Muertos is dedicated to remembering deceased family members and loved ones.

In Mexican tradition, the holiday celebrates their continuing place in family life and the belief that their spirits return to visit the living. Its customs differ from Halloween, combining remembrance with food, music, flowers and colorful decorations.

Hall 11 will become the PEDRO Kids’ Zone from 1 p.m. to 7 p.m., with a program designed for children and families.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Holešovická tržnice (@holesovickatrznice)

Activities will include dance workshops, Mexican music, crafts, stories about the holiday and a game in which children throw balls at illuminated skulls. Visitors will also have the opportunity to meet a Xoloitzcuintle, the Mexican hairless dog traditionally associated with guiding souls to the afterlife.

Costumes are welcome, and the organizers have divided the program into six one-hour sessions beginning at 1 p.m., 2 p.m., 3 p.m., 4 p.m., 5 p.m. and 6 p.m.

Admission costs CZK 100 per person for adults and children aged three and older. Tickets are available through GoOut and at the venue, subject to availability. Each ticket covers one hour of activities, after which visitors can explore the rest of the festival.

The program will also feature mariachi musicians, stilt walkers, colorful masks and costumes, and a festival parade. DJs will provide music throughout the day, while a screening of the animated film Coco will offer another introduction to Mexican traditions surrounding death and remembrance.

World.title: Danish-Japanese Chain Sticks’n’Sushi to Open First Prague Restaurant
World.content:
Sticks’n’Sushi will open its first Czech restaurant in central Prague on Wednesday, November 4, introducing its combination of Japanese cuisine and Danish design to the local dining scene.



The restaurant will occupy a site on Jungmannovo náměstí in Prague 1. Ahead of the official opening, guests will be able to sample the menu at half price from November 1 to 3.

Those interested in attending the preview must register online. Registered guests will then receive a link to book a table for one of the available dates.

The menu combines sushi, sashimi and salads with kushiyaki, Japanese-style grilled skewers. The restaurant will also offer set menus intended for sharing, making them suitable for groups.

Among the dishes are Beef Tataki, served with miso aïoli, truffle ponzu and crispy Jerusalem artichoke, and the Temaki Setto, which allows diners to assemble their own hand rolls with ingredients including lobster, Wagyu tartare and avocado.

Another addition is the Ebi Sando, a sandwich featuring crispy shrimp, truffle and miso aïoli. The Sticks Setto features skewers of Japanese Wagyu beef, Iberian pork, shrimp and miso-marinated black cod, served on a hot stone at the table.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sticks’n’Sushi Czech Republic (@sticksnsushi_cz)

The drinks list includes sake, Japanese teas, cocktails and premium spirits. The restaurant will also serve a Japanese rice lager brewed for the chain by Danish brewery Mikkeller.

Zbyněk Pokorný, chief executive of Sushi Group s.r.o., which is bringing the concept to the Czech market, said the opening followed nearly two years of preparation.

“We believe that the combination of Japanese quality, Danish hospitality, and a strong focus on the overall guest experience is a perfect fit for Prague,” Pokorný said. He added that the company was looking forward to welcoming its first guests.

Reservations can be made through the company’s Czech website.

About Sticks’n’Sushi

Founded in Copenhagen in 1994, Sticks’n’Sushi was established by brothers Jens and Kim Rahbek, who have Danish and Japanese roots, and Thor Andersen. The first restaurant opened in a basement space in the Danish capital.

The business has since expanded into an international restaurant group, with locations in Denmark, Germany and the United Kingdom. Its interiors draw on Japanese and Danish influences, with individual restaurants featuring their own design elements within the brand’s overall concept.

World.title: Czechia Among Top 5 Destinations for Digital Nomads
World.content:
The Czech Republic has been ranked the fifth-best country in the world for digital nomads, outperforming popular destinations such as Portugal, France, and the United Arab Emirates.

The ranking, compiled by Global Citizen Solutions and reported by Euronews, assessed factors like visa accessibility, cost of living, and quality of life.



The study found that Europe dominates the list, with Spain taking first place, followed by the Netherlands, Uruguay, and Canada. Seven out of the top ten destinations for remote workers are in Europe, confirming the continent’s continued appeal for professionals seeking stability and mobility.

Spain secured the top position thanks to its dedicated digital nomad visa, which allows foreigners to work remotely either for international companies or for Spanish-based businesses, provided that domestic work accounts for no more than 20 percent of their total income.

From an economic perspective, Spain is described as more affordable than northern European countries, especially in smaller cities where living costs are lower but the quality of healthcare, safety, and services remains high.

The Czech Republic, meanwhile, ranked fifth globally and third within Europe, praised for its balance between affordability and high living standards. The country offers a stable environment, well-developed infrastructure, and a relatively low cost of living compared to Western Europe — qualities that continue to attract freelancers and remote professionals.

According to the report, “Many European jurisdictions offer direct paths to permanent residency and eventual citizenship, providing digital nomads with strong passports and long-term mobility. Add to that Europe’s reputation for safety, stable institutions, and cultural richness, and it’s easy to see why the continent remains such an attractive base.”

The Czech Republic was followed by Portugal, France, the UAE, Germany, and Malta rounding out the top ten. Interestingly, while Southeast Asia remains a favorite among travelers, its countries did not make it to the upper ranks of this year’s digital nomad list — a sign that security, stability, and residency options are becoming increasingly important to remote workers.

Here are the top ten countries for digital nomads in 2026:

Spain The Netherlands Uruguay Canada Czechia Portugal France United Arab Emirates Germany Malta

World.title: Micro Budapest: a free website turns 40 of Kolodko’s mini statues into a treasure hunt
World.content:
A new website invites locals and visitors to track down 40 of the tiny, mostly bronze figures that sculptor Mihály Kolodko has placed around Budapest.

Searching is part of the fun. Each entry on Micro Budapest therefore gives only an approximate address, enough to bring you to the right place and leave the figure for you to discover. If you still cannot find it, help is one tap away: the exact GPS coordinates open the spot in OpenStreetMap.

Visitors can browse by district or by theme, from “Hungarian Childhood” and “Politics & History” to “Curious & Touching”, open a map of the 40 selected figures, and use “My Location” to see which one is nearest. Micro Budapest is free to use and available in Hungarian, English, German, French, Greek, Italian and Spanish.

Every location was checked on the spot rather than copied from existing lists. The site also offers a background story for each statue. Kolodko rarely explains his works himself, so these stories are Micro Budapest’s own: independently researched from newspaper articles and Hungarian sources, and the team’s view of what each figure means, not an official explanation.

Photo: Kolodko Art / Facebook Photo: DNH Photo: DNH Photo: DNH Photo: DNH Photo: DNH

Most of the statues appear unannounced, and they can be stolen, moved or altered at any time. A news section reports new figures and losses, and three statues are currently marked as missing on the map. The site asks visitors to report anything they notice.

Micro Budapest is a curated selection, not a complete list, and has no connection to the artist.

Website: microbudapest.com

World.title: Hungary Weekly Briefing: Magyar–Zelensky talks, EU funding breakthrough and Hungary’s changing political landscape
World.content:
Hungary’s political and diplomatic landscape continues to evolve rapidly. This week brought important developments in relations with Ukraine, a potential breakthrough over billions of euros in frozen EU funds, and fresh debates over migration, economic policy and the country’s international partnerships.

The latest Hungary Weekly Briefing on Substack brings together the key stories of the week, with analysis and context for international readers, expats, investors and everyone following developments in Hungary.

What’s inside this week’s briefing?

The headline story is Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Brussels. Progress on minority education rights and Ukraine’s EU accession negotiations could mark a turning point in relations between Budapest and Kyiv.

On the economic front, Hungary has moved closer to unlocking EUR 4.2 billion in previously frozen EU funding, potentially opening the door to renewed Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe opportunities for Hungarian universities.

The briefing also examines the Hungarian government’s migration policy, a major EU court ruling concerning the release of convicted people smugglers, and new polling showing Tisza’s continued political lead despite criticism of its economic performance.

World.title: Sharjah International Book Fair 2026 to bring together 2,673 publishers and exhibitors from 124 countries for 1,500 events – photos
World.content:
The 45th Sharjah International Book Fair (SIBF 2026) will take place from November 4-15 at Expo Centre Sharjah under the theme ‘Made of Stories’, bringing together 2,673 publishers and exhibitors from 124 countries. This year’s edition will also host 106 writers, artists and intellectuals from 25 countries, with 1,500 cultural and artistic events, and welcome Oman as Guest of Honour, presenting a programme celebrating its literature, heritage, writers and artists.

The details were announced at a press conference held by the Sharjah Book Authority (SBA) at its headquarters in Sharjah. The Authority unveiled the dates of the Thriller Festival and Sharjah International Library Conference, and new visitor experiences, including ‘Poets’ Corner’, where visitors’ stories are transformed into poems in Arabic and English, and ‘Future Hands District’, an interactive educational city designed to introduce children to different professions.

Photo: SIBF

Stories that shape generations

In his keynote, H.E. Ahmed bin Rakkad Al Ameri, CEO of SBA, said: “For 45 years, SIBF has brought together readers, writers, publishers and creative minds from around the world. This year’s theme, ‘Made of Stories’, celebrates how the stories we read, hear and pass down through generations shape our memories, identity and understanding of the world, and how we create stories of our own to leave for future generations.”

H.E. Ahmed bin Rakkad Al Ameri, CEO of SBA. Photo: SIBF

He added: “The journey of SIBF is part of the wider cultural vision established by His Highness Sheikh Dr. Sultan bin Mohammed Al Qasimi, Supreme Council Member and Ruler of Sharjah, who made books and knowledge the foundation for human development and a bridge connecting cultures and peoples.”

“Today, under the guidance of Her Highness Sheikha Bodour bint Sultan Al Qasimi, Chairperson of SBA, we continue to advance this vision, strengthening the fair’s status as a global publishing platform and expanding opportunities for publishers and creative professionals to collaborate and reach new readers and markets,” he concluded.

Celebrating Omani culture

Discussing the Guest of Honour participation, H.E. Ahmed bin Saud bin Nasser Al Rawahi, Assistant Director General for Knowledge and Cultural Development at Oman’s Ministry of Culture, Sports and Youth, and Director of the Muscat International Book Fair said: “We see this celebration as a tribute to Oman and its culture, and an opportunity to strengthen the longstanding ties between our countries and peoples. Oman’s selection as Guest of Honour builds on a shared history and close relations rooted in brotherhood and neighbourliness.”

Hungarian embassy opened in Oman

He added: “Our participation will introduce visitors to Oman’s history, heritage and cultural achievements while encouraging dialogue and exchange between Oman and Sharjah. The programme includes literary and intellectual discussions, poetry evenings, historical and cultural events, and workshops for children and young people.”

Media coverage of the fair

Salem Ali Hamad Al Ghaithi, Director of the Sharjah Broadcasting Authority, outlined the fair’s media coverage plan, including special programmes and interviews with writers and intellectuals on Sharjah TV, Al Sharqiya TV, Al Wousta TV and Sharjah Sports TV. Coverage will also include more than 20 hours of live broadcasting on Plus Radio, major events streamed on the Maraya platform and round-the-clock updates across digital platforms.

Salem Ali Hamad Al Ghaithi, Director of the Sharjah Broadcasting Authority. Photo: SIBF

A partnership supporting knowledge and culture

Saood Ibrahim Mohammed Saleh, Vice President of Government Sales (Dubai and Northern Emirates) at Etisalat, said: “As Etisalat marks its 50th anniversary, we take pride in our longstanding sponsorship of this major cultural event. We see this strategic partnership as a national and cultural responsibility, rooted in our belief that investing in people and knowledge is as important as investing in digital and technological infrastructure. We remain committed to using the latest innovations and digital solutions to support publishers, authors and readers.”

Saood Ibrahim Mohammed Saleh, Vice President of Government Sales (Dubai and Northern Emirates) at Etisalat. Photo: SIBF

Support for culture and community development

For his part, Mohamed Hachicho, General Director of Equiti’s Sharjah Branch, the fair’s Financial Services Partner, said: “We are proud to partner with the Sharjah Book Authority and sponsor the fair, supporting culture, knowledge and the community. Sharjah holds a special place for us because of its vision for culture and education as foundations of community development. As we expand our presence in the emirate, we aim to be an active community partner, recognising the power of knowledge to empower people, create opportunities and build a better future.”

Mohamed Hachicho, General Director of Equiti’s Sharjah Branch, the fair’s Financial Services Partner. Photo: SIBF

Bringing stories to life

Khoula Al Mujaini, General Coordinator of SIBF, outlined the fair’s cultural and artistic programme, explaining how this year’s theme shapes the activities and experiences offered to visitors.

She said: “Stories have been part of our lives since childhood, shaping our memories and how we understand ourselves and the world. We also create stories through what we write, share and leave behind. This idea inspired the theme of the 45th edition and runs throughout its books, discussions and activities, giving every visitor the chance to discover a new story, experience a different chapter or begin one of their own.”

Khoula Al Mujaini, General Coordinator of SIBF. Photo: SIBF

Expanding opportunities for publishers

Mansour Al Hassani, Director of Publishing Services at SBA, outlined the professional programme accompanying the fair and the opportunities it offers publishers to develop their businesses, exchange expertise, and expand rights trading and translation activities across international markets.

He said: “The Sharjah International Book Fair’s programme brings together publishers and book industry professionals from around the world, giving them opportunities to discuss developments in publishing markets, develop their skills, and build new business relationships and partnerships.”

Mansour Al Hassani, Director of Publishing Services at SBA. Photo: SIBF

Participating publishers

SIBF 2026 will welcome 2,673 publishers, including 1,151 Arab and 1,122 international publishers, showcasing titles in multiple languages across literature, science, children’s books and other fields.

Cultural events and guest speakers

SIBF 2026 will feature 1,500 cultural, creative and artistic events, bringing together 106 guests from 25 countries. The programme includes panel discussions, literary talks, workshops, theatrical performances and interactive activities for children and adults.

Writers, poets, intellectuals and researchers from the UAE, the Arab world and beyond will explore topics spanning literature, poetry, literary criticism, history, science, technology and contemporary social and cultural issues.

Emirati and Arab speakers

SIBF 2026 will welcome Emirati writers, thinkers, poets and artists, including Dr. Sultan Al Ameemi, Ali Abu Al Reesh, Dr. Habib Ghuloom, Dr. Shihab Ghanem, Dr. Ahmed Al Khoori, Fathiya Al Nimr, Dubai Abulhoul, Aisha Sultan and Nasser Al Dhaheri.

Photo: SIBF

Arab guests will include Moroccan academic and researcher Dr. Said Yaktine, a specialist in narratology, literary theory and digital literature; Lebanese actor, writer and director Rafiq Ali Ahmad; and Lebanese novelist and journalist Najwa Barakat.

The programme will also feature Sudanese novelist Dr. Amir Tag Elsir, Kuwaiti novelist Saud Alsanousi, and Syrian-Canadian author Zoulfa Katouh.

International authors and academics

SIBF 2026 will welcome international writers, researchers and creative figures, including V.D. Satheesan, currently serving as the 13th Chief Minister of Kerala. He will join American writer, artist and translator Daisy Rockwell; American-Canadian novelist and journalist John Vaillant; Chinese novelist and screenwriter Liu Zhenyun; and Filipino historian Ambeth R. Ocampo.

The programme will also feature Nigerian author Nnedi Okorafor; British novelist Clare Mackintosh; and Indian actress, writer and content creator Shenaz Treasurywala.

Other participants include Australian writer and designer Peter Gould; South African actress and producer Salamina Mosese; Singaporean poet Natalie Wang; German novelist Daniela Tully; and Thailand’s Rewat Panpipat

Workshops and creative activities

SIBF 2026 will also feature two specialised courses requiring advance registration. German novelist Daniela Tully will lead a course on narrative voice, character development, dialogue, editing and the publishing process. Meanwhile, Egyptian actor and writer Khaled El Sawy will present ‘Acting Studio: From Training to the Stage’, focusing on performance techniques, character development and improvisation.

Theatrical and family performances

The 12-day cultural extravaganza will present three productions requiring advance booking, beginning on November 7 with the exclusive premiere of the musical ‘When Memories Sing’. The show will revisit childhood songs and familiar voices remembered across generations.

On November 8, Abdullah Annan will present ‘Impossible or Science?!’, an interactive family show combining optical illusions and scientific experiments. Children and families will be invited to participate, vote and learn the scientific explanations behind seemingly impossible acts.

The outdoor stage at Expo Centre Sharjah will then host ‘Waterland’ on November 14 and 15, a theatrical production featuring Hussein Al Mahdi, Shaila Sabt, Ghorour Safar, Mohammed Al Musallam, Ahmed bin Hussein, Shamlan Al Omairi, Amani Al Dobb, Areej Al Attar, Najla Al Baloushi, Wahaj Al Anzi, Raghad Mohammed and Ahmed bin Jalal.

Thriller Festival returns November 7-10

SIBF 2026 will host the fifth edition of the ‘Thriller Festival’ from November 7-10, in collaboration with Capital Crime London and Thriller Festival New York. The event will bring together more than 12 specialists, including crime, mystery and thriller writers, literary agents and screenwriters.

Featured guests include British novelist and former police officer Clare Mackintosh; American author Karen Dionne, whose novel The Marsh King’s Daughter was adapted for film; and British writer and journalist Elizabeth Moore, known for her psychological thriller The Man on the Middle Floor.

They will be joined by Vaseem Khan, author of the Baby Ganesh Agency and Malabar House series; British novelist Abir Mukherjee, author of the Wyndham & Banerjee detective series; and British writer David Fennell, whose crime fiction includes the Sleeper and Grace Archer series.

Arab participants include Egyptian novelist Noha Dawoud, Emirati writer and director Ibrahim Al Marzouqi, and Emirati author Adel Al Sumaiti.

The festival will also welcome Emirati novelist Mohammed Ali Al Hammadi, Emirati writer Alia Nasser Al Zaabi, and Syrian novelist and journalist Islam Abu Shukair.

Cookery Corner

The Cookery Corner will bring together Arab and international chefs for live cooking demonstrations, introducing visitors to ingredients, flavours and techniques from different culinary traditions.

Participating chefs include Mohammad Orfali from Syria, Salam Daqqaq from Palestine, Jad Youssef from Lebanon, Kausar Raja from Pakistan and the UK, and Marina Georgallides from Greece and the UK.

They will be joined by Xavier Bramble from the Caribbean and the UK; Nitisha Patel, Romy Gill and Monisha Bharadwaj from India and the UK; and Sulaiman Al Kindi and Samira Al Aghbariya from Oman.

Oman’s Guest of Honour programme

Oman will be the Guest of Honour at SIBF 2026, with 50 participants, including 41 writers and poets. Its programme will explore the country’s history, heritage and cultural identity, alongside developments in Omani literature, poetry and the arts. Visitors will also be introduced to Omani cuisine, with activities for children and young people.

The agenda will include 15 cultural sessions, six children’s workshops and 20 artistic performances, including daily musical and traditional folk performances. Two additional artistic presentations and two cookery sessions will also be held.

Participating writers and poets include novelist Zahran Al Qasmi, Dr. Mohammed Al Yahyai, poet Hassan Al Matrooshi, winner of the Al Muallaqa Prize for Classical Arabic Poetry, Dr. Abdulaziz Al Omairi, winner of the Al Burda Award for Nabati Poetry, Dr. Mahmoud bin Mohammed Al Rahbi, and writer and storyteller Ahmed bin Nasser Al Rashdi.

Publishers’ Training Programme

SIBF 2026’s professional events will begin on October 31 with the Publishers’ Training Programme, organised by SBA in collaboration with New York University (NYU). The programme will bring together more than 200 publishers from 17 countries to develop their professional skills and understanding of changes in the global publishing industry.

Sessions will cover developments in the global audiobook market, video and social media marketing strategies, international translation rights markets, and the exchange of content and cultural assets between markets.

The 16th Sharjah Publishers Conference

The 16th Sharjah Publishers Conference will take place from November 1-3, bringing together publishers and book industry professionals. Nine countries will participate for the first time, including Angola, Aruba, Belarus, Burundi, Cambodia, Cape Verde, Myanmar, Trinidad and Tobago, and Niger.

Held under the theme ‘Publishing in an Accelerating Age’, the conference will feature more than 30 sessions and workshops covering artificial intelligence, developments in the audiobook market, publishing rights trading, children’s books and the growing role of comics in publishing.

Participants will also be able to apply for the Sharjah Translation Grant, which supports translating books between Arabic and other languages.

Sharjah International Library Conference

The Sharjah International Library Conference will take place from November 7-9, organised by SBA in partnership with the American Library Association (ALA). It will bring together more than 400 librarians, information professionals and library staff from academic, public, school, government and private institutions.

Discussions will cover guided and independent reading using the Destiny Discover platform; the contribution of partnerships, public policy and community leadership to building stronger communities; and ways to develop school libraries through student leadership.

Visitor services and transport

SBA is coordinating with the Sharjah Roads and Transport Authority to identify additional parking areas and arrange transport services to and from the fair. Details will be announced in the coming days.

Official partners and sponsors

SIBF 2026’s partners and sponsors include Etisalat as Official Telecommunications Partner, SAAS as Development Partner, Trends Group as Knowledge Partner, Sharjah Broadcasting Authority as Official Media Partner, Expo Centre Sharjah as Strategic Partner, Bank of Sharjah as Banking Partner, Equiti as Financial Services Partner, and Omeir Travel Agency and National Paints as Partners.

World.title: Hungary’s farmers need forecasts they can use, not just admire
World.content:
A sophisticated model has limited value to a farmer if the warning arrives too late or cannot be translated into a workable choice. Water resilience begins at the point where scientific confidence meets the practical calendar of planting, irrigation and transport.

Written by Abdulla Saeed Alhebsi (A.S. Alhebsi), Author and Researcher specializing in Security, Heritage, Risk Management, and Control Room Operations

On 9 October 2026, the Emirates News Agency reported that the UAE Research Program for Rain Enhancement Science had taken part in the Meteorological Technology World Expo and the World Meteorological Organization’s TECO conference in Amsterdam on 5–8 October. Its meetings concerned radar, remote sensing, forecasting, hydrological models and scientific cooperation, including discussions with the Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute. That is evidence of research engagement, not proof that rain-enhancement technology can end water scarcity.

Hungary’s agricultural and industrial users face water risks that differ from the Gulf, but its researchers and businesses can still draw lessons from the UAE’s interest in atmospheric observation and hydrological modelling. The scientific relationship should be measured through actionable data, not a shared slogan.

I would encourage universities, farm associations and water authorities to test forecast products against the decisions people actually make. A useful pilot with UAE counterparts could compare communication methods and quantify false alarms as well as missed warnings.

A weather forecast should not end on a screen. It should end with someone better prepared.

If you missed it: Hungary’s agriculture faces major crisis: Less than 3% of arable land is irrigated

For a Hungarian farmer, a climate model is not simply an academic achievement. It may influence irrigation planning, planting dates, crop choice and conversations with buyers. When forecasts change, decisions may need to change too. That makes clarity about uncertainty an economic necessity rather than a technical footnote.

The Emirates’ participation in the Amsterdam meetings is relevant because it draws attention to observation technologies and hydrological modelling. Yet science becomes useful only when its products are tested and communicated in language that working farms can act upon. An impressive radar image cannot substitute for a clear explanation of what the evidence does and does not show.

Hungary and the UAE face different water pressures, which makes methodological exchange valuable if it is conducted carefully. Researchers could compare how measurement uncertainty affects decisions in arid and temperate environments and whether warning formats help operators avoid costly delays. Any such work should be explicitly described as a proposal, not an existing collaboration.

I would like to see field-level evaluation take priority over promotional claims. Does an early warning change a farm decision? Does it reduce avoidable water use? Do users understand how quickly a forecast might change? These outcomes reveal whether investment in data is producing resilience.

Rain-enhancement research deserves scientific scrutiny, but it does not replace irrigation efficiency or maintenance. My argument is for a practical partnership between forecasters and the people whose livelihoods depend on them.

As we wrote before, Hungarian agriculture, as we know it, is nearing the end – but researchers already have a plan

World.title: Hungarian billionaire released from custody but placed under house arrest in corruption case
World.content:
Hungarian billionaire Dániel Jellinek has been granted release from pre-trial detention under strict conditions in a major corruption investigation involving the country’s former state-owned bus operator.

Hungarian billionaire to be placed under house arrest in major corruption case

Hungarian billionaire Dániel Jellinek is set to leave pre-trial detention under strict conditions in a major corruption investigation involving a state-owned transport company. Another prominent businessman, however, will remain behind bars.

Hungarian billionaire businessman Dániel Jellinek is to be released from pre-trial detention and placed under house arrest with electronic monitoring as a major corruption investigation continues. The decision was made on Friday by the Buda Central District Court, according to 24.hu.

Meanwhile, the court extended the detention of Norbert Szivek, former head of Hungarian National Asset Management, by another three months.

Both men were arrested in September in connection with suspected corruption involving Volánbusz, Hungary’s former state-owned regional bus operator.

Why was Jellinek granted house arrest?

According to the Budapest Metropolitan Court, which released details of the ruling, Jellinek had cooperated with investigators and provided a substantive statement during the proceedings.

Judges concluded that his suspected involvement in the alleged corruption network was relatively limited, reducing the risk that he could interfere with evidence or influence other individuals connected to the investigation.

However, the court still considered him a potential flight risk and found that the risk of further criminal activity had not disappeared. As a result, Jellinek must remain at a designated property, with his movements monitored electronically.

The court reached a different conclusion regarding Szivek, who is suspected of having played a more central role in the alleged corruption scheme.

Investigators are still examining the case and identifying potential witnesses. Judges therefore considered it necessary to keep Szivek in detention to prevent possible interference with the investigation. The court’s ruling is not yet final, and the criminal allegations against both men remain under investigation.

If you missed it: PM Magyar met Zelensky in Brussels: Here’s what they talked about

What is the Volánbusz corruption case about?

The investigation centres on suspected financial irregularities involving Volánbusz and related regional transport companies between 2015 and 2018.

According to investigators, more than 600 second-hand buses were allegedly purchased at inflated prices, causing estimated financial losses of around HUF 10 billion.

The authorities are also examining other transactions involving publicly owned assets and suspected financial misconduct. The case has attracted particular attention because of the prominent business figures involved.

Jellinek is the founder of the Indotek Group, a major Hungarian property investment company with interests in commercial real estate.

Szivek previously headed Hungarian National Asset Management, the state organisation responsible for exercising ownership rights over numerous publicly owned enterprises. Both were taken into custody in September as part of a wider investigation into suspected corruption connected to public transport contracts.

Investigation continues despite changes to detention

While Jellinek’s cooperation was considered sufficient to justify replacing detention with a less restrictive measure, judges did not conclude that the risks associated with his release had disappeared entirely.

In particular, the court considered his extensive business connections and financial resources when assessing the possibility of avoiding prosecution. In Szivek’s case, judges concluded that continued detention was necessary because of the possibility that he could influence other individuals involved in the proceedings.

The latest ruling therefore changes the conditions under which Jellinek is held while the investigation continues, but does not represent a dismissal of the allegations. Neither businessman has been convicted in connection with the case.

World.title: PM Péter Magyar: Strict border controls and migrant returns are the way forward
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has called for stricter border controls and the swift return of irregular migrants, backing a tough proposal during heated talks between EU leaders in Brussels.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar has backed tougher European measures against irregular migration, arguing that strict border protection and the swift return of migrants without legal permission to remain have become the preferred approach in most EU member states.

In a social media post shared during the final day of the European Council summit in Brussels on Friday, Magyar described the discussions among EU leaders as “heated and emotional”, according to Hungarian news agency MTI.

The prime minister said that strict, decisive and effective border protection had become the approach favoured by most European countries, although some member states continued to oppose tougher measures.

Hungary backs strict Polish, Italian and Danish proposal

“On behalf of Hungary, I support the toughest Polish-Italian-Danish proposal,” Magyar wrote, adding that the countries were working together to convince the remaining reluctant member states.

His comments came as EU leaders discussed how to strengthen the bloc’s external borders, tackle people smuggling and make procedures for returning irregular migrants more effective.

Migration remains one of the most divisive issues within the European Union, particularly when it comes to balancing border security, asylum procedures and the responsibilities of individual member states.

If you missed it: PM Magyar met Zelensky in Brussels: Here’s what they talked about

Several European governments have been calling for stricter migration policies, including stronger border controls and more effective returns. However, disagreements remain over how these measures should be implemented across the bloc.

Magyar’s remarks highlighted Hungary’s support for a tougher common approach, although the details of the Polish-Italian-Danish proposal and the positions of the opposing countries were not specified in his statement.

Hungary seeks EU support for border protection

Magyar’s latest remarks follow an announcement earlier this week that his government would seek additional EU funding to strengthen Hungary’s border fence and border protection measures.

Speaking in Brussels on Wednesday, the prime minister said his government would push for dedicated funding during negotiations over the EU’s next seven-year budget.

Hungary’s southern border has long played a central role in the country’s migration policy. The Tisza government has pledged to maintain strict border controls while seeking closer cooperation with European institutions.

Magyar has also criticised the former Orbán government’s decision to release convicted people smugglers from Hungarian prisons, saying his administration would pursue a different approach.

Meanwhile, the migration debate continued late into Friday evening, with EU leaders still discussing the issue nine hours into the summit’s second day. Magyar described himself as “somewhat tired, but determined”, saying he was representing Hungary’s interests as the talks continued.

He stressed that the negotiations concerned an important issue for Hungary and the European Union as a whole.

World.title: Hungarian international footballer Milos Kerkez removed from controversial Ukrainian blacklist
World.content:
Liverpool defender Milos Kerkez has been removed from a controversial Ukrainian blacklist, weeks after an incident involving the Hungarian international sparked outrage.

Milos Kerkez, the Hungarian international footballer currently playing for Liverpool, has been removed from the Ukrainian Myrotvorets database, which publishes information about individuals it considers hostile to Ukraine. According to HVG, the player’s removal may have been secured through the intervention of the Hungarian Football Federation and the country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

However, while Kerkez’s name has disappeared from the controversial website, his father remains listed.

How did the Liverpool defender end up on the list?

The controversy began following a Nations League match between Hungary and Ukraine in Budapest, when Kerkez became involved in an altercation with several Ukrainian players during the closing stages of the game.

His father subsequently shared footage of the incident on Instagram, accompanied by Russian Paradise, a song by Russian rap group AK-47. The choice of music sparked outrage in Ukraine, particularly given the ongoing war with Russia.

Shortly afterwards, both Kerkez and his father appeared on the Myrotvorets website, accused of supporting Russian aggression. His father was also described as a pro-Russian provocateur. The footballer strongly rejected the allegations, insisting that he had never supported aggression of any kind.

“I have never supported any form of aggression in my life, and I do not support it now,” Kerkez told Hungarian news outlet Telex earlier this month.

He also distanced himself from his father’s social media activity, stressing that he could not be held responsible for another person’s actions.

Kerkez explained that the confrontation on the pitch had been about defending a teammate and that he would have acted the same way regardless of the opposing team.

If you missed it: Former Budapest mayor makes striking claims about Orbán and corruption

Hungarian foreign ministry may have helped secure removal

Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán had previously condemned the inclusion of Kerkez and Fidesz politician Balázs Hidvéghi in the database, criticising what she described as the stigmatisation and intimidation of Hungarian citizens.

The incident also attracted attention because several Hungarian political figures, including former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, have appeared on the website.

Established in 2014, Myrotvorets, meaning Peacemaker, publishes personal information about people its operators consider pro-Russian or hostile to Ukraine.

Despite its name and activities, the website is not an official Ukrainian government database. Its operations have long attracted controversy, particularly over the publication of personal information and the criteria used to identify alleged enemies of Ukraine. Although Kerkez has now been removed, his father, Hidvéghi and Viktor Orbán remain listed.

The exact circumstances surrounding the Liverpool defender’s removal have not been disclosed, and it remains unclear what discussions, if any, took place between Hungarian officials and those operating the website.

World.title: Wizz Air CEO on night flights: “We’ll give passengers the minister’s phone number”
World.content:
Wizz Air CEO József Váradi has made a sarcastic remark about Hungary’s transport minister amid a dispute over night-time flights at Budapest Airport and warned of a difficult winter for European aviation.

Wizz Air CEO József Váradi has warned that efforts to restrict night-time flights at Budapest’s Ferenc Liszt International Airport could have serious consequences for passengers. Speaking at a press event on Friday, he discussed the challenges of avoiding late arrivals and made an ironic remark about Hungary’s Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy, as reported by HVG.

The government has been working with Budapest Airport, HungaroControl and Wizz Air to reduce aircraft noise during the night. A joint working group is examining how to protect residents living near the airport without unnecessarily disrupting flight operations.

Váradi acknowledged that residents’ concerns were justified, but argued that many delays are caused by circumstances beyond the airline’s control.

Wizz Air CEO’s sarcastic response to night flight restrictions

According to Váradi, a delay early in the morning can affect an aircraft’s entire daily schedule, potentially causing its final flight to arrive in Budapest during restricted night-time hours.

In such situations, the airline may have to cancel the flight or divert passengers to another airport, such as Bratislava, rather than land in Budapest.

“And we’ll give passengers the minister’s phone number so they can call him,” Váradi remarked.

He argued that government measures intended to protect consumers could sometimes have the opposite effect, leaving travellers to deal with the consequences of cancelled or diverted flights.

While Wizz Air is adjusting its schedules to minimise late-night arrivals, Váradi stressed that disruptions cannot always be prevented. He also claimed that the airline’s newer aircraft generate roughly half as much noise per flight as those of some competitors.

If you missed it: Wizz Air cancels several Eastern flights for the entire winter season

Strong growth in Hungary despite a difficult outlook

Váradi said the airline remains the market leader in Hungary with a 38% share, operating 19 aircraft from its Budapest base and serving 88 destinations from Budapest and Debrecen combined.

The company carried 2.6 million passengers in Hungary during the summer, a 30% increase compared with the previous year. It expects to transport around nine million passengers in the country by the end of 2026, exceeding its original target of 8.3 million.

“We consider ourselves Hungary’s national airline,” the CEO said, highlighting the company’s contribution to tourism and major international events. However, the CEO warned that the coming winter would be challenging for Europe’s aviation industry, as high fuel prices and supply chain disruptions continue to affect airlines.

Wizz Air believes it has an advantage over competitors, having secured 82% of its fuel requirements for the next six months at approximately half the current market price. More than three-quarters of its fleet also consists of fuel-efficient Airbus A321neo aircraft.

Despite the difficult environment, the airline is pursuing further expansion, including new bases in Madrid, Valencia, Pristina and Brașov. By 2030, Wizz Air aims to carry 127 million passengers annually, compared with fewer than 70 million in 2025, while expanding its fleet from 276 to 335 aircraft.
