World.title: Tougher Security Response Won’t Solve Albania’s Growing Crisis: Experts
World.content:
For three days, streets in central Tirana have been taken over by university students and high-school pupils who have boycotted classes to protest against the government.

Demonstrators throwing Molotov cocktails and stones have clashed with police, who have attempted to disperse them using tear gas, rubber batons and water cannon. The unrest has spread to other cities, including Shkodra, Durres and Korca.

The main demand of the protests is the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Since coming to power in 2013, Rama has become increasingly powerful as Prime Minister, while other democratic institutions have weakened, analysts argue. This is why the anger expressed at the protests has been directed at him personally.

The young participants have also voiced demands for better-quality education, improved living conditions and greater job opportunities.

World.title: Serbia Channels Public Funds to Pro-Vucic Diaspora Groups
World.content:
In Serbia itself, the Directorate regularly funnels money to local organisations that claim to support the Serb diaspora in the region.

The Izrazajnost association, for example, received a total of 23,800 euros in 2023-2024 for two projects promoting the use of Cyrillic.

Izrazajnost is led by actor Milan Bosiljcic, who in 2023 was among a host of public figures who put their signatures to a statement of support for the SNS.

In 2024, the Directorate awarded 9,400 euros to an association co-founded by Bosiljcic’s daughter, Sara, called Jeremija, for the purposes of a language camp. The association’s first project, which was not funded by the Directorate, was conducted in cooperation with Solidarité Kosovo, an organisation founded by SNS member Arnaud Gouillon, who was head of the Directorate at the time.

Since 2023, the Belgrade Centre for Education and Youth Development, CEROB, has received almost 34,000 euros from the Directorate for diaspora youth camps.

In late 2023, the Centre for Investigative Journalism of Serbia, CINS, reported that SNS activists tasked with canvassing voters for their support were being paid in cash at CEROB’s Belgrade office.

A year later, CEROB representative Ognjen Kocevic was appointed by the Serbian government to the Managing Board of the Institute for the Evaluation of Education Quality.

The Directorate also awarded two grants totalling 13,600 euros to the Association of Students of Republika Srpska in Serbia.

During local elections in 2024 in Serbia’s second city of Novi Sad, members of the association were caught on camera working in an SNS call centre at the Novi Sad Fairgrounds, where party operatives used voter records to track turnout.

Last year, the Directorate gave 8,500 euros to the Association of War Veterans of Serb Lands 1990–1999, for summer youth camps. The association’s leader, Zeljko Vukelic, previously sparked public outrage for sending children aged 11 to 15 to military training camps in Russia in 2017, where children were taught to handle guns and hand grenades.

None of the associations mentioned above responded to requests for comment.

Political scientist Dusko Radosavljevic said the direction of funding reflects the SNS roots in the ultranationalist Serbian Radical Party, which Vucic was a key part of through the bloody collapse of Yugoslavia in the 1990s, right up until 2008 when he broke away and formed the SNS.

“It must not be overlooked that this regime has, from its inception, carried a distinct ideological marker – a far-right stance,” Radosavljevic said.

“This is a regime rooted in the Serbian Radical Party, one of the most abhorrent political creations in Serbia. It exerts a malignant influence fueled by disputes with neighbours, nationalism, and support for war crimes.”

World.title: Week in Review: Bad Deals and Scandals
World.content:
Less than two weeks before parliamentary elections in Serbia, the public got a rare glimpse inside the workings of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party machine. In an exclusive interview for BIRN, Momcilo Marjanovic, an insider, revealed the workings of the party’s “security” machine.

Marjanovic discusses the ins and outs of vote buying, how party thugs are deployed to intimidate voters and protesters, or defend party offices, as well as how provocateurs are planted inside opposition protests. He also describes how public funds are used to pay for this special apparatus.

World.title: Croatian Football Fans’ Pro-Nazi Chants Prompt Arrests
World.content:
Torcida fan group march before match on Thursday. Photo: Torcida Split/Facebook

Police in Split have arrested several people after members of Torcida, a group of hardcore supporters of Hajduk Split football club, marched through the city chanting antisemitic slogans, including “Trample, trample the Jews,” “Auschwitz, Auschwitz,” and “Rise, Adolf”, referencing Adolf Hitler.

The incidents are being investigated for hate speech. Further arrests are expected on Friday. All those detained are members of Torcida and already known to the police. An investigating judge will decide whether to order pre-trial detention.

The chants occurred a few hours before Hajduk’s match against Dutch club Ajax – a club seen as having a longstanding Jewish connection.

The incident has been condemned by the Croatian government, the mayor of Split, political parties and members of the public.

“We strongly condemn the unacceptable chants glorifying the Nazi regime,” the government stated on its X profile. “Such shameful behaviour represents a negation of sport and the democratic values ​​that modern Croatia upholds,” the post added.

Torcida fans are known for expressing extremist views.

A series of incidents occurred before the Conference League match, when Hajduk chanted fans marched in a column led by a VW Golf Mk1 with a coffin on its roof, on which the word “Ajax” was written.

The Israeli embassy in Zagreb also condemned the incidents.

The embassy was “deeply shocked by the grave antisemitic incident that occurred yesterday in Split and condemns it in the strongest possible terms,” ​​a statement provided to the news agency Hina said.

“We are deeply grateful to the Government of the Republic of Croatia and to Sara Lustig, Special Advisor to the Prime Minister on Holocaust Issues, for their swift response and clear condemnation of this event,” it added, expressing confidence that “authorities will act quickly and decisively regarding this matter”.

“Such incidents should be unequivocally and decisively condemned by all competent authorities at every level,” it continued.

Croatian President Zoran Milanovic said verbal condemnation was not enough.

“Words of condemnation, such as those we hear from the government, are no longer sufficient; measures and sanctions are necessary to demonstrate that there is no place in Croatia for the glorification of Nazism and Ustasha ideology,” Milanovic said in a press release, referencing Croatia’s World War II fascist movement.

The game itself was halted for 12 minutes during the second half after Hajduk fans let off various pyrotechnic devices, including flares and powerful firecrackers.

Hajduk could face a heavy fine from UEFA. Following the match, Hajduk issued an official apology.

“When situations like today’s occur, we are obligated to apologise,” it stated. The club also apologised to the management and players of Ajax, who witnessed scenes “by which we do not wish to be remembered in Europe”. It did not mention the specific events before the match or the Nazi chants.

The match ended with a 2-1 victory for Hajduk.

World.title: Albania PM Defiant as Protests Spread to Provincial Cities
World.content:
Prime Minister Edi Rama blamed the opposition and “foreign actors” on Friday for the escalation of violence during student protests in Tirana, describing the continuing unrest as an attempt to hinder Albania’s progress toward the European Union.

Speaking from a kiosk that had been burned down during the protests, Rama tried to suggest that students weren’t the ones leading the violence that has accompanied demonstrations in recent days, while accusing his political opponents of exploiting the discontent of young people for their own ends.

World.title: Serbia’s ‘Captured’ TV Screens All Tell the Same Story
World.content:
Serbia approaches October 25 elections with a deeply polarized and uneven national media ecosystem. The media environment is characterized by systemic political influence, instrumentalization, government control, the independent regulator’s paralysis and heightened security risks for independent journalists and media outlets.

These worrying trends have greatly affected the pre-election media space, which has been defined by extreme structural asymmetry. Meanwhile, traditional television, dominated by heavy regime influence and a lack of critical voices, remains the main vehicle for political communication and voter mobilization.

Traditional TV is watched in Serbia for five hours daily on average, and is the main source of political information for the older population. On the other side, websites and social networks offer diverse views and are the main source of information for people aged 15 to 30.

Paradoxically, despite more than 2,500 registered media outlets, Serbia has been placed in a group of high-risk countries concerning media pluralism because of severe deficits in political independence of the media and lack of overall market plurality, according to the Media Pluralism Monitor 2026.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Polish Man Charged With Plotting to Kill PM, Suspected Saboteurs Arrested
World.content:
Czech Army chief warns of possible Russian attack; PM still has conflicts of interest

The chief of the general staff of the Czech Army, Miroslav Hlavac, this week warned that Russia could test the cohesion of NATO by launching a partial attack against one of its members. “I want to emphasise that we are ready and we will defend the Czech Republic with what we have,” he said in an interview with the Czech News Agency. “And I say this with all the force and responsibility for the army of the Czech Republic, also warning that the country’s response to a potential foreign attack did not only rely on Czechia’s military capabilities but also on the response from the entire state apparatus, defence industry and society. “State preparedness is a never-ending process. You will never be 100 per cent prepared. It is important that the state, and any state, not just the Czech Republic, has its security system prepared in such a way that it is able to respond to the threat and subsequently mitigate and address the consequences of the crisis,” Hlavac insisted.

“Based on the assessment of the information provided by the Czech national authorities, the Commission has concluded that [Czech Prime Minister Andrej] Babis’s situation constitutes a conflict of interest,” Elizabeth Werner, head of the European Commission’s directorate general for agriculture and rural development, was quoted as saying this week by Transparency International Czechia as part of DG Agri’s response to the Czech NGO’s previous complaint. Czech and foreign anti-corruption watchdogs have for months warned that the Czech PM’s steps to distance himself from his business interests – particularly the transfer of his shares of Agrofert into a trust fund back in February – in reality did nothing to mitigate the risks and ultimately did not resolve his conflicts of interest. Babis, meanwhile, insists the EU Commission’s evaluation is “nonsense”. Talking about his former agro-chemical empire, Babis insisted: “I did much more than I had to do. If I had followed the rules for conflicts of interest with European commissioners, I would have just reported the conflict and walked out the door… I will never get [Agrofert] back and I don’t receive any profit from it.”

It was an intense week of closed-door talks as parties from across the political spectrum launched negotiations following last weekend’s municipal elections. Less than a week after the ballot, the future leadership and coalition formats appear clearer in about half of Czechia’s 13 regional cities. Having emerged first in six of the country’s larger cities, Babis’s ruling ANO party has so far been able to reach an agreement with other partners in two of them – Karlovy Vary and Pilsen. On the contrary, ANO is likely to end up in the opposition in Czechia’s two largest cities, Brno where several parties have already entered coalition talks, as well as in the capital Prague where the centre-right and victorious STAN movement promised “to present the framework of cooperation” for the future municipal leadership by next week. Post-election talks remain largely open in the cities of Ostrava, Pardubice, Jihlava, Zlin and Ceske Budejovice.

World.title: German Newspaper: Greed for Profit Threatening Croatian Tourism
World.content:
October the 17th, 2026 – The well known German newspaper Die Welt has accused the country of greed, claiming it is threatening Croatian tourism.

The German newspaper Die Welt has published a somewhat accusative text about this year’s tourist season in Croatia. The paper warns that the short-term desire for higher earnings could endanger the country’s most important economic branch. DW has reported that the author of the article, Volker Corsten, describes his own impressions from the area between Zadar and Split and from the Adriatic islands. He points out that the beaches during the summer of 2026 were apparently “noticeably emptier than in previous years”, that there were “no usual traffic jams on the coastal roads”, and that even in August, the peak of the season, “one could walk through the old town centres of Zadar and Šibenik without large crowds”. We’re not sure how true that is.

ice cream, aperol and grilled squid…

What are the reasons for this claim, the author of the Berlin newspaper asks. At the same time he emphasises that it was by no means the climate, which he describes as almost ideal. The sea was, he notes, exceptionally clean and of a pleasant temperature, and the weather conditions were sunny and without extreme heat. “Everything was, as always, excellent – as long as nothing is consumed, nothing is wanted on the beach, and one does not look at the bill for accommodation and visits to restaurants.”

According to Die Welt, the problem begins precisely at the moment when tourists look at the bills, i.e. the prices – for accommodation, restaurants and other tourist facilities. The German newspaper cites prices in Zadar as an example. In the most visited tourist parts of the city a scoop of ice cream costs at least three euros, while in side streets it can still be found for around two euros, Die Welt writes. It adds that an Aperol Spritz, depending on the location of the hospitality establishment, costs between nine and eleven euros.

The German media outlet also notes that the price of one of the most popular Dalmatian dishes, grilled squid, in 2026 in many taverns has risen to around 25 euros, while “a year earlier it amounted to around 20 euros”. As a symbol of the price increase the newspaper highlights the example of pancakes at a kiosk on a beach near Šibenik: “Before the introduction of the euro in 2023 they cost seven kuna, or around one euro. After the switch to the euro the price rose to two euros, and this year to as much as five euros!”

prices have risen, but quality allegedly hasn’t

Referring to data from the Croatian Bureau of Statistics, Die Welt states that prices in tourism between 2015 and 2024 rose by 70 percent. At the same time it recalls that the current inflation rate in Croatia is 4.4 percent, while on the coast, according to the author’s assessment, the rise in prices is even more pronounced. Although the Croatian Ministry of Tourism officially claims that the number of officially registered overnight stays in July was slightly higher than a year earlier, the author of the text recalls numerous reports about empty beaches and hotels: “Anyone who compares those claims (of the Ministry of Tourism – ed.) with their own impressions thinks of Potemkin villages.”

a criticism of croatia’s tourism strategy

The German newspaper recalls that the Croatian authorities want to develop a more sustainable and higher-quality form of tourism, with Mallorca often mentioned as a model. However, according to the author’s assessment, when it comes to prices Croatia has already set off down that path, but the quality of infrastructure, hotels, private accommodation, gastronomy and service still lags behind the level of prices demanded from guests: “Almost fifty years of socialist Yugoslavia cannot be erased so quickly.”

World.title: Light and Dark “Rings” Appear Along the Northern Coast of Palagruža
World.content:
October the 17th, 2026 – Strange light and dark rings have appeared along the northern coast of Palagruža, resulting in all kinds of suspicions from those who saw them…

Unusual light and dark rings have appeared on the surface of the sea, arranged in almost regular oval circles that stretch in large arcs and are clearly visible from a great distance. Morski reports that this phenomenon has aroused the curiosity of autumn visitors to Palagruža who wondered what exactly was going on. Dalmacija danas sought the answer from the people who spend the most time on Palagruža and know the peculiarities of the local sea well, the lighthouse keepers.

They explained to them that this is a natural phenomenon connected with sea currents, which occasionally meet in that area and, as they picturesquely described it, “break”. The sea currents interact with each other, create vortex movements and areas of different current speeds.

In certain places where surface waters approach or diverge, zones of different roughness of the sea surface can form. Under certain lighting these are seen as lighter or darker stripes, arcs and other shapes, which explains the interesting “mystery” from Palagruža that nobody would be ridiculed for thinking aliens were coming!

World.title: Is Germany Pressuring Croatia Over Montenegro EU Entry?
World.content:
October the 17th, 2026 – According to a Euronews report, Germany is strongly pressuring Croatia over the Montenegro EU entry issue, but Andrej Plenković claims otherwise.

The German Government is allegedly intensifying its pressure on Croatia to resolve the open issues with Montenegro so that there is no standstill in its accession to the European Union, but the PM claims that isn’t what’s occurring. Index reports that Berlin has allegedly actively become involved in resolving the problem and is demanding a constructive approach from Zagreb, which four officials directly familiar with the situation claimed for Euronews.

This week, Croatia sent Podgorica a list of eight disputed points that it wants resolved before the conclusion of accession negotiations. Because of this, Germany is striving to ensure that the enlargement process continues without slowing down, as a blockade of Montenegro, which is considered the most advanced candidate, could jeopardise the entire process.

Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković stated on Thursday ahead of the European Council summit in Brussels that there are issues that have been pointed out to Montenegro for years. “In the last two years there has been no progress at all,” Plenković said, adding that Croatia has been “extremely constructive” in the negotiations.

war crimes and historical issues

The disputes mainly relate to the legacy of the wars of the 1990s, which includes property claims and unresolved border issues. These problems endanger Montenegro’s goal of becoming the 28th EU member by 2028. The Croatian side emphasises that the investigation of war crimes and compensation for victims are conditions that Podgorica must fulfil in order to conclude the negotiations. At the same time Zagreb faces accusations that it activated the disputes at the last moment in order to increase pressure on Podgorica. Croatia, for its part, replies that these are long-standing problems and that its demands are of a symbolic nature.

diplomatic engagement and criticism

The European Commission has also become involved in the talks in recent weeks, and several member states are trying to prevent bilateral issues from stopping the process. France wants to avoid problems with enlargement because of its internal political situation, while Luxembourg criticises the practice of using the accession process to resolve mutual disputes.

Although several governments are talking to Croatia, the strongest pressure is coming from Berlin. Germany recently also offered mediation, but that offer has not yet been realised. The government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz wants to act as an impartial mediator out of fear that bilateral disputes could jeopardise the entire enlargement process. Croatia’s position has also met with public criticism, including that of the EU High Representative for Foreign Policy Kaja Kallas. On the margins of the summit she stated that bilateral issues must not block the accession process.

the geopolitical angle

EU officials fear that the mood towards enlargement could change if Montenegro’s entry is not completed soon. Next year elections will be held in several key member states, including France, where polls are led by Marine Le Pen, known for her scepticism towards further expansion of the Union.

Montenegro’s accession is taking place in a context in which Brussels is using the enlargement policy to strengthen ties with neighbouring countries because of tensions with Russia. Since Montenegro is first in line for membership, a standstill due to bilateral issues could also negatively affect the other candidates – Albania, Moldova, and especially Ukraine, whose accession is linked to future peace negotiations with Moscow. Montenegro would at the same time be the first country to enter the bloc according to the new enlargement methodology. This year Podgorica is chairing the Berlin Process, an initiative for regional cooperation in the Western Balkans, and is closely cooperating with the German government. In that context Germany is also advocating new models of enlargement, such as the status of “associated candidate” for Ukraine. Germany therefore considers that, given Podgorica’s efforts and the geopolitical situation, it is crucial to make a breakthrough in Montenegro’s accession so that the enlargement process does not come to a halt.

World.title: Foreign Media Bash Torcida following Ajax Incident
World.content:
October the 17th, 2026 – Foreign media from a multitude of countries have bashed Torcida following the violent clash with Ajax in Split.

Antisemitic and Nazi chants by some Torcida members during the recent procession towards Poljud, a coffin with the inscription Ajax on it, and the interruption of the match due to pyrotechnics have resonated with the foreign media. Index reports that media outlets from Israel and the Netherlands to Germany, Poland and Russia, as well as numerous media outlets in neighbouring countries, wrote about the incidents in Split.

The most attention was attracted by the chants “Crush, crush the Jews”, “Auschwitz, Auschwitz”, “Rise, Adolf” and “Come on, come on, Ustaše”, which were heard during Torcida’s cortege ahead of the Hajduk–Ajax match in the Conference League. At the head of the procession was a yellow Golf with a coffin on the roof on which “Ajax” was written. The match itself did not pass without incidents either. The encounter at Poljud was interrupted in the 77th minute after home fans lit a large quantity of pyrotechnics. Because of the dense smoke the players left the pitch, and the match was resumed after 12 minutes. Hajduk won 2–1.

“shocking antisemitism”

Israel’s Ynet, one of the most-read portals in the country, published an article under the title “Auschwitz, Auschwitz: Antisemitism against the ‘Jewish club’ and its Israeli player”. The portal describes Torcida’s procession towards the stadium and the antisemitic chants shouted by individual fans. It particularly highlights the mentions of Auschwitz and Adolf Hitler, as well as the coffin with the inscription Ajax. On Thursday afternoon, before the start of the match, Israeli Israel Hayom published an article under the title “Auschwitz, crush the Jews: Shocking antisemitism against Oscar Gloukh”.

The paper states that the Hajduk–Ajax match was overshadowed by antisemitic and violent incidents and reports the chants “Crush the Jews”, “Auschwitz, Auschwitz”, “Rise, Adolf” and “Come on, Ustaše”.

Both Israeli media particularly emphasise Ajax’s historical connection with the Jewish community in Amsterdam. Part of Ajax’s fans have for decades used the name “Super Jews” and Jewish symbols as part of their supporter identity. That tradition developed, among other things, as a response to antisemitic insults from fans of rival clubs. Most Ajax fans who use that symbolism are not Jewish, but because of it the Dutch club is often the target of antisemitic messages from opposing fans. Israeli media also stress that their national-team player Oscar Gloukh plays for Ajax. Israel Hayom also reported on earlier attacks on Dutch fans, including two who sought medical help because of minor injuries, and on 57 people arrested after the riots in Split.

“disgusting insults”

The scandalous Torcida chants were also reported by the respected British The Telegraph, which published an article under the title “Croatian football fans chanted disgusting antisemitic insults”. The Telegraph also recalls the riots in Split during which the police detained dozens of fans, as well as the violence in Amsterdam in November 2024 linked to the Ajax–Maccabi Tel Aviv match. The British medium places the events in the broader context of earlier racist incidents in Croatian football. It recalls that the Croatian Football Federation has been fined several times over the years because of fans’ behaviour, including incidents at the Croatia–France match in March 2025.

“they showed themselves in the worst possible light”

The Dutch football portal FCUpdate published an article under the title “Scandalous chanting at the Hajduk Split – Ajax match”. “Hajduk Split fans showed themselves in the worst light ahead of the Conference League match against Ajax,” the Dutch portal writes.

FCUpdate states that a large group of Croatian fans on the way to the stadium sang shocking songs. “Videos are circulating on social networks in which dozens of Hajduk Split fans can be seen and heard singing antisemitic and Nazi songs on the way to the stadium,” the portal states. The Dutch medium reports the chants about Jews, Auschwitz and Hitler, and particularly singles out the coffin with the inscription Ajax. “But that was not the end,” FCUpdate writes, stating that the fans displayed a coffin with the name of the Dutch club which was later destroyed. FCUpdate also reports that the Croatian police have launched a criminal investigation because of the disputed chants during the cortege.

“they changed about auschwitz”

The scandal was also reported by the large Polish sports portal Przegląd Sportowy. The title of the article published late last night reads: “Rise, Adolf. They chanted about Auschwitz. Behaviour in the Conference League resonated”. The Polish medium particularly emphasises that Hajduk fans repeated the provocation from 1995, when Hajduk and Ajax played in the Champions League quarter-finals. Even then the fans carried a coffin with the inscription Ajax, and 31 years later they staged a similar scene again.

“Shocking scenes in Split before the Hajduk–Ajax match in the Conference League. Croatian fans repeated a horrific gesture from 31 years ago, encouraged violence against Jews and shouted antisemitic slogans,” Przegląd Sportowy writes. The portal reports the chants about Auschwitz, Hitler and the Ustaše, and particularly stresses that open glorification of Nazism was recorded during the cortege. It also reports the police statement about the investigation because of punishable chants during the procession.

the torcida scandal made it to the green, romanian and even chilean media

Torcida’s antisemitic chanting was also carried by numerous Greek media. The Greek public broadcaster ERT published an article under the title “Horrific Nazi chants and a coffin with the inscription Ajax during the procession of Hajduk fans”, while the sports portal Gazzetta wrote about “the coffin and Nazi chants of Hajduk fans”.

The incidents were also reported by the Romanian sports daily Gazeta Sporturilor, which published a text under the title “Rise, Adolf, light the ovens! Horrifying scenes in the Conference League, they disgraced themselves in front of Europe!” The Romanian medium describes the antisemitic chants and recalls the similar provocation with the coffin during the Hajduk–Ajax encounter back in 1995. The news also reached South America. Chilean Cooperativa reported on Nazi and antisemitic chants against Ajax, stating that Croatian fans shouted slogans about Jews, Auschwitz and Hitler and carried a coffin with the name of the Dutch club.

the german and even russian media weigh in

Unlike the Israeli, Dutch and Polish media, German reports mostly focused on the events during the match. Berlin’s Tagesspiegel carried the news of the German news agency dpa under the title “Defeat and interruption because of pyrotechnics: A bitter evening for ter Stegen”. The German agency writes that Ajax experienced a bitter start to the Conference League and that the match was close to a definitive interruption because of the mass use of pyrotechnics by home fans. Russian media, including RBC, Sport-Ekspress and Euro-Football, also reported on the interruption. In their reports the emphasis was also on the flare display, dense smoke and interruption of the match, while RBC also mentioned earlier fan clashes and extremist chants in Split.

regional media

Numerous regional media outlets also reported on the antisemitic chanting. The Serbian public broadcaster RTS published an article under the title “Scandal in Split – Hajduk fans sang ‘Auschwitz, Auschwitz’ and ‘Rise, Adolf’”. The Montenegrin public broadcaster RTCG also reported on the antisemitic chanting, while the Macedonian Sloboden pečat published a text and a recording of the events. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the scandal was carried by N1, Vijesti.ba and SportSport.ba, which even before the start of the match published a report on the cortege. Slovenian Siol reported on fan clashes in Split and police interventions, while Dnevnik carried information about the antisemitic chanting.

apologies from hajduk split

Split police confirmed that during Torcida’s cortege they recorded chants that have the characteristics of punishable behaviour and that they are conducting a criminal investigation in order to establish the circumstances and identify those responsible. After the match Hajduk also reacted, apologising for the behaviour of part of the fans who caused the interruption of the encounter by the mass use of pyrotechnics.

“We apologise to the competition organiser as well as to the management and players of Ajax who witnessed scenes by which we do not want Europe to remember us,” Hajduk stated. The club added that it had taken all prescribed measures, but that despite that something happened of which it is not proud and that it is ready to bear responsibility. Hajduk’s apology referred to the events at the stadium. The police are separately investigating the antisemitic and Nazi chants during the cortege.

World.title: Dinamo Beats Anderlecht With 96th-Minute Penalty
World.content:
Dinamo beat Anderlecht 1-0 in the second round of the Europa League, with Dion Drena Beljo scoring the only goal from the penalty spot in the 96th minute. It was Dinamo’s first goal in this season’s Europa League, after a goalless draw with Israel’s Hapoel in the opening round.

Dinamo started strongly and pressed the visitors from the first whistle. Anderlecht soon settled, however, and there were good chances at both ends in the first half.

Luka Stojković had the first in the 15th minute. Left unmarked after a Hoxha cross, he was in an excellent position ten meters from goal, but the ball took an awkward spin off an Anderlecht defender and he could not make clean contact.

What followed was a spell in which Anderlecht could easily have scored more than once. In the 21st minute the Belgian side hit the crossbar twice in the same attack, with Dinamo goalkeeper Dominik Kotarski getting a touch to the second effort.

In the 28th minute Tristan Degreef shot from close range, unmarked, but Kotarski again reacted superbly to keep it out. Dinamo responded towards the end of the half, when Iker Almena found himself well placed from a cut-back but failed to hit the target.

Dinamo created three very good chances in the second half. The best fell to Arber Hoxha in the 81st minute, who was through on goal before Anderlecht full-back Barry got back to knock the ball away from behind him. The home side still found a winner at the death.

Substitute Dani Rodríguez struck the arm of Anderlecht left-back Oleg Reabciuk, and after a VAR review Dinamo were awarded a penalty, which Beljo sent down the middle.

The goal and the win go a long way to improving the picture for Dinamo. They are now 14th in the table, a play-off place, with six matches still to play in the league phase. For Anderlecht, it was a second defeat in this season’s Europa League.

World.title: Hero from Omiš Who Saved 60 People From a Fire Receives Bravery Award
World.content:
October the 16th, 2026 – A hero from a small coastal settlement near Omiš who saved 60 people from a massive fire has received a well-deserved bravery award.

Milan Balić, a young man from Stanići near Omiš, selflessly saved around 60 people with two boats when the fire broke out back in August. He has since received the Croatian Grand Security Award for bravery. Index reports that the ceremony in Opatija he modestly said that he simply found himself at the scene of the fire and emphasised that many other people also took part in the rescue. The recognition was presented to him as part of the 20th Conference of Croatian Security Managers at the Hotel Ambasador in Opatija.

The Croatian Association of Security Managers (HUMS) otherwise awarded prizes in 14 categories, and among the winners are also the City of Split, the State Hydro-meteorological Institute, APIS IT, the City of Zagreb and RTL Danas.

“it was sheer horror”

“What can I tell you, is that it was sheer horror. It was pure horror. Everything started from the upper side of the road and we hoped it wouldn’t cross to the lower side. But the fire passed across. People were running towards the sea, which was the most logical thing to do in that situation,” Balić said at the time.

“My house is among the first by the shoreline and I tried to save it as much as I could. Luckily, nothing happened to it. People were coming down to the beach, everyone was. Older people, young people, children. I decided then and there during the fire to take my boat and try to help them” he added. He set off on the rescue with two vessels. He tied the smaller boat to the larger one and loaded a total of 60 people onto them, among them children, elderly and injured persons. “I put the older men in the small boat, and the women, children and elderly people in the large one. There was really great panic,” Balić said.

“people were screaming from the beach”

The journey to Omiš was extremely dangerous. A strong bora was blowing, and because of the dense smoke visibility was almost non-existent. During the voyage Balić was especially afraid for the people in the smaller boat he was towing. “After we boarded, people were still shouting from the beach. I would have liked to help everyone, but there simply wasn’t any more space. While we were towing the smaller boat, I was most afraid that it wouldn’t sink, because there were also injured people in it,” he said. The drama did not end even upon arrival in Omiš. When docking in the town harbour the smaller boat capsized and people ended up in the sea.

“Everyone fell into the sea. Luckily, the army and special police were there and helped us pull them all out,” Balić said. For the bravery shown during that action he has now received the Croatian Grand Security Award in the category Brave Act in the Service of Security. At the award presentation, he modestly thanked all those gathered for the recognition, stressing that at the moment of the fire he simply found himself at that place. He emphasised that credit for the rescue also belongs to numerous other colleagues who took part in the action.

World.title: Croatia Should Never be a Cheap Destination, Claim Experts
World.content:
October the 16th, 2026 – Croatia should under no circumstances ever be permitted to be a cheap Mediterranean destination claim experts, but just how far has it gone the other way?

Poreč has become the centre of discussion on the direction of Croatian tourism, with a special emphasis placed on the role of hospitality operators in the development of the tourism sector. Boris Bilas reports for Glas Istre that the Parentium Plava Laguna hotel was the host of the 38th Congress of Hospitality Operators and Tourism Workers of the Croatian Chamber of Trades and Crafts (HOK). It gathered together a record number of crafts owners, tourism sector leaders and numerous high-ranking state officials.

istria generates a third of total croatian tourist traffic

The central themes of this year’s three-day gathering focused on preserving profitability in conditions of strong growth in input costs, the chronic shortage of qualified labour, and upcoming legislative changes. Opening the congress, HOK president Dalibor Kratohvil pointed out that 12,094 crafts currently operate actively in the Guild of Hospitality Operators and Tourism Workers, which is 140 more than last year. Nevertheless, he warned of the harsh economic reality on the ground.

“Hospitality operators are the last in the price-formation chain and do not realise any extra profits. While input costs of energy, supplies and labour are relentlessly rising, our margins are constantly falling. We have not raised prices in order to get rich, but exclusively for bare survival and the preservation of jobs,” Kratohvil said, emphasising that HOK continues to insist uncompromisingly on the introduction of the right to a full old-age pension while continuing to perform a craft activity.

The host of the meeting, president of the Chamber of Trades and Crafts of Istria County Robert Momić, proudly highlighted the role of Istria, which generates as much as one third of total Croatian tourist traffic with 29.5 million overnight stays realised in the first nine months.

“In the area of Istria we have almost 12,000 craftsmen, of whom 1,200 are directly in hospitality. Top-quality tourism does not happen here by chance; it is created, and our enogastronomy sector is a key motive for guests’ arrival. Thanks to synergy with local self-government and tourist boards, we have a clear strategy for a bright future of the profession,” Momić stated. Deputy County Prefect of Istria Jessica Acquavita addressed the far-from-easy reality of the labour shortage, emphasising that foreign workers have become an economic necessity without which the tourism system could no longer function.

language issues in istria

“We’re currently facing the complex challenges of language barriers and preserving the recognisable Istrian hospitality. In Istria County we are thinking seriously about this and have launched an initiative to establish a regional support network for foreign workers. We want these employees to become part of the local community as quickly and painlessly as possible, because by facilitating their integration we are directly investing in the stability of your business and preserving authenticity. Sustainable tourism is a balance between economic growth and social responsibility,” Deputy County Prefect Jessica Acquavita said.

tourists are spending more and more

Director of the Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ) Kristjan Staničić stressed that the success of the season must no longer be measured exclusively by the number of arrivals and overnight stays, but by the overall economic effects on the economy. In doing so he exclusively presented the first data from the new comprehensive TOMAS survey that HTZ conducted in cooperation with the Institute for Tourism.

“The average daily expenditure of tourists in Croatia has risen to €160 per person per overnight stay, which is an increase of as much as 16 percent compared to a few years ago. Absolute record holders are guests from the USA who on average spend around €280 per day, followed by the British with €248. This justifies our strong investments in air traffic and digital promotion towards those emitting markets,” Staničić revealed. He also highlighted that as many as 68 percent of tourists choose mid-price restaurants, which means that “value for money” must remain at the centre of the offer.

The most important political message of the congress came from State Secretary in the Ministry of Tourism and Sport Monika Udovičić, who directly responded to the discontent of hospitality operators regarding complicated administrative obligations and the constant updating of price lists that was imposed on the sector this summer.

price increases remain a serious issue

“We’ve heard your voice and your opinion. The state’s intention was to prevent uncontrolled price increases that also affect you yourselves through procurement, but decisions in practice must not be unenforceable nor further stifle your business. That is precisely why those disputed rulebooks have been put out of force. New acts are being prepared and we will ensure enough time for us to discuss them together,” Udovičić announced.

She also addressed stories about Croatia’s expensiveness and prices in tourism and sent a clear message that Croatia must under no circumstances be the cheapest country on the Mediterranean.

“Croatia should not and must under no circumstances be a cheap destination on the Mediterranean. Our competition such as Italy or Greece is investing strongly and investing a lot. We must be a destination in which the price is fully justified by top quality and an authentic experience, and that is precisely what our craftsmen offer in their taverns and restaurants,” the State Secretary concluded, announcing that the new Hospitality Activity Act, which enters into force at the beginning of 2027, will bring a more effective fight against unfair competition and unregistered business, as well as simpler, digital procedures for all legal craftsmen.

istria’s 180-year-old tourism brochure

Poreč Mayor Loris Peršurić recalled a historical curiosity, a fascinating 180-year-old tourist brochure kept in the Poreč museum, proving that the tradition of hospitality across the region of Istria has some very deep roots. “Behind the success of Poreč stands not only natural beauty, but primarily local people, people who own crafts and their warm hospitality,” Peršurić concluded.

World.title: Turks to Purchase Uljanik for €12.05 Million
World.content:
October the 16th, 2026 – The Turks are set to purchase Uljanik for €12.05 million. The Kuzey Star Shipyard will now officially take over 97.13% of the shares of Brodogradnja 1856.

With the agreement on the transfer of business shares, Morski reports that the moves brings the months-long sales process to a close and opens a new chapter in the revitalisation of Pula’s shipbuilding industry.

The aforementioned Turkish company offered a purchase price for Uljanik of €12.05 million, which is higher than the initially sought €11.08 million. CERP therefore readily accepted Kuzey Star’s binding offer at the beginning of September, while the second received offer from the Luxembourg company Mira Finance Holding was not accepted because the payment of the prescribed guarantee wasn’t recorded in CERP’s account. Given that the buyer is from a country that is not within the EU, before the actual conclusion of the contract, it was also necessary to carry out a foreign investment screening procedure in order to determine whether the investment poses a risk to national security and public order.

the continuation of shipbuilding has been ensured

The key condition of the contract concerns the retention of the core shipbuilding activity, the construction, repair and overhaul of ships and floating objects, across the entire area of the maritime domain under concession. By taking over the company, the Turkish investor obtains the existing shipbuilding infrastructure and concession rights for the use of the maritime domain in the Bay of Pula, but not ownership of the entire land and sea space.

Minister of the Economy Ante Šušnjar emphasised the importance of this decision for this previously less than stable Croatian industry: “By signing this contract, Croatia is approaching the completion of the process of revitalising the shipbuilding industry in the Pula area. Through its decisions the Government has preserved the possibility of continuing shipbuilding in Pula. The further development of Uljanik will depend on the business decisions, investments and contracted work of the new investor.”

experience and existing business ties

The director of Uljanik Brodogradnja 1856, Samir Hadžić, assessed as positive the fact that the new owner comes precisely from the shipbuilding sector. The Kuzey Star group owns shipyards in the Turkish cities of Tuzla and Yalova and has extensive experience in the construction, overhaul, maintenance and conversion of ships, as well as in projects related to the energy sector.

In addition, the Turkish company is already well acquainted with the possibilities of the Pula shipyard. Namely, Kuzey Star and Uljanik are already cooperating on the project to complete Newbuilding (Novogradjna) 526 (a livestock carrier which had a hull that had stood unfinished for years), which gave the Turkish partner direct insight into the available infrastructure and the capacities of the workers. In a series of works, the Pula shipyard maintained production activity also through work on yacht hulls and the completion of a fishing vessel.

Kuzey Star is otherwise already present on the wider Croatian market, work on an additional re-gasification module intended to increase the capacity of the floating LNG terminal in Omišalj was carried out at their shipyard. In the recent period Uljanik Brodogradnja 1856 employed around 230 workers, while together with subcontractors between 250 and 300 people participated in production.

World.title: Reform Party unveils campaign slogan as PM touts economic growth
World.content:
Prime Minister and Reform Party chair Kristen Michal says Estonia's economy is growing twice as fast as the EU average, as Reform pledges a clear course in the 2027 elections.

Speaking at the party's council meeting in Tartu on Saturday, Michal said the largest income tax cut in Estonia's history had doubled economic growth.

"Estonia's economy is growing twice as fast as the EU average," he said, also citing rising wages, consumption, exports and manufacturing, alongside lower unemployment and easing inflation.

"The Reform Party can say with confidence: our plan is working," the prime minister emphasized. "Estonia has been led through a major test and is now on a solid growth path, moving forward even in the face of headwinds."

He noted that wages are rising, with consumer confidence up and people taking home an average of 10 percent more money this year. Defense spending of 5 percent GDP, he added, is also strengthening security and giving families and businesses confidence to plan for the future.

Even the opposition is starting to see that the Reform Party's plan is working, Michal said, accusing Isamaa and the Center Party of already making plans to form a coalition — potentially joined by the Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE).

"The Reform Party is their main enemy for a reason: they can only steal Estonia's prosperity and growth if we're out of the picture," the party chair said, emphasizing that the key issue in the March 2027 elections will be whether this prosperity will continue to grow or be taken away from them.

Michal said that incomes must rise faster than prices, as a wealthier Estonia can invest more in education, healthcare, a cleaner environment and a better quality of life.

"No other party in Estonia stands as firmly for the economy, national defense, liberal principles, Estonian-language education and culture, and European values," he said. "These are the foundations of Estonia's future."

'A clear course for the future'

The Reform Party also unveiled its campaign slogan: "A clear course for the future."

Tartu mayor and party council chair Urmas Klaas said it reflects the party's focus on security, economic growth and opportunities for families and businesses.

He recalled that Reform's "Blue, black and white plan" for Estonia, unveiled in March, centers on building a stronger middle class, bolstering security and making greater use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the economy and government.



"We're running for election to ensure that robust security can give families confidence, people's work and knowledge can create prosperity and technology can help businesses grow and the state operate more efficiently," Klaas said.

MP and Reform Party secretary general Kristo Enn Vaga said the slogan emphasizes that Estonia's future is up to its own choices.

"We in the Reform Party want Estonia to be secure and the economy to grow, because that gives people and businesses more opportunities to carry out their plans," Vaga said. "This is the future we want to build."

World.title: Gallery: Public bomb shelter in Tallinn hidden behind woodland mural
World.content:
A street-level public civil defense shelter in the heart of downtown Tallinn has been transformed with a mural featuring Estonian trees and wildlife.

Located next to Kalev Sports Hall in Tiigiveski Park, the modular concrete shelter cannot withstand a direct missile hit, but it can protect around 20 people from blast waves, shrapnel and debris from an explosion as close as 50 meters away.

Similar shelters are already widely used in Ukraine, including in Kramatorsk.

The concrete module, donated by security company Citysec, is also now fully wrapped in a woodland mural by Colorees Art's Helena Hanni and Vahur Agar, featuring a wild hare, a bear family, an owl in flight and a wolf.

While usually kept closed in peacetime, the shelter was open to visitors on Friday, when officials were on hand to explain its features to the public.

Tallinn unveiled a new street-level civil defense shelter on Juhkentali tänav. October 2026. Source: Ellen Rudi/Tallinn Strategic Management Office

City weighs dozens more shelters

Citysec CEO Eduard Rikkas said the module was developed on a 50-50 basis with partners in Ukraine, where the design has already been in use for years.

Deputy Mayor Tiit Terik (Center) said the shelter door can be opened remotely during an emergency, and will unlock automatically if power or communications fail.

The shelter door, he added, will be kept locked in peacetime.

Tallinn has mapped 40 to 50 potential sites for similar shelters, with public procurement to follow if the city decides to order more.

According to the manufacturer, the shelter model installed on Juhkentali tänav costs up to €70,000.

World.title: Nearly third of teachers at schools transitioning to Estonian unqualified
World.content:
Nearly a third of teachers at schools transitioning to Estonian lack the required qualifications, as heavy workloads and limited pay make recruitment and retention harder.

When Tallinn's Ehte High School of Humanities switched to Estonian-language instruction in 2024, it hired 17 new teachers. One in three has since left, and the school continues to hire 10–15 more a year to replace both retiring teachers and those who leave due to burnout.

Principal Marika Kranisver said teaching students whose first language is Russian can require more work, as teachers have to adapt materials and bridge students' language gaps. Some end up leaving for schools with more native Estonian-speaking kids.

"I have tremendous respect for the teachers who have taken on this challenge and come to a transitioning school," Kranisver said, acknowledging how much more work it involves than teaching at schools where Estonian is already the main language.

Higher pay has helped attract teachers, but increasing funding constraints are making this harder for schools.

Tartu Jogentaga School principal Alina Braziulene said their school has had to cut the bonus pay for qualified teachers from 20 percent to just 3 percent as state support for Ukrainian students has ended and enrollment is down.

"A third of our students came from Ukraine, and the state used to provide substantial funding to support them," Braziulene explained. "That support is gone now."

Empty classroom in an Estonian school. Photo is illustrative. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

When schools could no longer offer higher pay, some teachers quit. Meanwhile, the number of teachers required to teach in Estonian has grown, but funding has not, further squeezing budgets for bonus pay.

'The workload is killing them'

At Tallinn's Läänemere High School, principal Deniss Presnetsov said bonus pay is important, but the school can't offer it to everyone, especially as some applicants lack the required qualifications.

He said workloads are also taking a toll on teaching staff, who juggle heavy administrative demands, lesson planning and consultations on top of the teaching itself.

"That kind of constant workload is killing them," Presnetsov stressed, adding that it quickly drives young teachers away. "They end up leaving the school after a couple of years. Some leave after just one."

The Ministry of Education and Research recommends training to help teachers work with students with non-Estonian language backgrounds, adding that with the right methods, teaching Russian-speaking students isn't necessarily harder.

World.title: Estonia's Eneli Jefimova sweeps skins event, snags MVP at college swim meet
World.content:
Estonian swim star Eneli Jefimova swept the breaststroke skins event at California college meet Friday, snagging MVP honors, a personal best and a win for alma mater NC State.

Estonian swim star Eneli Jefimova swept the breaststroke skins event at California college meet Friday, snagging MVP honors, a personal best and a win for alma mater NC State.

Jefimova clocked 2:06.19 in the 200-yard breaststroke at the College Swimming League (CSL) meet in Walnut, California, pulling away in the second half to beat Stanford University's Addie Robillard by 2.12 seconds — and shave 0.14 seconds off her previous personal best from February.

Robillard finished in 2:08.31, with teammate Lucy Thomas third in 2:09.67.

NC State's relay win gave the team the right to choose the stroke for the women's knockout skins competition, in which eight swimmers start and the two slowest are eliminated after each round until two remain.

The team picked breaststroke, and Jefimova won every 50-yard round despite having less than two minutes to complete all four, leaving little time to recover.



Jefimova swam the first three rounds in 26.71, 26.89 and 26.68 seconds before clocking her fastest time of 26.65 in the final. Italy's Anita Bottazzo, swimming for Indiana University, finished 0.42 seconds behind.

About 15 minutes later, the Estonian also took second in the 100-yard breaststroke, finishing 0.49 seconds behind Bottazzo with 58.74.

Another 15 minutes on, she helped NC State reach the final of the 4x50-yard medley relay skins event, where the team narrowly lost to Indiana, 1:36.95 to 1:36.18.

'It was so hard, I teared up'

"That was an insane meet!" acknowledged Jefimova, a two-time Olympian and four-time European champion. "I even teared up during the last 50 yards of the relay because it was so hard."

She was pleased with her new 200-yard personal best, saying it showed her endurance was improving. "I showed good speed in the skins," Jefimova said. "And the 100 breastroke? That was just hard!"

North Carolina State University (NC State) won the meet with 544.83 points, well ahead of Indiana's 469.83. Fellow Estonian swimmer Egle Salu's University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) team placed third with 394.33, followed by Stanford with 311.

The season's main event for both Estonians is the short-course world championships in Beijing on December 1–6. Jefimova won bronze in the 100-meter breaststroke at the previous championships.

Estonian swimmers Egle Salu (UC Berkeley) and Eneli Jefimova (NC State) at the College Swimming League (CSL) meet in Walnut, California. October 2026. Source: Estonian Aquatics

World.title: Gallery: Central Estonia's upgraded Mäo junction reopens to traffic
World.content:
Mäo's upgraded highway junction has reopened with five bus stops, two roundabouts and a 30-space parking lot, improving long-distance bus connections in Central Estonia.

A Lux Express bus made the symbolic first stop at Mäo on Friday, marking the completion of construction and the launch of bus service at the junction.

"By Monday morning, ten Lux Express routes en route to Tallinn and another ten en route to Tartu will be stopping here," said Urmas Kupp, executive director of the Järva County Public Transport Center (JÜTK).

Other bus operators are also interested and could begin stopping there as early as November 2.

One key amenity, however, is still missing. Despite assurances at the opening that the upgraded junction is safer and ready to accommodate long-distance buses, passengers have no proper public bathroom at Mäo, with only a temporary portable toilet installed next to one of the bus shelters.

The Transport Administration says building a passenger terminal is not its responsibility.

A portable toilet next to one of the bus stops at the updated Mäo junction in Central Estonia. October 2026. Source: Olev Kenk/ERR

"Our job is to maintain and develop national roads," said Transport Administration director general Priit Sauk, adding that it's up to public transport centers and local governments to build stops and passenger terminals.

JÜTK plans to sell an unused terminal and use the proceeds to build a new one at Mäo, which would also solve the bathroom problem. Infrastructure Minister Kuldar Leis (Reform) said the project should be a joint effort with the state.

"I think the most logical approach for projects like this is for the state and local governments to work together," Leis said.

Next stretch of Tallinn–Tartu Highway roadwork begins

Friday also marked the start of reconstruction on an eight-kilometer stretch of Tallinn–Tartu Highway between Käsukonna and Imavere. The work, expected to take about two years, includes a multilevel interchange at Imavere that will connect traffic from Viljandi to the highway.

Sauk said another 15 to 16 kilometers between Mäo and Käsukonna also need rebuilding.

"It's included in our road maintenance plan and long-term plans," he noted. "If the next funding period allows, we'd like to get started on it within the next couple of years."

The updated Mäo junction in Central Estonia. October 2026. Source: Karli Saul/Transport Administration

World.title: Estonia, Latvia at odds over cross-border wind farm
World.content:
A hybrid wind farm under construction in northern Latvia is stirring tensions across the border, where nearby Estonian villages are facing the greater impact.

Utilitas Wind is building Lode Hybrid Park just across the border in Latvia, with 18 wind turbines and battery storage, and company executives say the site was chosen largely for its connection to the third electricity interconnection between Estonia and Latvia.

The Lode project is the first wind farm to be built directly on the border.

Earthworks are underway near Arakste, where the first foundations have been poured and equipment ordered. The park is expected to start generating electricity in about a year, with full completion planned for the first half of 2028.

The €200 million project also includes battery storage, and Utilitas hopes to build four additional turbines on the Estonian side as well.

"We have 18 wind turbines, along with battery storage capable of delivering 60 megawatts (MW) of power for four hours," said Utilitas Group CEO Priit Koit.

He said the entire complex is connected to the third Estonian-Latvian power link, "so electricity can flow in either direction depending on where demand is higher."

100 trucks a day

Latvia's Ministry of Climate and Energy says the project will bring local economic benefits.

"Up to €300,000 a year will go to the municipality and local residents," said ministry parliamentary secretary Einars Cilinskis, emphasizing that people will see economic benefits and regional development spurred by the wind farm.

But construction has also brought disruption to nearby Estonian villages. For the next six months, around 100 big trucks a day are expected to pass through the usually quiet village of Penuja, hauling sand and gravel from Estonia.

New speed limit signs have been installed and truck drivers are being careful, but a road originally intended to support tourism in the area is now carrying mainly construction traffic.

"We have a very good working relationship with the developer," said Penuja resident Reet Paju. "Some residents do object, of course, but since we had no say in the decision to build the wind farm, we have to accept it."

Mulgi Municipality tried to challenge the project in a Latvian court but lost, as Estonian local governments have no legal standing to appeal decisions made by Latvian ones.

'Too many wind farms'

Local leaders, however, say the concern extends beyond Lode, with several other wind farm projects planned in the wider area.

"This isn't just about the Lode wind farm, but wind farms more broadly," said Mulgi Municipal Mayor Imre Jagomäe.

He pointed to eight potential turbine sites in his municipality, two projects in neighboring Saarde Municipality and a planned development on the Latvian side in Ipiķi.

"Clearly, that's just too many wind farms for this area," he stressed.

With the municipality's support, the nonprofit Looduse ja Inimeste Eest is conducting environmental studies in the area.

"Underway and also partially completed are environmental studies of birdlife, bats and ecological coherence," said board member Urmas Maranik.

Lode Hybrid Park is expected to produce enough electricity to meet the annual needs of 110,000 households.

World.title: Canceled school trips abroad leave dozens of families chasing refunds
World.content:
Dozens of families in Estonia say they are out thousands of euros for canceled school language-learning trips abroad, with one organizer still owing about €50,000 in refunds.

Twelve students from Jüri School were due to travel to Spain this fall through organizer Gerri Vihman and his company Keeleõppereisid OÜ. Each family paid €1,260 for flights, host-family accommodation, language classes in Madrid and insurance.

According to one parent, everything seemed fine until their latest meeting with Vihman, where concerns were raised about his previous issues organizing trips, including a canceled trip to England for Lagedi School.

Asked whether the same thing could happen to them, Vihman replied that he had learned from his mistakes. Concerns grew, however, when Vihman failed to send the families their plane tickets and then canceled the trip.

When teachers inquired whether parents could book the kids' flights themselves, Vihman reportedly said he could not refund them because the money was gone. The parents later learned that he had made no payments in Spain either.

"We realized he had probably planned from the start to steal our money, or that this was fraud," one parent told ERR.

In all, Vihman had collected €15,120 from the Jüri School students' families.

Organizer: All but last two trips paid back

Vihman told ERR that he has organized language trips for nearly 20 years and has never deliberately canceled a trip to keep customers' money.

Every business, he said, has its ups and downs, and most trips have gone smoothly. Over the years, he has canceled seven organized trips for various reasons.

"Sometimes people have canceled by choice, sometimes I've had to cancel myself," Vihman said, admitting that there have certainly also been shortcomings in financial management involved.

Even so, he said he has refunded all but the two most recent canceled trips.

"I am working on the refund process, but everything takes time," the organizer said, adding that he has already been in touch with the Consumer Protection and Technical Regulatory Authority (TTJA).

About 40 students' families are still waiting for refunds totaling roughly €50,000.

Vihman also confirmed "in the interest of honesty and transparency" that a Tartu school's trip had been canceled under similar circumstances.

"Lessons learned, and we need to address the situation and work with the parties involved, whether that's the TTJA or the police," he said.

No stranger to consumer regulator

The TTJA's Consumer Disputes Committee has received four complaints this year involving Keeleõppereisid OÜ, said Margot Leen, a consumer rights adviser at the authority. Two consumers received refunds, one withdrew their complaint and one case remains under review.

In 2024, the committee received 10 complaints involving another Vihman-owned company, Keelereisid Eesti OÜ. Five consumers received refunds, four withdrew their complaints and one case was closed because the consumer did not provide the information missing from their complaint.

"Consumers are entitled to a refund if they have paid for a trip and then the organizer confirms it has been canceled," Leen said.

Consumers should first submit a written complaint clearly stating what they want. If the company fails to respond within 15 days or the consumer is dissatisfied with the response, they can turn to the Consumer Disputes Committee.

In contractual disputes, final decisions can be made either by the committee or in court.

Two troubled companies

Before buying anything or signing a contract, consumers can check whether a company is listed as noncompliant with the Consumer Disputes Committee.

Business register records show that Vihman owns both Keeleõppereisid OÜ, registered in 2013, and Keelereisid Eesti OÜ, registered in 2024. Neither company has submitted all required annual reports, and Keelereisid Eesti OÜ's latest filed report showed no sales revenue and a loss of €124,022 in 2023.

Under the Tourism Act, travel companies must not only register their activity with the register of economic activities but also maintain sufficient financial security to cover obligations such as customer refunds if they become insolvent, said Diana Lints, head of the TTJA's Services Supervision Office.

The authority launched supervisory proceedings against Keeleõppereisid OÜ on April 30, issued a precept over its failure to meet the financial security requirement and issued the company a penalty fine.

Schools say earlier trips went smoothly

Jüri School principal Triinu Luiga said the school had acted only as an intermediary for the planned Spain trip, with teachers recommending the organizer to parents who paid the company directly.

"The school had previously taken five successful language trips with companies run by the same person," she said, adding that the teacher involved had also run a background check on the organizer and found no obvious warning signs.

Luiga said the teacher eventually contacted the Madrid school directly to confirm whether the arrangements were still in place, only to learn that Vihman had not been in touch with them at all.

She said the company sent parents a letter on October 14 promising refunds within 14 days.

he school is seeking help from a municipal lawyer but has not filed a police report; because parents paid the company directly, they must file any reports themselves.

Lagedi School principal Oliver Hoole said his school had taken six trips with Vihman without any issues, however a trip planned for this spring was canceled about a week before departure. Vihman told the school that the host language school could no longer accommodate the students.

"Sixteen students were supposed to go, and so far, half of them have gotten their money back," Hoole said, adding that one parent had paid more than €1,000 for the trip.

World.title: Estonia's Soviet-era summer cottage culture to become museum exhibit
World.content:
Built to strict Soviet rules, they stand apart from what came before and after, embodying both state leisure and private dreams.

Nearly 50,000 were built between 1950 and 1980. Now art historians from the Estonian Academy of Arts and ethnologists from the University of Tartu have joined forces to understand this heritage — what people built, and how they spent their time there.

The classic Soviet-era suvila design followed very strict dimensions. Source: ERR

"The privately owned summer cottage is a type of building constructed en masse during the Soviet era that shows how the state sought to create opportunities for working citizens to enjoy leisure time," said Epp Lankots, dean of EKA, on "Tähelepanu! Tegemist on teadusega."

Dagmar Ingi, head of rural architecture at the Estonian Open Air Museum, stressed the human-centered approach. "For me as an ethnologist, it is extremely important that we study the person and their relationship with their summer cottage," she said.

Another standard suvila design was this A-frame variety. Source: ERR

The researchers spend their summers across Estonia, talking to owners and documenting history. Interviews are free-form, closer to conversation than survey. They examine the whole property — garden beds, small structures, interiors — and spatial specialists measure and draw up plans. "We photograph them if people allow us to, inspect the interiors and draw up site plans so that, at some point, if someone wants to study this subject, all this material will have been properly preserved," Ingi said.

They also dig into archives for rare types, like terraced summer cottages. Owners bring out old photo albums, receipts and construction plans kept for decades — insight into everyday building practices and people's ingenuity.

A more idiosyncratic design of suvila. Source: ERR

The researchers approach every participant without prejudice. "For us, it does not matter what work they do or what kind of life they have lived. Every person's story is important, significant and interesting precisely as they have lived it," Ingi said.

The work is limited by time and the subjectivity of memory. Decades-old events arrive filtered through nostalgia, lending emotional color but diminishing factual accuracy.

The knowledge won't gather dust. "The aim of this project is actually to find a Soviet-era summer cottage that can be relocated to the Open Air Museum, where we can tell the story of a summer cottage built in the 1960s or 1970s, together with the story of the person who owned it, what they dreamed of and what they needed the summer cottage for," Ingi concluded.

World.title: 52nd OIC Council of Foreign Ministers convenes in Baghdad with 55 nations
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The 52nd session of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) officially opened in the Iraqi capital, Baghdad, on Saturday, October 17, 2026. Convening under the banner of advancing regional solidarity, peace, and sustainable development, the two-day summit brings together diplomatic delegations representing 55 member states and observer nations.

The spokesperson for the 52nd ministerial session, Ambassador Hassanein Kamil, announced in a formal statement that proceedings commenced following the arrival of all participating international delegations in Baghdad.

The commencement follows an announcement by the Iraqi Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Friday confirming the completion of all logistical, technical, and security arrangements required to host the high-profile multilateral convention, which runs through October 17–18.

Baghdad’s stewardship of the OIC foreign ministers’ summit reinforces Iraq’s proactive diplomatic posture aimed at bridging regional divides and serving as a neutral convening hub for dialogue.

Ministerial agendas across the two-day meetings are set to address collective security frameworks, cross-border economic integration, humanitarian response mechanisms, and coordinated diplomatic strategies to de-escalate ongoing conflicts across the wider Islamic world.

World.title: AI is coming for every company, Nvidia boss says
World.content:
Stockholm – Artificial intelligence will ultimately become a key aspect of all companies, the head of AI chip giant Nvidia said during a visit to Stockholm, where he urged Europe to ramp up its AI industry.

“Every single company will be an AI company eventually. Every single industry will be impacted by AI,” Jensen Huang told an event late Thursday, part of a European tour that includes a Nvidia-hosted conference in Berlin next week.

“The important thing for us is to recognise that Europe needs to build out the entire stack,” he said, referring to the AI technology chain from data centres to chatbots and other apps.

Speaking later to AFP, Huang said his company had invested $8 billion in Europe over the past year.

“We’ve strategically invested in different parts of that ecosystem, really high quality companies that we believe could help lift it, the whole ecosystem in Europe,” he said, citing the British data centre and AI cloud provider Nscale and the Dutch cloud provider Nebius as examples.

“In the last one year, we’ve invested $8 billion already. We have another couple of billion dollars in the pipeline,” he added. “We’re helping Europe create the AI ecosystem.”

Huang was in Stockholm for the launch of Sferical One, a Swedish supercomputer using Nvidia chips that will keep sensitive Swedish data and expertise in the country.

During his visit, Volvo Cars also announced it was expanding its partnership with Nvidia to improve safety technology in its planned self-driving vehicles.

World.title: Asian stocks rise as tech bounces from rout, Warsh upbeat on AI
World.content:
Hong Kong – Most Asian markets bounced Friday after the previous day’s tech rout fuelled by concerns over the AI boom, which Federal Reserve boss Kevin Warsh said offered huge benefits to the global economy.

Seoul and Tokyo enjoyed healthy gains in early exchanges boosted by chipmakers SK hynix and Kioxia, after having been pummelled Thursday as investors bailed out of the once-dominant AI sector.

The selling had been fuelled by forecast-beating US inflation data that ramped up bets on Fed interest rate hikes, as well as concerns about the financial health of data centre operator CoreWeave owing to its huge debt pile.

The New Jersey firm — which has borrowed heavily to finance hefty purchases of pricey semiconductor chips from Nvidia — tanked 15.5 percent Wednesday in the US as yields on some of its bonds soared, reflecting heightened angst over its future.

That added to concerns about the whole AI-tech complex, but Nvidia chief Jensen Huang on Thursday lifted spirits by defending the company and its health.

“CoreWeave’s strength is improving every day,” he told Bloomberg. “I’m optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing.”

CoreWeave’s shares climbed almost six percent.

Huang’s “defence of CoreWeave’s financial position was enough to pull the NeoCloud complex off the floor, drag AI equities higher and give the broader market something resembling a pulse”, wrote SPI Asset Management’s Stephen Innes.

“One moment the market was pricing the possibility that the AI financing machine had started eating its own tail, the next it was listening to the high priest of the boom explain that the patient was getting stronger.

“AI Jesus had entered the trading room and, for a while at least, the machines found religion again.”

Seoul jumped more than two percent and Tokyo around 1.8 percent, though they slumped 7.6 percent and 4.9 percent respectively Thursday.

Hong Kong, Shanghai, Singapore, Taipei, Mumbai, Bangkok and Manila were also up.

Paris and Frankfurt opened higher but London fell.

Fed chief Warsh said Friday that AI was the “most consequential change” to the global economy in his lifetime, predicting its effects would be positive but the path forward “bumpy”.

At an event at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok he said the AI investment boom would drive prices up in the short term, but “there really is, I think, a huge benefit to the global economy, to the US economy over the horizon”.

He also reiterated his previously stated belief that the technology would “make economies and countries that put it to good use more productive”.

But he added: “The path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one, bumpy in our understanding of the technology, bumpy because we really don’t know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies.”

Shares in Jakarta tanked more than 11 percent — its heaviest loss since 1998 — after index compiler MSCI said it was “no longer appropriate” to maintain Indonesia’s emerging-market status, fuelling fears of an exodus of foreign investment.

The US firm said earlier this year that investors had raised concerns about “ongoing opacity in shareholding structures” as well as co-ordinated trading behaviour that affected price information.

Authorities said they had carried out changes but MSCI said Friday that investors had indicated the “sufficient progress has not been observed consistently across the Indonesian equity market”, adding “it considers Indonesia’s continued classification as an Emerging Market no longer appropriate”.
