World.title: Filipino composer Rom Dongeto and the song we thought we knew
World.content:
Decades after a TV commercial propelled it into the mainstream, the activist-born anthem ‘Kanlungan’ — popularized by the voice of Noel Cabangon — continues to transcend generations as a bittersweet classic, though few realize it was composed by Rom Dongeto

“Kanlungan” remains an enduring staple of Philippine popular music, recognized across generations for its emotional weight and social relevance. And while Noel Cabangon has become synonymous with the song, few know the story of the man who wrote it.

Rom Dongeto, the composer of “Kanlungan,” traces his artistic origins to the 1980s protest movement, recounting the song’s journey from an obscure track in the early 1990s to a timeless anthem.

Play Video

Tondo roots

Dongeto’s activism began in Tondo, where he joined student organizing efforts at Torres High School.

During those formative years, he attended a concert at the University of the Philippines Diliman featuring prominent protest musicians Jess Santiago, Paul Galang, and Susan Fernandez. Watching them perform made him realize that music was far more than just art.

“Na-inspire ako…sabi ko, ‘Ito ang gusto kong gawin. Ito ang gusto kong maging vocation bilang isang aktibista,’” said Dongeto.

(I was inspired…I said, ‘This is what I want to do. This is what I want my vocation to be as an activist.’)

Later in college at Far Eastern University, Dongeto founded the cultural group Sinaglahi, performing across the University Belt and Sta. Mesa.

During this period, he crossed paths with Rene Boncocan, a Fine Arts student at UP Diliman and founder of the artist collective Lingkod Sining.

From Bukluran to Buklod

In the early ’80s, the artist network gave birth to Bukluran ng Musikero para sa Bayan, an alliance of progressive bands, such as Nuklus Band and UP Sintunado, as part of the growing movement against the dictatorship.

As Dongeto described it, “Nagsama-sama ‘yan para lumikha ng mga progresibong kanta, mag-perform sa rallies, makatulong sa consolidation ng protest movement, at makapag-inspire ng marami pang mamamayan.”

(They came together to create progressive songs, perform at rallies, help consolidate the protest movement, and inspire many more people.)

Play Video

The political landscape shifted dramatically following the assassination of Ninoy Aquino in 1983. The tragedy rapidly accelerated mass mobilizations and galvanized artists, students, and workers nationwide.

Around this time, Dongeto was introduced to folk singer Noel Cabangon through the latter’s activist brother.

“Dahil trabaho kong mag-organize, ‘yon ang ginawa ko. Pinuntahan ko siya sa isang tugtugan sa Kamuning. Kinausap ko siya,” said Dongeto, recalling how he recruited Cabangon to join their growing circle of cultural workers, paving the way for their long-term musical partnership.

(Since my job is to organize, that’s what I did. I went to see him at a gig in Kamuning. I spoke with him.)

EDSA years and beyond

The 1986 EDSA People Power Revolution brought a wave of political uncertainty to the movement, particularly among student activists. At the time, Cabangon was in Malaysia.

Reflecting on the pivotal night Ferdinand Marcos Sr. fled the country, Dongeto found himself in Morayta alongside student leader Lean Alejandro.

“Magkasama kami ni Lean sa Morayta noon…I can still remember Lean was crying noong gabing ‘yon at sinabi niya, ‘Huwag tayong manlulumo, magpapatuloy ang pagkilos,’” he said.

(Lean and I were together in Morayta back then…I can still remember that Lean was crying that night, and he said, ‘Let us not lose heart, the movement will continue.’)

Returning home that night, Dongeto channeled the lingering tension and uncertainty into the lyrics of “Ang Ating Awit,” a track that would later appear on Buklod’s second album, Tatsulok (1991).

In the aftermath of EDSA, Buklod dissolved as an umbrella organization. Dongeto noted that fatigue had likely set in after years of relentless struggle, and many believed that the fight had ended following the fall of the dictatorship.

Dongeto, Cabangon, and Boncocan, however, made a conscious decision to carry on as a musical trio, retaining the name.

“So ang ginawa namin, minaintain namin ‘yong pangalan ng Buklod bilang isang musical organization,” said Dongeto.

(So what we did was, we maintained the name Buklod as a musical organization.)

The illusion of a democratic transition was shattered in January 1987 when state troops under the Aquino administration opened fire on protesting farmers in Manila — a tragedy now known as the Mendiola Massacre.

This incident, according to Dongeto, partly inspired the creation of Buklod’s debut album, Bukid at Buhay (1988), a purely acoustic album which he fondly refers to as “classic Buklod.”

Writing ‘Kanlungan’

“Kanlungan” would ultimately become part of Buklod’s third album, Sa Kandungan ng Kalikasan (1992), a project intended to reach a wider mainstream audience while expanding their advocacy toward environmental awareness.

Writing the song was a fluid experience for Dongeto, taking him just two days to compose it. Unlike earlier protest tracks like “Tatsulok” — where he felt the heavy burden of political analysis through an activist lens — the words and melody for “Kanlungan” simply flowed freely and naturally.

Dongeto noted that he did not feel emotionally or intellectually exhausted after completing it because it came straight from what he was feeling.

Though the song’s vivid imagery leads many listeners to assume Dongeto grew up in a rural coastal town, he clarifies that he wrote it in Tondo using pure creative imagination.

For Dongeto, “Kanlungan” is more than a nostalgic love song; it is an ecological lamentation on fragile ecosystems and human responsibility.

“Meron din siyang lamentation na, ‘Tsong, pag pinakawalan mo ‘to, pag nagkamali ka dito, baka hindi ka na makabalik,’” he shared.

(It features a lamentation, ‘Buddy, if you let this go, if you make a mistake here, you might not be able to come back.)

Dongeto emphasized the direct link between human affection and stewardship of nature: “Kasi gaano man ka-romantiko buhay mo, ‘pag tinamaan ka ng bagyo, bumagsak ang lupa, bumagsak ang bundok, patay ka, ‘di ba? Romantiko ka nga, pero patay ka naman…Kasi kaya tayong lipulin ng pagkakamali natin ‘pag pinabayaan natin ‘yan.”

(No matter how romantic your life may be, if a storm hits, if the ground gives way or a mountain collapses, you’re dead, right? You might be romantic, but you’d be dead… Because our own mistakes can wipe us out if we leave them unaddressed.)

Through its poetic metaphor, the song serves as an urgent reminder to safeguard our shared environment. In the end, no one wants to destroy their own sanctuary, only to be left grieving in the ruins and asking, as the song does: “Maibabalik ba ang kahapon? (Can the past be brought back?)”

Commercial shift and controversy

In 2003, while studying in the United States, Dongeto was surprised to receive a call from the Philippines. It was Cabangon, who wanted to discuss licensing “Kanlungan” for a McDonald’s commercial. After clearing up concerns regarding copyright, Dongeto agreed.

The release of the ad, which reframed the song around familial homecoming, triggered a backlash from national democratic activists.

Critics called the licensing a sellout, given McDonald’s status as a symbol of US imperialism. The friction was further heightened by the ad’s visual narrative, which featured a family member in military uniform — a stark point of contention given the Armed Forces’ long history of human rights violations in the country. Neither Dongeto nor Cabangon knew the commercial’s specific storyline in advance.

Dongeto shared that he understood and respected the sentiments of his fellow activists, but they stood by their decision. They wanted to push the song’s environmental and social themes beyond progressive circles and into the general public, believing that a far wider audience deserved to hear their work.

Beyond the commercial

While the McDonald’s commercial that elevated it to fame has long faded into memory, “Kanlungan” transcended generations to become one of the most beloved Filipino songs. Its mainstream success cemented its status in Philippine culture and sealed Noel Cabangon as its definitive voice.

“Si Noel talaga ang boses ng ‘Kanlungan.’ Kaya nga ang tao ‘pag sinabing ‘Kanlungan,’ si Noel kaagad ang naiisip,” Dongeto acknowledged.

(Noel is truly the voice of ‘Kanlungan.’ That is why, whenever ‘Kanlungan’ is mentioned, people immediately think of Noel.)

“Kanlungan” broke into the mainstream through the commercial world that its creators once stood apart from. Whether that journey represented compromise or cultural victory remains a matter of perspective.

But the song survived the backlash, outgrew the  that made it famous, and acquired a life of its own — continuing to resonate as both a song of longing and a warning against the destruction of our natural sanctuary. – Rappler.com

World.title: As Asia grays, can an aging Philippines avoid its neighbors’ fate?
World.content:
Japan, South Korea trends

Japan's working-age population (people 15 to 64) peaked at about 87 million in 1995 and has since fallen to about 73.5 million. Roughly three in 10 Japanese are now 65 or older, the highest share of any country with a population over 100,000.

The overall population has shrunk for 17 consecutive years. Tokyo has spent more than three decades trying to reverse the trend, including a pledge of about Â¥3.5 trillion a year (roughly P1.6 trillion) since 2024. Its fertility rate still fell to a record 1.14 in 2025. Adult diapers now outsell ones for babies, and the country has over 9 million vacant homes.

South Korea is on a similar path. In 2024, its working-age population fell below 70% of the total population for the first time.

After spending an estimated P17.5 trillion over 18 years to boost births, South Korea still has gaps in emergency care and too few neonatal doctors for its already small number of newborns. Its fertility rate is 0.80, among the lowest in the world.

The money in both nations has gone into a wide range of measures. Many are aimed at births, such as cash for new parents, better-paid parental leave, and housing help for young families.

Pronatal incentives, or efforts to encourage an increase in the births of children, "are not shooting up the fertility rate at all," said Ng.

That does not make them worthless. They matter for children's well-being and women's workforce participation, she said, even if they cannot necessarily reverse a decline in population growth.

Even with deep pockets, Japan and South Korea have seen limited results. What does that mean for countries with less money?

âThe current systems in Asia, in general, are not quite ready in terms of the influx of aging populations,â said Ng.

The pattern isnât limited to rich countries. Thailand became an aging society in 2004 with a gross national income per capita of P281,184, according to UN and World Bank data. In 2025, just 416,514 babies were born there, the fewest since 1950, and deaths outnumbered births by more than 143,000.

Vietnam is not far behind. It entered its aging transition in 2015 and is projected to become an aged society by the mid-2030s, according to the World Bank, when 14% of its population will be 65 or older.

Across Asia, a 2024 Asian Development Bank report found, 40% of people over 60 have no pension, and about 60% donât get regular health checks. Among workers 65 and older, 94% are in the informal sector.

Many Filipinos are no different: workers who are contractuals or in informal jobs have no pension and little savings. As they age, many will have to lean on a stretched public health system and on their children. But there will be fewer children to lean on.

World.title: Why every audience vote matters in PETA’s ‘Gen G’ play
World.content:
The choose-your-own-adventure format of ‘Gen G’ forces the audience to stay fully immersed in the story, with the active, live-voting feature directly dictating the fate of the characters

The show begins with the Joker asking the audience to help guide the story toward a satisfying ending. Most of the crowd belongs to the younger generation, or the digital natives widely known as “Gen Z.”

“Gen G began by listening to young people talk about how they make these choices,” said Ian Segarra, director of the interactive theater show Gen G: GG na ‘To!

“Through our conversations with them, what emerged is that choosing is rarely simple. Our decisions are shaped by our families, friends, fears, responsibilities, circumstances, and the systems we live in. What seems like the wrong choice from the outside may feel like the only choice available to us.”

Organized by the Philippine Educational Theater Association (PETA) and Move to Change Foundation, Inc. (M2C), Gen G: GG na ‘To allows viewers, particularly the younger audience, to make choices as they watch the play.

Inspired by what Filipinos commonly say, “Kabataan ang pag-asa ng bayan (The youth is the nation’s hope),” the story features the characters Dex, Achi, Chloe, and Sid, all fighting for survival amid rising floodwaters in Balangay Gen Zones.

“At the heart of Gen G is the image of the Balangay — a vessel built to carry people together. It becomes a symbol of community and of the systems we inherit and build together,” Segarra said.

“We may not have created the world we are given, but we are constantly participating in how it is maintained, shaped, and transformed.”

Perhaps more than entertainment, Gen G is a live exercise in democracy. The show relies on real-time choices from the crowd, which, Segarra noted, resulted in unpredictable choices during the play.

This, he shared, also provided the production team with fresh insights.

“There are surprising answers. Merong mga hindi namin ine-expect na makikita nila, na nakita nila (We see things we didn’t expect them to catch),” said Segarra.

“It’s surprising and sometimes it’s also enlightening. Na parang, ‘Ah okay, ganito pala talaga…ganito mag-isip ang mga kabataan ngayon (Ah okay, so this is how today’s youth actually think).”

This choose-your-own-adventure setup forces the audience to stay fully immersed in the story, with the active, live-voting feature directly dictating the fate of Dex, Achi, Chloe, and Sid as they navigate the rising waters.

Since the cast must adapt to the audience’s decisions, the story flow changes with every single performance.

“I thought that theater is very powerful in evoking the emotions or evoking the capacity and potential of the youth. Hence, we considered to mount this play with PETA,” said Liza Abaya, founder of Move to Change Foundation, Inc.

Youth-centered effort

The cast, all Gen Zs themselves, makes the play even more relatable to the young target audience.

On stage, they portray characters with clashing personalities and conflicting ideas — forcing the audience to carefully weigh options during crucial decision-making moments. Ultimately, the characters have to make choices to achieve their common goal: saving their Balangay.

“In our practice, we cannot prescribe it. We will always pick it up from the audience,” said PETA president Melvin Lee. “If they will bring up a specific issue, the audience has to resolve it and come up with their own stand about a specific issue. Us artists, we cannot prescribe it for the audience.”

Zoe Damag, the cast member who plays the Joker, emphasized how this interactive approach empowers both the actors and the students.

“When students perform and engage, they come alive and realize their true capabilities. You are forced to research and deeply understand your reality, because you cannot portray a character — or make a choice — with half-baked knowledge,” Damag said in Filipino.

Despite the different choices within the story, the casts come in well-prepared to execute different scenarios every show, having rehearsed all possibilities.

“​That’s why it’s difficult at times, challenging at times, but it’s beautiful also because you get to understand how the young people also react to what is [in front of them],” Damag said.

Gen G will continue to tour schools and universities until December 2026.

As the play respects the young audience’s real-time decisions, it also allows them to realize the weight of their choices.

“What if the future of our community depended on the choices we make today?” EO Masilungan, M2C’s executive director, asked.

“​Young people saw something that mattered, and they decided to do something about it. And that is change-making.” – Rappler.com

Angel Camille Dio is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at Polytechnic University of the Philippines.

World.title: Trend Intel: Chinese microdramas have Filipinos in a chokehold – are you watching?
World.content:
Hey trendsetters,

Remember when Linda Walker sprinted from our screens to our shores?

The Heiress Who Won with Brains, the vertical Chinese drama following a 17-year-old girl who used her academic excellence to prove herself to her toxic family, took social media by storm, with the actress behind the protagonist, Zhang Yingfei, even making a visit to the Philippines in June. (Yingfei was invited by the Filipino Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry, Inc., which tapped her to promote education.)

Play Video

This is just one facet of the rise of Chinese microdramas in the Philippines. Referred to as duanju in Mandarin, these are designed for mobile-first viewing, typically running from 60 to 90 seconds per episode. The rapid and serialized content often feeds viewers with over-the-top plots and multiple cliffhangers for instant dopamine hits, making the case for its pay-per-episode system.

Originally emerging on Douyin (the TikTok-equivalent app in China) in 2018, Chinese microdramas have now evolved into a billion-dollar industry worldwide, with revenue outside China poised to increase from $2.7 billion to $3.6 billion this year, then growing to $9.5 billion come 2031, according to Media Partners Asia.

Even brands are joining in the hype. This includes Valorant, a video game by American developers at RIOT, as seen with their fresh collaboration with Old Goat (老山羊): A four-part series called The Dragon King Returns — Brimstone’s Revenge! It’s tension-filled and a little bit outlandish, following the usual narrative DNA that works.

Play Video

Even Shopee, a non-streaming platform, is riding the wave through their Shopee Video Dramas hub, where Chinese microdramas are free to stream. In the app, users can earn Shopee Coins through watching episodes.

A preview of the Shopee Video Dramas lineup

The local appeal

Gathering data and scanning social media platforms from September 2025 to September 2026, The Nerve discovered that in the case of Pinoy viewership, familiarity breeds… fixation. Chinese microdramas quickly provide teleserye emotions.

Source: The Nerve

“The stories start off from humiliation to revelation and payoff within a short mobile session. Familiar melodrama makes the compressed format easy to enter,” wrote The Nerve. “Most of these stories start with a major injustice, pivot when a major secret comes to light, and end with payback, personal validation, or true love.”

Tagalog dubbing and less time commitment also contribute to their appeal.

Source: The Nerve

A form of livelihood

In June, Vera Files reported that Filipino women in provinces are turning the “attention economy” into profit, thanks to streaming and livestreaming apps. This includes Melolo, a Singapore-based platform where users can “earn ‘coins’ by watching series, completing daily missions, and inviting friends using referral codes.”

Chinese microdramas reward viewers emotionally and financially.

In The Nerve’s study, the checkpoints for earning include new-user bonuses and rewards for each time one finishes an episode. Referral codes and cash-out claims become promotional materials, pulling in more viewers. And even if there are cases when the rewards start to decrease after the initial incentives, viewers stay because they’re entertained by the dramas.

Source: The Nerve

In his column “The Vantage Point,” Val A. Villanueva analyzed how the format orchestrates different elements to make us addicted.

“The architects of the microdrama discovered something more potent: ordinary viewers do not always hunger for a two-hour movie. Frequently, our resolve dissolves before 90 seconds of unrestrained melodrama, an outrageous premise, and an unanswered question,” he said. “And the very moment our curiosity is piqued to discover what happens next, the price of finding out has already been calculated.”

Shaping consumption

The rise of Chinese microdramas has also influenced how studios in the Philippines create their online shows, but they still keep the stories within our entertainment palette.

Source: The Nerve

In late 2025, Viva launched VMB (Viva Movie Box), or what they call “the first Filipino microdrama app.” Meanwhile, iWant has aggressively expanded its roster of original microdramas with vertical shows like Runaway Love, Shadow CEO, The Heiress Deception, and I Am Your Daughter, with the last three having a similar overarching theme of pulling off fake identities and satisfying revenge.

The AI takeover

But as far as identity goes, the Chinese microdrama industry is hounded by concerns regarding the sudden massive use of AI to produce shows — a move caused by the need for cost efficiency and faster turnaround, as the behemoth of an entertainment market continues to expand, but is affecting copyright, livelihood, and other factors.

A South China Morning Post report said that China’s broadcasting regulator has pushed for greater support for live-action dramas. This follows the government’s aim to maintain quality and protect rights despite AI domination. The National Radio and Television Administration’s Wang Xiaolang revealed that among the 430,000 microdramas released in China during the first eight months of the year, AI dramas accounted for 90% of them.

For a format that tinkers with very human elements, the use of AI to maintain the rise is pretty ironic.

Entertainment (and emotional resonance) as a soft power

While these microdramas are becoming a new Chinese soft power, it might not be the first time that their form of entertainment got people happily addicted.

Ultimately, this culture boom teaches us that it may not be rocket science to strike a chord with people’s emotions, whether it’s through a shareable meme or a confrontation-filled one-minute episode. It can sometimes just take a simple vertical format, as long as you know how to integrate your way into people’s lives.

Until the next scroll!

Jelou Galang

Culture Desk Content Producer

World.title: The week in photos: October 10-16, 2026
World.content:
NORTHERN LIGHTS. People watch Aurora Borealis as it illuminates the sky over Rovaniemi, Finland on October 10, 2026.

A recap of news, sports, lifestyle, entertainment, and human interest images from the Philippines and around the globe

MANILA, Philippines — Pope Leo was hospitalized in Rome’s Gemelli hospital late morning on October 13, ahead of surgery to remove a small growth on one of his lungs. The 71-year-old pontiff has lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations.

The surgery to remove a small growth discovered during a recent routine health check lasted about 90 minutes and was successful, with no complications, according to Leo’s lead surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, and personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone.

Blood tests and a chest X-ray carried out on October 14, showed normal post-operative results, the Vatican said, adding that the pontiff had undergone respiratory physiotherapy. Pope Leo‘s recovery from surgery is progressing as expected and he has begun walking in his hospital room and eating normally.



Meanwhile, on October 13, the prosecution team in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte withdrew all but one of the articles of impeachment to expedite the proceedings. Lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro stated that focusing on one article allows for a more efficient trial, while the defense team expressed concerns about due process and the potential for a mistrial.

The court accepted the withdrawal of the other charges, which prevents the prosecution from reviving those cases during the current Congress, allowing the defense to concentrate on the remaining unexplained wealth allegation.
