World.title: 5 Supreme Court justices vie to become next chief justice
World.content:
HIGH COURT. In this file photo, the Supreme Court is holding oral arguments on the national budget and unprogrammed funds on April 7, 2026.

The candidates include two of the most senior justices: Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen and Associate Justice Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa

MANILA, Philippines — The Judicial and Bar Council (JBC), through the Supreme Court (SC), issued the list of five candidates vying to become the country’s next chief justice.

The next top magistrate will replace Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, who will retire on November 6. The appointee will be the country’s 28th chief justice and will sit at the High Court’s top post.

As the highest tribunal of the land, the SC oversees all courts in the country, including high level courts like the Sandiganbayan, Court of Appeals, and the Court of Tax Appeals.

According to the SC, the JBC will hold public interviews for the following candidates on October 22 and 26:

October 22

Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen (9 am to 12 pm)

Associate Justice Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa (1 pm to 4 pm)

October 26 (1 pm to 4:30 pm)

Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda

Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao

Associate Justice Jose Midas Marquez

JBC, the body tasked to screen candidates for justice and Ombudsman posts, traditionally invites the five most senior SC justices to apply for chief justice. Two of the most senior justices who are not yet for retirement — Associate Justice Ramon Paul Hernando and Associate Justice Henri Jean Paul Inting — were not on the JBC list.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will appoint the next chief justice based on the list of nominees from the JBC. As found under Article VIII, Sections 4 and 9 of the 1987 Constitution, the SC vacancy must be filled by Marcos within 90 days — which means he has until February 2027 to pick the chief magistrate.

After Gesmundo’s retirement and if Marcos has yet to appoint a chief justice at the time, Leonen will serve as acting chief justice in the meantime.

“This is pursuant to Section 12 of Republic Act No. 296, or the Judiciary Act of 1948, which provides that when the position of Chief Justice is vacant, the duties and powers of the Chief Justice shall be exercised by the most senior Associate Justice until a new Chief Justice is appointed and qualified,” SC spokesperson Camille Sue Mae Ting earlier told reporters.

Gesmundo has been serving for over five years now after his appointment as chief justice in April 2021 by former president Rodrigo Duterte.

The next chief justice will be Marcos’ third appointment to the SC, which is currently packed by Duterte appointees. Two of the chief justice candidates were appointees of former president Benigno Aquino III (Leonen and Caguioa), while the rest are Duterte appointees. – Rappler.com

World.title: Amar’e Stoudemire goes from Miami Heat to Miami police officer
World.content:
SECOND CAREER. Former NBA star Amar'e Stoudemire (left) graduates from the Miami Dade College School of Justice's Basic Law Enforcement Academy

Amar’e Stoudemire has traded in his jersey and shorts for a dress uniform and a badge.

Now 43, the former NBA All-Star player and recent enshrinee to the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame, graduated from the Miami Dade College School of Justice’s Basic Law Enforcement Academy on Thursday, October 15. He will move into a position as an officer with the county’s school police department.

TOWERING. Standing at nearly 7 feet, Amar’e Stoudemire towers over his fellow police officers. Photo from Miami Dade College

On its X account, the college posted photos of the smiling 6-foot-10 Stoudemire with his classmates and teachers.

A statement from Miami Dade College explained the motivation of Stoudemire, who enjoyed a decorated 14-year NBA career.

“For Amar’e, this is more than a second career,” the school announced in a post on X. “Becoming a police officer was a childhood dream, inspired in part by family members who served in law enforcement. Now, he will begin a new chapter as a police officer with the Miami Dade Schools Police Department, giving back to our community and serving as a positive influence for the next generation.”

Born in Florida, Stoudemire went straight from high school to the NBA, selected with the ninth overall pick in 2002 by the Phoenix Suns. He was named NBA Rookie of the Year in 2003 and was a six-time All-Star.

He played primarily for the Suns and New York Knicks, and briefly, at the end of his career, for the Dallas Mavericks and Heat. In his final NBA season, 2015-2016, he appeared in 52 games for Miami. The following season, he played for a pro team in Israel.

Stoudemire averaged 18.9 points and 7.8 rebounds over his 846 regular-season games (696 starts). – Rappler.com

World.title: US Holds Second Round of Talks With Myanmar Regime as Concerns Grow Over Policy Shift
World.content:
U.S. officials held a meeting with Myanmar miliary regime officials in Tokyo last week, Reuters reported on Friday, citing sources familiar with the meeting.

It was the second round of talks between the two countries within a month. A U.S. delegation led by Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance visited the regime’s capital Naypyitaw in mid-September.

Vance also led the delegation in Tokyo, which included over a dozen U.S. officials, while the identities of regime representatives and the issues discussed remained undisclosed, according to Reuters.

At the September talks, the U.S. delegation met with coup leader Min Aung Hlaing and secured the release of American businessman Adam Castillo, who had been detained upon returning to Yangon in June 2026 over a lawsuit filed against him.

The U.S. outreach led by Vance has focused on shutting down scam centers that target Americans, but could lead to broader engagement, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, Reuters reported, citing current and former officials as well as others familiar with the U.S. policy shift.

The Irrawaddy has learned that during the Naypyitaw meeting, the U.S. side urged the regime to reduce attacks on civilians, crack down on money-laundering gangs, engage with ethnic armed groups, release political prisoners and allow unfettered distribution of humanitarian assistance.

Observers noted that the Trump administration has shifted its policy from isolating the Myanmar military-installed government to engaging with it.

The National Unity Government (NUG), a leading anti-regime revolutionary organization, said it was not overly concerned by the increasing engagement between the U.S. and the military junta.

Speaking to The Irrawaddy, NUG Foreign Affairs Minister Zin Mar Aung said the U.S. is engaging with both sides—the military regime and the revolutionary groups—purely based on promoting its own interests, without granting legitimacy to anyone.

“Its [U.S.] policy is already clear. They are taking a transactional, practical approach to tackle issue like TOC [transnational organized crime]. They will discuss matters that are crucial to U.S. interests,” she said.

“So, this is nothing unusual. Nor is it a shift in policy. Since the Trump administration took office, this is how the U.S. has been dealing with [all] countries, not just Myanmar.”

Banya Khung Aung, Secretary 2 of the Interim Executive Council of Karenni (Kayah) State, which largely controls the eastern Myanmar state, told The Irrawaddy he is concerned that increased U.S. engagement with the regime will harm the country’s federal democracy and human rights movements, whether financially, technically or operationally. As evidence, he pointed to the Trump administration’s recent cuts to USAID funding for Myanmar.

“If you look carefully at Donald Trump’s policies, everyone knows that he engages with all [sides] and highly considers his national interests. So, I am not surprised with [the administration’s ongoing] engagement with the regime,” he said.

He noted that foreign governments are no longer prioritizing democracy and human rights, and are instead focusing on their national and common interests.

“Because of that, whether it is a government or a dictatorship, if there are benefits for America, it is almost certain they will engage.”

Bertil Lintner, a Swedish journalist, author and strategic consultant who has been writing about Asia for more than four decades, echoed Banya’s comments.

“I am not surprised. Democracy has never been a top priority for the Trump administration. And more countries are starting to acquiesce to a fait accompli. The military-dominated government is there to stay for the foreseeable future.”

Following the 2021 coup, the U.S. under Joe Biden imposed sweeping sanctions against top regime generals—including Min Aung Hlaing and his family—as well as military-owned conglomerates.

But Trump has shifted U.S. policy from isolating the regime to engaging with it, including delisting junta cronies accused of aiding and abetting regime war crimes and crime against humanity committed against their own people.

Meanwhile, the country, whose economy has collapsed under the regime, has become a hotspot of transnational organized crime. Chinese-run scam syndicates under the protection of several armed organizations, including regime-controlled or aligned militia groups, defraud huge sums from victims globally, including Americans, who have lost billions of dollars annually in recent years.

Regarding U.S. engagement with the regime, Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of the Alternative Asean Network on Burma, said, “It looks like President Trump has been scammed by sham President Min Aung Hlaing. Trump is rewarding a criminal for committing more crimes.”

She warned that U.S. engagement with the regime not only poses risks to the country’s pro-democracy movement, but also endangers civilians in Myanmar and across the region. She noted that Min Aung Hlaing has escalated the country’s conflicts, causing mass displacement, while also driving a boom in transnational crime that targets victims regionally and globally.

“Embracing Min Aung Hlaing is embracing a nest of vipers. He has been intensifying threats to regional human security and economic stability,” Stothard said.

The U.S. State Department said it engages will all groups in Myanmar on issues affecting U.S. interests and has raised the need to cease violence and release political prisoners, according to the Reuters report.

World.title: Chinese Jet-Fuel Refinery to Bypass Sanctions, Myanmar’s Blood Timber Flows to China, and More
World.content:
China‑backed refinery lets regime bypass jet fuel sanctions

Myanmar’s military regime has restarted the Thanlyin No.1 Oil Refinery near Yangon, allowing it to bypass jet fuel sanctions and sustain its deadly air raids on the civilian population. According to Nikkei Asia, Phase 1 is designed to produce 150,000 metric tons of jet fuel annually, roughly equal to Myanmar’s import volume last year.

The refinery, operated by Myanma Petrochemical Enterprise (MPE), was taken offline in 2017 but rebuilt after the 2021 coup. The engineering, procurement and construction contract was awarded to Peiyang Chemical Engineering Service Corporation (PCCS), a Singapore-registered subsidiary of Peiyang Chemical Equipment in Tianjin.

Anhui Tiankang Group supplied nearly 400 measuring devices for the various chemical processes, coordinated by Tianjin Sainuo Oil & Gas Technology. Some modules were fabricated in China and shipped via Singapore to Thilawa Port.

The regime says the project will reduce foreign currency outflow and stabilize supply. It has heavily relied on air power since 2022, killing thousands of civilians, and this dependency has only increased as the territory it controls continues to shrink. In the most recent atrocity, 50 civilians died and nearly 60 were injured when the regime bombed a busy market in Rakhine’s Kyauktaw.

China becomes biggest buyer of Myanmar’s blood timber

China has become the dominant buyer of Myanmar’s timber since the 2021 coup, according to UN Comtrade data cited by Australia’s Wood Central.

Last year, China’s purchases climbed to US$147.3 million, nearly double the pre-coup total of $78 million, while Western imports collapsed from roughly the same amount to just $1.2 million worth, according to Forest Trends, a Washington‑based non‑profit that monitors global forest trade and conservation finance.

The group’s analysis shows China’s share of Myanmar’s reported wood exports rose from 25.5 percent in 2019 to a peak of $228.7 million in 2024, nearly 80 percent of the total, before settling at 74.1% in 2025. Nearly three‑quarters of China’s imports since the coup were bound for companies registered in Yunnan Province.

Myanmar’s total reported wood exports rose from $304.3 million in 2019 to $370.6 million in 2022 but then fell to $198.9 million last year after the regime lost control over most of the border with Yunnan in Shan and Kachin states. But China continues to import timber through border crossings now controlled by ethnic armed groups.

Western buyers’ share now accounts for just 0.6 of Myanmar’s blood timber, but Forest Trends warns that the decline does not necessarily mean sanctions are working. Instead, the group believes much is “re-exported” to the West after “transiting through China,” though the flow is harder to trace.

Kokang scam warlord sentenced to death

A Chinese court on Tuesday sentenced three leaders of Myanmar’s notorious Wei clan to death as Beijing continues its public reckoning with the Kokang scam syndicates. The Quanzhou Intermediate People’s Court convicted Wei Huairen and two others of running violent fraud compounds that trafficked Chinese nationals, forced them into online scams, and murdered at least two victims.

According to Chinese state media, the Wei family’s network generated 12.2 billion yuan (US$1.8 billion) through online scams, drug trafficking, illegal casinos, and prostitution. Courts also handed life sentences to three associates and prison terms to 55 others, describing the gang as the “most violent criminal force in northern Myanmar.”

The Wei clan was one of four family crime syndicates in Kokang, which is now controlled by the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA). Wei Huairen was the chief of the regime-aligned Kokang Border Guard Force (BGF), in which capacity he created a much-emulated model of quasi-official armed protection of online fraud parks. The ruling follows earlier executions of Ming and Bai clan members.

Beijing renews outreach to Myanmar’s party leaders

The director‑general of the Chines Communist Party’s International Liaison Department, Peng Xiubin, met leaders of nine Myanmar political parties in Yangon on Tuesday, though none associated with the bona-fide opposition.

Present at the meeting were the usual suspects from the ruling Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) as well as a few co-opted ethnic political parties like the Arakan Front Party (AFP) and Shan and Nationalities Democratic Party (SNDP). Discussions focused on “bilateral ties” and Myanmar’s “peace and reconciliation,” according to participants.

SNDP chair Sai Aik Pao told the Popular News propaganda outlet that he urged Peng to help the central regime regain control over the Muse–Mandalay trade corridor, pushing out the MNDAA and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA).

“China has influence” over those armed groups, he was quoted as saying.

While the USDP remains at the center of party-to-party ties, China also often flies other party leaders to Kunming and Beijing for “study tours” and “cooperation forums.” Shortly after the regime announced its planned elections last year, the department hosted a delegation of several Myanmar political parties in Beijing.

Shan groups warn against MNDAA’s ‘Sinicization’

Eight Shan civil society and youth groups published an open letter to the MNDAA on Oct. 9, warning that its boorish cultural and administrative practices in northern Shan State threaten ethnic coexistence and China–Myanmar border stability.

The letter warns that the MNDAA’s military control is only temporary and urges it to respect local ethnic traditions, languages, and rights. The groups accuse the Chinese-speaking group of erasing Shan, Ta’ang and Burmese scripts from public signboards and replacing them with Chinese characters. They argue that imposing Chinese-style governance and financial systems without consultation undermines trust and risks fueling resistance.

Such actions could even jeopardize the future of the China–Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC), the letter warns, referring to the pet project of the MNDAA’s paymasters in Beijing.

Ta’ang civil society groups have similarly condemned the MNDAA’s actions. In April, six Ta’ang organizations said replacing Ta’ang signs with Chinese amounted to erasing an ethnic identity—a violation of international human rights law.

The MNDAA is busy consolidating its control of all major trade corridors linking to Yunnan Province.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Regime Turns to Belarus for High Interest Loans as Fiscal Crisis Deepens
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime, squeezed by a worsening fiscal crisis, has turned to its ally Belarus for high‑interest loans, with its rubber-stamp parliament granting approval to borrow at rates nearing 10 percent.

On Wednesday, lawmakers endorsed coup leader Min Aung Hlaing’s proposal to secure loans from Belarus just eight days after he submitted the request to the Union Parliament. The loans will be used to purchase goods from Belarus.

The loans will come from the state-controlled Development Bank of the Republic of Belarus (DBRB) and Belinvestbank JSC, with maturities ranging from one to five years. The regime has not disclosed the total amount, but the high interest rates have already drawn criticism.

Deputy Finance Minister Than Than Lin told parliament on October 6 that rates would range from 2.25 to 9.33 percent. Her colleague Kyaw Htin argued on October 14 that the short‑term nature of the loans — capped at five years — would limit exposure to market volatility.

The loans can be denominated in Russian rubles, Belarusian rubles, yuan, US dollars, or euros, with interest rates varying by currency type and commodity group. The regime says it will pre‑screen payment channels to avoid currencies subject to sanctions.

Authorities plan to use the loans to import capital goods (machinery), intermediate goods (raw/semi-finished products), consumer products, and other commodities. Purchases of Belarusian‑made goods, machinery, technology, and services will be financed through Belarusian banks, with Myanmar ministries, agencies, or private firms acting as buyers. In effect, Belarusian exporters will supply the goods while Myanmar entities serve as importers.

Three state‑owned banks, Myanmar Economic Bank, Myanmar Foreign Trade Bank, and Myanmar Investment and Commercial Bank, have already signed banking arrangements with Belarus, and talks are underway to open accounts.

During Min Aung Hlaing’s August trip to Minsk, the regime signed nine agreements, including a loan framework deal between Myanmar’s Ministry of Finance and JSC Development Bank of Belarus.

While the junta chief has repeatedly insisted Myanmar must rely on domestic resources rather than foreign loans, his regime’s rush to secure Belarussian credit underscores the depth of its fiscal crisis. The loan approval came the same day that lawmakers nodded through the regime’s proposal to “borrow” up to 2.1 trillion kyats from the Central Bank of Myanmar to fill its 2026-27 budget deficit.

“Myanmar’s public will suffer from the high-interest loans, which will be repaid at the expense of education and health budgets,” said a Myanmar analyst.

Myanmar’s ties with Belarus were once limited to arms sales, but since the 2021 coup cooperation has expanded into politics, economics, and now finance. Belarus has emerged as a key ally alongside Russia, with Min Aung Hlaing visiting Minsk frequently while also hosting Belarusian strongman Alexander Lukashenko in Naypyitaw.

Lukashenko was the first foreign leader to visit Myanmar after Min Aung Hlaing installed himself as head of state in April.

Reports suggest the regime may next lean on Russia for credit, with President Vladimir Putin pledging financial sector cooperation in August while hosting Min Aung Hlaing in Moscow.

Meanwhile, the junta has cut imports of basic goods including fuel, cooking oil, and steel to save foreign currency, while squeezing revenue through tax hikes, natural resource sales, and tighter remittance rules for migrant workers.

After the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, and Western governments suspended aid and imposed sanctions following the coup, Min Aung Hlaing’s regime has been increasingly dependent on loans and support from his authoritarian allies, analysts say.

World.title: China’s Shrinking Politburo Has a Diversity Problem
World.content:
China’s Communist Party chose 24 men for its Politburo in October 2022, all of them Han Chinese. It was the first Politburo without a woman in 25 years, and it included nobody from any of China’s 55 officially recognized ethnic minority groups. After four years, the group is even more exclusive.

In October 2025, the party expelled Central Military Commission Vice Chairman He Weidong. Former Xinjiang Party Secretary Ma Xingrui followed in July 2026, and top general Zhang Youxia last month. Official notices accused all three of serious violations; the notice on Zhang also alleged disloyalty, “faction-building” and a remarkably large number of bribes. Their removal leaves an active Politburo of 21—a concentration that tells us something important about power under Xi Jinping. Diversity exists farther down the political system, often through quotas and administrative rules. It disappears where the most consequential decisions are made.

A narrowing funnel

The contrast starts with the membership. At the end of 2025, women accounted for 31.5 percent of the Communist Party of China’s 101.3 million members, while ethnic minority members made up 7.8 percent. Among people admitted in 2025, women made up 46.5 percent and ethnic minorities 10.2 percent, according to the Central Organization Department.

Representation was also visible at the 20th Party Congress. Its 2,296 delegates included 619 women or 27 percent, and 264 ethnic minority members or 11.5 percent, drawn from 40 minority groups. Then the funnel thins. Only 11 of the 205 full members elected to the 20th Central Committee were women, while nine came from ethnic minority groups. At the Politburo level, both figures fell to zero.

This isn’t a simple story of too few qualified candidates. Shen Yiqin, an ethnic Bai woman, had served as Guizhou governor and provincial party secretary before the 2022 congress. She became a state councilor in 2023 and later president of the All-China Women’s Federation, yet never entered the Politburo. Her current brief covers civil affairs, human resources, social security, veterans, sports and liaison with the ethnic affairs bureaucracy. Those duties matter, but a state councilor ranks below the Politburo members.

Rules stop below the top

China has spent decades building representation requirements. A 2001 party directive called for at least one woman in provincial and prefectural party, government, legislature and political advisory leadership teams, as well as in county party and government teams. It gave early priority to women in education, culture, health, family planning, civil affairs and similar departments. The 2021-2030 national program for women calls for more women in local government leadership, more female principal officials and better access to training, rotation and key posts.

Yet many targets use the phrase “gradually increase” without a numerical floor for the Central Committee, Politburo or its Standing Committee. The result is presence without a reliable route to the top.

A peer-reviewed study of every prefectural mayor and party secretary serving between 2003 and 2020 found that women followed faster but more restricted careers. Female officials were younger and better educated, but more often came through the Women’s Federation, Communist Youth League and other less powerful portfolios. Men had greater access to finance, development and core party offices. Women held only 135 of 1,987 mayoral posts and 88 of 1,694 party secretary posts.

The study also found a revealing pattern: about 20 percent of women mayors were ethnic minority members, compared with 13 percent of male mayors. One appointment could therefore satisfy expectations for both gender and ethnic representation, while leaving more positions open for Han Chinese men. The evidence supports this “tandem quota” effect at the prefectural mayor level, but it doesn’t establish that top leaders consciously use the same calculation when selecting the Politburo.

Ethnic glass ceiling

Ethnic minority cadres face a parallel divide. China’s ethnic autonomy law reserves the head-of-government in autonomous areas for a member of the relevant minority, but the more powerful party secretary post has generally gone to a Han Chinese official. For decades, minorities held roughly 10 percent to 11 percent of full and alternate Central Committee seats, yet most sat in the alternate tier.

No ethnic minority official has ever joined the Politburo Standing Committee. A handful reached the wider Politburo: Zhuang general Wei Guoqing and Mongolian leader Ulanhu served there during the Mao and early reform years; Hui Liangyu later served in the body and became a vice premier. Those cases show the barrier isn’t formal, but they also highlight how rarely it has been crossed.

Under Xi, official ethnic policy increasingly centers on “forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation.” At the 2021 Central Ethnic Work Conference, Xi linked good cadre standards to firm support for centralized party leadership and commitment to his national community project. The policy stresses political unity, shared identity and security more than representation by distinct groups.

Perhaps this policy did not directly cause the all-Han Politburo. Public records don’t reveal the bargaining, vetting or rejected candidates behind elite appointments. Still, the roster fits a system where minority identity can warrant representation in congresses and autonomous governments but offers little access to the center.

Diversity and decision quality

An all-male, all-Han Chinese Politburo doesn’t mean every member thinks alike. Nor does adding women or minority officials guarantee different policies. Officials who rise through the same selection system may share its priorities. But there is evidence that representation can affect what institutions do. Women held about one-fifth of the seats in China’s 12th National People’s Congress but sponsored 44 percent of legislative bill proposals and more than half of proposals concerning women’s rights and interests. That finding comes from the first systematic study of female legislators’ behaviour in the national legislature.

The useful question isn’t whether one woman or minority official would transform policy but whether the leadership is drawing on the country’s full pool of political experience. The body, after all, makes decisions on birthrates, employment, Xinjiang, Tibet and social welfare.

The practical tests are clear. Party authorities could publish measurable targets for women and ethnic minority officials at each rung of the promotion ladder, report compliance and place more candidates in finance, security, organization and provincial party secretary jobs that feed Politburo selection. They could also stop treating one minority woman as sufficient evidence that two representation goals have been met.

Watch the 21st Party Congress, expected in 2027. Count who enters the full Central Committee, who receives powerful provincial and central portfolios, and who reaches the Politburo. Speeches about equality are easy to issue. Twenty-one occupied seats provide the harder evidence.

Chandu Doddi is an Assistant Professor at the Centre for Chinese Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi.

World.title: New ID Rules Tighten Regime’s Grip on Migrant Remittances From Thailand
World.content:
Desperate for revenue, the Min Aung Hlaing regime is again using the Certificate of Identity (CI) process to extract money from undocumented Myanmar migrants in Thailand, forcing them to shoulder even greater financial hardship.

The regime recently added new rules to the CI process, requiring migrants to use the regime’s official channels for 25 percent of their remittances before applying for the certificate.

The CI is a temporary document intermittently issued by Myanmar that serves as an alternative to a passport for migrant workers in Thailand, allowing them to secure a legal work permit.

Regime Labor Minister Maung Myint told Parliament on Thursday that five centers issuing CIs started operating on Wednesday in Thailand’s Samut Sakhon, Samut Prakan, Chiang Mai, Chon Buri and Surat Thani.

The new order requires workers to provide proof of remitting 6,000 baht (about US$180) through official channels, equivalent to 25 percent of three months’ wages calculated on a fixed monthly salary of 8,000 baht, as well as proof of payment of 2 percent income tax. Newly appointed regime Labor Minister Maung Myint said remittances are a matter of “national interest,” and workers should consider them “a donation” to the country.

The move is part of the regime’s longstanding effort to extract foreign currency from overseas workers, including through the income tax and mandatory 25-percent remittance rule introduced in 2023.

Groups assisting migrant workers said the new requirements would complicate the employment process, potentially leading to higher costs for workers.

“Many workers do not have stable jobs,” a member of a migrant assistance group told The Irrawaddy. “How can they transfer the money, when they are already struggling with the cost?”

Complicating the process by requiring more documents would create space for service providers to charge more money, he said.

The CI application costs around 3,600 baht, but workers must rely on service providers or agents, who normally charge between 7,000 and 15,000 baht, including service fees, though precise costs under the latest rules remain unclear.

A migrant worker in Thailand told The Irrawaddy that the agent who managed his CI application process charged around 15,000 baht.

The amount is paid in installments to his employer through deductions from his monthly wages, reducing the amount he could send home.

“I send less money to my family. Everyone around me has to do the same thing,” he said.

Meanwhile, service providers said families of some workers in Myanmar do not have access to the banking system, making it more difficult to obtain proof of remittance transfers.

“Some workers’ families live in remote areas. It is not easy for them to withdraw the money,” a service provider told The Irrawaddy. He added that the regime was also likely to introduce stricter checks on applicants and their supporting documents.

U Set Aung, an economist and former deputy minister of planning and finance under the ousted civilian government led by Aung San Suu Kyi, wrote on his Facebook page on Thursday that low-wage Myanmar workers in Thailand were struggling to cover their living expenses and could not afford to remit 25 percent of their wages.

“The amount workers send home should be their own decision,” he said.

He added that the policy was designed solely to benefit the regime, rather than to support families and formal banking use.

“When remittances are converted at exchange rates below prevailing market rates, workers and their families suffer additional financial losses,” he said. “It raises serious concerns about freedom of movement, the right to pursue a livelihood, and fundamental labor rights.”

As the Myanmar regime steps up efforts to squeeze remittances from overseas workers, workers in Thailand are a prime target. Thailand hosted nearly 3 million Myanmar workers as of November 2025, according to official Thai figures. But the real number is likely to be much higher as many workers are undocumented.

Labor Minister Maung Myint said on Thursday that remittances from Myanmar migrant workers abroad totaled $5.6 billion in 2025. Experts say the regime’s remittance controls have cut a vital financial lifeline for the Myanmar population, which has been badly affected by conflict and economic collapse triggered by the 2021 coup that brought the regime to power.

World.title: Kyat Slides Again as Regime Wins Approval for 2.1 Trillion-Kyat Borrowing Plan
World.content:
The kyat lost value again this week after the regime-backed parliament on Wednesday approved borrowing of up to 2.1 trillion kyats (approximately US$1 billion at the fixed official rate) for a junta struggling with ballooning defense costs.

The kyat has weakened drastically since the 2021 coup plunged Myanmar into a dollar crisis, with economic sanctions, the withdrawal of foreign investment, declining exports and fighting in border trade zones taking a toll on the regime’s coffers.

On Wednesday, the rubber-stamp parliament approved the regime’s proposal to “borrow” up to 2.1 trillion kyats from the Central Bank of Myanmar to fill its budget deficit for fiscal year 2026-27. The legislature has already approved the regime’s plan to borrow money from major arms supplier Belarus, which will be used to import goods from Minsk.

Prior to Wednesday’s parliamentary approval, the regime had already raised nearly 14 trillion kyats through multiple treasury bill and bond auctions to finance its budget deficit for fiscal year 2026–27, according to Central Bank Deputy Governor Thet Htun Aung. He admitted the regime had also relied on treasury bond issuances and borrowing from the Central Bank to address budget shortfalls in previous years.

Analysts warn that borrowing from the Central Bank will accelerate inflation and the kyat’s depreciation. Currency traders report the dollar rose to 4,670 kyats in the unofficial market on Thursday, up from 4,450 kyats earlier this month, while the baht has risen from 129 to 139 kyats. Before the coup, the kyat was trading at less than 1,300 to the dollar.

“This surge is linked to the new loans. The market jumped from 4,400 to nearly 4,700 within days. Whether it will continue to increase, or decline—or if the regime will make arrests—remains to be seen,” one trader told The Irrawaddy. The regime has repeatedly arrested foreign exchange traders during currency spikes, accusing them of speculation and market manipulation.

The loan proposal has triggered fears that the revenue-deprived regime will simply print more banknotes to address the shortfall.

Deputy Finance and Revenue Minister Kyaw Htin explained that the regime has other plans to address the shortfall, apart from borrowing money. “We are working to reduce reliance on Central Bank financing to boost state revenue. We are developing taxation policies,” he told the parliament.

Recently, the regime has escalated its efforts to enforce remittance rules requiring Myanmar migrant workers to send at least 25 percent of their salaries back home at the official exchange rate of 2,100 kyats per dollar.

Officially, the Central Bank pegs the dollar at 2,100 kyats, while the trading rate between banks is 3,660 kyats and the market rate currently hovers at around 4,670 kyats. Meanwhile, the regime has restricted imports to reduce dollar spending, which has proved counterproductive for a war-ravaged economy heavily reliant on imports ranging from cooking oil and pharmaceuticals to fuel and fertilizer.

Rising dollar rates are expected to push up the cost of imported fuel, medicines, food, consumer goods and machinery, with knock-on effects for transport and production costs. Domestic industries face mounting pressure as expenses rise.

Meanwhile, the Belarus loan package, arranged through the Development Bank of the Republic of Belarus (DBRB) and Belinvestbank JSC, carries interest rates of between 2.25 and 9.33 percent. The loans will be used to import goods including capital goods from Minsk, but the total amount was not revealed.

Myanmar can receive loans in five currencies—the dollar, euro, Russian ruble, Belarusian ruble and Chinese yuan—said Kyaw Htin, who admitted exchange rate fluctuations would affect the amount of money Myanmar will actually receive.

Unlike concessional loans from Japan’s aid agency JICA—which carry a 40‑year repayment term at just 0.01 percent interest—analysts note that the Belarusian loan is a “tied” arrangement, warning the regime is locking itself into costly debt that will further deepen Myanmar’s economic crisis.

International organizations and Japan suspended development aid to Myanmar following the coup.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Launches ‘ASEAN Affairs’ Panel to Clinch Full Reintegration
World.content:
Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has formed a new ASEAN Affairs Committee to “regain the country’s original role and rights” in the regional bloc, which continues to bar his regime from summits months after it rebranded as an “elected” government.

The committee’s inaugural meeting on Tuesday was chaired by Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe, with representatives from the President’s Office and ministries of Defense, Home Affairs, Information, and Social Welfare also in attendance.

While the Foreign Ministry normally serves as the focal point for international relations, the new body includes the defense and home affairs ministries, underscoring the junta’s bid to institutionalize its efforts to reintegrate into the regional bloc.

Reintegration is crucial for coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, who is seeking international legitimacy after installing himself as president in April following an election widely denounced as a sham by Western nations and rights groups.

While individual members including Thailand have recognized Min Aung Hlaing’s presidency, ASEAN as a whole remains divided, prompting continuous regime demands for full integration as a “legitimate elected government.”

Tin Maung Swe told the meeting that Myanmar had suffered “discriminatory treatment” since 2021, when ASEAN excluded Min Aung Hlaing from top-level meetings for ignoring its Five‑Point Consensus agreed in Jakarta. The bloc’s peace plan calls for an immediate end to violence, dialogue among all parties, and humanitarian access—conditions the junta has refused to meet.

Tuesday’s meeting came just weeks ahead of the next ASEAN Summit in Manila. Since assuming the presidency, Min Aung Hlaing has made official visits to five bloc members, securing support for Myanmar’s reintegration from Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia. Analysts say the committee was formed in an effort to win over the remaining five members.

“The regime is attempting to win a majority consensus through bilateral engagement with individual member states,” said political analyst Htin Kyaw Aye.

“The committee is designed for this purpose. But it remains difficult for ASEAN to allow Myanmar’s return while there is no visible progress on the Five-Point Consensus.”

Since assuming office in April, the pseudo-civilian regime has dismissed the Five-Point Consensus as a non-binding declaration, before formally rejecting the peace deal through its rubber-stamp parliament.

The regime said Tuesday’s meeting tabled “Myanmar‑led approaches” to restore the country’s role in ASEAN—a statement reiterating defiance of the Five-Point Consensus spearheaded by an ongoing military campaign that has killed over 8,500 civilians since the coup.

While rights groups warn that countries hosting Min Aung Hlaing risk legitimizing a regime still committing atrocities, others have different views after more than five years of isolation has delivered no results.

Former Japanese prime minister Fumio Kishida told Nikkei Asia on October 12 that Japan should help Myanmar rejoin ASEAN. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. recently hailed Min Aung Hlaing’s visits to fellow ASEAN countries as part of a “new approach” to resolving the country’s crisis. Meanwhile, Brunei and Indonesia plan to invite Min Aung Hlaing for official visits, according to junta spokeswoman Khaing Khaing Soe, leaving only Timor-Leste and Singapore standing firm against the regime.

As the bloc’s newest member, Timor-Leste has backed Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement while initiating legal action against the military regime in February over alleged war crimes. Meanwhile Singapore, which will take over the rotating chairmanship at year-end, recently affirmed that there can be “no political representation” for Myanmar at ASEAN meets.

Mon Mon Myat, a lecturer in the Department of Peace Studies at Thailand’s Payap University, said: “It appears that the Philippines wants to reintegrate Myanmar into the bloc before Singapore takes the chair next year. ASEAN countries that are stepping up their diplomatic engagement with Myanmar regime must exercise extra caution to avoid legitimizing war criminals.”

She added that ASEAN must set clear rules for accountability if the regime refuses to obey the Five-Point Consensus.

“Otherwise, the regime may secure full legitimacy as a leader of an ASEAN nation.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Denies Drafting College Students Into Army
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime has denied reports that university students must suspend their studies for two years to serve in the army, but fears persist among students and parents.

Earlier this month, a panic broke out when rumors said that young men selected in conscription lotteries must serve in the army even if they are registered university students, and those drawing numbers under 100 would be called up within three months.

Conscripts are selected randomly at ward levels by drawing lots from a box. Those with smaller numbers are drafted first, and those with larger numbers later.

In Mandalay, even high school students who just turned 18 were forced to participate in the conscription lottery last month, according to parents.

“High school students were also told to draw lots. I drew on my son’s behalf and got a large number, over 500,” said a mother from Mandalay. “But we are still really scared because of reports that university students would be called up.”

In denying the rumors, the regime’s central conscription committee this week cited Article 15 (a)(3) of the Conscription Law, which allows deferment for students in education. It said official newspapers “repeatedly stressed this point.”

But concerns persist as township administrative offices in regime-controlled areas including major cities like Naypyitaw, Yangon and Mandalay have called in lists of university and high school students, apparently separating out those with spectacles, health problems, disabilities or on long‑term medication.

In August, the regime centralized the draft, with regional and district authorities taking over management from township and lower-level conscription offices. Since early September, a new wave of lotteries have been held in wards and villages across Mandalay but not yet in Yangon.

“Ward offices summon us according to lists from the Population Department,” one young man said. “Everyone aged 18 to 35 including students must draw. In our ward alone, over 40 students were included. One 12th grader drew a number under 100, but officials said high school students would be granted temporary deferment.”

Previously, families with eligible young men could pay a monthly fee to the authorities for deferment, in theory so someone else could be paid to take their place. But the regime abolished the substitution fee in September, declaring that all those selected must serve in order of their lottery numbers.

The department also denied reports that ward offices are confiscating ID cards and smart cards of selected youths, requiring monthly check‑ins, and demanding parents sign pledges to prevent their sons’ escape.

A Mandalay conscription official told The Irrawaddy that the process strictly follows laws and regulations.

“Students who can prove they are genuinely enrolled, with proper documents and forms, are granted temporary deferment,” the official said.

According to the 2019 census, nearly 13 million people are eligible for conscription under the Conscription Law—6.3 million men and 7.7 million women. So far, about 140,000 men have been called up by the regime, assuming that around 5,000 recruits are drafted per batch.

When the long-dormant Conscription Law was revived in 2024, it forced a mass exodus of young people, and the regime has since been struggling to meet its quotas despite barring eligible men from working abroad and even snatching young men from streets and homes.

In Yangon, an eerie quiet descends after 8 p.m. as regime-backed thugs prowl the streets on the hunt for eligible young men to abduct, a practice that has swiftly degenerated into a black economy of kidnappings for ransom.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Cambodia Seek AI Cooperation and Stronger Trade Ties
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Cambodia are looking to expand cooperation in artificial intelligence, energy, agriculture and trade, while exploring direct air links, as President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet held talks on Oct. 17.

The discussions marked the first visit to Kazakhstan by a Cambodian prime minister and came as the two countries mark 32 years of diplomatic relations. Tokayev said the visit could open a new chapter in bilateral ties, with both countries seeking to translate shared intentions into practical cooperation, Akorda reported.

“Kazakhstan considers Cambodia a reliable partner in Southeast Asia and an important link in expanding our partnership with ASEAN countries,” Tokayev said during the expanded-format talks.

He added that the countries would adopt a joint statement outlining their shared vision for future relations and sign several bilateral documents.

AI and digital government

Technology emerged as a key area for cooperation, with Tokayev highlighting opportunities in artificial intelligence and digital government. Hun Manet and his delegation were scheduled to visit the Alem.ai International Center to learn about Kazakhstan’s AI initiatives and technological developments.

Tokayev noted Kazakhstan’s progress in the United Nations E-Government Development Index and said the two countries could achieve significant results by combining mutual interest with political commitment.

“I am convinced that, given mutual interest and firm political will, we can achieve significant progress in expanding cooperation across many areas of mutual interest,” he said.

The two leaders also discussed energy cooperation. During their one-on-one meeting earlier in the day, Tokayev proposed exploring direct air links to facilitate tourism and people-to-people exchanges.

“Many Kazakh people would like to visit Cambodia and discover its attractions. We need to discuss the possibility of establishing direct air links between our countries,” Tokayev said.

Trade, agriculture and education

Hun Manet expressed Cambodia’s interest in expanding cooperation in food security, agriculture and manufacturing, alongside energy and digitalization.

He also emphasized the longstanding humanitarian ties between the countries, noting that more than 120 Cambodian students had studied in Kazakhstan. Many have since taken up senior positions in public administration, including as provincial governors, state secretaries and ministry officials.

“Our countries are connected by a shared history and strong people-to-people ties,” Hun Manet said.

Tokayev praised Cambodia’s socioeconomic progress and expressed support for its long-term development goals under Cambodia Vision 2050 and the Pentagonal Strategy.

The leaders also highlighted their constructive political dialogue and engagement at the international level, including through their respective permanent missions to the United Nations. Tokayev commended Cambodia’s support for Kazakhstan’s initiatives on several topics on the UN General Assembly agenda.

Both officials expressed confidence that the talks would help increase bilateral trade, strengthen business ties and create new opportunities for partnership.

In the presence of Tokayev and Hun Manet, the two sides exchanged six memorandums of understanding covering cooperation in artificial intelligence and digital development, digital government and information and communication technologies, trade and economic relations, culture and the arts, and tourism. The documents also established sister-city relations between Astana and Phnom Penh.

Earlier, Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos Kanat Tumysh told The Astana Times that the countries were seeking to expand trade, explore investment opportunities and strengthen transport and technology cooperation.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s PARAQTA Platform Turns Reading Into Daily Habit
World.content:
ASTANA – A Kazakh digital platform called PARAQTA is helping readers build consistent reading habits through page tracking, personalized goals and interactive features, bringing together more than 8,400 registered users who have collectively read almost 1 million pages over the past year.

The platform was created by Yerdaulet Ayanuly, an engineer by profession who wanted to make reading a more accessible part of everyday life. Speaking on the Jibek Joly television channel’s program on Oct. 15, he said the project grew out of his own experience with books and efforts to build a reading community in Astana, reported Kazinform.

Ayanuly first joined a book club before organizing reading-related activities with volunteers. When the group struggled to find a suitable venue for meetings, the team opened a café for book lovers. Financial difficulties eventually forced it to close, but Ayanuly continued looking for ways to promote reading.

“It was a special, cozy place that was close to my heart. We held various creative events there and managed to bring together Astana residents who enjoyed reading. Closing the project was difficult, but I did not want to give up on the idea of developing a reading culture,” he said.

The team had previously used a Telegram bot to record the number of pages members read. Ayanuly later decided to turn the simple tracking tool into a dedicated website.

From page tracking to a reading community

Artificial intelligence helped him develop the first version of the website in three months. Over the following four to five months, he added features and improved the design, bringing the total development period to approximately eight or nine months.

PARAQTA allows users to set reading goals, record completed pages and track their progress, whether they read printed books or digital editions. Users can also access books directly through the platform’s online library, which currently contains 148 titles.

The collection includes Kazakh folk tales, Abai’s “Words of Edification”, works in Kazakh, Russian and English, and translated literature. According to Ayanuly, users show particular interest in Kazakh classics and national literature.

The platform also uses gamification to encourage readers to return regularly. Users earn stars for reading, which they can exchange for profile customization options and virtual room decorations. Personal accounts allow readers to track their activity and see their progress over time.

“We believe people should not be forced to read books. Instead, we need to find other ways to interest them,” Ayanuly said, explaining that small rewards can encourage users to read more consistently.

He cited four platform members who each read 60 books in a year as examples of how a regular reading habit can develop.

Digital tools and offline connections

PARAQTA offers both free and paid features. Paid options allow users to read the same book alongside other participants, compare reading progress and pace, join book clubs and take part in rankings. The platform has collected around 600 book reviews.

Beyond its digital functions, the project aims to connect readers offline. Astana’s book club currently has around 300 members, with people aged 20 to 25 among its most active participants. Members meet to discuss books and exchange perspectives on what they have read.

For Ayanuly, building this community is as important as developing the technology itself. He said books can influence how people think and understand the world, motivating him to share his enthusiasm for reading with others.

PARAQTA remains a small operation, with a team of two people. Ayanuly continues to work in his main profession as a design engineer while developing the platform, which began as a personal hobby and is gradually becoming an independent business.

The next step is to expand access through mobile applications. Ayanuly is awaiting approval to publish the iPhone version on the App Store, while an Android version is also planned. The application will be free to download, with paid subscriptions remaining available.

He believes that making reading convenient and rewarding is essential to building a stronger reading culture, particularly when digital platforms compete for people’s attention.

Kazakhstan’s wider reading initiative

PARAQTA’s development coincides with Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to promote reading. In September, Kazakh singer Dimash Kudaibergen joined the nationwide Reading Nation marathon in its Parasat category, which encourages reading through the personal example of public figures rather than competition for prizes. The marathon runs from Sept. this year to April 2027 and brings together participants including schoolchildren, students, teachers, families and civil servants.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Cambodia Seek to Expand Trade and Explore New Investment Opportunities, Ambassador Says
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Cambodia are seeking to turn political dialogue into tangible economic outcomes by expanding agricultural exports, strengthening business ties and exploring transport and technology partnerships, Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos said ahead of Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet’s visit to Kazakhstan.

“The principal expected outcome of the visit is agreement on practical next steps in priority areas and the creation of favourable conditions for new trade and investment projects,” Kanat Tumysh said in written responses to questions from The Astana Times.

Trade and investment potential

Bilateral trade reached $40.7 million in 2025, up from $33.8 million in 2024. In the first half of this year, it amounted to $20.6 million, up 1.4% year on year. Trade remains heavily weighted towards Cambodian exports, particularly textiles, knitwear, footwear and other consumer goods.

“The priority now is to realise more fully the potential of our partnership,” Tumysh said, identifying agriculture, food processing, tourism, construction, transport and logistics as promising areas.

At a meeting in Shanghai on July 17, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Hun Manet discussed cooperation in these sectors, as well as the textile industry and technology. Kazakhstan expressed readiness to increase supplies of grain, fertilizers and other agricultural products and share its expertise in advanced technologies.

Investment ties remain modest. No gross inflows of direct investment from Cambodia into Kazakhstan have been recorded, while gross outflows of direct investment from Kazakhstan to Cambodia amounted to $30,000 in January-June. As of Sept. 1, four legal entities with Cambodian capital participation were registered and operating in Kazakhstan.

“The presence of businesses with Cambodian capital does not automatically imply substantial direct investment inflows,” Tumysh said, adding that these companies could nevertheless provide a basis for stronger commercial ties.

Agriculture offers opportunities for two-way trade

Kazakhstan sees opportunities to supply Cambodia with wheat, fertilizers and other agricultural products, while importing Cambodian rice.

“Cambodia, in turn, can export its rice to Kazakhstan, and we are ready to purchase it. This offers an opportunity to develop mutually beneficial trade in both directions,” Tumysh said.

Cambodia has a population of approximately 17.8 million and imported around $34 billion worth of goods in 2025. Its agricultural exports that year reached approximately 14.9 million tons, worth around $5 billion, including rice, rubber, cassava, maize, cashew nuts and tropical fruit.

Expanding Kazakh agricultural exports will require identifying buyers, establishing product specifications and assessing transportation costs, certification requirements and seasonal demand.

“For grain, it would be useful to assess the requirements of flour mills and food-processing companies, including quality specifications and opportunities to supply both raw materials and processed products,” Tumysh said.

Fertilizer exports would require similar assessments of demand, registration procedures and potential local partners. Agricultural processing, packaging, storage and distribution could offer additional opportunities.

Kazakhstan’s total exports to Cambodia amounted to just $47,000 in 2024, with control and measuring instruments accounting for the principal export items. Confirmed figures for agricultural supplies in 2025 and the first half of 2026 are not yet available, and no quantitative targets for future shipments have been announced.

“At this stage, it is therefore appropriate to speak of exploring opportunities rather than guaranteeing supplies of a particular volume,” Tumysh said.

Transport and regional connectivity

Kazakhstan is working towards accession to the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia, also known as the Bali Treaty. Tumysh said Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia had supported the initiative, which Kazakhstan views as an important step towards strengthening engagement with ASEAN.

“We aim to translate this partnership into practical outcomes by expanding trade, strengthening business ties, exploring investment opportunities and improving transport connectivity between Central Asia and Southeast Asia,” he said.

One proposed step is to assess multimodal routes with exporters, importers, carriers and freight forwarders, comparing costs, delivery times, transshipment, storage and documentation requirements. Cambodia’s Sihanoukville port, its principal maritime gateway, could be considered in these assessments. However, no dedicated Kazakhstan-Cambodia transport corridor has been agreed.

The two countries also have experience with direct air services. In October 2024, SCAT Airlines launched charter passenger flights from Astana and Almaty to Sihanoukville to serve tourist demand, but the services were subsequently suspended. Their experience could inform future assessments of passenger demand and commercial viability.

Tourism remains another potential area for cooperation. Cambodia welcomed approximately 5.57 million international visitors in 2025, creating opportunities for engagement between tourism authorities, tour operators and airlines.

Digital cooperation and next steps

Both countries could also explore partnerships in digital technologies and public services. Kazakhstan has offered to share its technological expertise, while Cambodia is developing e-commerce, digital financial services and digital government services.

The institutional framework for cooperation has developed through a February 2025 memorandum establishing a mechanism for political consultations between the two foreign ministries and a May 29 intergovernmental agreement providing visa exemptions for holders of diplomatic and service or official passports.

Tumysh said the immediate priority was to arrange business meetings, exchange information on export offerings and import requirements, consult logistics operators and assess trial shipments.

“Realistic targets can then be set, with progress measured through signed contracts, repeat deliveries, investments actually made and the reliability of transport services. Ultimately, the guiding principle is a practical approach: moving from general expressions of interest to commercially sound solutions that deliver mutual benefits for businesses and strengthen links between the two regions,” Tumysh said.

World.title: IMF Expects Kazakhstan’s Inflation to Ease and Economic Growth to Accelerate in 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s inflation is projected to decline to 8.2% in 2027, while economic growth is expected to accelerate to 4.9%, according to the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) latest World Economic Outlook, released Oct. 13 at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.

The IMF forecasts inflation to fall from 11.4% in 2025 to 10.3% in 2026 before declining further next year. Economic growth is projected at 4.4% in 2026, rising to 4.9% in 2027.

The report also identifies Kazakhstan among the countries outside the Persian Gulf that increased oil production and helped the global market adjust to disruptions in supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.

Kazakhstan’s economic outlook

The IMF expects Kazakhstan’s unemployment rate to remain at 4.6% in 2026 before easing to 4.5% in 2027. The country’s current account balance is projected to remain positive at 0.5% of gross domestic product in 2026.

Kazakhstan is also mentioned in the report’s assessment of the economic effects of the artificial intelligence boom. The fund identifies the country among commodity exporters benefiting from increased exports of technology-related goods produced by major Asian manufacturing economies.

Oil supply and the Strait of Hormuz

The report examines how the conflict in the Middle East disrupted global energy markets, with supplies through the Strait of Hormuz nearly halted in the spring. The disruption affected a route responsible for approximately 20% of global oil supplies, pushing prices to $126 per barrel in late March, according to the information cited in the report.

The IMF said the market adapted partly because countries outside the Persian Gulf increased production. Brazil, Kazakhstan, the United States and Venezuela were among those identified as helping offset the supply shortfall.

The report’s global outlook remains closely tied to developments in the Middle East. The IMF assumes that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March 2027 and that shipping will return to previous levels by October 2027. Under this scenario, oil prices are projected to average $96 per barrel in 2026 and $87 in 2027.

Artificial intelligence supports global growth

The IMF raised its forecast for global economic growth in 2026 to 3.1%, up from 3% in its July projection. The global economy grew by 3.5% in 2025, while growth is expected to reach 3.4% in 2027.

The fund attributes the improved outlook partly to substantial investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, which is helping offset the economic effects of higher energy prices and the prolonged conflict in the Middle East.

Economies building AI platforms and manufacturing the equipment needed to support them are among those receiving upgraded forecasts. The report highlights South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico and Thailand in this context.

According to Reuters, Petya Koeva Brooks, deputy director of the IMF’s Research Department, said the global economy would have grown more slowly in 2026 without measures taken by governments and businesses following the oil shock. These included drawing on inventories, finding alternative suppliers and reducing oil consumption.

However, the IMF cautions that the effects of these adjustments are weakening as the conflict continues.

The benefits of AI-related investment are also becoming increasingly concentrated. According to the report’s assessment cited by Reuters, 32 countries now account for 95% of global growth, compared with 54 countries in April. Since then, the IMF has downgraded its growth forecasts for 47% of the world’s economies.

Diverging growth prospects

The United States is projected to grow by 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, supported by consumer spending, tax cuts and investment in AI. The IMF raised its 2026 growth forecast for the euro area from 0.9% to 1.1% and expects the United Kingdom’s economy to expand by 1.3%. Investment in AI is among the factors supporting these projections, alongside higher defense spending in Europe.

China’s economy is projected to grow by 4.5% in 2026 and 4% in 2027. Higher oil prices are weighing on domestic demand, although strong exports continue to provide support. India is expected to remain the fastest-growing major economy, with projected growth of 7% annually.

By contrast, the Middle East’s oil-producing economies face significant pressure. The IMF forecasts Saudi Arabia’s economy to contract by 3.3% in 2026, reversing its July projection of 1.7% growth. The fund also expects deep economic contractions in Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.

Inflation and risks to the global outlook

Global inflation is projected to reach 4.7% in 2026 before easing to 4.1% in 2027. However, the outlook depends heavily on how the conflict in the Middle East develops and whether energy supplies recover as anticipated.

The IMF also highlights uncertainty surrounding AI investment. Faster adoption of the technology could add 0.6% to global gross domestic product by 2029. Conversely, if the expected productivity gains fail to materialize and investment falls sharply, global economic output could be 1.1% lower by 2028, with the United States facing a potential decline of 1.8%.

High public debt, particularly in advanced economies, presents another challenge. The IMF urges governments to rebuild fiscal buffers and establish credible plans to return public debt to sustainable levels.

“The global economy has proved resilient, but this resilience is reaching its limits, so we need to move from simply surviving to rebuilding,” the IMF’s chief economist, Silvana Tenreyro, said, according to Reuters.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Regional Ties, AI Rules and Middle Corridor Plans
World.content:
ASTANA — The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest covers Kazakhstan’s partnerships with Azerbaijan and Belgium, proposed AI rules for newsrooms, and plans to expand Middle Corridor logistics infrastructure.

President Ilham Aliyev meets with Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and officially inaugurates Trans-Caspian Fiber Optic Cable

President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev met with President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Oct. 15, reported Trend.

During the meeting, the sides hailed the successful development of the strategic partnership and allied relations between Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan.

They highlighted the successful organization of the 7th CICA Summit in Baku, adding that the event had provided a good opportunity to discuss cooperation among countries in the Asian region.

Subsequently, Presidents Ilham Aliyev and Kassym-Jomart Tokayev officially inaugurated the Trans-Caspian Fiber-Optic Cable Line in an online format.

Kazakhstan weighs AI rules for newsrooms amid growing digital risks

Kazakhstan is considering new rules governing the use of artificial intelligence in newsrooms, including requirements to label AI-generated content. The proposal was discussed at the tenth Astana Media Week, which also focused on digital threats and children’s online safety, reported AnewZ on Oct. 15.

“Dmitriy Mun, CEO of Q.AI, predicted that AI could generate much of the content for some radio programmes and commentary within two to three years.

With automated content expected to become more common, Mun argued that the real challenge for journalists would be earning public trust rather than simply delivering information.

Fact-checking, accuracy and editorial independence could therefore become crucial in distinguishing professional journalism from machine-generated content,” reads the article.

Kazakhstan and Belgium to open new chapter in their partnership

EU Reporter published an article on Oct.12, written by Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Belgium Roman Vassilenko, exploring how the first Belgian state visit to Central Asia could strengthen Kazakhstan-Belgium ties through trade, investment, transport connectivity, and broader economic, academic and cultural cooperation.

“For Kazakhstan, relations with Belgium also have an important European dimension. Brussels combines bilateral diplomacy with dialogue with the European Union institutions. Transport connectivity, investment and resilient supply chains form a shared agenda in which Belgian expertise and Kazakhstan’s potential can, and do, complement each other,” reads the article.

Belgian royals in Kazakhstan: first state visit to Central Asia

Brussels-based VRT News released an article on Oct. 12 about the first-ever state visit to Central Asia by Belgium’s King Philippe and Queen Mathilde, aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation with Kazakhstan in trade, critical minerals, technology, and science.

German logistics group Rhenus plans up to 14 terminals along the Middle Corridor

Global logistics company Rhenus Group plans to build a new multimodal hub in the Kazakh city of Aktau and develop up to 14 terminals along the Middle Corridor. This network will link Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Türkiye, and connect the route to the company’s infrastructure in Europe, reported Euronews on Oct. 9.

German logistics giant Rhenus Group is set to roll out a network of up to 14 terminals along the Middle Corridor, also known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), with a new trimodal container terminal in Aktau.

Azerbaijan–Kazakhstan ties could reorient Central Asian integration

The five Central Asian presidents met with Azerbaijan’s Ilham Aliyev in Avaza on Oct. 8 for the Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and the Republic of Azerbaijan, reported The Times of Central Asia on Oct. 12.

Azerbaijan’s participation brings a principal outlet for Central Asian trade into the six governments’ economic deliberations. Within their consultative format, the states can coordinate industrial projects with the transport services through which regional producers reach foreign markets. If Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan connect cross-Caspian transport more closely to industrial cooperation, the corridor could become an organizing axis for regional integration.

World.title: From Saiga Recovery to Caspian Seal Decline, Tokayev Outlines Kazakhstan’s Biodiversity Agenda
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan is seeking international support for a fund to protect rare species and conserve biodiversity, while proposing Almaty as the host city for a regional office of the UN Convention on Biological Diversity Secretariat, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said at a Leaders’ Summit ahead of the UN biodiversity conference COP17 in Yerevan on Oct. 16.

Addressing the summit, Tokayev highlighted Kazakhstan’s progress in restoring endangered species, including the saiga antelope, while warning of mounting threats to the Caspian Sea ecosystem, notably the declining population of the Caspian seal, reported Akorda.

He called for stronger international cooperation, emphasizing that biodiversity protection was a shared responsibility essential to human well-being, economic resilience and long-term security.

“Environmental priorities, grounded in a balanced approach and concrete measures, must prevail over political disagreements,” Tokayev said, urging countries to focus on practical results and genuine partnerships.

Saiga population reaches 4.7 million

Tokayev cited the recovery of the saiga antelope as one of Kazakhstan’s major conservation achievements. The country is now home to approximately 98% of the world’s saigas, whose numbers have risen from 21,000 in 2003 to 4.7 million as of spring this year.

He also reported progress in protecting the snow leopard, whose population in Kazakhstan has grown from critically low levels in the 1990s to approximately 190 animals. Around 70% of the species’ habitat in the country falls within protected areas.

Tokayev thanked Russia, the United Nations Development Program, the World Wide Fund for Nature and other international partners for supporting efforts to reintroduce the Turan tiger to Kazakhstan. In June, a tiger was released into the wild for the first time in the country in 70 years.

Kazakhstan is also working with partners in the Czech Republic, Germany and Hungary to restore the population of Przewalski’s horse.

Tokayev said these achievements reflected years of sustained efforts by government agencies, scientists and international partners.

Caspian seal population falls to 270,000

Despite progress in restoring some species, Tokayev warned that the Caspian Sea’s fragile ecosystem faces growing pressure, with the future of the Caspian seal a particular concern.

According to Tokayev, the seal population has fallen from approximately one million to 270,000 over the past century. Kazakhstan has officially included the species on its list of rare and endangered animals.

He called on the five Caspian littoral states and the international community to intensify conservation efforts, warning against repeating the environmental disaster that befell the Aral Sea.

“We must not allow the Caspian Sea to suffer the same fate,” Tokayev said.

At the first Caspian Ecological Summit in Turkmenistan, he said, Kazakhstan had called for immediate, coordinated action to prevent irreversible damage to the vulnerable ecosystem.

Kazakhstan renews push for international conservation fund

Tokayev informed summit participants of Kazakhstan’s proposal to establish an International Fund for Rare Species and Biodiversity Conservation and invited international partners to join the initiative.

Kazakhstan has also adopted a 10-year National Biodiversity Conservation Program focused on restoring natural habitats, protecting species and expanding the network of specially protected natural areas. A National Genetic Biodiversity Bank is also being established.

Tokayev highlighted broader regional initiatives, including the Astana Declaration on Environmental Solidarity in Central Asia, adopted following the April summit. Kazakhstan is also advocating an interstate program to conserve the Caspian Sea’s resources, with the support of Caspian littoral states.

AI and regional cooperation in conservation

Tokayev called for greater use of digital technologies and artificial intelligence to improve ecosystem monitoring, natural resource management and early-warning systems for environmental threats.

He proposed using the International Center for Artificial Intelligence in Astana as a platform for joint scientific research, biodiversity data analysis, environmental risk forecasting and specialist training.

Tokayev also proposed hosting a regional office of the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity in Almaty. The office could help Central Asian countries implement the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, facilitate scientific exchange and advance joint conservation projects.

Tokayev reiterated Kazakhstan’s proposal to establish an International Water Organization within the UN system. The initiative, first proposed in 2025, aims to strengthen regional cooperation while remaining open to all interested countries.
