World.title: The best hotels in Europe with five-star vibes at three-star prices
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Three stars (the good ones) are for the great romantics. For people who don’t like golf or the gym, who value what a star-rating system cannot measure: character, beauty, warmth – those qualities that make them unforgettable. Here are some of the loveliest in Europe.

But how to find such a place? The star rating system is of little help. Many of Europe’s hotels are lumped into the three-star category, which is dominated by budget chains and dreary B&Bs. Yet it is also home to some ineffably charming small stays – sustainability passion projects and ancestral homes turned boutique boltholes. Often, the very things that prevent these small hotels from winning more stars is what keeps them special: their intimate scale; their refusal to install a lift in a Renaissance palazzo.

Marvellousness is to be expected if you’re staying at a five-star grande dame. But winkling out something that’s cheap and lovely – that’s the real buzz.

Is there any greater holiday pleasure than that self-congratulatory thrill on arriving at your hotel to find it is pinch-me marvellous?

This handsome hacienda, bougainvillea clambering all over its lemon and white facade, still feels like a grand family home, though it took a 10-year restoration from neglected olive farmhouse to get there. There are inviting spaces indoors and out – cane chairs in a shady corner, dining tables in the courtyard, squishy sofas beside a fireplace, books, paintings, heirlooms and antique beds in the 14 rooms and casitas. Gardens are glorious: paths through towering oleander, arbours strewn with cushions, a mosaic-tiled pool. The kitchen serves simple, seasonal dishes beautifully cooked. Seville and Jerez de la Frontera aren’t far, but it’s tempting not to leave at all. Doubles from $476 a night.

Imagine Vivienne Westwood let loose in a colonial Cuban casa and you’ll have some idea of Chic&Basic Habana Hoose, in Barcelona’s El Born neighbourhood. It’s Scottish meets punk meets Cuba – young and hip and chic, though hardly basic. Rooms are bonkers-bold and fabulous, bathrooms dark and inviting, beds large and well-dressed. There’s a restaurant too. Doubles from $135 a night.

The quintessential Mallorcan hideaway: a dreamy, ochre-stone agriturismo in native gardens, a few kilometres from the sandy coves of the south-east coast. Inside is cool and high-beamed. There are 12 rooms and suites, some with green-shuttered windows, others with private terraces. In the morning, breakfast comes courtesy of the vegetable garden, served on the sun-dappled terrace beneath the pines. Doubles from $160 a night.

Tucked in a quiet bay on the island’s west coast is Hotel Bahia, with a beach and the brightest aquamarine sea right at the foot of the steps down from the terrace. This unfussy, sandy-toes kind of place has simple rooms and a laid-back restaurant that serves excellent fish and paella. Doubles from $180, including breakfast.

It’s easy to forget that Marbs, with all its glitzy five-star resorts, is in Spain’s most fiery, passionate region of Andalusia. Hotel Claude is a reminder of where you are – it’s a classic 17th-century Andalusian house, once home to Eugenie, Empress of France, with a colonnaded Moorish courtyard at its heart, a peaceful roof terrace, and galleried upper floors leading to seven rooms and suites, decorated with contemporary furnishings and irreverent art. Doubles from $333 a night.

Superstars have been taking dips in Como’s green-blue waters since the Golden Age of Hollywood, Italian nobility far longer, and its waterside villas tend to be five-star fancy. So three-star Casa Olea is quite the find – a 19th-century rectory turned eco hotel, completely solar-powered, with six sophisticated, contemporary rooms, a saltwater pool and a garden overlooking the lake, plus a bird hide in the neighbouring woodland for spotting bee-eaters, golden orioles and turtles. Doubles from $299 a night.

An eclectic mix of modern and historic come together at AdAstra, a characterful 16-room hotel set within a family-owned mansion with expansive gardens in the groovy Oltrarno neighbourhood. Design is bold and beautifully curated: mid-century flea market finds offset frescoed ceilings and antique chandeliers, and books and fireplaces give it the feel of a new-generation aristo’s apartment. Ineffably romantic in a wholly original way. Doubles from $224 a night.

The ceilings steal the show at Palazzo Vannoni, in the old heart of Levanto on the Italian Riviera. The seaside town is just outside the Cinque Terre, making it a good base for exploring the candy-coloured coast on foot or by car. Levanto has its own smattering of pink and yellow houses, churches and castles, piazzas and restaurants – plus the only sandy beach on this stretch of coast. Doubles from $258 a night.

Youthful spirit in the Eternal City? Whatever next? Converted from an early 1900s apartment block in Rome’s boho Monti neighbourhood, whippersnapper Condominio Monti is refreshingly modern – velvet headboards, bold wallpapers, art deco lighting – designed by two young locals. Breakfast is served on the rooftop, and there’s a proper Roman restaurant on the ground floor. Doubles from $156 a night.

Back in the 1920s, the owner of this mountain refuge eschewed the trad chalet detailing in favour of clean-lined modernism, and today Hotel Brio cuts a sharp silhouette against the pine-forested slopes. Rooms in Briol are alpine-adorable – lots of hefty scrubbed pine and white linen, windows opening onto truly uplifting views, and air so clean you’ll break into song. In recent years they’ve added a treehouse suite, plus a few family apartments in the forest below the hotel. Doubles from $221 per person half-board.

Relais Monastero Santa Teresa, Nardo, Puglia

The regal rooms of Relais Monastero Santa Teresa are scattered across two palazzi.

The regal rooms of Relais Monastero Santa Teresa are scattered across two palazzi and a medieval monastery in Nardo, down in Italy’s hot heel. This once-grand little city has a many-layered history apparent in its art and architecture – Roman, Norman, Byzantine, Renaissance, Baroque – and a stay at this splendid albergo diffuso (“scattered hotel”) literally immerses you in its past and present glories. Vaulted ceilings, ornate gateways, cloisters and colonnades – deeply romantic and completely unique. Doubles from $169 a night.

FRANCE

La Maison de Lucie, Honfleur

La Maison de Lucie, a charming antique-filled hotel in Honfleur, France. Alamy

Take a morning train or drive out from Paris and you can be in Honfleur in time for lunch – which, on the Normandy coast, means oysters and a bottle of white. Tucked away in the medieval streets behind Honfleur’s impossibly quaint harbour is 12-bedroom La Maison de Lucie, a beautiful house that’s furnished with antiques, warm colours and art all over the oak-panelled walls. Some rooms have terraces, others terrific views through shuttered windows that let in the light that drew Monet and Turner to this spot. Doubles from $265 a night.

Les Florets, Provence

Family-run Les Florêts is Provence in a nutshell.

All the trademarks of Provence are found at family-run Les Florets: a sun-dappled stone terrace set with wrought-iron chairs; views over the painterly Vaucluse landscapes and forested slopes of the Dentelles, surrounding villages of absurd prettiness. The pool is swisher than you might expect, the restaurant smart but jolly, and the wine list 350 vintages long. Doubles from $124 a night.

Chateau Richeux, Mont-Saint-Michel, Brittany

World-class dining to match those views over Mont-Saint-Michel bay at Chateau Richeux, Brittany.

A 1920s three-star hotel with a three-Michelin-starred restaurant. Chateau Richeux looks out across Mont-Saint-Michel Bay and is part of the Roellinger family’s Maisons de Bricourt estate, where Hugo Roellinger’s Le Coquillage is the main attraction, but rooms upstairs in the chateau are exquisite too: warm-hued, wood-panelled, with deep modern beds and antique French furniture. Doubles from $400 a night.

Hotel Le Sud, French Riviera

Hotel Le Sud in Juan-les-Pins featuring bright Riviera-chic design. Stephanie Lizee

Over the Cap from Antibes, the more down-to-earth Juan-Les-Pins is home to Hotel Le Sud, a Riviera three-star gem of a hotel. Inside, it’s all-white simplicity with citrus zings of colour and bamboo furniture; outside, there’s a delicious little courtyard garden and deckchairs around a pool shaded by palms and pine trees. Settle in with Francois Sagan’s 1954 Bonjour Tristesse, set right here. Doubles from $130 a night.

La Planque Hotel, Paris

Eclectic interiors and bold hues in a Cosy Room at La Planque Hotel in Paris.

“The Hideaway” is right at home in the hip enclave between Belleville and the Canal Saint-Martin. Interiors are beautiful, en-vogue-eclectic, mixing up jewel-coloured fabrics, brocantes and modern finishes. The former apartment block has 36 rooms upstairs and, in what was a sweet shop, a vibrant salon on the ground floor, with reception staff on hand 24/7 for insider tips on Paris. Doubles from $233 a night.

Chateau de la Bourdaisiere, Loire Valley

A fairy tale stay at Chateau de la Bourdaisiere in Montlouis-sur-Loire.

Your classic Loire Renaissance fairy tale: turreted on top, redly damasked within, with the kind of soul-stirring grounds that are de rigueur round here. Less de rigueur is the price: rooms start from around $188. There’s a formal restaurant and, in the delightful kitchen garden, a tomato bar. Ah, oui – they are very proud of their tomatoes. Come in September for the Tomato Festival, not to be confused with Spain’s fruit-flinging La Tomatina. In the Loire, that kind of behaviour will have you chucked out on your ear. Doubles from $177 a night.

La Roseraie, Dordogne

La Roseraie has the most magical gardens stretching down to the Vezere river.

Unapologetically flowery, as the name suggests, La Roseraie has the most magical gardens – lawns and trees, pool and pergola rose walk – stretching down to the Vezere river, flowing serenely and greenly through the Dordogne (you can take canoes out). The rooms and suites are equally floral, dressed up French country style. White tablecloths in the restaurant, naturally – but it welcomes children too. Doubles from $160 a night.

PORTUGAL

Noah Surf House, Santa Cruz

A laidback beachside haven Noah Surf House.

You don’t have to surf to stay here – many come for the astounding location, cantilevered over the most glorious, deserted sandy beach on Portugal’s Atlantic coast, with sea views to stir the soul. But if you ever wanted to try it, this is the spot. Noah’s instructors teach all levels and ages from six up, on a lagoon or west-coast breakers, both surfing and paddleboarding. There’s also Pilates, yoga, hiking, a long pool, driftwood-chic restaurant and roof terrace hosting barbecues and sundowners. Beach houses (sleeping up to three) from $312 a night, including breakfast.

Chalet Saudade, Sintra

Chalet Saudade. All the romance of Sintra is encapsulated in this historic townhouse. Antonio Chaves

All the romance of Sintra is encapsulated in this historic townhouse, with its white-icing balconies, intricate carvings and pastel exterior of rose and sea-blue. Homely charm runs throughout, from garden to living rooms with fireplaces and vintage furniture. Breakfast is served in-house at sunny Cafe Saudade. Doubles from $139 a night.

Aldeia de Pedralva, Vila do Bispo, Algarve

Charming, whitewashed stone cottages in the countryside at Aldeia de Pedralva, Algarve.

It took 25 years to rebuild the abandoned village of Aldeia da Pedralva, down in the south-west corner of the Algarve. Sensitively restored, retaining plenty of rustic charm, it is now an offline retreat of 26 gorgeous one- to three-bedroom stone cottages – whitewashed and terracotta-roofed, doors painted blue and yellow and red – along with a restaurant in the village square and a swimming pool. It’s a year-round kind of place for outdoor types – go horse riding, dolphin watching, kayaking, sailing, surfing, cycling and hiking the Algarve’s coast paths and rugged interior. Cottages from $122 a night.

Herdade do Touril, Alentejo

Donkeys graze next to sunflower fields at Herdade do Touril in Alentejo.

This former 19th-century farmhouse, daubed with the primary blues and yellows of Portuguese pottery, is set on its own 365-hectare estate along the Costa Vicentina in Portugal’s south-west corner. There are 18 rooms and suites spread across five houses and cottages with shady terraces. Chill by the pool, with views of the Atlantic, or find your own beach along the estate’s own 2.9 kilometres of coastline. Doubles from $241 a night.

Grande Hotel do Porto

Pastel perfection in a classic guest room at Grande Hotel do Porto in Porto, Portugal.

The Dalai Lama, Edward VIII and Brazil’s Emperor Pedro II have all been put up at the Grande. Despite its illustrious guests, old-fashioned opulence and silver service, this fin-de-siecle hotel remains a three-star steal. While its 90-odd rooms have been updated since 1880, they remain grandma-pleasing in pastels and florals, while marble bathrooms retain an art deco air. Doubles from $88 a night.

GREECE

Anemomilos, Folegandros

Serene clifftop sanctuary Anemomilos, Folegandros.

Folegandros gets overshadowed by its superstar neighbour, Santorini – precisely why thoughtful travellers love this island, which still feels wild and undiscovered. Clifftop eyrie Anemomilos has, over the past three decades, elevated simple Greek chic to an art form. Stylish but unpretentious, it has large individual suites with terraces, a delightful pool, cocktail bar and all-day restaurant dishing up locally sourced salads, fish and mezze – all with sensational views, shared with precious few others, over the Aegean. Suites from $410 a night.

Nostos, Serifos

Nostos, Serifos … thoughtful, organic design just a short stroll from Serifos’ pristine shores.

Stone, wood and natural materials create the earthy aesthetic of Nostos, an understatedly stylish, unbelievably good-value boutique hotel on rugged Serifos. Owners Harrys and Bianca, a Greek-Swiss couple, brought in leading architects and designers to breathe fresh life into Harrys’s grandfather’s property in Livadi and create a 17-room mindful modern retreat. There’s no pool, but Livadakia beach is a five-minute walk away and the knockout Psili Ammos a short scooter ride over the headland. Doubles from $118 a night.

Onar, Andros

Onar, Andros’ stone suites seamlessly integrated into the rocky shore above Ahla beach.

For most of the past century, Andros was an exclusive enclave for holidaying shipping magnates. Luckily for us, one of them recently built a superb hotel where anyone can stay and experience this enchanting Cycladic island. Onar, the passion project of Mateo Pantzopoulos, is a collection of low-slung contemporary suites and villas, some with private pools, stacked on the hillside above the otherwise deserted Ahla beach in the island’s north-east – a region riven with secret coves and sensational hiking trails. Suites from $431 a night, including breakfast.

Eumelia, Peloponnese

Eumelia has authenticity in spades.

If sustainability, authenticity and wellbeing are the new luxury, then Eumelia has it in spades. This agriturismo is set on a regenerative farm that encompasses olive groves, orchards and vineyards, and the produce is made into natural wines, oils, and farm-to-fork dishes. Cooking classes are also on offer, along with yoga. Five barn-like houses of raw timber and concrete have living rooms with fireplaces for winter stays, full kitchens, private gardens and verandahs overlooking the Peloponnese mountainscapes – glorious hiking and biking territory. Houses (sleeping up to four) from $400; two-night minimum stay.

The Merchant’s House, Corfu

Meticulously restored stone cottages in Corfu’s oldest village … The Merchant’s House.

A trio of abandoned 200-year-old cottages were sensitively restored to form the five-suite Merchant’s House in Old Perithia, Corfu’s oldest village. Interiors are appropriately traditional, though not without mod cons (air-conditioning, TV, Wi-Fi, high-quality bed linen) and each suite has an outdoor seating area. A stay in this hinterland hideaway, in what was until fairly recently a ghost town, gives an insight into a side of Corfu most don’t witness. Doubles from $190 a night, including breakfast.

The Telegraph, London

World.title: The WNBA is shattering records. Is women’s sport in Australia falling behind?
World.content:
What can Australian women’s sports learn from a thundering success of the WNBA

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The sound is deafening. It’s July 10 and Bell Centre stadium in Montreal is packed, with 20,996 fans on their feet screaming as the Toronto Tempo and Dallas Wings take to the court against a backdrop of indigo strobe lights and rock music. The crowd shattered the WNBA’s regular-season attendance record for a single game, an extraordinary statistic given Montreal doesn’t even have its own WNBA team. It didn’t take long for an avalanche of posts on social media. “Tough day for the ‘No-one watches women’s sports’ crowd,” one user cheekily proclaimed alongside footage of the roaring crowd. The records didn’t stop there. Last week the WNBA announced the first round of the play-offs was the most-watched yet, with an average of 1.3 million viewers tuning in across the network over 10 days. Meanwhile, an analysis from Sports Business Journal found the WNBA drew a league-high record of 3.79 million fans to games in 2026.



The WNBA’s skyrocketing popularity is the accumulation of what many people in women’s sports spaces have been dreaming about for decades. The league’s record-breaking attendance, sold-out stadiums, in-demand merchandise, fan activations and superstar players have set the benchmark for what marketing in women’s sports can do. But what about here in Australia? Dr Kasey Symons, a lecturer in sports media at Deakin University, says Australia has fallen behind the United States when it comes to creativity and innovation for marketing in women’s sports. WNBA superstar Angel Reese. Getty Images “I want to be generous to where we are in our sporting landscape in terms of resources, revenue, and support, but we are undoubtedly behind,” she said. “It’s not enough any more just to say, ‘One day we’ll get there’. ‘One day’ is now, and we can take some examples from other sports to see what they’re doing.”



We’ve contacted athletes, player agents, content creators, academics and marketing experts to ask which women’s sports in Australia are thriving in today’s marketing landscape. More importantly – which ones need to catch up? What’s behind the WNBA’s meteoric growth, and why isn’t the WNBL as popular? Not many have had a closer look at the WNBA’s expansion than Australia’s most-decorated basketballer, Lauren Jackson. Over more than a decade in the American league, Jackson won two championships, was crowned MVP three times and was a seven-time WNBA All-Star. Now, as chief strategy and partnerships officer in Australia’s WNBL (in which she also played, winning seven championships), Jackson has the task of trying to emulate domestically some of that success she’s been privy to abroad. Australian basketball legend Lauren Jackson. Louis Trerise “There are so many moments that are contributing to us being here right now and in a position where we are starting to grow – we are getting eyeballs,” Jackson said of the WNBL. “We’re able to start making a little bit of noise around the game and the global women’s basketball movement is happening, and it’s real. There’s a lot of investment going into it. For us, it’s about trying to capitalise on that, trying to grow with it, and [to] stay globally relevant.”



Jackson said the way the WNBA is now marketing its players – where individual stars have become household names – has been a big contributor to its success. “When I first went into the WNBA, they made us not be ourselves, we weren’t being marketed as ourselves, it was more what they thought society wanted to see,” she said. “Whereas, I think what’s happened in the last 10 years or so is that you start to see way more authenticity. The athletes are stepping into their own power, and it’s resonating with society.” Symons has a theory about why the US has been able to produce these cult-like figures, noting American sporting culture allows “individual personalities to shine and be themselves”. “I think in Australian sports we still have a bit of that tall-poppy syndrome, where individualism is a bit less celebrated, and we do like athletes to stay more humble.” Symons also praised the multipurpose marketing campaign implemented by the WNBA for fans across a diverse demographic, highlighting the impact of New York Liberty’s famous mascot, Ellie the Elephant – who has dedicated fan pages and had appeared in Vogue. The WNBA also attracts investors such as Serena Williams (part-owner of the Tempo), Tom Brady (who has a stake in the Las Vegas Aces), Magic Johnson (part owner of the Los Angeles Sparks) and Karlie Kloss, who is an investor in the group that owns the Liberty.



The WNBL has recently introduced private ownership and Jackson believes will help propel opportunities in, and visibility of, the league. Why netball is falling behind other sports Netball remains one of the most interesting women’s sports in this conversation. It attracts a largely female fan base and has mammoth participation numbers in grassroots levels. While total attendance numbers during the Super Netball league have increased this year, the sport is still battling for attention. Alexa Prinno is a Perth-based presenter and content creator of Your Netball Bestie – a media platform with a combined 120,000 followers. From a marketing perspective, Prinno believes netball is falling behind other sports and is eager to see more branding, media visibility and sponsorship opportunities to transform netballers into household names. “I’d say from a fan perspective, yes, I would say netball is behind, from what I’ve seen there’s no denying that,” she told this masthead.

World.title: Nice is a millionaire’s playground, but I found plenty of affordable ways to play there
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life Nice is a millionaire’s playground, but I found plenty of affordable ways to play there Hayley Peppin October 18, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This story is part of the October 18 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

Most of us know the south of France, even if we’ve never been. The feeling flows from the uncorking of your first summer rosé to the scent of lavender sachets lightly perfuming one’s intimates. It’s there in the wistful imagery from films like La Piscine with Jane Birkin and Alain Delon, and the TikToks inspiring us to leave it all behind for the good life: “POV: You quit your job to move to a vineyard in the south of France.” It’s a temptation I’ve indulgently tasted five or six times (the wine haze makes it a little difficult to separate) over the past two years, and somehow it never wears off. You can dip your toes in the sandpit at Saint-Tropez’s eye-wateringly expensive beach clubs, or retreat to the slower, “touching grass” corners of a region that stretches from rugged mountains to sun-baked fields and sapphire coastlines. It’s this high-low tension that makes the south of France as seductive as it is approachable. The high-low tension makes the south of France as seductive as it is approachable. Sonya Khegay / Stocksy United I’ve made jambon-beurres at a party for my friend’s 30th birthday on a rural farmstead just outside Nîmes, and dined on organic escargot and lobster bisque pasta at La Rotonde, the gold-leaf and carousel-horse dining room inside Nice’s grand dame, Le Negresco. I’ve even hugged my parents (and an obligatory bowl of frites and a Campari Spritz) while watching a local pétanque game in Saint-Paul-de-Vence. But it was my most recent visit, for winemaker Whispering Angel’s 20th anniversary – which was serendipitously timed with the Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity – that captured this euphoria best. There was rosé sipped in the shower, then dancing under the moonlight at Zuma, the izakaya-style destination that seemed to twinkle even more with the glam festival crowd pouring through it.



By the next morning, back in Nice, the Riviera had slipped into its easygoing Mediterranean warmth, freshly baked croissants and all. That’s the beauty of the Riviera: it lets you lose yourself in the night, then return to the ease of the morning after. Now the south of France hardly needs more buzz online, but if you’re planning your own escape, allow me to sweet talk you into a few of my favourites. If you’re a first-timer, base yourself in Nice. Few cities layer history, culture and nature so effortlessly. It’s also home to the region’s main international airport and is well-connected by public transport. The Cote d’Azur in France. Getty Images/iStockphoto If you want the best of both worlds, stay at Anantara Plaza Nice. Belle Époque grandeur meets earthy, minimalist interiors, with the historic Old Town on one side and the Mediterranean on the other. Take it all in from SEEN, the sweeping rooftop restaurant and bar, with 360-degree views of the rolling hills, palm-fringed Jardin Albert 1er public gardens and the people-watching parade of the Promenade des Anglais. Against the hotel’s honeyed façade, it’s golden hour the Niçoise way (the sun shines here more than 300 days a year). Craving something softer? Antibes is a gentler alternative just along the coast, where the Cap d’Antibes Beach Hotel feels wonderfully secluded, fusing Palm Springs-inspired geometry with classic Mediterranean villa styling.



Then head to Ruhl Plage, one of the oldest beach clubs in Nice. Just steps from Anantara on the Baie des Anges (Bay of Angels), the institution built in 1920 is all blue-and-white parasols, blond wood and maritime motifs, with sunbeds that won’t smash your daily budget — though you can spend €130 on a front-row double bed if you fancy. It was once the beach club of the old Hotel Ruhl, where F. Scott and Zelda Fitzgerald wrote of dining on the terrace as “stars fell in our plates … and we were alone with the deep blue grandeur and the filet de sole Ruhl, and the second bottle of champagne”. From Nice, it’s a 30-minute taxi to the Fondation Maeght museum in Saint-Paul-de-Vence (public transport more than doubles the journey). Art lovers will know it, Dua Lipa fans might, too, since the English singer hosted a Service95 Book Club event there in June. France’s first private art foundation was born from grief: after losing their young son, art dealers Aimé and Marguerite Maeght built a Catalan-inspired village on a pine-covered hill where artists could gather, create and exhibit. Come for the sculpture garden, stay for the views over medieval Saint-Paul-de-Vence and the scent of pine resin and rosemary. Related Article Sunday Life What three strangers taught a single mum on a trip to New Zealand Save another day for Èze, a winding taxi ride (or bus) from Nice. Inhale the boundless sky from the cactus-filled Jardin Exotique, perched high in the “eagle’s nest” village, then settle in at the luxurious Château de la Chèvre d’Or hotel. The menu may induce financial vertigo (though the complimentary snacks are replenishable), but the yacht-dotted views over Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat are worth nursing one glass of champagne. Rosé purists should make the pilgrimage inland to the home of the summer tonic: Château d’Esclans, the inland Provence estate behind Whispering Angel, about 90 minutes’ drive from Nice. Book a tour and tasting among the vines, and enjoy the view of the surreal blue hydrangeas while you’re there.



And no south of France visit is complete without a beach picnic. It can be as curated as a feast from one of the region’s markets – Nice’s Marché aux Fleurs, Cannes’ Marché Forville or my favourite, Antibes’ Marché Provençal – or as simple as a deli run. One of my most memorable afternoons was also the least complicated: a cheap bottle of rosé, paper cups and a bag of crisps on the beach in Italianate Villefranche-sur-Mer. Moments like that make leaving feel impossible. So when my flight out of Nice was delayed by three hours, I didn’t mind in the slightest. The writer was hosted by Whispering Angel.
