World.title: Fresh call for sugar tax to combat children's deteriorating oral health
World.content:
A sugar tax is needed to address deteriorating oral health across the country, the New Zealand Dental Association says.

The number of children having decayed teeth removed is steadily increasing each year, with children undergoing almost 8000 extractions of multiple teeth in the last year.

In the 2024/2025 year on 7973 occasions children aged between 0 and 14 were hospitalised to have more than one tooth removed.

That is an increase from 7351 in the 2023/24 year, 6865 in 2022/23 and 5540 in 2021/22.

Dr Robin Whyman, the director of dental policy for the New Zealand Dental Association, said dental decay was to blame.

He said 140 countries have a sugar tax, and the latest figures showed New Zealand should join them.

"Dental decay is a relatively complex range of issues that are going on, but often dietary related.

"The more sugar and more sugar-containing diets that children have, the more we tend to see in some young children very high levels of dental decay," said Dr Whyman.

Extractions for children tend to peak between the ages of three and eight, he said.

While a sugar tax was likely to increase the cost of high sugar foods, it would also encourage food producers to reduce the sugar in some items, he said.

"Those sort of measures have been shown to brings things like dental decay levels and general anaesthetic use rates down in the countries we would compare ourselves with, not the least the UK."

World.title: 'Overuse of state power': Documents detail Gloriavale school's fight to stay open
World.content:
The closure of Gloriavale Christian School for student safety reasons would be unlawful, and an overuse of state power on a religious and cultural minority, the governing board says.

The High Court will hear arguments about the future of the West Coast Christian community's private school on Monday, following the Secretary for Education's decision to cancel its registration over serious concerns that the school is not a physically and emotionally safe place for students.

Documents released to RNZ under the Official Information Act detail the board's response to secretary Ellen Macgregor-Reid's moves to shut the school, after a second failed Education Review Office (ERO) audit in as many years.

In a letter to MacGregor-Reid on 14 November last year, the board said it was deeply concerned that the Ministry of Education's approach was legally flawed and procedurally unfair, and the school's closure would be a disproportionate response.

"It is an overuse of state power on a religious and cultural minority," the letter said. "The school has wholeheartedly committed to doing whatever is asked of it to meet the required standard (if it does not already).

"There is no lack of engagement, passion or goodwill to do what is required. The very significant improvements made to the school over the last two years testify to that - and the work is continuing.

"There are significant flaws in the proposed decision to close the school such that it is unlawful."

The ministry had not shown any evidence that it had considered the effects of closing the school on Gloriavale children, and members were deeply concerned about schooling outside the community, the board said.

"Parents wish to exercise their rights to educate their children consistently with their religion and values," the board said. "They regard this as a protected right.

"The school enables them to manifest their religion and enjoy the unique culture of their community, as part of their educational experience. This experience would not be available to them at a state school.

"They are entitled to these rights and the ministry must act consistently with them when making a decision."

The board said the ministry had also failed to consider the practical effects of closing the school, with the nearest primary school, Lake Brunner School, a 40-minute drive and Greymouth High School a one-hour drive from Gloriavale.

"These are unacceptable distances for children to be travelling back and forth each day, and to do so would not be in the best interests of the children. The ministry would need to put on school buses to enable this transport, but this does not negate the impact of 1-2 hours of travel time daily."

An on-site satellite school would not seem to address the issues raised and boarding schools were not an option, the board said.

"This would take children away from their families, and their religious and cultural life at the community. Concerns as to discrimination and bullying would be exacerbated by fulltime attendance at the school, and boarding is especially unacceptable to parents, whose children should not be taken away from them through the week without their consent and against their wishes.

"Children being dislocated from their parents, community, culture and religion is unacceptable.

"There is also no evidence provided that community children will be physically and emotionally safer at state schools."

MacGregor-Reid told school leaders in December that she was cancelling its registration, but the 80-student school has remained open, pending judicial review, as a result of a High Court challenge by the board.

She again confirmed the move in September, after considering the findings of a special ERO review, with the ministry applying to lift interim court orders preventing the school's closure.

The July review found the school had failed to meet one of the eight registration criteria - to be a physically and emotionally safe place for students - after falling short of three criteria in 2025 and six in 2023.

"Inconsistencies between the school and community child protection policies limit assurance that governance oversight is effective, and that the school is consistently a physically and emotionally safe place for students," the ERO report said.

"Information was withheld from ERO in relation to provision, monitoring and reporting requirements for health and safety to and by the premises owners."

The report noted that the teaching council was investigating two allegations of staff misconduct. The school had provided ERO with a letter of suspension for one staff member.

While there had been improvements overall, ERO said it was not confident that the school's systems were "sufficiently embedded, consistent and reliable to ensure ongoing compliance with the requirements for registration over time".

Last November, the school board said information relied on by the ministry failed to distinguish between the school and the wider community.

"While it is not accepted that there remain unaddressed issues in the Gloriavale community, the school and the community are not the same. The relevant question for the ministry is whether the school meets the criteria for registration, not whether the wider community does."

The board said there had been no instances of any "sexualised misbehaviour" at the school and systems were in place to mitigate risk, including a comprehensive child protection policy.

Teachers were trained to recognise, and respond to any concerns or disclosures of abuse.

"The school is a safe, student-centred, externally assured learning environment, where historical patterns of harm are neither present nor possible."

The ministry was relying on irrelevant evidence, a flawed process, and had failed to take relevant considerations into account, such as the children's best interests, said the board, which claimed "mixed and evolving" ministry concerns had "created uncertainty about what the actual concerns for physical and emotional safety are, suggesting an underlying agenda".

"We strongly affirm that Gloriavale Christian School meets the statutory requirements for registration under the Education and Training Act 2020."

RNZ initially sought documents relating to the ministry's decision in December 2025, with a response provided in May.

The ministry letters to Gloriavale detailed concerns that the school existed to indoctrinate children, maintain a caste system and grow a workforce, rather than for teaching and learning.

They also outlined concerns over most teenagers being prevented from progressing beyond Year 11, a lack of support for young victims and abusers, and students not being able to use school toilets without fear.

The ministry's points were rejected by the board.

In October, the ministry released a further 11 documents, after re-assessing its response to RNZ's request, consisting of letters and supporting information received from the school board between 3 October and 21 December 2025.

"Unfortunately, we have identified that, due to an administrative error while processing your request, some communications that the ministry received from Gloriavale Christian School were omitted when preparing the response. As a result, we have identified a further 11 documents in scope of your request.

"I can confirm that the information contained in these documents was considered in the decision made by the Secretary for Education in December 2025 and apologise for the oversight in our earlier response to your request."

World.title: Aitutaki residents urged to heed updates as Wati approaches
World.content:
Tropical Cyclone Wati is moving southeast towards the Southern Cook Islands, with conditions expected to deteriorate over the coming days according to the Cook Islands Meteorological Service.

Wati currently has maximum sustained winds of around 75 km/h with gusts reaching 100 km/h. The system is moving southeast at around 14 km/h.

On its current track, Tropical Cyclone Wati is expected to be approximately:

530 km north-northwest of Aitutaki by 10am on Saturday 17 October.

100 km north of Aitutaki by 10am on Sunday, 18 October.

Aitutaki residents have been told to pay close attention to official updates as the system approaches.

Forecasts

For Aitutaki, fresh to strong winds of 35-45 km/h with gusts up to 80 km/h.

Winds are expected to strengthen to damaging gale force from early Sunday morning, averaging 75 km/h, with gusts up to 100 km/h.

Cloudy periods with showers, increasing to periods of heavy rain and squally thunderstorms from tomorrow, Saturday.

Rough seas with moderate to heavy swells. High seas are expected from Sunday morning.

For the rest of the Southern Cook Islands, moderate to fresh southeast winds, strengthening from later tomorrow.

Strong winds averaging up to 45 km/h, with gusts up to 90 km/h.

Cloudy periods with showers, increasing to periods of heavy rain and squally thunderstorms from tomorrow.

Seas becoming very rough, with moderate to heavy swells expected from early Sunday morning.

World.title: World Cup: Tonga upsets England with Olakau'atu double
World.content:
Tonga recorded their first-ever win over England in their opening pool clash at the 2026 Rugby League World Cup in Perth on Saturday night, with a 30-12 victory.

It was a Haumole Olakau'atu double that inspired the Tongan XIII to the win.

The win is the Pacific nation's first over England in their history and helps avenge a two-point loss in the 2017 World Cup semifinal.

Kristian Woolf's men repelled multiple waves of England attack before scoring twice in three minutes to turn a 10-6 lead into a 22-6 advantage midway through the second half.

England fought back through Dom Young before Haumole Olakau'atu's second try with 10 minutes to play put the game to bed and secured a hard-fought 30-12 victory.

The result puts Tonga in pole position to progress to the semi-final.

With Samoa also winning their pool match against France, England must defeat France and Papua New Guinea and hope Tonga beats Samoa when the two Pacific nations face off at a sold-out CommBank Stadium in the final game of the group stage on 1 November.

A total of 18,302 vocal fans turned up at HBF Park, painting the stadium red.

Jason Taumalolo paid tribute to the players and the fans.

"We got a group of talented players and one thing that has brought this group of players together is the sacrifice they made," Taumalolo said.

"Some of the boys could have played for the bigger countries. Forever grateful to the man above.

"Grateful for all the Tongan fans who turned up to support the boys.

"Obviously England was a tough game, talented players too. We were in for the fight the whole 80 minutes."

Head coach Kristian Woolf said they put themselves under pressure a couple of times, but "the longer the game went the better we got".

"The efforts were really important."

Woolf said they had done extraordinary things before, by beating Australia and New Zealand.

He said it is a big thing beating Tier One nations.

Co-captain Addin Fonua-Blake said they regrouped at halftime and came back strong in the second half.

"It was a physical game. They capitalised on some of our ill-discipline."

Fonua-Blake said they were able to swing the momentum back in their favour, after the initial English attack in the earlier part of the second half.

Tonga struck first in the match through Stefano Utoikamanu, and managed to keep a clean sheet in the first half as two Isaiya Katoa penalty goals made it 10-0 at the break.

England were finally rewarded for their effort in the 46th minute when Hugo Savala went through a hole.

A second English try appeared imminent before a high shot on Tongan winger Dallin Watene-Zelezniak swung the momentum.

Tonga capitalised on the opening, Olakau'atu and Tolu Koula crossing for tries in successive sets to put their nation in control.

England cut the deficit to 12 through Dominic Young before Olakau'atu pounced on an Isaiya Katoa grubber in the dying minutes.

World.title: Olivia Dean concert stopped due to sound issues
World.content:
Olivia Dean was forced to stop her sold-out concert at Western Springs Bowl on Saturday night due to sound issues.



Dean was playing to more than 40,000 people at the revamped venue as part of her Art of Loving Live tour.



RNZ executive editor Jeremy Rees, who was at the concert, said Dean played three songs to a jubilant crowd, before leaving the stage, saying the sound needed to be "reset".



"We're looking at an empty stage at the moment and it's a real disappointment for people who had been looking forward to the Olivia Dean concert for a long, long time,” Rees said.



At 9.30pm, a stage manager announced the sound at the stadium was being reset.



Rees said the first few songs sounded very good, although Dean's voice cut out in places.



"The crowd were right into it and singing along and happy, and then just as I say, she said she had to stop. She improvised for a moment, talking about love and her latest album, while people were trying to fix the sound."



The concert restarted just after 10pm, with Dean apologising to the crowd and saying the show would not be cut short, before launching into a song.

World.title: Bledisloe Cup: Josh Moorby's try double highlights All Blacks' game of two halves
World.content:
Picking just one of the seven All Blacks tries that best summed up their 43-21 victory over Australia in a masterclass in cohesive attack and decision making in Sydney on Saturday was difficult - but Josh Moorby's second five-pointer might be it.

After a bruising run by second-five Timoci Tavatavanawai - a late replacement following the withdrawal, before kickoff, of Jordie Barrett - the ball found left wing Moorby, who showed it to Wallabies right wing Max Jorgensen and halfback Ryan Lonergan, and went over untouched.

Ultimately, that converted score was the All Blacks' final points of an extraordinary afternoon in front of 73,000 at Accor Stadium, as the Wallabies, swept again in the Bledisloe Cup for the sixth successive year, finally found something.

The home side had the better of the second half - helped by the fact the All Blacks played the final 12 minutes shorthanded - and five minutes with just 13 players - due to debutant Chay Fihaki's yellow card for a high tackle and, before that, replacement hooker Samisoni Taukei'aho's injury, which left them with no more players on the bench.

The visitors were scoring at almost a point a minute, when Damian McKenzie's conversion for Moorby's second try went over and - led by skipper Codie Taylor, loose forward Peter Lakai and a rejuvenated Beauden Barrett, who also scored a double - Dave Rennie's men looked as good as they have all year.

They committed to backing up last weekend's victory at Eden Park and, perhaps inspired by the bright afternoon sunshine, played with a continuity and skill that blew the Wallabies away in the first half.

They did it despite Jordie Barrett's calf problem, which ruled him out hours before kickoff, and fellow midfielder Quinn Tupaea's head injury within two minutes of the start.

Despite a very much reshuffled line-up, the intensity with which the All Blacks went about their work was almost as impressive as their short-passing game, which showed an incredible appreciation for time and space against a Wallabies team determined to right the wrongs of last weekend.

Beauden Barrett also had a try double against Australia. www.photosport.nz

The All Blacks had four tries in the space of 14 minutes, Moorby, Beauden Barrett, Lakai and Rieko Ioane - on for Tupaea - all finishing scores that highlighted their killer instinct.

Lock Jeremy Williams' reply for the Wallabies was only a blip, as the All Blacks made the most of Williams' yellow card for offside after the re-start for Wallace Sititi to over from a scrum and Barrett putting an exclamation on the half with an intercept try from 70m out.

"I thought we were awesome in that first 40 - just backing ourselves and playing what was in front of us - but the second 40 was a bit different," Taylor said afterwards.

Counterpart Harry Wilson said: "I'm gutted. When you give a team like the All Blacks a headstart, it's tough... we're going to have to improve a lot."

Australia fought back with two tries to one in the second half, but this was a devastating loss for them in their final home game of the year. Their next home test is in Perth on Anzac Day, 2027.

Unfortunately for them, their opponents are the All Blacks.

Wing Will Jordan's absence in the second half may spark concerns about a potential injury and Shannon Frizell's leg issue after he come into the test off the bench may also be a problem.

As Taylor hinted, the second-half performance may come under some scrutiny by Rennie and company, but maintain such intensity is difficult, when the game is all but over at halftime, and after last weekend's second-half performance at Eden Park, it was a reminder that if this team get it right, they can be devastating.

All Blacks 43 (Beauden Barrett 2, Josh Moorby 2, Peter Lakai, Rieko Ioane & Wallace Sititi tries; Damian McKenzie 4 conversions) Australia 21 (Jeremy Williams, Tom Wright & Filipo Daugunu tries; Ryan Lonergan 2 conversions, Declan Meredith conversion)

World.title: Shorthanded All Blacks too strong for Wallabies in Bledisloe Cup sweep
World.content:
The All Blacks ended the game with just 14 fit players, as they beat the Wallabies 43-21 in the second Bledisloe Cup test in Sydney.

The visitors scored seven tries to the hosts' three to claim back-to-back wins over Australia.

Midfielder Quinn Tupaea left the field for an HIA, after hitting his head on the ground early in the match and didn't return, with Rieko Ioane coming on to take his place.

Both sides started well, but the All Blacks struck first through wing Josh Moorby, who scored out wide, after a period of attack in the Wallabies 22. First-five Damian McKenzie was unsuccessful with the conversion.

The visitors were soon in again, with fullback Beauden Barrett stepping over for a try, after a nice break from flanker Peter Lakai.

McKenzie was unable to add the extras, with the All Blacks leading 10-0 nearing the 20 minute mark.

Peter Lakai of New Zealand goes over to score. www.photosport.nz

Lakai was rewarded for some good support play, taking a short ball from halfback Cam Roigard to barge over for the All Blacks' third try. McKenzie nailed the sideline conversion to make it 17-0 to New Zealand.

The All Blacks' next try was superb, with some slick handling and good running lines putting Ioane in the clear, before the replacement back beat the last defender to help the visitors extend their lead to 22-0.

Australia had barely had the ball, but they looked good when they had it, and lock Jeremy Williams scored their first try, after some nice attacking play inside the All Blacks 22. The conversion was successful to make it a 15-point game at 22-7 to the All Blacks.

Williams was then yellow-carded, after being penalised with the All Blacks hot on attack, leaving the Wallabies a man down for the last 10 minutes of the first half.

The All Blacks made the most of the numerical advantage and scored on the next play, with No.8 Wallace Sititi storming over from the back of the scrum. McKenzie added the extras to push their lead out to 29-7.

The Wallabies then went on the attack and were making inroads into the All Blacks defence, when Barrett intercepted an Australian pass and sprinted 70 metres to put a dagger in the home side's hearts just before halftime. McKenzie kicked the extras for a 36-7 lead at the break.

Beauden Barrett of New Zealand dives over to score. www.photosport.nz

A big break from midfielder Timoci Tavatavanawai led to another try for Moorby, who sold a dummy to two Australian defenders, before trotting over the line. McKenzie's conversion was good to put the All Blacks ahead 43-7.

Replacement back Chay Fihaki came off the bench for his All Blacks debut and made a nice break, before not quite connecting with an attempted grubber kick.

The All Blacks had made 14 linebreaks by the 53rd minute and continued to stretch the Wallabies defence, although the hosts were also hard to handle with ball in hand and they scored next through fullback Tom Wright, who had been impressive all game.

The conversion was successful to cut the All Blacks lead to 43-14 with about 25 minutes remaining.

The Wallabies cut that lead to 43-21, with Filipo Daugunu scoring a try for the hosts, and the All Blacks then went down to 14 men for the final 11 minutes of the match, due to too many injuries.

They then had Fihaki yellow-carded for a high tackle, but managed to hold on for a 43-21 victory for 13 straight wins over Australia.

The All Blacks had already retained the Bledisloe Cup, after winning last week's first test at Eden Park 50-19.

Recap all the action with our live blog below:

World.title: Orchids and Kumuls pile on tries in respective World Cup victories
World.content:
The Papua New Guinea Orchids started their 2026 Rugby League World Cup campaign on a high, with a convincing 58-4 win over France in Port Moresby on Saturday afternoon.

Playing their first-ever world cup game at home, at Santos National Football Stadium, in their first international against France, the Orchids ran in 12 tries in total - four to winger Naomi Kelly, who scored one in the first 35-minute spell before adding three in the second half.

In the process she also equalled the record for the most tries in a single match by any PNG Orchids player.

The previous record was held by Belinda Gwasamun, who scored four tries against Brazil during the 2022 Women's Rugby League World Cup.

Tia Molo, Shelly Long and Fleur Ginn got a double each against France.

The Orchids led 32-0 at halftime, with six tries recorded in the first 35 minutes.

Relna Wuruki-Hosea of the Canberra Raiders notched the first try for the home side in the seventh minute, with a powerful run from a scrum outside the French 10-metre zone.

North Queensland Cowboys' Emily Veivers converted the goal kick to give the Orchids an early 6-0 lead.

Hooker Ua Ravu at dummy half led their attacks, with Cynthiah Peters at seven directing play.

Captain Elsie Albert was a powerful runner up front.

France attacked from their line in a good set in the 12th minute and won a penalty on the PNG 30-metre line.

Dummy half Cristina Song directed their attacks as forwards Elodie Pacull, Perrine Monsarrat, Stacy Bessiere and Leila Bessahli started gaining valuable metres with their strong forward drives upfield.

That resulted in a close drive for the corner flag but it ended in a knock-on close to the PNG line.

Shellie Long ran through the French defence to score the Orchids' second try, followed by Paramatta Eeels Fleur Ginn, who stepped her way through a gap, dummied and ran in to score between the posts after the PNG team attacked from the restart.

Tia Molo claimed the team's fourth try in the 24th minute, before Naomi Kelly finished off wide out for the Orchids five minutes later, after Molo stepped inside two players to leave Kelly free out wide. Veivers kicked the goal and PNG were up 28-0.

Former Wallaroos rugby union player Ivania Wong then showed her speed out wide on the right and ran back in between the posts to score.

PNG Orchids led 32-0 after the first 35-minute spell.

Closed off

France went straight to attack from the restart and their persistence was rewarded when Manon Samarra went over after playmaker Lisa Diraison set up the attack.

The try was the only one the visitors managed in the game as PNG responded and closed off the game, with a dominating second half performance, running in six more tries.

Kelly kicked off their scoring in the second spell, after the Orchids varied their play with Ginn and Peters going through the defensive gaps to set her up.

Then it was Ginn who picked up a loose pass and ran through the French defensive line to score between the posts again for her second try.

Veivers' goal kick gave them a 42-4 lead.

Replacement Essay Banu combined well with captain Albert as the two big forwards kept the momentum on through the middle of the field.

With 20 minutes to go Molo went over to score her second from a penalty, after Albert was stopped on the line. Molo picked up from the ruck and dived over for the 46-4 lead.

Then it was Kelly's turn again for her third try with 18 minutes to go. She received the pass from Molo, who had chased Peters' grubber towards the corner flag.

The Orchids then capped off their afternoon with Kelly's fourth try before Long crashed over in the right corner for the team's 12th try of the afternoon.

Captain Elsie Albert said the team had prepared well for the game and the tournament.

"It was a great win, in front of the home crowd," she said.

"I thought we had a good preparation leading up to this game and I thought everyone went out there and did what we exactly needed to do.

"It's great to be back home playing and to get a win in front of the home crowd."

PNG Orchids coach Craig Sandercock said post-match it was a great game and a good start to their campaign.

"I was really pleased," he said.

"They've trained so hard. Really pleased for them and having the crowd support - it was fantastic."

PNG Kumuls Facebook

Kumuls also victorious

It was the first of a double-header in Port Moresby, with the PNG Kumuls paying Lebanon also on Saturday afternoon.

The PNG Kumuls made it a double win for the home teams, defeating Lebanon 42-18.

The side scored seven tries to Lebanon's three, and open their campaign on a high, in front of their vocal local fans.

The Kumuls scored tries through Gairo Voro, Robert Derby, Nixon Putt, Finley Glare, Epel Kapinias, Ryse Martin and Bailey Biondi Odo.

Martin added the other points through his boots.

Lebanon got their three tries from Abbas Miski, who got two, and Tony Sukkar.

World.title: Wallaroos not content with simply being 'better versions' of themselves
World.content:
Among Siokapesi Palu Sekona's many impressive qualities as Wallaroos captain is her uncompromising approach.

Wallabies outclassed by All Blacks The Wallabies fall to the All Blacks for the 13th straight time, as their trans-Tasman rivals record a convincing 43-21 win in Sydney.

As such, it does not come as a shock to learn she feels the Wallaroos still have much room for improvement following their dominant 56-12 win over Scotland in this afternoon's Global XV Series Test.

The eight-tries-to-two victory did not represent a complete performance in Palu Sekona's eyes, which should serve as music to the ears of Wallaroos supporters.

Why?

It shows the Wallaroos are setting the highest possible standards for themselves.

"We still know there is room for improvement and we definitely know what to do to clean that up," Palu Sekona said.

Wallaroos skipper Siokapesi Palu Sekona put in a solid shift on both sides of the ball. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The Wallaroos defeated Scotland 30-10 three weeks ago in Edinburgh during their three-Test swing through Great Britain and France as part of the Global XV Series.

The victory snapped a six-match losing streak but left Wallaroos players and coaches dissatisfied.

It was a sign of the Wallaroos' quickly developing harder edge, which Palu Sekona wants carried through to the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup.

"We knew we could put together a better performance," she said.

"Ultimately results and scores are what people look at. But if we want to break down our rugby, there are so many things to clean up.

"From discipline, to our ruck, to the accuracy of our set-piece. There are things we can continue to work on."

Wallaroos set bar high

The Wallaroos, ranked seventh in the world, are starting from behind scratch when compared to teams such as England and New Zealand.

Both enjoy the benefit of being full-time programs, with their respective governing bodies making a wise move to invest in the women's game.

The Wallaroos are still semi-professional, but a shift to full-time status — as part of an integrated program alongside the women's sevens squad — is in progress.

There is no doubt the Wallaroos' rate of improvement will be accelerated once they go full-time in the lead-up to the World Cup, which Australia will host.

"We don't want to only be the better versions of ourselves," Palu Sekona said.

" We want to be the best in the world. "

Winger Amelia Whitaker scored a double in the Wallaroos' victory. (Getty Images/Corbis: Steve Christo)

The Wallaroos' makeshift coaching team, under the leadership of Rugby Australia's director of women's high performance Tim Walsh, has had a positive influence on the playing group.

Sione Fukofuka will take over as head coach next year and work alongside Walsh, who enjoyed tremendous success in charge of the Australian women's sevens squad.

Like Palu Sekona, Walsh was not completely satisfied with the Wallaroos' display against Scotland.

But he saw enough to know they are heading in the right direction.

"I think it was another step forward, for sure," Walsh said.

The Wallaroos will complete their 2026 Test season when they meet Scotland in Canberra on Friday night.

World.title: World Cup heartbreak for Kangaroos half as Tonga notches first win over England
World.content:
Mitchell Moses will miss the remainder of the Rugby League World Cup, after being ruled out of the Kangaroos' title defence with a lower leg injury that continues his representative misery.

The Parramatta playmaker suffered the injury during Australia's 24-22 win over New Zealand in the tournament opener on Thursday night in Sydney.

He attempted to play on but eventually left the field less than two minutes into the second half.

Meanwhile, England's hopes of reaching the World Cup semi-finals are already on life support after suffering a 30-12 loss to world No.5 Tonga in their blockbuster showdown in Perth.

Moses was injured during the Kangaroos' World Cup opener against New Zealand. (Getty Images: Matt King)

While initially believed to be a calf issue or a hairline fracture, scans following the match revealed Moses had suffered an unspecified "high-grade muscle tear", meaning his World Cup campaign is over.

It's a blow to the Kangaroos, who are already missing Nathan Cleary with a serious leg injury, with Moses the Kangaroos' strongest last-tackle kicker.

Moses switched allegiance to play for Australia at this tournament after captaining Lebanon at the 2022 World Cup.

In Perth, Tonga produced a defensive masterclass in its four-tries-to-two victory over England.

The result put Tonga in the box seat to reach the semis, with games against Lebanon and Samoa to round out the group stage.

England's World Cup campaign is already on life support after Tonga's statement win in Perth. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

In contrast, world No.3 England have been left on the brink of elimination — even if it wins its remaining two games against France and PNG.

Under the confusing group stage system employed for the World Cup, only two teams from across pools B and C will progress to the last four.

If England finish on the same number of wins as Tonga, then Tonga will go through given they won Saturday's head-to-head battle.

World Cup opener a reminder of Australia's glory days There was a time when Test matches were rugby league's biggest, best and bloodiest spectacles, and last night's World Cup opener between Australia and New Zealand was a reminder of those days.

Should England and Samoa end up with the same number of wins, the tiebreaker will be which nation has the better points-for-and-against differential.

Samoa opened its campaign with a 78-4 smashing of France, leaving England needing to post some massive wins in its remaining two games to stay alive.

Stefano Utoikamanu opened the scoring in the 24th minute when he found a hole in England's defence to stroll over untouched.

A pair of Isaiya Katoa penalty goals extended the margin to 10 points by half-time, with England left to rue a series of fumbles and near misses.

England started the second half full of steam, resulting in a team-lifting try to AJ Brimson in the 46th minute.

But in a game where hard work was king, it was a slice of fortune that ended up giving Tonga a vital edge with Haumole Olakau'atu scoring the first of his two tries after he soccered the ball into an opponent's arm and then gathered the bouncing rebound.

And when Tuimoala Lolohea's neat dribble found Tolutau Koula in the corner to make it 22-6 in the 58th minute, it was as good as game over.

The win was a powerful statement from Tonga, whose only previous taste of international success against England came in 2019 when they beat Great Britain.

In Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea's men's side earned a gritty 42-18 win over Lebanon hours after the country's women's team had dispatched France 58-4.

Veteran Rhyse Martin began his farewell tournament in style, scoring a try and going perfect from seven conversions against a dogged Lebanon outfit.

His try with nine minutes left on the clock finished off the Cedars, who were fading in humid conditions.

But Lebanon never stopped trying, with fullback Jacob Kiraz (207 metres) and winger Tony Frances (292 metres) constant threats in attack, while Wests Tigers stalwart Alex Twal led the defence with 48 tackles.

Winger Naomi Kelly crossed four times in the women's game as the Orchids ran in 12 tries to one.

England ended the day's women's action in comprehensive fashion against Wales, with Connie Boyd and Anna Davies both scoring hat-tricks in the 70-6 rout in Perth.

AAP/ABC

World.title: 'Terrible to watch': Ohope Wins euthanased after fall in Caulfield Cup
World.content:
New Zealand mare Ohope Wins has been euthanased after a fall in the Caulfield Cup that also included 2025 Melbourne Cup winner Half Yours.

With about 200 metres to go in the 2,400m race, which was won by Gavin Bedggood's Kingswood, Half Yours was in the middle of the pack when there appeared to be contact with Kings Valley.

Half Yours went down hard, sending jockey Mark Zahra into the turf, with Ohope Wins also coming down after Jye McNeil was unable to avoid the fallen McEvoy Racing product.

Racing Victoria Stewards later confirmed Ohope Wins, from Chris Waller Racing, was euthanased by the on-course veterinarian.

Jye McNeil on Ohope Wins in the mounting yard before the Caulfield Cup. (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri)

"The mare was unable to be saved due to the nature of the injury sustained," a Racing Victoria (RV) statement read.

"RV extends its condolences to Yulong, the owners of Ohope Wins, her trainer Chris Waller and their stable staff who cared for the horse and are deeply saddened by their loss."

Yulong and Waller released a statement, saying "few words can express our current emotions".

"Ohope Wins was a true star of the turf, but to the people who looked after her everyday, she was so much more," the statement read.

"She was brave. She was kind. She was full of character, but more importantly, she was loved.

Ohope Wins won the Oaks at Randwick in April. (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri)

"Our hearts go out to all involved throughout her career, especially those who cared for her on a daily basis."

Half Yours, the defending Caulfield Cup victor, got up and eventually crossed the finish line without a jockey.

The stewards said Half Yours would undergo a "thorough veterinary examination" after falling in "a racing incident", which would be subject to an inquiry.

Half Yours got up and crossed the line without a rider. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Half Yours returned to his stall, while stewards said Zahra and McNeil were both "conscious and alert" and transported to hospital for further assessment.

Trainer Tony McEvoy said after the race that Half Yours had suffered some abrasions but looked OK, all things considered.

"That was terrible to watch," McEvoy said.

"The horse, he's got a couple of lacerations, he seems bright, he seems composed in himself.

"He's got a laceration under his arm, he's got a laceration on a hind leg. They look superficial."

The final race of the day at Caulfield was delayed.

World.title: Cats underline AFLW premiership credentials as Crows snap Suns' winning run
World.content:
Geelong has underlined its AFLW premiership credentials with a 53-point rout of West Coast in Perth.

Midfielder Georgie Prespakis (39 disposals, six tackles, five clearances) was at her dominant best as teammate Mikayla Bowen (27 disposals) also impressed in the 8.18 (66) to 1.7 (13) victory.

In Adelaide, the Crows boosted their hopes of a finals appearance with victory over Gold Coast, while Brisbane and the Western Bulldogs also claimed victories as the competition's top eight continued to take shape on Saturday.

The Eagles challenged early at Leederville Oval but had to wait until late into the fourth quarter to kick their first major of the afternoon, with Isabella Lewis slotting from a forward-half stoppage.

The Cats boasted eight different goalkickers and Prespakis registered a career-high 13 score involvements as Geelong finished the day in first.

Former leader North Melbourne can reclaim top spot with victory over Essendon on Sunday.

Earlier, Adelaide moved back into the finals frame after ending Gold Coast's six-game winning run.

Sisters Niamh (right) and Grace Kelly (left) combined for an early Adelaide goal. (Getty Images: Sarah Reed/AFL Photos)

Led throughout by Irish sisters Grace (three goals, 12 disposals) and Niamh Kelly (two goals, 20 disposals), and 18-year-old Chloe Bown (one goal, 25 disposals) in the final quarter, the Crows scored back-to-back wins for just the second time this season in a 10.3 (63) to 7.11 (53) win.

The bad news for the Crows was the loss of influential midfielder Maddi Newman who went down twice with a knee injury.

She stayed down after a non-contact incident midway through the third quarter and got subbed off to have her left knee strapped before coming back onto the field.

Later in the term, she was hit hard by Gold Coast's Charlie Rowbottom and was carried off again, later appearing on the sidelines on crutches with ice on the back of her knee.

The win left the Crows eighth on the ladder with five wins and five losses, equal on points with Hawthorn, and four points ahead of Fremantle, West Coast, Port Adelaide and Richmond, although the Dockers have a game in hand.

And the Suns fell out of the league's top four just hours later, with the Western Bulldogs notching a convincing 30-point win over Carlton at Princes Park.

Midfielder Mikala Cann was among the Bulldogs' best with 27 disposals and a goal, while key forward Emma McDonald kicked two majors in her side's 8.8 (56) to 3.8 (26) victory.

The victory saw the Bulldogs leapfrog both the Blues and the Suns into fourth, as Carlton fell to a first defeat in four games.

The Bulldogs are now tied on competition points with North Melbourne and Melbourne in second and third, respectively — although the Kangaroos are yet to play in Round 10.

In Ipswich, Port Adelaide's hopes of pushing into finals contention took a hit with a 16-point loss to Brisbane.

The victory ended a five-game losing streak for the Lions, who were led by midfielders Isabel Dawes (16 disposals, one goal), Sophie Conway (19 disposals, one goal) and Alexandra Anderson (24 disposals).

Conway was especially electric in the opening quarter, reaching the first break with 15 disposals and a goal, as her side made its way to a 5.4 (34) to 2.6 (18) victory, just its third of the season.

The defeat means the Power remains four competition points and percentage from the finals places.

World.title: Wallabies outclassed as All Blacks continue Bledisloe Cup domination
World.content:
The Wallabies have slumped to a 13th straight defeat to the All Blacks, with their trans-Tasman rivals recording a convincing 43-21 victory at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

The result meant the All Blacks swept the two-Test Bledisloe Cup series, having thrashed the Wallabies 50-19 at Auckland's Eden Park a week ago.

A dominant first half from the visitors set up this afternoon's win.

They scored six tries to one to lead 36-7 at half-time, before extending their lead to 43-7 shortly after the break when winger Josh Moorby completed a double.

To the Wallabies' credit, they refused to give up.

Tom Wright and Filipo Daugunu crossed the stripe for the home side, but the two converted tries only served to limit the damage on the scoreboard.

Filipo Daugunu crossed for one of the Wallabies' second-half tries. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Alongside Moorby, All Blacks veteran Beauden Barrett touched down for a brace of tries, with his second coming after a 70-metre dash to the line.

The Wallabies had high hopes before the back-to-back Bledisloe Cup Tests, but they are forced to return to the drawing board.

Coach Les Kiss and his squad will now turn their attention to their remaining Nations Championship Tests in the UK.

They play England (November 9, AEDT), Scotland (November 16) and Wales (November 22).

The Wallabies will have to wait until next year's historic Anzac Day Test in Brisbane to face the All Blacks again.

The Wallaroos were too strong for Scotland to post a second straight Test win. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Earlier on Saturday, the Wallaroos scored a massive 56-12 win over Scotland to kick off the quadruple header.

It is the Wallaroos' second straight win over the Scots, and they will meet again in Canberra on Friday night.

Meanwhile, the world champion Australian women's sevens team fell to New Zealand in their preseason match, 21-12.

In the men's sevens match, which was also a preseason fixture, Australia drew 19-19 with Fiji.

It is the first time all four of Australia's national rugby teams have appeared on the same match-day schedule.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: 'Decision next year': Nawaqanitawase keeps Wallabies options open
World.content:
Mark Nawaqanitawase is refusing to rule out turning his back on Australia for next year's home Rugby World Cup as a three-nation tug-of-war for the cross-code super talent escalates.

While Wallabies captain Harry Wilson and coach Les Kiss have no doubts Nawaqanitawase will be wearing the gold jumper at the 2027 global showpiece, the player himself is keeping his options open.

The in-demand winger's manager this week suggested Nawaqanitawase may choose to represent Fiji, to honour his father's heritage, or Italy, who the dual international is also eligible for through his grandmother.

Still only 26, the prospect of Nawaqanitawase defecting from Australia had seemed improbable.

Under World Rugby laws, if he chose to switch allegiances, following 11 Test appearances for Australia in 2022-23 before enjoying a hugely successful two-year stint in the NRL, the dual international would not be allowed to wear the Wallabies jumper ever again.

Wallabies in awe of Nawaqanitawase It was not just the 80,000 spectators, nor the millions of TV viewers in Australia, who were left in awe of Mark Nawaqanitawase's performance in the NRL grand final.

Representing Fiji or Italy could appear a more appealing scenario in the twilight of his career, but not his pomp.

However, the newly-crowned NRL premiership winner took to social media yesterday to reveal he had yet to make any decisions about his playing future beyond a looming two-year, $3 million stint in Japan under former Wallabies coach Robbie Deans.

"I just thought I would jump on here as there has been a lot of speculation on my future," Nawaqanitawase posted on Instagram.

"My only focus right now is moving to Japan in a couple of weeks and connecting with my new team at Saitama Wild Knights.

"I will weigh up my options and make a decision next year on my international future.

"Love, Marky."

After taking in the Kangaroos' thrilling Rugby League World Cup win over New Zealand on Thursday night with Nawaqanitawase in Sydney, Wilson is confident the free agent will be playing for Australia next year.

"I don't have to convince him," Wilson said ahead of the Wallabies' second Bledisloe Cup clash with the All Blacks in Sydney today.

" I played junior Wallabies with him, played Wallabies with him, saw him last night supporting the Kangaroos, so I think it's pretty obvious who he wants to play for. "

Coach Kiss is also optimistic about the 2023 Olympic sevens star opting for a Wallabies return next year.

"I think there's no doubt that he wants to be back in the game for us, that's for sure," Kiss said.

"We'll continue our conversations and go from there. I'm not going to speak on his behalf at all. But we know where he wants to play."

AAP

World.title: Tattoo artist brings queer joy to AFLW pride jumper
World.content:
When it comes to elite sporting teams, some adopt roaring tigers or bucking horses on the guernseys, but sometimes a "fruity" dolphin works best.

The playful design for the Gold Coast Suns' Pride Round guernsey, by Sunshine Coast tattoo artist Mady Peters, is bringing fun, and maybe some luck, to the Queensland AFLW side.

Ms Peters's design features a rainbow football boot, which she says highlights the support of the LGBTQIA+ community for women's football, as well as a carabiner, a symbol historically associated with the women-loving-women community.

She said the colours and characters reinforced Pride Round's message of self-expression.

Mady Peters, also known as Pokey Pokes, in her tattoo studio. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Nykayla Dux)

"It just came from a place of joy," Ms Peters said.

" I think that's everything that the Pride Round kind of stands for — this celebration and to show up authentically and as yourself. "

Among the more light-hearted illustrations is a dolphin holding a non-binary flag.

"I believe dolphins are a bit fruity," Ms Peters said.

Peters, Mithen and Lynch all shared the same vision for the 2026 Pride Guernsey: queer joy, self-expression, and a little bit of silliness. (Facebook: Gold Coast Suns)

The Sunshine Coast artist said she hoped Pride Round would help queer people relish and celebrate their identities.

"There is a world that still exists where people would rather not be here than be themselves, and that's so sad to see," she said.

Her work has won the endorsement of Mitch Brown, who last year became the AFL's first past or present player to openly come out as part of the LGBTQIA+ community.

Gold Coast Suns AFLW players Lily Mithen and Katie Lynch worked with Ms Peters to develop the guernsey.

LGBTQIA+ community 'in the fabric' of AFLW

Mithen said the team wanted the design to reflect their individual personalities.

"Katie and I are a bit loud and fun and silly and we wanted that to be felt through the jumper," she said.

Mithen said helping design the guernsey was an important way to honour the LGBTQIA+ community, which she said had been "woven into the fabric of the AFLW from the very beginning".

"[The AFLW has] always been a place where people have been really free to be themselves," she said.

Lily Mithen says Pride Round celebrates everyone’s individual strengths. (Supplied: Gold Coast SUNS)

For Lynch, her connection to football began playing with "the boys" at the age of four and grew into an enduring love of the game and a place where she felt accepted.

She said many in the AFLW had grown up knowing they "maybe did see themselves doing things a little differently", and that shone through in their sport.

Lynch said it was important to acknowledge a "very brave and courageous group" continuing to challenge perceptions of the LGBTQIA+ community in sport, including in the men's competition.

Head of AFLW at the AFL Players Association Julia Chiera said she could remember feeling like the "odd one out" as the only young girl playing football in her community, before finding a sense of belonging at Melbourne's Darebin Football Club as an adult.

Chiera said women's football had provided a welcoming environment for many queer people at the community level well before the national competition began.

She said football had historically attracted many queer women and gender-nonconforming people because of their "fearlessness" to challenge social expectations.

"It felt empowering to be amongst women who loved football and didn't really care if it was not socially acceptable for women to play sport," she said reflecting on her time at Darebin.

Julia Chiera says the AFLW’s culture of authenticity and acceptance extended beyond sexuality and is celebrated year-round in the women’s league. (Supplied: AFL Players’ Association)

However, Chiera said more work was needed to improve inclusion in the men's game, which did not have a dedicated Pride Round.

She said meaningful support for the LGBTQIA+ community required clubs, players, administrators and supporters to demonstrate genuine inclusion throughout the season and behind closed doors, rather than relying on a single round.

Ms Peters said she hoped the guernsey would bring the Gold Coast side the same good luck for their second and final game of Pride Round 2026 after the Suns won their first match last week.

"I knew it was lucky. I put lucky vibes into it," she said.

The Gold Coast Suns will wear the Pride guernsey for a final time against the Adelaide Crows in Adelaide on Saturday afternoon.

World.title: Dees dismantle Tigers to seal AFLW finals series berth
World.content:
Melbourne has secured a spot in the AFLW finals series after dismantling Richmond with ease in Pride Round.

Last night's 14.10 (94) to 5.2 (32) win was a return to form after the Demons' surprise first-ever AFLW loss to Gold Coast the previous week.

The defeat to the Suns was front of mind for Demons coach Tom Wilson ahead of the Tigers clash at Melbourne's Princes Park.

"We understood last week was far from our best performance," Wilson said before the first bounce.

"We thought around the ball we probably got a bit of a lesson in that space.

"Contest is going to be really important. (Richmond) having Monique Conti and Ellie McKenzie in there, it's a real weapon for them."

Conti returned to the field for the first time since an Achilles injury in round three and wasted no time getting to work.

Within seconds of the first bounce, the club's seven-time consecutive best-and-fairest winner won the centre clearance for the Tigers.

It was a welcome return given Richmond's struggles this season to win the loose ball. The Tigers rank second-last in the competition for contested possession.

But despite Conti's return, and Richmond ruck Poppy Kelly dominating with 23 hit-outs, the Demons won the centre contest time and again through Olivia Purcell and Tyla Hanks.

The pair heeded coach Wilson's call, with each picking up more than 30 disposals and a combined 13 clearances.

Their dominance set up Melbourne's 47 inside-50s to Richmond's 18, and spelled a long night for the Tigers' defence.

Ryleigh Wotherspoon kicked four goals to give the Demons some reassurance ahead of a finals series in which they may be without lead goal kicker Mia Austin, who has undergone throat surgery and does not yet have a set return date.

"We've got a lot of forwards that can kick goals, and even the mids can come through and kick goals, and so we're well supported and well balanced," Wotherspoon said after the game.

"We're pretty unstoppable."

AAP

Tech.title: Mercedes-AMG’s first ground-up SUV is a 1,150hp electric beast
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Earlier this year, Mercedes’ AMG performance brand grabbed our attention with the GT four-door coupe, a souped-up sports sedan with three axial flux motors delivering over 1,150 horsepower. Well, now meet its beefier cousin, the 2028 Mercedes-AMG GT SUV, an equally powerful, ultra-fast-charging electric people-hauler.

The AMG GT SUV (say that five times fast) marks the first time in the performance brand’s 59-year history that it has developed a full-size SUV entirely in-house from the ground up. Scheduled to hit the US next summer, the new EV is built on Merc’s high-performance AMG.EA architecture to combine sports-car handling with full-size SUV suburban practicality.

It will be available in three trims — GT 53, GT 55, and the flagship GT 63 — with the top model delivering 1,153hp via the same three axial flux motors powering the four-door coupe. That beats the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric with Launch Control, which is sure to make for some awkward run-ins around Stuttgart.

Previous Next

















1 / 10

Thanks to an 800-volt architecture, the SUV supports blistering-fast charging speeds up to 710kW on the 128kWh battery (GT 63 / GT 55) and 600kW on the 106kWh battery (GT 53). Drivers can charge 10–80 percent in 12 minutes or gain up to 450km (around 280 miles) of WLTP range in just 10 minutes. The 128kWh battery trims will have an estimated max range of 435 miles.

That battery, by the way? It utilizes F1-inspired technology with specialized NCMA cathodes, silicon-containing anodes, and cylindrical cells. An electrically nonconductive oil flows directly around each individual cell for uniform thermal management, enabling continuous high-power delivery and long battery life. Mercedes has quietly been on the vanguard of battery technology for a while now, with the AMG GT SUV just the latest example. The 710kW charging speed, in particular, could give Mercedes another edge over Porsche’s 320kW speeds.

For a full-size SUV, the AMG GT sounds like it could handle like a vehicle half its size. Mercedes-AMG replaced the traditional mechanical roll bars with a newly developed suspension that uses active hydraulic elements to eliminate pitch and roll during acceleration, heavy braking, and cornering. Combined with three-stage air springs and standard six-degree active rear-axle steering, it purports to balance track precision with long-distance comfort.

But just because it’s a beefy lad doesn’t mean it’ll tip the scales. The AMG GT 63 SUV weighs in at 5,941lbs, making it slightly lighter than the Lotus Eletre R (6,007lbs) and Lucid Gravity (6,100lbs), and nearly identical to the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric (5,960lbs).

Previous Next















1 / 9

Silence is golden — except to a performance brand’s EV engineering team. That means piping in recorded sounds of real AMGs — in this case, the legendary AMG V8 and six-cylinder engines — to preserve the “emotional” AMG identity. Mercedes is proud that it’s using real engine sounds over synthetic EV tones, though some may disagree. The system even simulates mechanical gear shifts with paddle controls, offers adjustable sound profiles, and integrates physical seat vibrations — so you can still feel like there’s a real engine under that hood instead of a 78-liter frunk. The so-called AMGFORCE Sport+ drive program is offered as standard across all three trims of the Mercedes-AMG GT SUV.

Inside, you’ll find the MB.OS platform on your 14-inch display, with an army of AI agents from ChatGPT, Microsoft, and Google at your disposal to boss around. Use them to set navigation, discover random locations, do web searches, tell bad jokes, or whatever else people use AI for in their cars. Merc’s own onboard AI system can handle the physical stuff, like adjusting HVAC, changing drive modes, or fiddling with the lighting — all through voice commands.

Previous Next 1 / 1

Beyond voice and navigation, the AMG GT SUV applies AI to high-performance track driving through something called the Predictive Performance Manager. Mercedes says the PPM uses track-mapping data to dynamically throttle or boost electric motor output depending on topography, conserving battery energy on downhill or technical winding sections so full power is available on steep inclines and long straights. That could also mean faster, more consistent overall lap times by eliminating battery overheating and power throttling during track driving — something an AMG lover would likely appreciate.

Mercedes didn’t release the official pricing yet, though we can expect something closer to its official launch.

Tech.title: Elon Musk settles lawsuits over $1 million voter giveaway
Tech.content:
In 2024, Elon Musk promised to give away $1 million a day to a randomly selected registered voter in a swing state. That prompted legal challenges, raised questions about its legality, and drew lawsuits from two Arizona residents claiming the lottery was a fraud. Musk has now agreed to settle the two lawsuits filed in Austin, Texas, though the details of the settlement have not been made public.

That directly contradicted Musk’s claim that the drawings were random. The plaintiffs say they never would have signed the petition required to enter the giveaway if they had known it wasn’t random. They accused Musk and America PAC of using it as a ploy to obtain user data and said the petition “places no limitations on America PAC’s use of or sale of the personal data it collects, nor does it provide any additional information about the planned use of data.”

Tech.title: Meta removes language that may have allowed it to scrape news sites
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After backlash, Meta is updating its terms again to remove language that suggested it could scrape content from sites, including news sites, to train its AI. Specifically, the following language no longer appears on the commercial terms page:

… Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.

Many, including Neiman Lab and James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell, interpreted it as an attempt to give Meta the right to use content scraped from sites to train its AI products for free and supersede blocking instructions in a site’s robots.txt file.

Andy Stone, Meta’s vice president of communications, and spokesperson Daniel Roberts pushed back, saying that “There is no change to how Meta uses web crawlers; any suggestion to the contrary is false.” Today’s update to its terms and a new statement go further, removing the controversial language entirely. Roberts said in a follow-up statement to The Verge this morning:

“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves. It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers. As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences. This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”
